News.title: Serial thief banned from EVERY Greggs in UK after repeatedly stealing soft drinks and doughnuts from bakery chain
News.content:
Next

A PROLIFIC thief has been banned from every Greggs store in the UK after she repeatedly stole doughnuts and soft drinks from the chain.

Since May, Tiffany O’Neill, 28, has stolen more than £2,000 worth of goods.



She has been arrested, charged and remanded to court 11 times.

O’Neill was ultimately charged with 69 theft offences.



She appeared for sentencing at Croydon Magistrates’ Court today, November 11, and pleaded guilty to a total of 80 offences.

She swerved spending time behind bars but was given a 26-week sentence, suspended for 12 months.

In addition to the suspended sentence, a Criminal Behaviour Order was also granted banning her from Brixton town centre and all Greggs stores in the UK for two years.

New rules on magistrates and judges that came into force earlier this year require a sentence of less than a year to be suspended unless very specific exceptions apply.



The Met Police estimates its officers spent more than 120 hours on the case since O’Neill’s arrest in May, including preparing case files, carrying out further arrests and attending court hearings.

At all but one court appearance in recent months she was granted bail, despite repeatedly breaching her bail conditions and returning to target the same Greggs store on Electric Avenue in Brixton, South London.

O’Neill was initially banned from entering the London Borough of Lambeth and required to wear a GPS tag as a condition of her bail.

However, despite repeated offending whilst on bail, the GPS tag was never fitted.

Three sentencing hearings were previously adjourned because she failed to appear in court, and a fourth was delayed earlier this week due to tech issues at the court.



Sergeant Chris Wilkinson, who led the investigation, said: “Our officers worked relentlessly over several months to build the evidence needed to bring this prolific offender before the courts.

“Despite multiple arrests and repeated offences, we remained focused on securing a positive outcome for our community.

“Her persistent offending caused repeated distress to staff, harmed the business and placed a significant demand on police resources.

“We recognise that courts are obliged to follow the guidelines on suspending sentences, but it’s obviously a disappointment that someone who we know has reoffended so frequently is now back out in the community.

“We hope this marks a change in her offending, but if it doesn’t we will be there to intervene and put her back before the courts.”



Greggs chief exec Roisin Currie said: “The safety and wellbeing of our colleagues and customers is always our priority, and persistent incidents of theft can have a real impact on those in our shops.

“We are grateful to the Metropolitan Police for their continued work with retailers, including Greggs, to tackle repeat offending.

“Retail crime is an industry-wide issue and we continue to strengthen our approach, including the rollout of Auror technology across all of our shops, investment in CCTV and trials of a new shop format in a small number of locations exposed to higher levels of anti-social behaviour.

“We also work closely with law enforcement and industry partners to share intelligence, helping us to better prevent and respond to these incidents and maintain safe, welcoming environments for our colleagues and customers.

“We support efforts to apprehend repeat offenders, and we welcome calls for meaningful consequences for those who repeatedly target retailers.



“Importantly, we would like to see a renewed focus on positive interventions and services that prevent reoffending.”

Her spree beats the previous record holder, Adam “Hamster” Gosling, 39, who stole £1,817 over a six week period this year.

The Sun’s Bake and Take campaign last year revealed that Greggs was being hit by thieves multiple times a day.

Our reporters saw thieves swiping goods from branches across the country, with staff unable to act.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

At one branch in Stockwell, South London, we saw at least one shoplifting raid an hour. In some locations, Greggs has scrapped self-service displays.



Our investigation prompted pledges from ministers to clamp down on shoplifting, which has risen 60 per cent in three years.

News.title: Woman ‘raped’ in cemetery during broad daylight as cops appeal for witnesses
News.content:
‘RAPE’ ATTACK Woman ‘raped’ in cemetery during broad daylight as cops appeal for witnesses







Next

A WOMAN was allegedly raped in a cemetery in broad daylight as cops launch an urgent appeal for witnesses.

The shocking incident is said to have happened on the afternoon of Sunday, October 18 between 1pm and 3pm in Worcestershire.

West Mercia Police said a woman was raped in the grounds of Redditch Crematorium.

The force has subsequently charged two men – aged 19 and 33 – with rape.





Officers believe there were people around the location at the time who could be “key witnesses” as they urge them to come forward.

DC Ashleigh Willetts from the Public Protection Unit (PPU) said: “We would like to speak to anyone who was in the area at the time and may have seen anything captured evidence on their dashcam in relation to this serious incident.

“We believe there was a black car in the area at the time that someone may have seen and would like details on that also.”

Anyone with information or footage is urged to contact the force quoting quoting 22/102885/26.

News.title: Woman, 29, ‘burned alive in car after ambulance call handler failed to tell fire crews Mini had gone up in flames’
News.content:
BLAZE TRAGEDY Woman, 29, ‘burned alive in car after ambulance call handler failed to tell fire crews Mini had gone up in flames’







Next

A WOMAN is said to have been burned alive in her car after an ambulance call handler failed to tell the fire brigade a Mini had burst into flames, an inquest has concluded.

Nursery worker Amanda Edwards, 29, was rendered unconscious and trapped in her Vauxhall Corsa after being hit head-on by a speeding drink driver on the morning of April 13.



Cheshire Coroner’s Court heard that Miss Edwards, who was commuting to her place of work, survived the impact and was seen to be breathing by one, or potentially two, bystanders.

The witnesses were part of what the coroner hailed as a “valiant” effort to rescue her and 59-year-old Andrew Dean, who caused the crash by speeding on the wrong side of the road.



Following the impact, a fuel leak led to Mr Dean’s Mini Cooper catching fire which then spread to the Corsa.

But a bungling call handler failed to categorise the incident correctly, meaning that the fire service turned up 13 minutes later than they could have been on scene – and long enough that Miss Edwards succumbed to the flames.

Ben Staham, who alerted emergency services to the crash in Frodsham, Cheshire, was able to put a fire extinguisher to the blaze, initially having some success before it reignited.

He was joined by a highway maintenance worker who exhausted four or five extinguishers on the flames, but the inferno could not ultimately be prevented from taking a hold of Mr Dean’s Mini Cooper, with its driver still trapped inside.



Though bystanders were battling to save the two drivers, and with the flames now spreading to Miss Edwards’ car, they were thwarted by a North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) call handler who delayed a decision to notify the fire brigade by 13 minutes.

While police and paramedics arrived on the scene promptly, they were powerless to attempt a rescue.

One bystander had bravely attempted to prise open Miss Edwards’ driver side door with a crowbar, to no avail, before medics arrived to urge would-be rescuers back just moments before the Mini Cooper exploded and was engulfed in flames.

In a statement read out in court, call handler Jennifer Campbell admitted she was immediately told of a fire underneath one of the vehicles, but rather than notifying the outbound desk, who would alert the ambulance service, she prioritised triaging the two patients over the phone.

Ms Campbell said she was “overwhelmed” by the call, and had “multiple concerns, including the best way to manage competing priorities, when to pause triage to alert the fire service and police, and what to say to callers asking for instructions on how to put out a fire and remove patients from their vehicles.”



Later that shift, Ms Campbell said her team manager called her into a meeting, where he revealed that both cars had caught fire and that the drivers had died.

Since then, Ms Campbell said she has “undertaken an extensive programme of learning”, despite already having been a fully qualified handler at the time.

The court heard how she was not comfortable seeking support from senior colleagues, or from her team manager.

Of the two managers due to be on the shift, one was absent, which she said “made me hesitate before seeking help as I was conscious of the limited management resources available and the competing demands for those limited resources.”

Giving evidence, Christopher Dempsey, of the North West Ambulance Service, said that the incident should have been marked as a category 1 incident and an ambulance deployed within three minutes of Campbell taking the call.



At the same time, a report should have been passed to the outbound desk, who would notify the fire department.

However, the desk was not alerted, and Ms Campbell’s triage resulted in a category 5 classification, a non-urgent incident not requiring an ambulance.

It wasn’t until she approached her manager that the incident was correctly categorised and the outbound desk alerted to the need for fire and rescue services at the scene.

The call, which was taken at 8.15am, did not result in a category 1 classification until 8.27, and the fire service was not alerted until 8.31, a delay that the coroner ruled precluded any possibility of rescuing Miss Edwards from the fire which burned her alive.

When it was put to Mr Dempsey that Ms Campbell had all the information required to initiate a category 1 response at the start of the call, he agreed, telling the court that “if the handler had passed it to the desk at the onset of the call, it would have reduced the delay.”



When tactical fire commanders arrived on the scene of the crash in Manley Road in their personal vehicles, they were said to be shocked that there were no fire engines present.

The evidence from Aaron Collis, head of operational policy at Cheshire Fire and Rescue, was that – on the balance of probabilities – had they been notified of the fire earlier, then firefighters “would have been able to prevent the second vehicle [Amanda’s car] becoming fully involved in fire, or otherwise sufficiently suppressed the fire to attempt a rescue of Amanda Edwards.”

Paramedic Tammy Scarrat described the scene as “frantic”, with members of the public “screaming” to help the drivers out of their cars.

But rising black smoke and the heat of the flames prevented her from attempting a rescue.

A forensic collision investigator found that Mr Dean had potentially been travelling above 70mph round a bend in a 50-mph zone.



A toxicology test determined he had a blood alcohol level of 124mg per d/l, over the drink drive limit of 80mg.

In a statement read out in court, Sarah Dean, Mr Dean’s wife, said that her husband had “a couple of glasses of wine” over the weekend.

A toxicologist though said the quantity of alcohol found in his blood “suggests a greater quantity was consumed on the Sunday night, or that drinking may have continued later than can be understood from the account, or a combination of both.”

Concluding, senior coroner Victoria Davies found the crash was caused by Mr Dean’s “manner of driving” which was likely contributed to by alcohol intoxication and the speed at which he was driving, estimated to be between 67 and 76 mph in a 50-mph zone.

Ms Davies ruled that a category 1 classification could have been issued within a minute of the call being placed, and that by 8.18am, three minutes later, the outbound desk should have been told about the presence of fire.



But this was not done.

Instead, the call handler delayed, an “error” which was attributed to “a lack of experience and confidence, a reluctance to seek help, and a mistaken belief she should be focusing on triage first.”

The coroner concluded that this delay proved deadly.

Had the fire brigade been called at the appropriate time, resources could have been on the scene at around 8.34am and thereby be in a position to suppress or extinguish the flames, and attempt a rescue of Miss Edwards, from Runcorn.

As it was, they did not arrive on the scene until 8.46am, 31 minutes after the first call was placed to the ambulance service, and by the time the fire was defeated, Miss Edwards was already dead.



The coroner declined to issue a Prevention of Future Deaths Report and said she was satisfied that NWAS had taken the incident seriously and put an action plan in place.

Concluding, she said: “Her death was due to the fire combined with effects of the injuries she sustained in the collision.

“I give the cause of death as 1 effects of a fire and 2 multiple injuries sustained in a road traffic collision.

“Had they been notified when they should have, the fire service would have arrived at 8.34 at which point the fire which had started under the Mini Cooper had not yet spread to her car, and Amanda would have been rescued from her car prior to the fire taking hold…

“Once the fire was extinguished, Amanda’s death was confirmed, which was contributed to by the delay of the ambulance service to notify the fire service.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Recognition must be made of valiant efforts of bystanders who selflessly attempted to put fires out and rescue the drivers at great risk to their own safety.

“I hope they know their efforts are very much appreciated.”

News.title: Chaos in Barcelona as rioters light fires and clash with cops while Spain grinds to a halt with millions on strike
News.content:
Next

BARCELONA has descended into chaos as protesters set fire to barricades and clash with cops during heated demonstrations.

Spain was brought to a standstill today due to a 24-hour nationwide strike over soaring rents and real estate prices.



Millions of employees across the country walked out of airports, public transport hubs, and shops.

Nearly 60 people have been arrested so far as part of mass demonstrations which have taken place in several major cities.



But what had started as peaceful marches in Barcelona spiralled into carnage this evening as thugs threw makeshift Molotovs at shops and shot fireworks towards officers.

The city’s Passeig de Gràcia and Gran Via areas saw demonstrators light fires and tear down barriers, according to Spanish media.



Activists claimed 400,000 people turned out in Barcelona while local authorities put the number closer to 55,000.

Local cops said eight people in Passeig de Gràcia were cuffed tonight for smashing shop windows and burning containers.

Meanwhile, at least 120,000 took to the streets in Madrid alone, authorities say.



A sea of umbrellas packed into central neighbourhoods in the Spanish capital amid a heavy downpour.

Protesters in several cities were heard chanting slogans demanding housing and wage increases.

Shocking images showed dramatic brawls between riot police and crowds – with some officers firing smoke grenades.



One astonishing clip recorded this morning appeared to show a flaming barricade in the middle of a road, with cars seen driving around the terrifying inferno.

It is the first general strike of its kind in 14 years.

Organisers said the strikes were a “massive” success despite the torrential rain battering parts of the country tonight.



Some protests in cities including Seville and Cadiz had to be axed due to Storm Charles and the severe weather.

One union put the total number of people who took part in the strike at four million.

Housing activists hope the massive show of force will lead to more regulations to protect tenants and crack down on real estate speculation.



Yesterday it was said the scheduled industrial action would “bring the country to a complete standstill”.

Travel between Spain and the UK was feared to be severely disrupted – potentially sparking chaos for Brit tourists.

The protests come after weeks of similar chaos in France.

Paris and several other major cities descended into carnage after what had started as demonstrations over poor school conditions.

Riots were widespread – with dramatic images showing massive clashes between crowds and armed officers.



Unrest also unfolded in other European countries like Italy and Albania over a range of other issues.

Today’s chaos comes as Spain’s socialist leader Pedro Sanchez is hoping to mobilise voters ahead of a national election.

He is currently trailing in the polls.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last decade, eating into household budgets and upsetting voters.

Public anger reached a boiling point following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month.



Maricarmen became a symbol of Spaniards who can’t dream of owning a home.

She died just weeks after being forcibly removed from the home she lived in for over 70 years.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Protests wreaked havoc across the country over recent weeks since her story gained traction.

News.title: 6 unanswered questions after ‘bright spark’ runner, 23, found dead by stream with drugs in her system after 5-day search
News.content:
Next

A “BRIGHT spark” runner was tragically found dead by a stream with drugs in her system, an inquest heard.

But there still remains a host of unanswered questions after Jenny Hall, 23, vanished without a trace for five days – sparking a major search operation.



Keen long-distance runner Jenny was last seen leaving her home in Tow Law, County Durham, just after 3pm on February 18, 2025.

After the 23-year-old’s sudden disappearance, mountain rescue teams and cops scoured almost 100km of running trails.



Her body was found at 9:30am on February 23, roughly 13 miles away in a stream in a “very remote” area of Teesdale.

Senior coroner Crispin Oliver recorded the cause of death as “the effects of amphetamine and paracetamol” – but mystery continues to swirl over Jenny’s tragic death.



Did she die shortly after disappearing? Or was she alive during the five days?

Jenny, described as 6ft with long dark hair, was last seen wearing a blue hoodie with a John Deere logo and dark jogging bottoms.

Across five days, specially-trained police, mountain rescue teams and coastguard crews scoured miles of moorland.



Among the areas they searched were running trails between Eggleston and Hamsterley, Durham, which Jenny frequently used.

It was later revealed that turbulent weather and rough ground was prevalent in the area where Jenny disappeared.

Cops confirmed searchers had come up against “challenging weather conditions and terrain”.

So did Jenny come into difficulty while on her run? And did she die shortly after her disappearance?

Why did she drive to the remote stretch of road?

A red Ford Focus belonging to the keen runner was found parked in a lay-by on a remote stretch of the B6278.



Dashcam footage taken by a passing motorist showed her abandoned car just one hour after the jogger left her home.

The driver who captured the video later spoke of his increasing fears for the 23-year-old.

He said: “It is an incredibly remote area. My fears for the missing woman are growing.

“I really hope she is found safe and well.”

So why did she stop out there? Was this the spot for her run, was she planning to meet someone or perhaps dealing with an emergency?



Was the fatal cocktail of drugs taken deliberately?

Jenny was a dedicated runner and described as “super-fit” by her training partner Mariagrazia Panaccio.

So it seems unlikely that her disappearance and subsequent death came as a result of exhaustion or difficulty while running.

But how is it that she came to ingest a fatal combination of amphetamine and paracetamol?

Was Jenny alone when she parked her car?

Dashcam footage from a passing motorist shows a missing woman’s car abandoned in a remote moor.

The video was taken just one hour after Jenny Hall left her home in Tow Law, County Durham, shortly after 3pm on Tuesday February 18.



In the footage, Jenny’s red Ford Focus can be seen parked in a remote lay-by surrounded by empty moorland.

Jenny’s vehicle was found completely abandoned, sparking a 100-mile wide search.

The car, a red Ford Focus, was found parked on the B6278, between Eggleston and Stanhope the following day.

Was Jenny alone when she parked her car and walked into the woods, or was anyone with her in the hours or days leading up to her death?

Will the full inquest rule the death an accident, misadventure, suicide, or an open verdict?

An inquest into her death was opened at Crook Coroners Court on Tuesday (November 10), 18 months after she was reported missing.



The County Durham runner died from the effects of amphetamine and paracetamol, an inquest has heard

While the medical cause is now confirmed as drug toxicity, the legal conclusion remains open.

Mountain rescue teams worked “around the clock” to search the area between Eggleston and Stanhope before her body was recovered five days later.

Police later ruled out any suspicious circumstances.

Will the full inquest rule the death an accident, misadventure, suicide, or an open verdict?



Did hypothermia contribute to Jenny’s tragic death?

The average daily highest temperature in County Durham when Jenny went missing was between 4-7C.

But temperatures dipped to just below freezing overnight on February 19, the day after she was last seen.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And with police confirming that rescuers came up against “turbulent weather” during the search for Jenny, hypothermia caused by cold wind and rain may have contributed to her death.

Did exposure or hypothermia in remote winter woodland contribute to the fatal outcome alongside the physical effects of the substances?

News.title: Haunting cellphone clue in search for missing DoorDash driver Zachariah Schuck, 32, led cops to most-crucial evidence
News.content:
Next

A CHILLING clue from a missing DoorDash driver’s cellphone led cops to a bridge where he was last tracked, before footage emerged of someone abandoning his car miles away.

Zachariah “Zach” Schuck, 32, mysteriously vanished on October 22 after completing a food delivery in Beaver County, Pennsylvania, and telling his wife he was heading home.



But the father-of-two never made it back, and his cellphone suddenly lost coverage around 8 pm, sparking a desperate search that has now stretched into its third week.

His terrified wife used the Life360 tracking app to pinpoint his last known location near the Vanport Bridge, around 11 miles from where his car would later be found abandoned.



Zach’s dad, Carl Schuck, told Pittsburgh’s Action News 4, “His wife went out to the Vanport Bridge, where the last cell tower communication was with his phone.”

Officers searched the area but found no trace of her missing husband or his cellphone.



Investigators later discovered that Zach’s black Chevrolet Impala had been parked along Croxall Avenue in Hopewell Township around the same time his phone went dead.

A doorbell camera captured the vehicle pulling up around 8 pm before a mystery figure climbed out and walked away down the road.

But the footage was too grainy to tell whether the person behind the wheel was Zach, leaving his family fearing something sinister may have happened to him.

“Was it Zach? Or wasn’t it Zach?” Carl asked, questioning what could have happened.



Speaking exclusively to The U.S. Sun, Carl said, “Once we can identify who got out of the vehicle, then we could determine what to do next.”

Police revealed the vehicle was found with its keys still in the ignition and the car had no gas left in it.

The vehicle was not located until October 24, two days after Zach vanished, when a tip shared on social media helped lead his family to the vehicle.



Investigators have since pieced together a timeline showing Zach completed his final known DoorDash delivery around 6.30 pm.

North Sewickley Township Police Chief Tyler Kelosky said Zach had been in contact with his wife during his deliveries and reassured her that he would be returning home.

Police have also confirmed that his phone remains switched off and that he has not used his credit cards since disappearing.

Search teams have combed the area surrounding the abandoned vehicle, including nearby woodland, using drones and search-and-rescue dogs, but have found nothing.

Kelosky said investigators were exploring every possibility, including whether Zach had fallen victim to a crime.



“We’re not ruling foul play out,” the police chief said, adding that detectives did not want to speculate before establishing the facts.

Zach’s father has also traveled from upstate New York to Pennsylvania to retrace his son’s final movements and speak with residents near where his car was found.

Carl fears his son may have been carjacked, although he acknowledged that there is still no evidence proving what happened to him.

He previously revealed to The U.S. Sun that Zach had recently lost his job managing Penske truck-leasing branches and had been making DoorDash deliveries while supporting his young family, including a newborn baby.

Police are now urging residents in the Davidson Heights neighborhood, particularly around Croxall Avenue, to review home security footage.



Carl told The U.S. Sun, “He has all of our support. And all we want is for him to come home. And then we can work everything out.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Zach is described as six feet tall, with brown hair and green eyes, and was last seen wearing a blue-and-red flannel shirt, jeans and brown boots.

Anyone with information is urged to contact North Sewickley Township Police at 724-843-3421 or 724-843-8118.

News.title: Plans for proposed migrant camp on RAF base in Barnham drawn up despite village referendum on ‘leaving UK’
News.content:
Next

HOME Office chiefs are spending £4.6 million to prepare two new controversial migrant camps, The Sun can reveal.

Deals have been struck to prepare ground for sites in Piddington near Bicester, Oxfordshire and at RAF Barnham in Suffolk.



There has been widespread opposition to both sites which are near to small, rural communities.

The camps form part of the Government’s plan to move away from costly hotel accommodation.



Paperwork seen by The Sun shows that a deal has been struck to refurbish land and provide foundations for modular buildings at the Suffolk site.

Kier Construction have been awarded the £3.4 million deal with the work planned to be concluded by the end of January.



The site has been subject of fierce local protests, with plans to house 1,250 male migrants scaled back to 931.

Millions of pounds have already been spent on the site which was a former munitions and nuclear weapons store.



It is currently used by Norfolk and Suffolk police forces for specialist training.

The latest cash is thought to be going on major upgrades to sewerage and utilities needed to increase the capacity of the site.

In Bicester, company ‘Reds(10) UK’ has been given a £1.2m contract to prepare the ground, by January 5 next year.

The contract is for “architectural, engineering and surveying services” and “engineering design services”.

In September residents of Piddington, which is the closest village to the Bicester base took part in a symbolic referendum and voted for independence from the UK.



Home Office officials want to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a nearby site and will be in use for a minimum of 10 years.

It has lodged an Urgent Crown Development Application which bypasses planning normal procedures.

Just the cost of the paperwork for the application by the Home Office to the Ministry of Housing has cost taxpayers £76,482.



The Home Office say that they are “considering” the use of both sites as asylum accommodation and there are still routine feasibility assessments taking place.

They say that no final decision has been made on the camps, despite the preparatory works taking place.

Both contracts have been published but have been heavily redacted meaning plans or payment schedules are not possible to be viewed by the public.

The Government is also attempting to open a migrant camp at the former Ministry of Defence site at Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire.

It comes after The Sun revealed that Clearsprings Ready Homes, a key Home Office provider, is still raking in £3.26 million a day despite the move away from hotels.



Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “This is a catastrophic waste of money.

“These young, male illegal immigrants should not be getting accommodated on these sites – they should be getting deported.

“This weak Labour government is imposing thousands of these young men on small villages.

“Women and girls are rightly worried given the large numbers of sex offences and rapes these asylum seekers have committed.

“This money should be spent deporting them – not putting them up.”



A Home Office spokesperson said: “No money has been paid upfront for these contracts.

“They simply allow work to be commissioned and paid for only if needed while we assess whether the sites are suitable.

“Since the election, this government has saved taxpayers more than £1billion and is delivering a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are closing asylum hotels, which were costing taxpayers £9 million a day, and returning them to local communities.

“Alternative accommodation, including former military sites, has 24/7 security and CCTV in place to minimise disruption for residents.”

News.title: Storm Charles batters Europe with torrential rain and 99mph winds as streets turn into rivers & flights cancelled
News.content:
Next

STORM Charles has battered Europe with gale-force winds and biblical rain causing over 200 flights to be grounded across Portugal.

Schools and hundreds of supermarkets were forced to close as the intense storm drew in on Wednesday with streets turned into raging rivers.



The extreme weather is set to cause havoc across the entire country, which was slapped with an urgent red warning for torrential rain and destructive 99mph winds.

Flash floods have already struck the Portuguese island of Madeira, sending torrents of muddy water bursting through a swollen stream near Caminho Velho da Igreja.



Heavy machinery and emergency teams were deployed to clear debris-laden roads across the island as many streets were turned into raging rivers.

Torrents of rain battered Lisbon this afternoon, swamping streets as drivers struggled to get through floodwaters.



Pictures show a row of parked cars submerged up to their wheels.

The rough weather is forecast to reach most of southern Portugal and the Lisbon ​region into the evening.



As a precaution many hospitals altered or suspended surgeries as officials urged people to stay in their homes during the worst of the rain and the wind.

According to Net Weather, an official red alert covers the southern half of Portugal’s mainland and the Madeira archipelago.

People in areas under red alert can expect heavy rain, rough seas, and risk of flooding from river overflows.



The National Authority for Emergency and Civil Protection warned of the possibility of floods, landslides, falling trees, slippery road surfaces and power cuts.

Residents should stay clear of flooded areas as there is a real risk of people and vehicles being swept away by powerful torrents, authorities warn.

Across the water, heavy downpours and high winds are expected to reach the Spanish islands by Wednesday afternoon.

The country’s weather service ​AEMET warned ⁠of “very serious” impact from heavy rain, strong winds and rough seas.

Large parts of the Canaries were placed on a high alert on Tuesday night as wind speeds are predicted to exceed 99mph.



The storm is carrying warm tropical air, meaning it will bring heavy rain, particularly in mountainous areas, with La Palma and Tenerife’s peaks expected to be the worst hit.

Officials say downpours may lash in the south and west of Tenerife as schools were shut and roads blocked as a result of the warning.

Holiday hotspots including Lanzarote, Gran Canaria and Fuerteventura have been placed on a wind alert, where gusts could exceed 55mph.

Sea conditions will be hazardous around exposed shores, authorities say.

In central Spain, authorities maintained the evacuation of more than ⁠3,000 ​people in Piedralaves, who they removed from their homes ​on Tuesday due to the risk of a local dam overflowing.



The whole of the mainland, except for Asturias and Cantabria, were on alert on Wednesday for heavy rain or gale-force winds.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Rain will fall across almost the entire country, at times accompanied by storms, although the intensity will decrease the further north-east — except in the Pyrenees.

The fresh warning comes just days after Spain and Portugal were threatened by Storm Bruna earlier this week.

News.title: Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry
News.content:
Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.

Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".

An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.

HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.

In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".

Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

News.title: 'I felt like I was being manipulated': Woman alleges Walliams groomed her as a teenager
News.content:
Lilly Creightmore, who has alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager, has told BBC Newsnight that she was "angry" at his behaviour.

She said that Walliams invited her to move in with him while she was "in between living situations". She was 18 at the time. She says she "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him" but told him she was not interested in him in a romantic way.

After about a week of refusing Walliams's advances, Creightmore said "he started to become very moody and rude and cold".

According to ITV, Walliams says he did not act inappropriately and did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

TV agent Dermot McNamara, who has represented someone allegedly groomed by Walliams, told BBC Newsnight he had informed "authorities and broadcasters" about Walliams's alleged "inappropriate behaviour" but no action was taken.

Walliams denies all allegations, and in a statement to journalists shared by the Guardian said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He acknowledged that "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

News.title: Scottish DJ, 32, confirmed as victim of Krakow shooting
News.content:
Det Ch Insp David McAlinden, senior investigating officer from Police Scotland's Counter Terrorism Policing unit, said the force was "aware of the tragic death of a Scottish man in Krakow".

He added: "Working in conjunction with COPFS (the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service), Police Scotland is supporting the UK counter-terrorism policing network and the Polish authorities.

"The immediate shared priority is to ensure that identification is properly established for the family, so that repatriation can take place as quickly as possible.

"The family has asked for their privacy to be respected. Our thoughts are with them and everyone impacted by this incident."

Mark Jewell, a close friend of Campbell's who regularly DJ'd with him, described him as "a quiet, kind and soft-hearted person, who wouldn't have harmed a fly".

He added: "It's just so tragic that he had to be in the wrong place at the wrong time.

"I had been speaking with him when he was headed over to Poland and I messaged him as soon as I heard about the terrible attack, to ask if he was safe - not for one minute expecting that he would have been caught up in it all.

"I was fully expecting a funny message back from him, saying not to worry. I can't quite get my head round it all."

News.title: Trump says 'we won' Iran war during Veterans Day service
News.content: US President Donald Trump placed a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before making remarks at the Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. Trump spoke about the ongoing US-Iran war, saying that "we won" but it's "just a question of when we want to end it." Arlington National Cemetery is a short distance away from Memorial Circle, the proposed site for Trump's 250-foot triumphal arch.

News.title: Ex-parliamentary aide acquitted for spying tells BBC he was 'fall guy' but also 'naive'
News.content:
A British man who was acquitted of spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".

Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us, revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.

In his first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", Cash admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, Chris Berry, who was in China at the time.

Berry, who was also acquitted of espionage, declined to comment on this story, but previously denied any wrongdoing and said he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media".

The BBC's politics investigations correspondent Joe Pike speaks to Cash about the allegations.

Read the story behind the interview.

News.title: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home
News.content:
Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.

Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.

They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.

Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.

In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith, who wasn't part of the trial, said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.

"I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."

The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.

Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.

"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

News.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
News.content:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime.

The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident at RAF Fairford.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were allegedly both in Iran at the time of the incident, the indictment claims.

Meanwhile, al-Saadi was coordinating with the pair through third parties from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges after being arrested in August, it adds.

US court records show that al-Saadi is due in court on 19 November, though it is not clear whether this status conference - which is usually a routine scheduled appearance - relates to the new charges or the previous ones. The BBC has asked the Southern District of New York for comment.

News.title: Richmond upon Thames is happiest place to live in Britain, survey finds
News.content:
Richmond upon Thames has been named as the happiest place to live in Britain in an annual survey.

Residents of the south-west London borough have easy access to central London and strolls along the Thames on their doorstep, as well as boutiques, cafes and opportunities to spot roaming deer in their local parks.

Richmond ranked particularly highly across several aspects of local life in Rightmove's "happy at home index", including access to nature and green spaces, essential local services, shops and restaurants, employment opportunities as well as residents' pride in their area.

But, living there comes at a cost, with the average asking price for a home in the borough standing at more than Â£1m.

Harrogate in North Yorkshire and Cirencester in Gloucestershire came in second and third places respectively in Rightmove's 15th annual "happy at home index".

In Wales, Monmouth was the highest ranked, while Kirkcaldy took the top spot for Scotland.

News.title: No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government minister
News.content:
The education secretary told MSPs that she had held a meeting with police and local authorities.

"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," Mairi McAllan said.

"I would take this opportunity to repeat Police Scotland's advice that there is nothing to suggest any threats to the public from the content of the emails."

The cabinet secretary added there was a "considerable amount of work" ongoing by Police Scotland and partners across the UK to "understand the motivations and the individuals behind this".

Most local authorities contacted by BBC Scotland said schools were operating as normal but some confirmed pupils had been evacuated.

More than 300 calls were made to police when a similar message was sent to schools around the country on 19 October.

In many areas, pupils were off due to half-term holidays.

On Wednesday the majority of schools in Dumfries and Galloway received the email and some were evacuated as a precaution.

A spokesperson for the local authority said: "Each school community/setting is unique and as such has its own way of supporting and reassuring learners and staff.

"We also know that local police have attended some school settings in a community capacity to assist and reassure."

In Edinburgh Queensferry High School was evacuated and pupils were sent home.

Highland Council confirmed a number of its schools "made the decision to activate their emergency protocols".

Local authorities in Glasgow, Edinburgh, East Lothian, Aberdeenshire and Orkney also confirmed their schools received the message.

In Northern Ireland, the Education Authority (EA) said the "message has similarities with a bogus threat sent last month" which was treated as a hoax by the (PSNI).

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the email originated from outside the UK.

Italian reports said 280 school head teachers had received threats in recent days. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has called a meeting of top ministers and intelligence chiefs over the issue.

News.title: Police believed Huntingdon train attacker had schizophrenia, jury told
News.content:
Police dealing with a man accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train noted he had schizophrenia following his arrest, a court has been told.

Anthony Williams denies attempting to murder passengers and staff on a London-bound train, which made an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November last year.

Cambridge Crown Court heard PC Caitlin Brown, who was involved in transporting Williams to hospital then to the police station, said he "appeared to be talking to himself" and spoke about the devil.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, also denies four other counts of attempted murder related to earlier attacks in Peterborough and London.

Jurors were shown footage of Williams' arrest in the car park of Huntingdon railway station, and the court heard a Taser and a baton gun - which fires less lethal objects - were used against the defendant.

In a statement read to court, the arresting officer said Williams had said something along the lines of "kill me, kill me".

PC Matt Panks, another officer involved in transporting Williams, said in his statement he saw the suspect "acting strangely, appeared completely unphased by what had occurred... he was rocking and laughing".

News.title: Reform boycotts Senedd after member banned for saying white people are being replaced
News.content:
Jenner confirmed her party's boycott on the steps of the Senedd on Wednesday afternoon.

"It is now clear that the freedom of speech of one of our Senedd members is being curtailed, meaning his constituents are being silenced," she said.

"We stand behind Joe, and we will not attend today's plenary session in protest at his treatment.

"Every Reform MS [Member of the Senedd] will be in their Senedd office working hard for our constituents."

Martin said he would not apologise.

"My voters sent me to the Senedd to speak on their behalf," he said.

"I am being blocked from doing so, and now it's clear that I have fewer rights than the people who elected me.

"That cannot be the situation in a national parliament."

Asked by BBC Wales if he genuinely believed white people were being "replaced" in the UK, Martin said: "That's obviously a fact."

Aliya Mohammed, chief executive of the charity Race Equality First, said "the idea that white people are being 'replaced' is linked to a conspiracy theory that creates division and wrongly portrays people from minority ethnic backgrounds as a threat".

"Immigration can and should be debated, but language that fuels fear and hostility has no place in public discourse," she said.

"Being Welsh or British is not defined by race or skin colour.

"Wales belongs to all of us, and our diversity is one of our greatest strengths."

News.title: Former minister calls for phone tech to block live-streamed child sex abuse
News.content:
Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips has joined calls from campaigners for the government to back new technology that blocks the live-streaming of child sexual abuse.

The UK National Crime Agency has flagged the UK as the third biggest market in the world, external for live-streamed abuse, where children are sexually abused live on camera to order.

Device-level blockers can prevent this material being filmed and viewed on smartphones, laptops and tablets in the first place, Phillips said, at the launch of a policy report in Parliament.

Anti-abuse campaigners claim keeping the technology at device level maintains privacy and encryption. Civil liberties campaigners Big Brother Watch dispute this.

The government has already legislated to demand tech firms like Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, block under-18s from taking or sharing nude images on smartphones and other devices.

However, three-quarters of child sexual abuse material (CSA) was not self-generated but likely captured on adult devices, according to 2025 research from the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), which works to eliminate child sexual abuse imagery online.

Some 1.8 million men in the UK admitted to some form of online sexual offending against children, according to research from child safety institute Childlight.

Phillips, who complained of repeated delays to work to tackle CSA when she resigned as safeguarding minister in May, is demanding action to tackle the source of the crime and reduce the number of British offenders.

"This should be a source of national shame, and we must stop it," the Labour MP said.

"The technology, the evidence and the public support are all there - I want to work with ministers to extend on-device blocking to child sexual abuse material on every device sold in Britain, making children here and over the world safer."

The software uses AI to classify known child abuse images in the phone's operating system, and blocks the material at the moment it is viewed or created, whatever app is in use.

Nothing is logged, stored or sent anywhere, and the tech would work alongside encryption.

The AI classifier has been trained against a database of known child abuse images so it can differentiate between harmless material such as children at the beach, and sexual abuse.

Phillips said online child sexual abuse is "an issue that we did not keep control of" as legislators and now must be prioritised, at the event in Parliament.

She was joined by survivors of online child sexual abuse, who said they should not have to beg for the removal of images of themselves being abused from the internet.

Phil Eccles, from the National Crime Agency (NCA), said the scale of the problem was "at crisis point".

"This would cut off at source somebody on the UK their ability to direct a live stream for a child to be abused," he said.

"To me, safeguarding children will always supersede the ability to prosecute. If we can stop that abuse we must.

"But it's so important that tech companies come onboard - we cannot arrest our way out of this problem."

News.title: Jailed undertaker lodges bid to appeal against sentence
News.content:
Victims of the Legacy funeral scandal say it is an "insult" Hull undertaker Robert Bush has lodged an application to appeal against his 20-year prison sentence.

Bush, 48, admitted keeping 30 bodies after their funerals, presenting families with the ashes of strangers and selling fake funeral plans.

He pleaded guilty to 67 separate offences and was sentenced in July 2026.

Humberside Police said it had been notified by the Criminal Appeal Office at the Royal Courts of Justice and added "any decision regarding the appeal will be a matter for the courts".

In August, Bush wrote to families impacted by his crimes to express regret and said he was "deeply sorry".

Prosecutors said he ran a "shambolic and chaotic" funeral business at premises on Hessle Road in Hull and his "appalling" offending had caused "extreme emotional pain, anguish and upset".

His crimes over a 12-year period involved more than 300 victims.

News.title: 'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
News.content:
Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.

There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".

But in a sign of the division within the party, about a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns about approving it during a Westminster Hall debate in Parliament.

Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.

One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate".

"The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.

Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.

Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test.

"It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."

Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh. She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance.

News.title: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review
News.content:
Successive governments have been "asleep at the wheel" on adult social care, says the head of the independent commission looking into the sector in England.

Baroness Louise Casey said care services for older people and adults with disabilities had been developed in a largely uncontrolled and unintended way, unlike the deliberate design of the NHS in 1948.

As a result, she suggested a postcode lottery had developed with different levels of services available depending on where people live.

And she also highlighted the fees that self-funders pay, saying they were much higher than councils were charged for people entitled to state support.

Baroness Casey said care services, such as home adaptations and personal care like helping people out of bed and with washing, were simply not valued enough.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said the NHS had become a "national hospital service: that was focussed on medical care".

News.title: UK falls silent to mark Armistice Day
News.content:
The UK has fallen silent on Armistice Day, commemorating the end of World War One and to remember those who have died in conflicts.

A national remembrance service took place at the Cenotaph in London, with a two-minute silence observed at 11:00 during ceremonies across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting laid a wreath at the Cenotaph, which was also attended by senior military figures, children and cadets.

In Staffordshire, the Duke and Duchess of Gloucester laid a wreath at the Royal British Legion National Remembrance Gardens.

Hundreds of people gathered at the Armed Forces memorial in the gardens, formerly known as the National Memorial Arboretum.

Geoffrey Spencer, 101, who joined the RAF in 1943, was among the veterans attending the event.

He told the BBC he felt "lucky" to be one of the last surviving World War Two veterans, adding that he had "two very narrow escapes" during his service.

Spencer described having survived a crash landing and, on a different mission, he said one of the planes he was with was lost completely, with 22 men on board.

People who served in more recent conflicts, from the Falklands to Afghanistan, were also present at the memorial.

News.title: New details emerge after LAPD officer died during dive training in backyard pool
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An LAPD officer may have been testing an underwater breathing device when he died during a police training exercise, according to a new report.

First responders rushed to a home in Huntington Beach on Thursday at around 11 a.m. after a call about a drowning in a backyard pool. Officer Thomas Denton, a member of LAPD's Metropolitan Division and dive team, was taken to the hospital where he was pronounced dead.

Denton may have been testing a device known as a closed-circuit rebreather, which is used by Navy SEALS and other military divers to remain undetected under water, sources told The Los Angeles Times.

“Because of the way it was being operated or because of some failure inside the rebreather, it puts too much oxygen in the mix,” David McMurdie, California Recovery Divers co-founder and former chief of Alameda County Sheriff’s Department’s dive team, told the publication. “And because it causes this sort of neurological response, the first signal you have that something’s gone wrong is you go into a seizure and you die because you’re underwater.”

LAPD declined to release further details about Denton’s death when approached by the LA Times. The police department and California Division of Occupational Safety and Health are investigating what led up to the accident, which occurred at a private residence rather than a department facility.

“The department is in the process of conducting a comprehensive investigation and will make the public aware of its findings at the appropriate time,” LAPD spokesperson Lt. Elpidio Orozco told the publication.

Denton had served with the department for 20 years and is survived by his wife and two children, according to Gov. Gavin Newsom who ordered flags at the state Capitol lowered to half-staff in Denton's memory.

"Today, we honor Officer Denton's lasting legacy to the people of Los Angeles," Newsom said in a statement. "Jennifer and I deeply mourn his loss and our thoughts are with his family, friends, and colleagues. May he be remembered for his dedication and honorable service."

Denton served at the Metropolitan Division, "but his heart belong to the Dive Unit,” according to the Los Angeles Police Protective League, the union for LAPD officers.

"It was more than an assignment. It was his passion, and where he built lifelong friendships with those who shared his love for the work," the union wrote on social media Friday.

"His loss leaves a void that will never be filled, but his friendship, dedication and years of service will never be forgotten."
