World.title: Which key races remain undecided one week after the US midterms?
World.content:
Democrats hope several races that are still too close to call will further expand their majorities in the US Congress.

Share Which key races remain undecided one week after the US midterms? on social media

It has been more than a week since voters in the United States cast ballots in the midterm elections.

But the size of Democrats’ majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate remained undetermined. More than a dozen congressional races are still waiting to be called.

Democrats have already won 54 Senate seats in the incoming Congress in January, but they could pick up one or two more as votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi.

Meanwhile, in the House of Representatives, Democrats have notched their largest elected majority since 2008, with 255 seats in the 435-member chamber. But they have the potential to add to their lead with several more seats as the remaining races are decided.

Here’s a look at where things stand in some of the uncalled races:

Mississippi’s Senate seat remains too early to call

Late on Tuesday, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for the US Senate in Mississippi.

There are two key deadlines in the vote-counting process in Mississippi this week: Mail-in absentee ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday.

It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.

Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, journalists from The Associated Press and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.



The state will certify its results on December 3.

On Monday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said about 14,200 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80 percent were accepted, and about 2,700 mail-in absentee ballots had not yet been returned.

Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The Associated Press may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

The vote count is ongoing in Alaska’s Senate race

Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes in Alaska’s US Senate race as of Tuesday, with an estimated 76 percent of the vote counted.

Absentee ballots are among those that continue to be counted. The final absentee ballots mailed from outside the US are accepted as late as November 18, which is 15 days after Election Day.

Ranked-choice voting could also affect the timeline. Peltola is just over one percentage point short of the majority needed to win outright. If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked-choice tabulation on November 18.

The state’s “target date” for certifying the election results is November 25.

Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state’s certification.

A dozen House races are still up in the air

In most of the US House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than one percentage point among votes counted, as of late Tuesday afternoon.

In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in each one. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is one percent or less of the total votes.

The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on November 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results on November 24.

In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber’s balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail-in ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties must certify their results by December 3. The state will certify its results on December 11.



In South Carolina’s 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalifa. Wilson led Khalifa by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99 percent of the votes had been counted.

In Minnesota’s 1st District, the race was still undecided late by Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99 percent of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25 percent of the vote.

In Tennessee’s 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of Tuesday. In that state, recounts are held only as part of a legal challenge in the courts. There are no automatic recounts, and losing candidates may not request recounts.

Two governorships remain undecided

In the race to be Kansas’s next governor, Democratic state Senator Cindy Holscher led state Republican Senate President Ty Masterson by less than one percentage point on Tuesday.

On November 4, the state announced that a close-race audit had been triggered in six close Kansas races, including the gubernatorial race.

That process requires a hand count of selected ballots, and it must be completed before November 16, the day by which counties must certify their results.

In the race for governor of Alaska, only about 76 percent of votes were estimated to have been counted by Tuesday.

The Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Jonathan Kreiss‑Tomkins, was leading Bernadette Wilson by about 45,000 votes, 49.6 percent to 28.9 percent. The race will advance to ranked-choice tabulation if no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote.

World.title: More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages, UN says
World.content:
UN warns hunger crisis affecting almost quarter of Lebanon’s population could escalate without ‘urgent action’.

Share More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages, UN says on social media

Nearly a quarter of Lebanon’s population, or more than one million people, is facing acute food shortages due to two consecutive conflicts in less than two years and a dire economic situation, according to the United Nations.

The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme (WFP) and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture warned in a joint statement published on Wednesday that the number is expected to rise to 1.15 million by the middle of next year.

“Employment opportunities remain limited, savings have been depleted, and debt remains high, while the cost of food, fuel and other essentials continues to strain household budgets,” the joint statement said.

“Some households can still draw on savings, borrow, cut expenses or find other ways to put food on the table. For others, those options are being exhausted. When families have nothing left to fall back on, even a small additional shock can push them deeper into crisis,” Allison Oman Lawi, WFP representative and country director in Lebanon, said.

Lebanon’s Agriculture Minister Nizar Hani said: “These findings call for a coordinated national response that addresses urgent food needs while protecting livelihoods and restoring productive capacity.”

Lebanon’s authorities estimate that the cost of two wars between Israel and the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah since October 2023 amounts to about $27bn.



The last war, launched in March, displaced more than one million people in Lebanon. That number has fallen to about 300,000 since violence subsided in June.

Despite a United States-brokered framework deal signed between Israel and Lebanon’s government in June to bring fighting to an end, Israel is still occupying land in Lebanon.

Under the terms, Israeli forces were to withdraw, and Lebanon’s army was to take up positions in vacated territory.

Lebanon was meant to disarm Hezbollah, which is not a party to the agreement.

The fighting broke out as Lebanon struggled to recover from its worst-ever economic crisis, which began in 2019.

Beirut has been seeking a bailout from the International Monetary Fund but has yet to implement reforms demanded by the institution to release the aid.

World.title: Will Sheikh Hasina return to Bangladesh?
World.content:
The former Bangladeshi PM says she is planning to go back, despite a death sentence.

She faces being hanged. Yet, Sheikh Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh and would rather die in her country.

She served twice as prime minister, but was forced to resign and flee after large-scale street protests more than two years ago.

Since then, she has been living in India, which has refused a request by Bangladesh to hand her over.

Hasina says she asked for a new passport to return. But the government in Dhaka turned down the request.

The former leader announced she will return home in December, no matter what.

So, what would her possible return mean for politics in Bangladesh?

Presenter: James Bays

Guests:

Shahab Enam Khan – Professor at the Department of International Relations at Jahangirnagar University

Sanjay Kumar Bhardwaj – Professor at the Centre for South Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, specialising in India-Bangladesh relations

Taqbir Huda – Human rights lawyer and a Clarendon scholar at the University of Oxford

World.title: Zohran Mamdani’s influence grows as Democrats eye 2028 strategies
World.content:
Progressive strategists explain how Mamdani’s 2025 mayoral campaign offered a ‘real model’ for other progressives during the midterms.

Democrats have notched their strongest showing in decades in the 2026 midterm elections, taking control of both chambers of the United States Congress, as well as a share of the country’s gubernatorial races.

In the aftermath, television networks scrambled to book the night’s biggest winners and most recognisable faces to comment on the results.

But one of the most sought-after figures was not a longtime Democratic leader like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer or House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. It was Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City – and a figurehead for a burgeoning progressive movement.

At New York Governor Kathy Hochul’s re-election watch party in Midtown Manhattan, a newly shaven, moustache-wearing Mamdani took the stage to celebrate what he described as a victory for the broader left-wing political movement.

“We have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to working people once again,” Mamdani told a roaring crowd.

In the days that followed, Mamdani appeared on networks ranging from left-leaning MS NOW to the more conservative Fox News to discuss the growing clout of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the organisation with which he is affiliated.

Several DSA-backed candidates succeeded in the November 3 midterms, including the Mamdani-endorsed politician Claire Valdez, who won New York’s seventh congressional district.

Democratic socialists also triumphed in mayoral elections from Washington, DC, to Providence, Rhode Island, and Los Angeles, California. Elsewhere, progressives captured key races around the country, including toss-up Senate contests in Maine and Michigan.



Supporters of the progressive movement see this year’s midterms as a turning point for Democratic politics overall. They credit Mamdani with setting the landslide in motion.

“On the candidate and campaign side, we now have a path – cleared by Zohran and now being paved by others – for this kind of authentic, populist and competent progressive leadership,” Adin Lenchner, founder of New York-based political consultancy Carroll Street Campaigns, told Al Jazeera.

Lenchner called figures like Mamdani “a real model nationally” for the left wing.

Mayoral sway

New York City’s mayors have long occupied a prominent place in US politics, commanding a national profile well beyond the city’s limits.

Rudy Giuliani, for example, was dubbed “America’s mayor” after the attacks on September 11, 2001. Bill de Blasio became a fixture on national television during the COVID-19 pandemic. But Mamdani’s ascent has been different.

At the start of 2025, Mamdani was a relatively unknown state assemblyman from Queens. His mayoral bid was widely regarded as a long shot. But his grassroots organising, social media operation and economic message quickly turned his campaign into a national phenomenon.

That message – focused largely on affordability – resonated with political strategist Nomiki Konst, who worked on the 2016 presidential campaign for US Senator Bernie Sanders, another democratic socialist.

She remembers connecting with the Sanders campaign in a way she had not with mainstream Democrats.

“I couldn’t necessarily articulate my frustration with the Democratic Party and what they were not providing for me,” Konst said.

“But then suddenly Bernie Sanders started talking about student loan debt, and I was like, ‘Oh, that’s the thing that’s killing me right now. That is why I feel like I can’t get by, like I’m just constantly on a hamster wheel.'”

Konst is currently organising for other progressive candidates to compete in the 2028 elections, building on this year’s midterm momentum.

She anticipates campaigns like Mamdani’s – that focus on the “crushing weight of this monopoly-driven crony capitalism” – will continue to be relevant in 2028, just as they were this year.

For Lenchner, the success of progressive and democratic socialist candidates in the 2026 midterms hinged on affordability issues. Voters consistently ranked the cost of living among their top concerns in pre-election polls.

He pointed to the parallel with Mamdani’s 2025 campaign, which included videos explaining how street food had become so expensive.



“Understanding that the same forces that make halal trucks expensive and limit immigrants from being able to run food carts are the same forces that are keeping people off healthcare and keeping their rent high,” Lenchner said.

“I think that is the connective tissue that Zohran has so expertly told the story of and connected for voters.”

Upending the establishment

Political insiders say Mamdani’s victory in 2025 also offered a lesson for midterm candidates today: that the political establishment is not invincible, and candidates willing to challenge it can win.

In 2025, Mamdani’s main opponent was former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, a candidate who had name recognition, political connections and institutional backing.

Despite resigning his governorship in 2021 over sexual misconduct allegations, Cuomo was long thought to be the frontrunner.

Instead, he lost the Democratic primary to Mamdani, 56 percent to 44. He ran in the general election as an independent, only to lose again, with Mamdani taking just over 50 percent of the vote to Cuomo’s nearly 42 percent.

Progressive operatives see that willingness to stare down long odds as one of the biggest takeaways from Mamdani’s dark-horse campaign.

Early in his campaign, the future mayor was polling at barely 1 percent in pre-election polls, with Cuomo by far the frontrunner. At the time, his identity as a democratic socialist was seen as a weakness.

To Konst, the lesson is that political affiliation matters less than overarching questions of economic inequality.

“The people who are holding up this country are the corporate class, which likes to divide us based on its designation of what left and right is,” Konst said.

“It’s up versus down. There’s no left or right in this country, and people are changing their minds every day.”

Mamdani’s campaign also demonstrated the appeal of small-dollar fundraising, with the vast majority of its contributions coming in amounts under $250.

In 2026, DSA candidates in New York also banked on a lot of small donors.

Looking to 2028

Political insiders trace Mamdani’s strategy of redirecting attention to the economy to some of this year’s most surprising victories.

In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in the Senate race, becoming the first Democrat to win statewide office in the state in more than 30 years.

In Michigan, another Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, faced repeated questions about his position on Israel and Gaza, but instead centred his campaign on a pledge to redirect money for the war towards domestic priorities.

Konst, the political strategist, said she has already started to look at how to leverage last week’s midterm success into future races.

“I think, on the left, we need to take the momentum out of our wins on Tuesday and channel it into something,” Konst said.

In her case, that has meant scoping out potential 2028 presidential candidates. She is co-chairing a draft committee urging US Representative Ro Khanna of California, an outspoken progressive, to run.



Whether Mamdani’s influence can translate into a lasting national movement remains to be seen.

Critics warn that the 2026 midterm victories may reflect more the backlash to US President Donald Trump than support for a progressive political surge.

But Konst hopes that, on election night in 2028, she might find herself experiencing the same anticipation and enthusiasm she felt during the midterms.

Only this time, her eyes are not on the halls of Congress or city hall, but the White House.

World.title: ‘Malign actors’: Ireland fears undersea cables face threat from Russia
World.content:
Wexford, Ireland – They cross the ocean floor between continents, carrying nearly all our data, from messages and calls to trillions of dollars in financial transactions each day.

Subsea cables underpin global communications and power economies, but they are also increasingly seen as vulnerable to sabotage.

About 75 percent of transatlantic subsea cables pass through or near Irish waters, according to the Irish government, connecting North America with Europe – giving the small European Union member outsized strategic importance.

Ireland is also a major hub for United States tech multinationals, including Google, Microsoft and Meta, with a growing concentration of data centres supporting the digital economy.

But increased activity by Russian vessels near undersea infrastructure in recent years has raised concerns that cables around Ireland could become targets of interference.

In November 2024, the Russian ship Yantar, officially an oceanographic research vessel but described by the United Kingdom Ministry of Defence as a spy ship, was monitored near undersea infrastructure in the Irish Sea before being escorted out of Ireland’s exclusive economic zone by the Irish Navy.

Two months later, the UK’s Defence Ministry said the vessel had been “caught loitering over critical undersea infrastructure in UK waters.”

In late 2025, the British government accused Yantar of directing lasers at Royal Air Force (RAF) pilots monitoring its movements in the North Sea.

‘Ireland is absolutely Europe’s weakest link when it comes to defence’

Ireland has limited capability to monitor its waters – it has the lowest defence spending as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) in the EU, and its navy has no submarines. It is militarily neutral and not part of NATO.



Irish senator Tom Clonan, a strong supporter of Irish neutrality, argued that it should not be a barrier to boosting defence.

“Because of the end of the violence and the conflict in Ireland, and with the ceasefires and the peace agreement, we’ve had a peace dividend. So for the last 30 years, successive governments have really taken their foot off the accelerator when it comes to defence and security. And then, more broadly, Europe has enjoyed a peace dividend after the fall of the Berlin Wall,” he told Al Jazeera.

“So as a consequence of those two things, Ireland is absolutely Europe’s weakest link when it comes to defence in the air, maritime, ground and cyber domains,” he added.

The Irish government recently boosted its naval powers, allowing the navy to board and inspect suspicious vessels.

Ensuring defence against “emerging threats in our waters, particularly from vessels linked to the Russian shadow fleet” is a priority, Defence Minister Helen McEntee said in March, referring to the ageing, often uninsured tankers used to transport Russian oil and circumvent Western sanctions.

Their presence in Irish waters has raised concerns about both accidental damage and deliberate interference with undersea infrastructure. Moscow disputes the term “shadow fleet” as a political fabrication.

“Recent events in the Baltic Sea and the activities of Russia’s shadow fleet have highlighted the importance of ensuring that we have the legal framework necessary to respond to evolving threats,” McEntee continued.

In December 2024, a tanker suspected of belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet was investigated after power and telecoms cables were damaged in the Gulf of Finland.

A year later, in December 2025, a cargo ship sailing from St Petersburg under the flag of St Vincent and the Grenadines damaged telecommunications cables between Finland and Estonia. A Finnish court convicted its Russian captain and Azerbaijani boatswain of aggravated sabotage, according to the Reuters news agency. Both denied wrongdoing, and the conviction can be appealed.

For Daniel Mulhall, Ireland’s former ambassador to the US, that much of the world’s digital infrastructure passes through Irish waters means the country can no longer assume that its geographical position offers protection.

“It’s the fact that there are 850 US multinationals that have operations in Ireland. Many of them have big data centres to manage their data in our country,” he told Al Jazeera. “We are an integral part of the Western digital economy. And therefore, any sort of cyber threat to that economy is going to be potentially aimed at Ireland, or at least we could be victims of it, even if we’re not the prime target. So I think the world has become a far more complex place. And I think Irish people are waking up to that fact.”



Mulhall argued that protecting the cables will require international cooperation.

“I don’t think anyone can guarantee that those cables will be safe, least of all Ireland. But I think with collective effort, we can make reasonable preparations to strengthen our ability to protect those cables from malign actors that might wish to interfere with them,” he added.

“They’re the bloodstream of our economy. And if that bloodstream is interfered with, the economy will have serious trouble.”

World.title: Russia’s ambassador to US, Alexander Darchiev, dies at 66
World.content:
Share Moscow announces sudden death of Russia’s envoy to US on social media

Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died at the age of 66, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry.

The ministry said in a statement that he “passed away suddenly” on Wednesday, just a year and a half after being appointed to the US role.

Moscow did not provide more details on his death.

Darchiev was an “outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader and a kind colleague” and worked “in one of the most critical areas of Russian foreign policy”, the ministry said. He was a specialist in Russia-US relations.

He was appointed last March, shortly after US President Donald Trump returned to power, and several years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In 2022, when Russia launched its offensive against Ukraine, Darchiev called the move a “necessary measure”.

Darchiev was born into the family of a diplomat and minister-counsellor of the Russian Embassy in Hungary, Nikita Ivanovich Darchiev, according to the state-owned TASS news agency.

He first entered diplomatic service in 1992, becoming first secretary and head of the North America department in Russia’s Foreign Ministry.

He served as an adviser to the Russian Embassy in the US in 1997 and later took the post of minister-counsellor from 2005 to 2010. He also previously served as Russia’s ambassador to Canada between 2014 and 2021.

Darchiev returned to the North America department in the Foreign Ministry as its director in 2010 and later held the post again until last year.

World.title: Spain faces nationwide protests over soaring housing costs
World.content:
NewsFeed Spain faces nationwide protests over soaring housing costs

Spain has been rocked by nationwide protests and a general strike over its worsening housing crisis. The death of 87-year-old Maricarmen, who was evicted after her rent was set to increase fivefold, has become a symbol of the crisis.

World.title: Portugal cancels more than 300 flights, shuts schools due to Storm Charles
World.content:
Authorities spared no effort in preparation for the Atlantic storm after criticism following January’s Storm Kristin.

Share Portugal cancels more than 300 flights, shuts schools due to Storm Charles on social media

More than 300 flights in and out of Portugal have been cancelled, while businesses and all schools nationwide shut down before Storm Charles hit the country’s mainland, but the heavy rainfall and intense winds passed without causing severe damage.

Operations shut down on Wednesday across four different international airports, as well as hundreds of supermarkets and all non-essential public services across the country.

For the first time in living memory, about 8,000 of Portugal’s schools cancelled classes over the significant Atlantic storm forecast.

Streets were largely deserted when Storm Charles arrived, because the government had told people to stay at home, fearing the worst.

The national weather agency, IPMA, recorded wind gusts of more than 120km/h (75mph) in some areas.

Buses without passengers drove through the country’s capital, Lisbon, where some streets flooded due to clogged drains.

A national supermarket chain closed its stores, while the Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon, attended by about 70,000 people, called off the day’s events.

Government response

By mid-afternoon, only the southern Algarve region, a popular European tourist destination, remained on red alert, the highest level of emergency warning, which initially had covered more than half of the country.

Storm Charles had struck the Portuguese island of Madeira, off northwest Africa, on Tuesday with 130km/h (81mph) winds.



In January, the country’s centre-right government faced harsh criticism for its weak response when Storm Kristin hit central Portugal, felling thousands of trees and causing widespread property damage that is still being repaired.

In February, a 70-year-old man died in the southern region of Alentejo after flooding swept his vehicle off a street in the aftermath of Storm Leonardo.

Prime Minister Luis Montenegro chaired a crisis unit along with eight government ministers and other officials to monitor the storm.

Interior Minister Luis Neves, who oversees public safety, dismissed suggestions that authorities had overreacted, saying the government organised its response in accordance with the weather forecast.

Storm Charles was forecast to head later into Spain, where workers staged a general strike Wednesday. Strike organisers cancelled or postponed demonstrations in some southern cities, including Cordoba, Huelva and Cadiz.

World.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
World.content:
Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Ãlvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.

Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.

The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.

Ãlvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.

He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay â¬1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.

"It's absolutely crazyâ¦ with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."

He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."

With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".

However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.

"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.

Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.

Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.

Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red ElÃ©ctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

World.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
World.content:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.

Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.

However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.

Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.

The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.

For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.

For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.

That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.

Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.

There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.

Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.

Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.

Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.

Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.

Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.

"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

World.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
World.content:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.

CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.

Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.

While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.

"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.

Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.

Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.

In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.

The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.

Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

World.title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
World.content:
Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.

In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".

"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.

Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.

It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.

Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.

"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.

Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.

The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.

The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project.

Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.

Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

World.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
World.content:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.

It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.

The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.

The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.

"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.

It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.

Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.

On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.

Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.

His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.

In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

World.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
World.content:
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.

Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.

His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.

Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.

He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.

Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.

When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.

Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper ClarÃ­n.

However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.

A nationwide manhunt is now under way.

Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.

Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.

However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.

Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".

He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.

Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.

The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.

Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

World.title: Missing 11-month-old baby found buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
World.content:
An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.

Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.

The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.

The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.

Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.

The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.

Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.

World.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
World.content:

The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".

He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".

Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.

"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.

Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.

The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.

"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.

"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

World.title: COP31: Guterres faults fossil fuel lobby, demands $1.3tn for developing countries
World.content:
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has called on developed countries and international financial institutions to mobilise at least $1.3 trillion annually for developing countries by 2035, warning that the global response to climate change is falling far behind the scale of the crisis.

Mr Guterres said climate finance commitments must translate into accessible funding for countries struggling to adapt to rising temperatures, build resilient infrastructure and transition to cleaner energy sources.

He also demanded an accelerated transition away from fossil fuels, accusing powerful industry interests of obstructing climate action while continuing to profit from activities contributing to global warming.

Mr Guterres made the demands on Wednesday at the World Leaders Summit of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, where heads of state and government gathered to discuss the implementation of international climate commitments.

He said global emissions needed to decline by about six per cent annually, arguing that existing national climate plans, even if fully implemented, would deliver only about a third of the required reductions.

“Our first climate duty is to tell the truth. The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. Emissions in 2025 reached all-time highs. Heat records keep shattering. The last four years were the hottest ever,” he said.

Climate finance gap

Mr Guterres’ demand comes amid continuing concerns over the availability and accessibility of climate finance for developing countries, many of which face high costs in responding to extreme weather, protecting vulnerable communities and reducing emissions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The $1.3 trillion annual financing ambition is not an entirely new commitment. It builds on the climate finance agreement reached at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, which established a goal of mobilising at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, led by developed countries, alongside a broader call to scale up funding from all sources to at least $1.3 trillion annually by the same year.

However, Mr Guterres said the wider financing ambition must move beyond political declarations to become actual funding available to countries that need it.

“Developed countries must lead in delivering at least $300 billion a year by 2035, and set out concrete plans with clear milestones to at least triple adaptation finance by then”.

“The $1.3 trillion goal must become real finance flowing to developing countries, and this demands that every source of finance pull its weight,” he said.

He noted that emerging and developing economies outside China account for nearly two-thirds of the world’s population but receive less than one-fifth of global clean energy investments.

He added that many of these countries pay two to three times more to borrow, making it difficult to finance renewable energy projects and climate adaptation programmes.

According to him, the disparity risks deepening dependence on fossil fuels, as countries unable to secure affordable clean-energy financing may continue investing in conventional energy infrastructure.

He called for greater contributions from multilateral development banks, private investors and donor countries, including more favourable lending arrangements and innovative financing instruments.

He also urged governments to strengthen funding for the Green Climate Fund and the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which supports vulnerable countries dealing with the consequences of climate-related disasters.

Fossil fuel industry under scrutiny

Beyond financing, Mr Guterres criticised the influence of fossil fuel companies on climate policy, arguing that the industry’s lobbying activities were slowing the transition to renewable energy.

He said the world could no longer justify continued dependence on coal, oil and gas when the economic and environmental costs of their use were becoming increasingly apparent.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” he said.

He accused fossil fuel interests of distorting scientific evidence, delaying policy decisions and avoiding accountability for environmental damage.

He argued that renewable energy had become increasingly competitive, noting that solar power, which accounted for only one per cent of global electricity generation a decade ago, met nearly three-quarters of the growth in electricity demand in the previous year.

He also cited the growing adoption of electric vehicles, saying nearly one in three new cars sold globally was expected to be electric in 2026.

Mr Guterres said three-quarters of the world’s population live in countries that import fossil fuels, leaving them vulnerable to international price fluctuations and energy insecurity.

He called for a just and orderly transition that would include ending new unabated coal development, reducing methane emissions and expanding electricity grids, energy storage and clean electrification.

He also urged governments to tax windfall profits made by fossil fuel companies and direct the proceeds towards countries affected by climate disasters.

Citing the financial disparity between oil companies and climate-vulnerable countries, he said the nine largest oil companies made $95 billion in profits in the last quarter, while the Loss and Damage Fund had received approximately $600 million.

“That is what these companies made in about 14 hours,” he said.

Leaders seek stronger climate action

The COP31 World Leaders Summit, taking place on 11 and 12 November, is part of the conference’s high-level discussions, which run from 9 to 20 November in Antalya.

The conference is being hosted by Türkiye, while Australia is leading the formal negotiations under an agreed partnership arrangement.

Other leaders at the summit also called for increased climate financing and practical interventions to protect vulnerable countries.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the growing threat of rising sea levels to Pacific island nations, particularly Tuvalu, where the average elevation of the islands is approximately 1.83 metres above sea level.

He recounted meeting a 13-year-old student in the country who feared for the future of her home, despite aspiring to become a doctor.

Reading her message to world leaders, Mr Albanese said the student was asking for international cooperation to protect communities threatened by rising oceans.

He said Australia had doubled its renewable electricity generation over six years, with renewables now accounting for half of the country’s electricity mix. He also disclosed that more than 600,000 home batteries had been installed in the country in the past year.

Meanwhile, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed called for climate action to be integrated into economic development planning, particularly in countries where changing weather patterns threaten agriculture and livelihoods.

“In Ethiopia, climate action is economic policy,” he said.

Mr Abiy said more than 90 per cent of Ethiopia’s electricity came from hydropower, while the country was expanding investments in wind, solar and geothermal energy.

He also highlighted Ethiopia’s Green Legacy Initiative, through which more than 56 billion seedlings had been planted to restore degraded land and expand forest cover.

He said climate financing must be predictable and accessible early enough to enable vulnerable countries to prepare for extreme weather events.

He urged international financiers to make their commitments measurable, asking them to specify the amount of funding available, when it would be delivered, and the conditions attached.

World.title: Flamingos’ victory shows Tinubu will be re-elected  – Akpabio
World.content:
The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, has said Nigeria’s historic victory at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco is a sign that President Bola Tinubu will be re-elected in 2027.

Mr Akpabio said the Flamingos’ triumph ahead of the 2027 general elections signalled that Nigerians would vote massively for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) and return Mr Tinubu for a second term.

He stated this on Wednesday when he received members of the Flamingos at the Senate wing of the National Assembly in Abuja.

“Perhaps, the prominence in choosing this hour for your triumph, just as we are about to go for the 2027 election, you brought this World Cup to us, which means that we have won the next election. It is the same way Nigerians are going to choose us in January 2027,” he said.

Mr Akpabio further said that Mr Tinubu’s receipt of the trophy from the team was an indication that he would also emerge victorious in the 2027 presidential election.

“And for the president to be a president that receives this World Cup from you, it means he’s also going to receive a bigger trophy of his re-election into office as president of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. So, continue the good work and continue to make us proud. The transformative spirit is already touching every sector of our economy,” he said.

The 2027 presidential election is scheduled for 16 January 2027, according to the timetable released by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

INEC has cleared 18 presidential candidates and their running mates to participate in the election, after political parties concluded their primaries and INEC published its final list of candidates on 12 September.

The candidates include Mr Tinubu of the APC; former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar of the All Progressives Congress (ADC); former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC); and Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM).

Other candidates include Sandy Onor of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP); Omoyele Sowore of the African Action Congress (AAC); and Adewole Adebayo of the Social Democratic Party (SDP).

The governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections are scheduled for 6 February 2027.

Flamingos’ historic victory

Nigeria defeated Japan 2-1 in Saturday’s final at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat, Morocco, to become the first African country to win the competition.

Awawu Bashiru opened the scoring in the 39th minute before Oluebube Umejiaku doubled Nigeria’s lead shortly after the restart. Japan’s Fuki Ito reduced the deficit in the 80th minute, but the Flamingos held on to secure the title.

The Flamingos lost their opening group-stage match 2-1 to Poland but recovered, winning six consecutive matches to lift the trophy. They became the first team in the competition’s history to lose their opening fixture and still win the tournament.

They defeated Puerto Rico 2-0 and defending champions Korea DPR 3-1 in the group stage before overcoming Mexico 2-1 in the round of 16. They subsequently edged Venezuela in the quarter-finals and defeated Brazil 3-1 in the semi-finals to reach their first-ever final.

The victory also made Nigeria the first African country to win both the men’s and women’s FIFA U-17 World Cup titles.

On Tuesday, the Senate announced a donation of N100 million to the team in recognition of their historic achievement and to encourage the players.

At Wednesday’s meeting, Mr Akpabio presented the cash donation to members of the team.

He urged the players to remain united and encouraged the technical crew, including the coaches, to sustain their training and development to prepare them for promotion to the senior women’s national team, the Super Falcons.

World.title: Police linked to 118 civic space violations in 2025 -WSCIJ Report
World.content:
The Nigeria Police Force has been linked to 118 out of 245 civic space violations, according to a report by the Wole Soyinka Centre for Investigative Journalism (WSCIJ) on the status of journalism and the civic space.

The Executive Director of Media Rights Agenda, Edetaen Ojo, made this known on Tuesday during his presentation of findings from the 153-page documented report on civic space violations. The event was held virtually on X Spaces.

The report, titled “Silenced Voices, Shrinking Space: Civic Freedoms Under Pressure,” relied on evidence from the WSCIJ monitoring work regarding patterns of intimidation against media and civil society actors.

The findings indicate that 89 per cent of recorded violations were perpetrated by state actors, with the Force accounting for 54 per cent of those incidents.

Police response

Aliyu Giwa, the Force spokesperson, said in response to the report’s findings that the Force is training 10,000 officers in election security management and human rights ahead of the 2027 elections.

Mr Giwa, who was represented by Kondom Joseph, a police superintendent, clarified that while police act as gatekeepers for law and order, they recognise journalists as core partners in society.

He emphasised that the police maintain internal mechanisms, such as the Public Complaints Bureau, to investigate officer misconduct through dismissals or demotions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The conversation

The online programme featured prominent figures, including human rights lawyer Ayo Obe; Peter Maduoma, executive director of the CLEEN Foundation; Edetaen Ojo and Motunrayo Alaka, executive director and CEO of WSCIJ.

Nabilah Usman, general manager of Radio Now 95.3 FM, moderated the online event.

In his remarks, Mr Ojo identified a culture of impunity as a primary challenge, noting that many violations occur because perpetrators believe that they would not face transparent punishment.

He called for legal reforms to close loopholes that allow laws to be used to restrict legitimate expression and assembly.

Mr Ojo noted that journalists are essential for democratic participation, accountability and rule of law in Nigeria.

On her part, WSCIJ’s CEO, Mrs Alaka, stressed that media organisations must remain persistent in their advocacy, despite the risk of state repression.

She said documented threats are increasing, with a notable spike during recent election cycles since 2021.

Data from the report shows significant spikes in incidents during election periods and public protests throughout 2023, 2024, and 2025.

While journalists were historically most affected, recent trends show more harassment directed toward general citizens in civic spaces.

Legal perspective on civic rights

Human rights lawyer Ms Obe highlighted that while the constitution guarantees freedom of expression, journalists face targeted harassment.

She warned against using laws such as cyberbullying or criminal defamation as tools by powerful figures to harass critics through arbitrary arrests.

She identified the lack of independent discretion by police when handling reports involving public figures for politicians.

Mr Maduoma of CLEEN Foundation said there is a significant gap between security agencies and civil society regarding public trust.

He noted that accountability must be a continuous process involving intelligence sharing and community policing at the state level.

The report

The 2025 Journalism and Civic Space Status Report, “Silenced Voices, Shrinking Space: Civic Freedoms Under Pressure”, presents an analysis of reported civic space violations.

The incidents were documented through systematic monitoring of reports published by 54 media organisations between January and December 2025.

“Data was collected through continuous monitoring of reports on civic space violations across physical and digital spaces. Every incident was verified through cross-checking with multiple credible sources before inclusion in the dataset. Where additional context was required, Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) were conducted,” the report stated.

The report said it counted incidents reported by multiple media organisations as a single verified incident to avoid duplication.

It added that the 245 incidents analysed were referenced in reports published by 54 media organisations, comprising 16 newspapers with print and online editors, 26 online-only news platforms, 10 television stations and two radio stations.

The report said the findings showed that Nigeria’s civic space remained under significant pressure despite the country’s democratic system and constitutional guarantees of fundamental rights.

It also identified the Nigeria Police Force as being involved in 118 of the 219 incidents involving state actors.

World.title: Seven organisations pledge $65m to reduce maternal, newborn deaths in Nigeria
World.content:
Seven private sector and philanthropic organisations have proposed commitments worth more than $65 million to strengthen maternal and newborn healthcare services in Nigeria.

The commitments, announced on Wednesday during the 2026 Joint Annual Review of the health sector in Abuja, are expected to support interventions in 172 local government areas (LGAs) identified as having a high burden of maternal deaths.

According to a statement issued following the event, the organisations submitted letters of intent under the Maternal and Neonatal Mortality Reduction Innovation Initiative (MAMII) Private Sector Compact, a government-led framework designed to coordinate investments and technical support for maternal and newborn healthcare.

The seven organisations are DP World, Bayer, UNICEF, dsm-firmenich, Nestlé Nutrition Institute, Roche and Ferring Pharmaceuticals.

The proposed contributions include financial resources, medical products, technical expertise, supply chain support and other services intended to address gaps in maternal and newborn healthcare delivery.

Nigeria’s maternal mortality burden

The announcement comes as Nigeria continues to record high numbers of preventable maternal and newborn deaths.

According to estimates contained in the statement, approximately 40,000 women and 300,000 newborns die annually in Nigeria, representing more than 100 maternal deaths and 800 newborn deaths every day.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

These estimates highlight persistent challenges in access to skilled birth attendants, emergency obstetric services, essential medicines and timely referrals, particularly in underserved communities.

MAMII, launched in November 2024, prioritises 172 LGAs across 33 states, which account for more than half of Nigeria’s maternal deaths, according to the programme’s targeting analysis.

The initiative focuses on improving emergency obstetric and newborn care, strengthening referral systems, providing emergency transport and increasing access to essential medical supplies and trained health workers.

Speaking at the event, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Muhammad Pate said reducing preventable maternal and newborn deaths remained a national priority.

“Through the Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and our Sector-Wide Approach, we are bringing federal and state governments, the private sector and development partners together around a common national plan, with particular attention to the 172 local government areas where the burden of maternal mortality is greatest,” Mr Pate said.

He described the commitments as an important step towards improving healthcare delivery and an important expression of confidence in Nigeria’s reform agenda.

“Our responsibility is to ensure that every commitment is aligned with national priorities, every investment is accounted for, and every intervention contributes to measurable improvements in the lives of Nigerian women and children,” he said.

Partners pledge technical support

The Nigeria Country Director of the Gates Foundation, Uche Amaonwu, said the partnership would help coordinate resources and expertise towards reducing preventable deaths.

Mr Amaonwu said the burden of maternal mortality continues to affect too many Nigerian families.

“The MAMII compact brings focus to this challenge, coordinating public, private and philanthropic efforts to reduce preventable maternal and newborn deaths,” he said.

He said the foundation was working with partners, including MSD for Mothers, MTN Group Foundation and the World Economic Forum’s Global Alliance for Women’s Health, to strengthen maternal and newborn healthcare.

Similarly, MTN Foundation Executive Director Odunayo Sanya said the organisation would support the initiative through connectivity, artificial intelligence and digital solutions.

“MTN believes technology has its greatest value when it removes real barriers to essential services,” she said.

Ms Sanya said the partnership would help provide women, frontline health workers and healthcare facilities with information and digital tools to improve maternal health outcomes.

The Head of the Centre for Health and Healthcare at the World Economic Forum, Shyam Bishen, said private sector participation could contribute more than financial support.

Mr Bishen said businesses could provide products, technology, supply chains and expertise needed to improve healthcare delivery, particularly in underserved communities.

The Executive Director of Social Impact and Sustainability at MSD for Mothers, Jacquelyn Caglia, said the organisation would invest in the Training for Emergency Action, Management and Workflows in Midwifery, Obstetrics and Neonatal Care (TEAM OB/NEO).

The programme is designed to equip health workers with the skills needed to manage life-threatening complications during pregnancy, childbirth and newborn care, including severe bleeding, infections and breathing difficulties in babies.

Ms Caglia said the company had spent 15 years supporting efforts to reduce maternal deaths, including in Nigeria, through its MSD for Mothers initiative.

“By investing in TEAM OB/NEO as part of the MAMII Compact, we reaffirm our commitment to Nigeria and to collaborating with other private sector partners to pool resources, expertise and innovation aligned to the national effort to expand access to quality maternity care services for women across Nigeria,” she said.

Platform to track investments

The government also unveiled a digital platform designed to coordinate and monitor contributions under the MAMII Private Sector Compact.

The platform, developed through the SWAp Coordination Office, is expected to show the geographical distribution of interventions, partner contributions and outstanding healthcare gaps across participating states and LGAs.

It is also intended to help prevent the concentration of donor-funded projects in some locations while other communities remain underserved.

However, the platform is still at the prototype stage, with its operational and reporting arrangements yet to be finalised.

The MAMII National Lead at the SWAp Coordination Office, Dayo Adeyanju, said the platform would support better coordination and investment decisions.

“It shows clearly where the gaps are and which delivery partners are supporting which LGAs,” Mr Adeyanju said.

He added that the platform would help prevent the duplication of interventions and improve resource allocation, with information expected to support partner decisions from December 2026.

The government said the next phase of the Compact would involve agreeing on implementation milestones, deploying resources to priority areas and monitoring progress against maternal and newborn health outcomes.

World.title: INEC chairman’s scheduled appearance in Sowore’s cyberbulling trial stalled
World.content:
The cyberstalking trial of the African Action Congress (AAC) presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore stalled at the Federal High Court in Abuja on Wednesday earlier scheduled for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) chairman, Joash Amupitan, to appear on subpoena.

The case was rescheduled for 17 November after court officials informed Mr Sowore and the prosecution lawyers at about 11 a.m. that Judge Mohammed Garba Umar could not sit because he was indisposed. About 28 other cases on the cause list were also adjourned.

The federal government, through the State Security Service (SSS), is prosecuting Mr Sowore, the publisher of Sahara Reporters, over social media posts in which he described President Bola Tinubu as a criminal.

The SSS had accused the activist of publishing false information about the president and charged him with cyberstalking under the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act.

Mr Sowore pleaded not guilty to the charges and is currently presenting his defence before the court.

At the previous 9 November hearing, Judge Umar granted Mr Sowore’s request to summon All Progressives Congress (APC) figure Joe Igbokwe and INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan as defence witnesses.

The court subsequently adjourned the trial until Wednesday for the appearance of the two witnesses.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But it was unclear if any of the two men would have appeared on Wednesday had proceedings continued.

INEC opposes subpoena

Ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, INEC had opposed the subpoena summoning its chairman to produce President Tinubu’s electoral records from the 1999 Lagos governorship election and the 2023 presidential election.

The commission filed a motion on notice asking the court to set aside the subpoena on Tuesday.

In the motion, Mr Amupitan asked the court to set aside a subpoena dated 26 October and served on INEC headquarters in Abuja on 6 November.

The subpoena also required him to appear as a defence witness and produce two sets of electoral records.

These include Mr Tinubu’s INEC Form CF01 for the 1999 Lagos governorship election, including an affidavit concerning lost certificates. It also requested his Form CF01 for the 2023 presidential election.

INEC argued that the subpoena was invalid because it was not personally served on Mr Amupitan, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) and professor of law at the University of Jos. It also said the document was served on INEC’s Litigation and Prosecution Department.

The commission also argued that he was not a party to the criminal case and that the requested documents did not exist in the form described. He therefore argued that he could not give evidence about them.

He also alleged that the request was made in bad faith and could embarrass the commission. He asked the court to set it aside.

How the case started

The case arose from the posts Mr Sowore published on X and Facebook in August 2025 calling President Tinubu a criminal in response to the comment the president made about corruption during a visit to Brazil.

The SSS subsequently wrote to X, demanding the suspension of Mr Sowore’s account. The agency also asked him to retract the posts and publish an apology, a request Mr Sowore rebuffed.

After Mr Sowore declined to comply, the agency filed five charges on 23 September 2025, initially listing Mr Sowore alongside X Corporation, formerly Twitter, and Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook, as co-defendants. But the prosecution subsequently removed the names of the tech firms, leaving Mr Sowore behind as the sole defendant.

The SSS eventually arraigned him on 2 December 2025, when he pleaded not guilty and was granted bail.

On 19 January, the prosecution amended the case, reducing the number of counts from five to two and officially removing X and Meta as defendants, leaving Mr Sowore as the sole defendant.

The amended charge accused him of cyberstalking under Section 24 of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Amendment Act, 2024. The allegations concerned his publications on X and Facebook.

The prosecution called one witness before closing its case in March. It also tendered evidence, including screenshots of Mr Sowore’s posts and video recordings.

On 8 May, Judge Umar dismissed Mr Sowore’s no-case submission, ruling that the prosecution had established a prima facie case requiring him to warrant him to enter defence.

Mr Sowore opened his defence in July, calling a lawyer and public commentator Deji Adeyanju as his first witness.

Other defence witnesses who have appeared are SSS official Uwem Davies, who appeared on subpoena, former member of Mr Sowore’s legal team, Wayne Elijah, and SSS investigator Michael Jego, and another subpoenaed witness.

Mr Davies testified about a letter the SSS sent to Mr Sowore concerning his social media posts. Mr Elijah appeared in connection with documents the defence sought to tender.

Mr Jego was called after the court ruled that an authorised SSS official could testify in place of the agency’s Director-General.

The latest development began in October when the court rejected an application to compel SSS Director General Oluwatosin Ajayi to appear personally as a defence witness. But, the judge held that another authorised official could testify on behalf of the agency.

The defence subsequently sought to compel the SSS’s lead lawyer, Mr Kehinde, to testify, but Judge Umar set aside the subpoena, citing the duty of professional confidentiality between lawyers and their clients.

The defence then requested subpoenas against Mr Igbokwe and Mr Amupitan. This time, the judge granted the application and directed both men to appear.

World.title: NILDS urges Sergeant-at-Arms personnel to uphold professionalism
World.content:
‌‌‍‌The Director-General, National Institute for Legislative and Democratic Studies (NILDS), Abubakar Sulaiman, has urged Sergeant-at-Arms personnel to uphold discipline and professionalism in protecting the National Assembly.

Mr Sulaiman, a professor, gave the advice at the closing ceremony of a three-day training programme on Effective Legislative Security Policy: A Management Strategy for Safety and Protection of the National Assembly, in Abuja on Wednesday.

The training was organised by NILDS in collaboration with the National Assembly.

Mr Sulaiman said securing the National Assembly goes beyond protecting buildings, emphasising that it involves safeguarding democracy, constitutional order, and the integrity of the legislature.

According to him, the Sergeant-at-Arms’ responsibilities extend beyond conventional security duties to maintaining order, protecting lawmakers, staff and visitors, and enforcing parliamentary authority.

He said the responsibilities required discipline, emotional intelligence, sound judgment, restraint, loyalty and professionalism, rather than physical strength and the authority to enforce instructions.
