If your comments are mean-spirited, irrelevant or impractical to enact, it's probably better to stay silent. 🗣️ Would I want to hear this? Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the other person doesn't want to hear it. A 2022 survey found that people often underestimate others' desire for feedback even when it is constructive.

Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the other person doesn't want to hear it. A 2022 survey found that people often underestimate others' desire for feedback even when it is constructive. 🗣️ Do they want your feedback? When in doubt, don't assume you know what someone needs. Pre-assessing how valuable your advice is or how well someone can handle the truth can make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing.

Sponsor Message

For more guidance on how to share good and bad news, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

Volunteer musicians from Musicians On Call perform for veterans at the VA Medical Center in Washington, D.C., and other hospitalized patients nationwide. They typically visit hospitals three to four times a month. The Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam came alive recently as a renowned tattoo artist brought 17th-century masterpieces to life on visitors' skin. The Professional Women's Hockey League has announced the name of its new women's hockey team: the San José Sea Lions. (via KQED)

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: An Iran-backed trio is accused of plotting attacks on a U.K. base hosting U.S. jets
World.content:
An Iran-backed trio is accused of plotting attacks on a U.K. base hosting U.S. jets

toggle caption i Alastair Grant/AP

LONDON — Federal prosecutors in New York have charged three men with terrorism offenses over what they describe as an Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The charges include a September plot against a British air base where American forces were stationed.

The indictment, unsealed on Tuesday, names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, 32, who holds Iranian and Iraqi citizenship, Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi.

Prosecutors allege the men acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah to orchestrate, plan and conduct the attacks through a network of associates across Europe and the U.S., targeting Jewish communities and a British base hosting American troops. The indictment cites plots against synagogues in London and in New York. Both Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hezbollah are designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organizations.

Sponsor Message

The court filings describe an operation that was directed, in part, by the suspects who were thousands of miles away. In April, prosecutors have alleged, the three men gathered in a room and watched an attack unfold live on a large screen via Apple's FaceTime video calling app. Al-Hassani allegedly coached the attacker through igniting and hurling a series of seemingly incendiary devices while Al-Saadi filmed.

The following day, Al-Hassani is accused of guiding another man on a video call as he lit an improvised explosive and threw it at a synagogue in London.

The men "helped orchestrate a campaign of terror" on behalf of the two designated terror groups, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald.

The RAF Fairford plot

The United Kingdom seems to have been a central target of the plot allegedly perpetrated by the three men: among the roughly 18 attacks claimed last spring by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, which prosecutors say was a front for Kata'ib Hezbollah, as many as seven took place in the U.K. It was the most intensely targeted country in Europe, though the indictment does not specify the location of other plots or attacks.

Sponsor Message

These included arson attacks, the use of explosives, and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London — one of whom was a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Prosecutors say that in April the men sat in a room, and directed an attack remotely, in real time, over FaceTime, telling the attacker when to light and throw what seems to have been some kind of incendiary device.

The next day, one of the men, Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, allegedly told another man attacking a London synagogue to "light it up like a Christmas tree."

According to the indictment, Al-Hassani was operating from Iran, but he began paying associates in Britain in August to film the perimeter of Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, in Gloucestershire, several hours west of London.

They allegedly obtained vans and drums of fuel, looked into buying chemical accelerants, and gathered metal items that could potentially serve as shrapnel. The vans were fitted with sham branding for a fuel delivery firm as well as a pool supply company.

On Sept. 26, three of these vans had set off toward the base that housed large numbers of U.S. military aircraft. At least two vehicles were stopped at a security roadblock, and British authorities seized all three early the next morning and arrested those inside.

The U.S. almost immediately redeployed several of its long range bombing aircraft from the base at the time of this incident.

The indictment said Al-Saadi had been detained abroad in May and brought to the United States, where prosecutors say he kept directing the network from his jail cell by relaying coded messages through phone calls with relatives in Iraq. He used aliases to refer to his alleged co-conspirators and referred to terrorist activity, including ongoing alleged plots, as "work," while those he spoke to used the phrase "international section" to mean overseas travel, according to the indictment. His sister and mother were among his interlocutors on some of those calls. Three days before the plot, in late September, he allegedly asked them to get money to Al-Hassani for the RAF Fairford operation.

Sponsor Message

British authorities had earlier charged two men with national security related offenses tied to the incident.

U.S. soldier held over Russia allegations

In a separate case, British counterterrorism police said on Tuesday it arrested a 41-year-old member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain's National Security Act 2023.

The suspect, who has not been named by authorities, is a senior U.S. soldier who was stationed at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, in western England, which is home to NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the U.S. Army's Counterintelligence Command told NPR.

Officers have been searching two addresses in the same region of Gloucestershire, to the west of London. The man is being held at a London police station. Police said the allegations concern Russia, and the investigation was "very much ongoing," according to Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing in the U.K.

FBI Director Kash Patel called the arrest important in the context of an uptick in FBI counterintelligence arrest, and said it "involves allegations of espionage" — without giving further details.

"The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement to NPR.

The U.S. footprint in Britain

Though unrelated, both these cases have occurred in the U.K., a country which hosts a large American military presence. At the start of the war in Iran, Britain's Defense Ministry confirmed to the U.K. Parliament in March that U.S. forces operate eleven RAF bases across the country, with approximately 12,300 American military and civilian defense personnel at various sites.

Responding in January to a written question from a member of Parliament, the ministry said that there were around 11,000 uniformed U.S. personnel in the country, excluding families, civilians and contractors.

Sponsor Message

The ministry has declined to give figures for individual bases, citing the security of personnel.

The U.S. Air Force's two main operating bases are RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, in eastern England. Other sites include RAF Croughton, a communications station in Northamptonshire, and RAF Menwith Hill in North Yorkshire, used primarily by the National Security Agency, according to a House of Commons Library briefing. RAF Fairford serves as a forward operating base for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command.

In March, the British government allowed the U.S. to use British bases for limited strikes against missile sites in Iran, according to a parliamentary research service, which identifies Fairford as one of the bases potentially involved.

The threat picture around some U.S. bases seems to have sharpened in recent days. The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the U.S. military had moved aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall on Monday because of a threat from Iran. NPR did not independently confirm the reports.

Neither the U.K. nor the U.S. government has confirmed the reason for the aircraft movements that have been reported. Britain's Defense Ministry has said aircraft relocate routinely for operational reasons.

World.title: Pilot killed in aircraft crash linked to Remembrance Day ceremony in Quebec's Beauce region
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A pilot has died in a plane crash linked to a Remembrance Day ceremony in Quebec's Beauce region Wednesday morning.

The Sûreté du Québec (SQ) says the pilot was a man in his 60s. He was alone in the plane at the time of the crash, according to SQ spokesperson Sgt. Audrey-Anne Bilodeau.

The fatal crash happened in a wooded area near 10th Street and close to the Saint-Georges airport, about 100 kilometres south of Quebec City.

The SQ was informed of the crash shortly after 11 a.m.

The mayor of Saint-Georges told CBC the crash occurred during a Remembrance Day ceremony.

"A formation of six aircraft was performing the Missing Man formation as part of the ceremony when one of the pilots crashed," Manon Bougie said via email.

"It was a deeply sad and tragic moment, and our thoughts are with everyone affected by this terrible accident."

The SQ initially said the pilot was seriously injured and then confirmed the death shortly before 1:30 p.m.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon posted his condolences to the pilot's family and loved ones on X.

The premier has said he's closely monitoring the situation and is in touch with Domestic Security Minister Guy Lapointe Jr.

The aircraft crash is still under investigation. (Edouard Dubois/Radio-Canada)

Provincial police are still on scene responding to the incident.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada will also be investigating the crash, and has sent a team to the site.

It's still not known what happened to cause the plane to go down.

World.title: The remarkable story behind the secret Canadian guerrilla force you've never heard of
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Brent G. Hoy's father, Charles Hoy, didn't talk much about what he did during the Second World War.

It wasn't just that it was difficult. He also was part of a covert Chinese Canadian force, sworn to secrecy.

Force 136, part of Britain's Special Operations Executive, was trained in espionage, guerilla warfare and jungle survival for parachute deployment behind enemy lines in Southeast Asia.

These soldiers wore a Canadian uniform and were prepared to sacrifice their lives, despite being shunned by their country, both in law and daily discrimination.

"Fighting for a country that really didn't want you, but nevertheless having that deep sense to contribute," Hoy said of his father.

That complicated legacy is being spotlighted in a black and white photograph selected by Canada Post for a new stamp, to commemorate the country's military history.

It shows 10 out of about 150 Chinese Canadian soldiers who served the Allied war effort with Force 136 and, after the war was won in 1945, came home to become part of a broader push to change how their community was treated. In 1947, the Chinese Exclusion Act was repealed and the entrenched racism Chinese Canadians experienced began to shift.

It was a double victory, says Catherine Clement, a historian and curator whose work excavates stories of the Chinese Canadian experience.

"Helping the Allies win the war, but also helping the Chinese community to win the right, like equal rights, full rights of citizens of Canada".

Canada Post's new Remembrance Day stamp shows 10 soldiers from Force 136 awaiting repatriation in 1945. Brent G. Hoy's father, Charles Hoy, is in the bottom row, second from the right. (Canada Post)

Between 1885 and 1923, Chinese immigrants who came to Canada had to pay at least $50 to enter. The head tax was later raised to $100, then $500, before all Chinese immigration was banned in July 1923.

From then until 1947, all Chinese people — even those born in Canada — were required to register with the government or risk fines, detainment or deportation. They were segregated within society too, like being prevented from working in some professions or swimming in some public pools.

Operation Oblivion

It was under those laws, designed to exclude or ostracize people on the basis of their Chinese ethnicity, that Hoy's father, at the age of 26, still decided to volunteer in the war effort for Canada.

It was the same story for Rick Wong's father, Hank Wong, the son of a head tax payer and a member of Force 136, also called Operation Oblivion. Hank, who died in 2019, was the last surviving member of the original 13 members of the top secret mission to sabotage supply lines and equipment within Japanese-occupied territory in the Pacific.

Wong says despite first being rejected from the navy, because it was "for white men only," his father eventually joined the Kent Regiment and learned to parachute out of planes and rapidly deploy from moving trucks.

It was in the 1940s, when Japan entered the Second World War and began to quickly invade and occupy large parts of Southeast Asia, that the British realised it needed agents in the region to support local resistance fighters.

Undercover resistance

An undated photo of the first recruits of Force 136 training in Darwin, Australia. (Chinese Canadian Military Museum)

Chinese Canadians were the perfect recruits, from the perspective of Britain's Special Operations Executive, easily blending in with local populations with language skills in English and Cantonese.

Force 136 was born.

Then began intense training in Canada and abroad, including in espionage, wireless operation and jungle survival. Their mission was to gather intelligence, support local resistance fighters and carry out sabotage operations.

They were told to expect extreme heat, insects and disease, alongside the dangers of capture, torture or death.

Members of Force 136 training in Queensland, Australia in 1945. (Chinese Canadian Military Museum)

'A suicide mission'

One recruit, dropped into Borneo, recalled living on crocodile meat, monkeys and wild pigs, in a story highlighted by the Chinese Canadian Military Museum.

"They were told to save your last bullet for yourself, carry cyanide, if you're captured don't reveal any secrets," said Wong.

He says he once asked his father if he was afraid about what was "essentially a suicide mission" while he was awaiting his deployment in Australia.

His father replied, "you gotta do what you gotta do."

Then the Americans, under President Harry Truman, dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in early August 1945. There's long been difficulty in estimating total casualties, but more than 120,000 people were killed instantly in both cities, with many more dying from radiation in the years following, according to the Harry S. Truman Presidential Library & Museum. A few days later, the war ended and so too did Operation Oblivion.

While most of Force 136 sailed back to Canada through England, some men, including Wong's father, were abandoned in Australia.

" They had to work their way back on a freighter in order to get back," said Wong.

When they did get back to Canada, it took another two years until discriminatory laws were repealed. Many see Force 136 and the dismembering of legislation like the Chinese Exclusion Act as inseparably linked.

When those men returned they continued fighting, says Melissa Karmen Lee, the CEO of the Chinese Canadian Museum in Vancouver. It's the only place in Canada, including the War Museum in Ottawa, where the public can see a permanent exhibit on Chinese Canadian soldiers.

"Their faces belong on a Canadian stamp, their stories belong in our history books, and their legacy belongs to every Canadian," Lee said.

Rick Wong, left, and Brent G. Hoy unveil the new Canada Post stamp in Vancouver on Nov. 3. (Spill Studios)

'That's my dad there'

Hoy told an audience at the unveiling of the stamp in Vancouver that he could visualize his father's "broad and knowing closed lip smile of approval" that the contributions of Force 136 would be memorialized in such a way.

His father, who died in 2002, appears in the stamp in the bottom row, second from the right.

Hoy says he was thrilled "beyond words" when he was sent a mock-up of the stamp.

"I thought, hey gee, you know that's my dad there."

While the stamp features only a handful of the faces behind Force 136, Hoy says it marks an acknowledgement of gratitude for the Chinese Canadians that were prepared to sacrifice their lives. None lived long enough to see this commemoration.

"This selfless sense of duty shines a bright light on the fact that we, as a generation after them, are the offspring of our ancestors' courage, persistence, commitment and sacrifice."

World.title: Did Stellantis violate its deals with the feds? Funding contract provided exceptions around Brampton, Ont.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney called Stellantis' now-confirmed plans to sell an automotive assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., "a betrayal" of the global automaker's "obligations to Canada and by extension to all Canadians."

But a previously obtained copy of the multi-million-dollar funding deal between Stellantis and the federal government suggests the carmaker had a way out when it came to closing the Brampton plant.

The copy of the 2022 agreement, obtained earlier this year by CBC News, is partially redacted, so not all the terms are visible.

Still, a provision added to the deal in 2023 specifically says closing the Brampton plant before 2035 would be a violation of the contract if circumstances beyond the automaker’s "reasonable control" made the facility "commercially unviable," and Stellantis was "unable to produce substantial evidence that it has promptly taken all reasonable commercial efforts to secure alternative mandates for the Brampton."

In more basic terms, if Stellantis could provide "substantial evidence" that it had tried to find other options for Brampton, it might not be in violation of the deal, under which the company has received at least $220 million in federal funding for its facilities in Brampton and Windsor, Ont.

The Brampton Assembly Plant, in Brampton, Ont., is pictured on Oct. 15, 2025 — the day Stellantis announced it would be moving vehicle production to the U.S. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The specific language around Stellantis' contractual commitments with Ottawa has returned to the political forefront since Monday, when the automaker confirmed plans to sell the Brampton plant to defence contractor Roshel.

Windsor West MP Harb Gill, who serves as the Conservative shadow minister responsible for the auto sector, says the language in the deal around circumstances beyond Stellantis' "reasonable control" needed to be more specific.

"Obviously Stellantis is going to say it was the tariff or the trade war and things of that nature," Gill said Tuesday. "But what sort of proof or evidence did the government ask in return to say, why is this not commercially viable? Tell us how it's not viable because you're still producing or you're just moving production from Canada to the U.S. and you're still selling the same product."

Harb Gill, the Conservative MP for Windsor West, in Windsor, Ont., in July 2026. (Samantha Craggs/CBC)

The federal government on Tuesday did not answer questions about why it agreed to that language or whether Stellantis has argued that tariffs have made the plant commercially unviable.

Stellantis, for its part, said the company is "not commenting on specific legal interpretations or discussions with the government while those matters are being addressed." The spokesperson also noted the sale of the plant to defence contractor Roshel is not complete; rather, the parties have signed an asset purchase agreement, "a step toward the proposed transaction."

Stellantis announced last year that it was shifting planned production of the Jeep Compass from Brampton to Belvedere, Ill., unleashing a political firestorm over the public funding the company has received.

In December, Industry Minister M é lanie Joly said the federal government would serve Stellantis with a notice of default under its contracts with Ottawa.

Stellantis was also a party to funding agreements worth up to billions with the NextStar Energy battery plant in Windsor, formerly a joint venture between the automaker and LG Energy Solution. However, Stellantis sold its stake in the project earlier this year.

It's unclear where, exactly, the formal contractual dispute process over Brampton stands. Asked about it Tuesday, a spokesperson for the federal industry department said that for "over a year, [the] government and Unifor have worked in good faith to find a resolution, yet Stellantis has chosen once again to breach the commitments it made.

"This is a direct betrayal of Brampton workers and its obligations to Canadians," the spokesperson added.

"As the Prime Minister made clear, our government will use every tool at our disposal and the full force of the law to enforce our rights, safeguard Canadian tax dollars, and fight for justice and jobs for these workers."

A source with direct knowledge of the sale of the Stellantis Brampton plant said the federal government had been engaged regularly on the deal since August. The source said both the Prime Minister's Office and Industry Minister Melanie Joly's office had been briefed on the details of what was going to be announced. CTV News first reported the government's involvement in the talks, citing three unnamed sources.

WATCH | Joly shows 'complete and utter lack of credibility': CPC labour critic: Joly shows 'complete and utter lack of credibility': CPC labour critic | Duration closed caption 6:00 Stellantis’s decision to sell its Brampton, Ont., auto assembly plant to defence vehicle manufacturer Roshel has sparked immediate political fallout, with Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre calling for Industry Minister Mélanie Joly to be fired even as the company repays its federal funding. Power & Politics speaks with Kyle Seeback, the Conservative Party's labour critic.

In a statement Monday confirming the purchase agreement, Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said the automaker is "opening new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry, and creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.”

The news has prompted backlash from opposition MPs and Unifor, which represents the Brampton plant's more than 2,000 unionized employees who have been laid off since 2023.

Stellantis said Tuesday that it recognizes "that Canadians expect accountability for public funding" and that the company "has offered to voluntarily return the government support received for Brampton Assembly's original retooling plan."

But the company declined to say how much of the funding it will return and when, citing confidentiality provisions in the contracts.

The industry department said Joly "will convene a meeting in Toronto" on Thursday with Stellantis executives, Unifor National President Lana Payne, and the province.

Payne's office declined an interview request Tuesday, but told CBC's Power and Politics that the government still has options to halt the sale of the Brampton plant — and finding out the conditions of the sale will be key.

"All we needed here was for the government to hold the line, said Payne, whose union has reached a stalemate with Stellantis in its latest round of collective bargaining. "We've already seen conditions for this trade war changing in the U.S."

Gill, for his part, says Conservatives on the House's industry committee will want to look into the Stellantis situation and call Joly before the panel soon.

World.title: TV providers say Rogers' Monday hockey move inflates prices, 'erodes' sports viewing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A trio of television providers are accusing Rogers Communications Inc. of violating competition rules and inflating Canadian sports fans' bills by moving Monday night hockey broadcasts exclusively to its Sportsnet Plus streaming service for the current NHL season.

In a letter to Canada's broadcasting regulator on Tuesday, the companies — Cogeco Inc., Eastlink and SaskTel — say Rogers is forcing fans to pay a $12.99 monthly add-on fee to access hockey games on Monday nights, unless they already subscribe to Sportsnet on Rogers TV or Sportsnet Plus.

The rival providers are asking the CRTC to order Rogers to immediately offer the content to independent companies for distribution to their customers for free, "ensuring parity" with Rogers' offering.

"Without swift, decisive, and binding regulatory intervention by the commission, this predatory siphoning of must-have live sports content will inflict immediate and irreversible structural damage on the Canadian broadcasting ecosystem," stated the letter, adding that without regulatory action, Rogers' actions would establish "a dangerous precedent."

"Left unchecked, this strategy erodes consumer choice, forces Canadian households into mandatory fee-stacking, and distorts fair market dynamics."

In September, Rogers announced Monday night NHL games would stream exclusively on its streaming platform this season for the first time. It clarified that Rogers, Rogers West and Shaw Direct customers who have Sportsnet in their TV package would receive access to that content without any extra charge.

The company also added three new digital channels with the exclusive content to Rogers Xfinity TV packages that have Sportsnet.

However, those who subscribe to Sportsnet through other TV providers have to shell out an additional $12.99 per month for the add-on package.

The rival TV providers said the dynamic is "deliberately degrading the user experience on other distributors' platforms" and leading to the "erosion of sports on television," as such companies are unable to assemble a comprehensible sports lineup for their own subscribers.

They called it a "predatory rate squeeze" that forces independent distributors to "absorb severe content devaluation" or pass inflated costs onto consumers.

"Consequently, the commission must intervene without delay and put a definitive end to Rogers' anti-competitive practice in order to preserve the integrity of the Canadian broadcasting system and properly defend Canadian consumers' interests from coast to coast to coast," they said.

In a statement, Sportsnet spokesperson Jason Jackson said the company would address all issues raised through the CRTC proceeding, "including Sportsnet's right to distribute content exclusively on Sportsnet Plus."

"Rogers Cable has paid Sportsnet fair market value to provide Sportsnet Plus exclusive content to their TV customers and decided to make it available to them at no extra cost," Jackson said.

"All TV providers, including Cogeco, Eastlink and SaskTel, have the same opportunity to make the content available as part of their TV offering, but so far have chosen not to. Fans can contact their TV provider about this option."

The CRTC complaint also alleged that Rogers' move violates conditions of its 2023 merger with Shaw. That $26-billion takeover was approved by the CRTC subject to requirements that Rogers would preserve competitive market dynamics.

In particular, the telecommunications giant made a commitment to "refrain from entering into any agreement for exclusive or referential distribution of any online programming service or rights necessary for its distribution."

But the rival companies said Rogers is using its national NHL media rights covering multiplatform distribution "to grant preferential access to its own distribution network while effectively withholding full linear carriage from independent (distributors)."

The current NHL season marks the first under Rogers' 12-year, $11-billion national TV rights deal for English broadcasts.

The shift of Monday broadcasts exclusively to Rogers' streaming platform is one of a few significant changes for hockey fans this season.

Those include the end of a sublicensing agreement that allowed Saturday night NHL broadcasts to air on CBC under the "Hockey Night in Canada" brand. Those games continue to air on Sportsnet under new "Saturday Night Hockey" branding.

It marks the first time since Hockey Night in Canada's television debut in 1952 that NHL games are not available to Canadian viewers via the public broadcaster. The CBC plans to broadcast Professional Women's Hockey League games on Hockey Night in Canada this season.

Rogers also raised the annual cost of Sportsnet Plus for premium subscribers to $344.99. The $20 price hike comes after streaming subscribers were hit with a $75 increase to annual plans last season.

Meanwhile, Rogers announced a 12-year agreement with Amazon for Prime Video in Canada to exclusively broadcast Wednesday night regular-season national games starting this season.

A previous sublicensing deal between Rogers and Amazon saw Monday night regular-season games air on Prime Video for the previous two seasons.

World.title: Canadian family finds long-lost WW II baby in England after 80 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Rod Anderson grew up in England always wondering who his father was.

He was born at the end of the Second World War to a British mother.

At 81 years old, he received a call out of the blue this year with news he never expected — his dad was actually a Canadian soldier.

"I was knocked down by it all. It was just such a shock," Rodney told CBC News.

"Still, you could knock me down with a feather. Even today."

Anderson learned the truth about a family secret buried for generations. He was one of thousands of babies born in England and other countries where Canadian troops and allied forces were stationed during the Second World War.

WATCH | British man discovers his father was Canadian WW II soldier: He discovered his father was a Canadian soldier — 80 years later | Duration closed caption 6:11 After 80 years, Englishman Rod Anderson discovered a stunning truth: his father was a Canadian soldier during the Second World War stationed in Britain, but he had a family back home in New Brunswick. CBC's Ashley Burke speaks to Anderson and the Canadian relatives who searched for him for 20 years.



In the 1940s, mothers were blamed and shamed for these pregnancies out of wedlock. Children were given up for adoption. Families were torn apart. Some parents hid the truth until the day they died.

"My grandmother, my mother, none of them said a word," Anderson said.

Rod Anderson when he was a baby in his mother Yvonne Anderson's arms. He was born in 1945. (Submitted by Dawn Anderson)

But little did Anderson know, a family on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean spent almost two decades searching for him, hoping it wasn't too late.

Now after a remarkable turn of events, Anderson has connected with family in Canada he never knew existed.

An 18-year search

Canadian Bethany Allen spent almost two decades searching for Rodney Anderson.

She said it all started with a "persistent" family rumour about her grandfather Charles Blakney that never went away.

"After the war, there were rumors that my grandfather had a child with a woman in England," said Allen. "Some people heard it. Some people were well aware of it. While others have never heard a whisper of it."

Blakney was married and had a baby girl in New Brunswick when he stepped aboard the HMT Andes to travel across the Atlantic to serve in England in 1942.

Charles Blakney in uniform with his Canadian wife and baby (Bethany Allen's mother). (Submitted by Linda Rowe)

His military records describe him as a "very soft spoken" and reliable soldier. He served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers until he returned home in 1945.

Rod Anderson was born in Farnham, England, that same year.

Allen requested her grandfather's divorce records from the archives in 2008. She says they contained the "mother lode of information." The documents confirmed the baby in England was indeed real.

"The moment that I saw it, I was so surprised because it was so obvious," said Allen. "It was so definitive … turned all the rumours into fact."

Bethany Allen in New Brunswick holding her grandfather's divorce records that confirmed he had a baby during the Second World War while stationed in the United Kingdom. (Pierre Fournier/CBC)

But the mystery was far from over. Allen had no idea who the baby was.

Before Allen's mother died, she asked her daughter to keep searching for her sibling overseas no matter what.

"My mother had always wanted to know that he had a good life and was happy," she said.

Suddenly this past spring, "everything changed very quickly" when she did a DNA test through the U.S.-based company Ancestry, Allen said.

The results pointed to Rod Anderson as her half-uncle.

"I was like, oh my god, there he is," said Allen. "Oh my god, his name is Rodney!"

'I thought this is a wind up'

That same day, she managed to track down Rod Anderson's daughter, Dawn Roberts, in England.

Roberts called her dad and asked if he was sitting down.

"She said I had a phone call from a lady in Canada who said that you're her long lost relative," Rod Anderson said.

"I thought this is a wind up. It has to be. But it wasn't. You can't believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge."

Anderson had once done his own DNA test. For 50 years he tried to find the man he always suspected was his father. But in a crushing blow years ago, the test results found they weren't related.

In the end, that DNA test was the key that connected him to his newfound family in Canada.

WATCH | Rod Anderson describes a stunning call from his daughter with the news: British man finds out at 81 his father was a Canadian soldier in WW II | Duration closed caption 0:36 Rod Anderson in Surrey, U.K., says he got a call out of the blue from his daughter in March with news he never expected. At 81 years old, he learned his father was a Canadian soldier stationed in England during the Second World War and that he has family in Canada he never knew existed.

Second World War historian Jeff Noakes at the Canadian War Museum says the parents of wartime babies whose fathers were Canadian or allied soldiers often kept the details about these children hidden.

'Unbelievable amount of stigma'

There was an "unbelievable amount of stigma," he said, back in the 1940s around having children outside of marriage.

"Eighty years ago, there would have been a tremendous amount of shame for many people attached to this," Noakes said.

"The blame also fell disproportionately on women who were involved rather than the men."

A photo of Charles Blakney taken during a family gathering. (Submitted by Bethany Allen)

Noakes said there was so much public attention around it, Canadian military commander Lt.-Gen. Guy Simonds held a news conference in 1945 to defend his troops. Dutch newspapers had written editorials about an alleged decline in Dutch morality because of the Canadian soldiers stationed in the Netherlands.

Now, decades after these parents have died and there's far less stigma, some Canadian relatives are searching for these war babies before it's too late.

Toine van der Weerden lives in the Netherlands and helps families do the detective work needed to track down the truth.

"They are always happy when they find out," said van der Weerden.

"Everybody wants to know where they come from. Where you got those gestures from, where you got your posture from."

'You've got the same ears'

Since Anderson's revelation about his father, he's connected with his 77-year-old half-sister Barb Lowe in St. Thomas, Ont. They now talk every week.

They said they felt instantly connected the first time they spoke. They both like to laugh, share the same sense of humour and joke about the mischief they got into growing up.

Lowe said he reminds her of their father, who died in 1987.

"You've got the same ears," Lowe told him on one of their calls that CBC News filmed.

'Everything you do is a challenge, especially when you've got one arm and one eye. You have to conquer those challenges no matter how,' said Anderson. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

Rodney joked she once called them big "elephant-like" ears.

Despite never knowing his biological father, Anderson was amazed to find out he takes after him.

Like father, like son

As a child, Anderson lost his eye and an arm in a rail accident.

In the 1960s, a government assessment found the only job he couldn't do because of his injuries was work as a mechanic.

In true Rod Anderson fashion, he proved them wrong and became one.

Rod Anderson's photos that show his work as a motor mechanic over the years. He eventually opened his own business. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

It turns out, that's the exact job his Canadian father did for a living and during the war.

"That did surprise me. Isn't it strange?" Anderson said.

These newfound siblings can't quite believe they found each other before it's too late.

"It means the world," Lowe said. "My sister had passed away, my half-sister had passed away. And I finally found Rod. He's everything."

"Don't give up. You never know what the DNA can do."

Barb Lowe lives in St. Thomas, Ont., and said it means 'the world' to her that she's connected with her half-sibling Rod Anderson in England. She's photographed on a video call with Rod. They speak every week. (Yan Theoret/CBC)

But for this family, the mystery may not be over yet.

The divorce records that helped the Canadians find Anderson said his father had another baby in Britain during the war.

"There's still more mysteries to be had," said Allen while laughing. "There's still a search going on, and now we have two sides of the Atlantic trying to solve that mystery."

For now, Anderson's booked his plane ticket to New Brunswick this summer.

He's bringing his granddaughter Samantha Eldridge with him to finally meet the extended family he almost never knew.

"It'll make a difference to my children and their children and their children's children. It will go on," Anderson said.

"Never give up looking."

World.title: Solemn Remembrance Day ceremonies in Alberta pay tribute to Wainwright's fallen soldiers
World.content:
4 fallen soldiers in last month's tragedy top of mind at ceremonies in Wainwright, St. Albert, Edmonton

Remembrance Day | Solemn wreath-laying ceremony honours 4 killed in CFB Wainwright fire | Duration closed caption 5:01

People came together during a Remembrance Day ceremony in St. Albert, Alta., on Wednesday to honour Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, who were killed in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base.

World.title: Flood warnings issued for parts of southern B.C., as storm batters province
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. Hydro is warning that some drenched areas of the province could be without power for days, as a fall storm continued to make its presence felt on Wednesday.

Some areas of British Columbia have been without power since late last week after a series of storms rolled through, with more than 400,000 customers in total left without power between Friday and Monday, according to B.C. Hydro.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) has maintained a number of rainfall and wind warnings throughout B.C. on Wednesday, saying more than 250 millimetres of rain is possible for parts of western and inland Vancouver Island.

The River Forecast Centre has upgraded to a flood warning for the South Coast including the Howe Sound, Sea-to-Sky and North Shore mountains regions.

It also upgraded Pemberton Valley, including Lillooet River mainstem and tributaries, to a flood warning.

Flood watches are also in place throughout southwest B.C., as officials warn drivers to be prepared for pooling water and debris on the South Coast after the storm made landfall on Tuesday.

In an update on Tuesday night, B.C. Hydro said that restoring power after the parade of storms has proven challenging due to the extensive repairs required.

"Access remains challenging in some areas due to fallen trees, debris and soft ground conditions," the utility said.

The #BC River Forecast Centre has issued a High Streamflow Advisory for the Fraser Valley including areas around #Chilliwack and #HopeBC, the Fraser Canyon and #Chilcotin. Stay away from fast-flowing rivers & potentially unstable riverbanks. More info: https://t.co/W87tVOtUlp #BCFlood —EmergencyInfoBC

The village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island, where an evacuation order was issued last week due to a landslide, will likely remain without power for a few more days yet, it said.

"Specialized equipment is required and must be transported by helicopter due to the remote location and challenging terrain," the B.C. Hydro update reads. "The earliest crews can access the site is Thursday, provided weather conditions allow safe access."

Warning for drivers

The weather warnings posted throughout B.C. cover the entirety of Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii, as well as the Sunshine Coast, the central Interior and Prince George areas, and portions of Metro Vancouver and the Fraser Canyon.

In west and inland Vancouver Island, ECCC says that rainfall rates could go as high as 20 millimetres per hour at times on Wednesday, and up to 160 millimetres of rain could fall on the Sea-to-Sky Highway by Thursday morning.

"Localized flooding is likely. Some roads may become impassable," the warning reads.

The Ministry of Transportation and Transit has issued a Traffic Advisory for the South Coast region, including the Lower Mainland, #SunshineCoast, #VancouverIsland & the Fraser Valley. Drivers should prepare for winds, heavy rainfall & possible flooding. Never drive across flooded roads, bridges or river crossings. Follow @DriveBC for updates. More info: https://t.co/sHy7chVK6E #BCStorm #BCFlood #BC —EmergencyInfoBC

B.C.'s Ministry of Transportation issued a traffic advisory on Tuesday, warning commuters on the South Coast to be prepared and check DriveBC before heading out.

Areas that could be most affected, according to the ministry's traffic advisory, are the Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 1 through the Fraser Valley and Fraser Canyon, and the Malahat and western coast communities on Vancouver Island.

World.title: Missing baby rescued after being buried alive in a dog crate in South Carolina
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A missing 11-month-old infant was rescued Tuesday after being buried alive in a dog crate in South Carolina.

A county sheriff says little Koah Sharp had been underground for about 24 hours but survived, likely due to an air pocket created by a towel wrapped around the crate. Cool temperatures may also have helped.

Dozens of first responders combed the countryside for the "bright boy with reddish blond hair" that the sheriff's office said had disappeared while his grandmother ran errands.

After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil in the woods not far from the home of the boy's grandfather. They began digging and soon unearthed the baby, who was "clinging to life," the sheriff said.

"Certainly, God is good," Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference, not long after Koah was found. "He was screaming at the top of his lungs, which is a good thing in the baby world, I would guess."

A photo provided by the Lexington County Sheriff's office in Lexington, S.C., shows Michael Comer in custody after his son was found buried alive. (Lexington County Sheriff's Office/The Associated Press)

The child's father, Michael Comer, 25, was arrested and was being held without bond on a burglary charge, Koon said. Investigators were working with prosecutors to confirm further charges, he said.

Koah, who disappeared Monday in the county just west of Columbia, was taken to a hospital. His condition was not immediately known Wednesday.

"We're better now that we know that Koah is safe," his great aunt, Amber Hammond, told The Associated Press in an interview. She was watching as he was freed from the crate.

100 people helped in search

Deputies who searched the grandfather's home found the doors open and baby belongings inside, but they did not see Comer or the child, the sheriff said. Then the digging started.

"It was shallow," Koon said. "It was probably about at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground."

It was not immediately known if Comer had a lawyer. A phone number could not be found for him. The Associated Press sent emails seeking information to the public defender and prosecutors.

Nearly 100 first responders participated in the search.

Authorities said Koah had been in the care of Comer's mother. She had to run an errand and left the boy in Comer's care. Another caregiver was on the way, Koon said.

"By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him," Koon said.

Surveillance video from several businesses in the area showed Comer without the infant on Monday afternoon, Koon said. The father was found Monday night and was arrested.

Koah's parents "have had some situations" regarding domestic violence charges, the sheriff said.

"Children," he said, "sometimes get caught in the middle."

WATCH | Happy ending to search for missing child: Montreal toddler found alive after 4-day search a rare ending, police say | Duration 2:32 A three-year-old toddler was found alive and well in Ontario on Wednesday, 72 hours after she went missing. Police say after such a long search period, it’s rare for a missing child to be found alive. They say although the girl is dehydrated, she is in good health.

Comer was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-peace charges related to an arrest in July, Lexington County online court records show. Prosecutors dropped a gun charge as part of the plea deal.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Cuba’s Revolution Is Even Taking Away Our Vices
World.content:
By Fabiana del Valle

HAVANA TIMES – There comes a day when you realize there are things you don’t need, and you decide to give them up as a voluntary, personal choice. But in Cuba, there are things you give up because they have become economically impossible.

My husband, for example, is discovering that the “Revolution” has found a way to force him to quit smoking. Not through anti-smoking campaigns, a terminal illness, the image of a lung reduced to a rag, or a personal decision born of a desire to be healthier.

Here, even vices are subject to inflation, and existential questions begin when, before lighting a cigarette, you look at it as if it were a diamond. Do I really need to smoke? Should I save the money to buy food, or just buy three cigarettes and save a little that way?

Every cigarette becomes an equation, and getting even the most die-hard smoker to develop the skills of an economist when lighting up a Popular brand cigarette is quite a revolutionary achievement.

The famous Popular cigarette, or “ration-store cigarette,” as all Cubans know it, deserves a special chapter in the life of anyone born on this island who has ever smoked.

It’s a domestic product made with so few resources that it seems to have been manufactured from the leftovers of a cigarette someone else already smoked. Sometimes you even find a tobacco stem or a cockroach wing in the filling. Its packaging, white paper with blue lettering, makes you suspect it has been through a war before reaching the consumer’s hands.

It turns up on the informal market at a frightening price, as though every cigarette were wrapped in gold leaf. One thing is for a product to be unavailable; quite another is for it to show up where it shouldn’t be, at a price far above its actual value.

It’s the same old game with every product manufactured in this country. It all begins in the warehouse of some factory, with a worker who knows someone else who knows how to get hold of the merchandise. Then there’s the famous “buddy” who always manages to obtain a few boxes, moves them around, resells them, and at the end of the chain are the same people as always: those trying to survive on wages that are laughable.

I’m not going to blame the person selling them. Unfortunately, that person is also trying to survive. This country’s economy resembles a game of dominoes in which everyone tries to play their tile and move forward however they can before night falls. And while some manage to get their hands on merchandise, others can barely afford to breathe.

I know smoking isn’t a basic necessity. It would never occur to me to convince anyone that a cigarette should take priority over rice, medicine, or electricity. Smoking is bad for your health, and if it’s also expensive, well, you just quit. Simple as that.

Except that the same thing is happening with anything that still gives us a little pleasure. We don’t smoke, we don’t drink coffee, we don’t eat meat because it costs too much, traveling is an impossible dream, and we don’t buy clothes. There are always other priorities. The sad thing is that when someone asks how we’re doing, we answer without hesitation: “We’re fine.” We’ve learned to survive without complaining too much.

In this tropical version of the Holy Trinity, the land of rum, sugar, and tobacco, you’d better have your wallet ready. My husband has the right to decide to quit smoking because he wants to, rather than having his choices dictated by economic misery.

Cigarette packs warn that smoking is harmful to your health, but in Cuba, smoking seriously damages your wallet, leaving it sick, very sick, with no chance of getting an appointment with a specialist.

Read more from the diary of Fabiana del Valle here on Havana Times.

World.title: Camaguey, Cuba, Governor Exposed for Corruption Resigns
World.content:
Sutil Sarabia had held the position since May 28, 2023. / Radio Agramonte

An independent journalist exposes serious irregularities, while readers of Cubadebate demand explanations about Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia’s “mistakes.”

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia, governor of Camagüey, submitted his resignation, which was accepted by Miguel Diaz-Canel on Tuesday, according to a statement published in official media. According to the official version, the resignation came “after acknowledging mistakes made in the performance of his duties that were incompatible with his responsibilities,” an explanation that has failed to satisfy public opinion.

The public is well aware that the word “corruption” is hidden behind this euphemism, and even some comments on the pro-government Cubadebate website demand transparency. Still fresh in everyone’s memory is the dismissal of former Minister of Economy and Planning Alejandro Gil in February 2024, which was initially presented as a “personnel reshuffle.” A few days later, however, it was announced that his removal was the result of “serious mistakes made in the performance of his duties.” The former high-ranking official was sentenced in December 2025 to life imprisonment for espionage and to 20 years in prison in a second trial for economic and administrative crimes.

Probably with that precedent in mind, citizens have not hesitated to demand clarity to prevent speculation. “The reason for the resignation, without euphemisms or secrecy. We’re not living in the 1970s. Nowadays everything is known, and the truth will come out in the coming days, but I’d rather hear the Government’s version,” wrote one reader. “Why not report the whole story, including the reasons for his resignation, and thus prevent speculation, lies, etc., from other media outlets?” urged another.

A third commenter was even more explicit: “Some time ago, the Social Communication Law was approved, and one of its provisions guaranteed citizens the right to transparency of information. However, there is ever greater secrecy. For some time now, corruption involving this official has been denounced on social media. Once again, they are beating us in the communications war. Credibility remains in crisis,” the reader lamented.

On social media, independent journalist Jose Luis Tan Estrada, a native of Camagüey, has claimed the governor’s removal as a success of his investigations, attributing it to the information he has published about the official. The reporter, now exiled in Mexico, says that a colonel from the province traveled to Havana to participate in the investigation into Sutil, which was based on his allegations.

“Why was it necessary to bring an investigator from the province to participate in an investigation of this magnitude? Was there distrust about the possibility of investigating these events independently from Camagüey? Now they will try to prevent all of this from turning into a public scandal,” he says.

Tan Estrada maintains that “among the matters under investigation is the fuel allocated to several private businesses in quantities exceeding established limits,” allegedly diverted from public services, including ambulances and taxis used to transport dialysis patients.

“Amid this scandal, and because of other acts of corruption that are under investigation and that we exposed, the director of Taxis Cuba in Camagüey has also been removed. Another case of corruption uncovered by the investigative commission involves resources belonging to state-owned companies that produce food and beverages. Certain contracts favored some private businesses, which ended up purchasing practically all of the production,” he adds.

Tan Estrada identifies the Beverage and Soft Drink Company, La Vaquita Dairy Industry, and the Meat Processing Industry as entities under investigation. These companies produced food and beverages but allegedly diverted their products to private businesses.

He adds that construction materials were also diverted, along with another specific case that “involves the Provincial Directorate of Community Services. Huge budgets allocated to repairing the vehicle fleet, purchasing spare parts and fuel, as well as resources used to support the private business Almaley, which is linked to that entity, are under investigation.”

The journalist directly implicates several executives from a wide range of sectors, including the cultural sector, through a project run by the Provincial Book Center that served to divert “millions of pesos.”

“Thanks to my sources for their courage. Several years of investigation and risk, and in the end we succeeded,” Tan Estrada concludes.

According to the official statement, Sutil Sarabia will be replaced by the current deputy governor until a new governor is chosen, a decision that the public finds difficult to understand, judging by the comments.

“I don’t understand anything. The deputy governors, who are the governor’s right-hand people, had nothing to do with the mistakes?”

Sutil Sarabia had held the position since May 28, 2023.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more news from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Prices in Today’s Cuba and Who Can Pay Them
World.content:
Photo Feature by Irina Pino

HAVANA TIMES – Several times a week, I visit private businesses in my neighborhood and surrounding areas, looking for the most affordable prices for my budget. And believe me, prices keep rising every day, going through the roof. And I’m certainly not talking about heaven, but rather prices that are outrageously high for anyone who doesn’t have dollars to exchange for Cuban pesos, a currency that has become completely devalued.
