Today, the exchange rate is 915 Cuban pesos to 1 US dollar. No one could have imagined this happening, even in their worst nightmares.

We live on an island that no longer has an economy. It produces nothing. Factories and sugar mills have disappeared, and the same has happened to Cuban coffee. All products are imported. State control over agriculture prevents productive forces from being unleashed. Dante Alighieri’s Inferno is child’s play compared to the hell we are living through.

Now I ask myself: How does a retiree survive on less than 4,000 pesos a month? What can they do to eat and buy the medicines they need? They won’t even be able to afford rice, because now one kilogram of the cheapest white rice costs 1,200 pesos. And eggs cost 150 pesos each.

Many people are dying from curable diseases. Soon we will see people lying dead in the streets from starvation.

Meanwhile, the state-run ration stores and the ration books have practically ceased to exist. Sometimes they offer a little bread that employees sell at 200 pesos for 10 small rolls.

Who can survive in this disaster? Only those who receive substantial remittances from abroad and those who own profitable businesses. I’ve seen many of my friends grow thin, and I’ve lost weight myself. It’s difficult to eat two meals a day, let alone have a simple glass of milk for breakfast when one kilogram of powdered milk costs 5,000 pesos.

How much longer will the state turn its back on what is happening to the people? Nobody controls prices. They couldn’t care less about us.

Here are some photos showing the prices at a nearby private store. Look at what things have come to in this country.

See more photo features here at Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Wednesday, November 11, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

House GOP Blocks Impeachment Charges Against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

Nov 11, 2026

House Republicans on Tuesday blocked impeachment charges against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. By a margin of just seven votes, Republicans managed to bury the charges in committee through a 211-204 party-line procedural vote. Eleven Democrats skipped the vote, including Democratic Congressmember Nancy Pelosi of California. While House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is vying for the speakership in January, expressed support for Hegseth’s impeachment, many wondered how it was such a surprise that he was unable to corral Democratic votes to impeach Hegseth. President Trump hailed the outcome as an “exoneration.” Hours before the vote, Hegseth blasted the impeachment articles and said he’d carry out the same operations again.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth: “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies, Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching, that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”

Sanders Says He Will Not Back Schumer for Senate Majority Leader

Nov 11, 2026

Vermont’s independent Senator Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he will not back Senator Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan also said she won’t support Schumer until he presents a plan to govern differently. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Troy Jackson of Maine, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Juliana Stratton of Illinois and Adam Hamilton of Kansas have all said they won’t support Schumer, as has Senate candidate Scott Colom of Mississippi. This comes as Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland indicated Monday he’s open to running for Senate majority leader when the new Congress convenes in January. This is Senator Sanders.

Sen. Bernie Sanders: “If this campaign was about anything, it was about change and the need for the Democratic Party, in my view, to move in a new and bold direction. I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

Rep. Jordan Elected as House GOP Leader as Senator Thune Reelected as Senate Republican Leader

Nov 11, 2026

House Republicans elected Congressmember Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump ally, as their leader after last week’s sweeping midterm losses. Jordan will replace Speaker Mike Johnson come January when a new Democratic majority takes office with at least 256 seats in the House. In the Senate, Republicans reelected Senator John Thune of South Dakota as leader. Democrats currently have a 54-seat majority in the Senate, with the races in Alaska and Mississippi leaning toward Democrats. The Democratic Senate candidate in Mississippi, Scott Colom, leads his Republican opponent by 3,000 votes.

Trump’s Former Lawyer Alina Habba Mildon Fired by Concord Partners

Nov 11, 2026

Image Credit: Gage Skidmore

President Trump’s former lawyer Alina Habba Mildon has been fired by Concord Partners, a secretive company with no public profile, set up by a prominent and wealthy Venezuelan family, which had previously signed Habba Mildon to a $50 million deal. Habba Mildon had received the contract shortly before Trump pardoned the head of the family, Julio Herrera Velutini, who was facing felony bribery charges in Puerto Rico. According to The New York Times, Trump recently erupted in anger after learning about Habba Mildon’s $50 million contract. In a letter from last week, Concord Partners said that Habba Mildon was fired due to a “failure to perform duties.” She will still keep $6.5 million that was paid to her, as well as an $8 million signing bonus.

U.S. Gov’t Received Over $12 Billion in Revenue from Venezuela’s Oil Exports

Nov 11, 2026

The U.S. government received over $12 billion in revenue from exports of Venezuela’s natural resources in the first nine months of this year, following the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. That’s according to a report by the global financial firm KPMG, which is among the first to provide detailed insight into the Trump administration’s financial holdings in Venezuela. The report was reviewed by The New York Times. After the U.S. removed Maduro from power in January, the Treasury Department reportedly established a “Venezuela Custody Account,” initially based in Qatar and then moved to Citibank in New York.

NYT: Immigrants Deported Back to Home Countries Despite Court Orders

Nov 11, 2026

The New York Times reports that foreign governments are accepting U.S. deportees and then sending them to their home countries, where they risk torture, sexual abuse or persecution. The Times identified more than 110 immigrants who were deported from the U.S. to third-party countries and then passed on to their home countries despite U.S. court orders. Alma David, a consultant with the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said, “It’s immigration colonialism — making these governments do the dirty work.”

WaPo: ICE Hired 19 Officers with Past Allegations of Misconduct, Violence and Criminal Charges

Nov 11, 2026

An investigation by The Washington Post reveals ICE hired at least 19 officers who had past allegations of misconduct, violence and criminal charges during a mass hiring spree after Trump took office in 2025. The findings come after a Homeland Security Department data breach in October leaked the names of an estimated 1,500 new ICE hires. The Washington Post ran a background check on about 300 of them, with over a dozen officers coming back with red flags, including a former Detroit police officer involved in a fatal shooting that resulted in a $2.5 million wrongful-death settlement.

Immigrants Jailed at Northwest Detention Center in Washington Hold Hunger Strike

Nov 11, 2026

Image Credit: La Resistencia

A group of immigrants jailed at the troubled Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, Washington, have been on a hunger strike for over eight days denouncing due process violations, medical neglect and inhumane conditions. They’re also demanding all ICE jails be shut down. This is at least the 22nd hunger strike inside the Northwest ICE jail this year alone. Despite mounting reports of abuse, Northwest will continue to operate for another 10 years, after the for-profit prison company GEO Group signed a $1.5 billion contract with the federal government in October.

Israeli Forces Kill at Least Eight Palestinians in Gaza

Nov 11, 2026

In news from Gaza, Israeli forces have killed ⁠at least eight Palestinians, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in attacks on Gaza City and Khan Younis. Israel has conducted near-daily attacks on Gaza despite a so-called ceasefire brokered by the U.S., killing more than 1,600 Palestinians since the deal went into effect last October. This comes as damage and destruction caused by Israel’s relentless bombings on Gaza’s infrastructure since 2023 have contributed to worsening flash floods as the enclave faces another winter with torrential rains. Gaza’s stormwater and sewage networks are so deteriorated that thousands of tents are being flooded. This is UNICEF spokesperson James Elder.

James Elder: “So, toxic sewage could flow into the streets and tents of Gaza City, forcing children and families from their makeshift home once more and grossly increasing the threat of disease. So we’re a bit baffled. Let’s do the rehabilitation before this becomes another entirely preventable killer of girls and boys in Gaza.”

Israeli Soldiers Kill 14-Year-Old Palestinian Boy in West Bank

Nov 11, 2026

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli soldiers have killed a 14-year-old Palestinian boy and wounded two other teens during a raid on the village of Burqa Tuesday. The boy was identified as Moataz Iyad Daghlas. This comes as more than 50 illegal Israeli settlers attacked a village south of Nablus, setting vehicles on fire. The U.N. has warned that attacks by Israeli settlers have escalated to an “unprecedented level,” with at least 1,143 Palestinians killed in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, including 250 children.

Russia and Ukraine Hold First Peace Talks in Nine Months

Nov 11, 2026

Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first peace talks in nine months in Abu Dhabi. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was not in attendance at the summit, where Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff renewed pressure to end the war.

In related news, a senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in Britain for allegedly attempting to steal secret NATO information and deliver it to Russia. The 41-year-old has not been identified. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied any links between Russia and the suspect.

Independent Russian Newspaper Novaya Gazeta Closes Moscow Office

Nov 11, 2026

In more news from Russia, the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue operating due to a campaign of state persecution. The investigative outlet was co-founded by the last Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, with money from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize. Russian President Vladimir Putin had designated the paper as a “foreign agent.” Last month, Novaya Gazeta’s landlord refused to renew the news outlet’s lease. Also, Russian banks said that they would stop processing donations from readers. In October, Russian authorities raided the home of editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov and took him in for questioning. Another editor, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April.

Dmitry Muratov, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning editor of Novaya Gazeta, said, “Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today. We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function.”

Egyptian Court Postpones Criminal Trial of Mada Masr’s Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah

Nov 11, 2026

A court in Egypt has postponed proceedings in the criminal trial of Mada Masr’s editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, until November 18. Attalah faces charges of publishing false news and managing a website without a license. Click here to see our recent interview with Lina Attalah.

Federal Appeals Court Rules Trump Admin Illegally Fired Head of Voice of America

Nov 11, 2026

Image Credit: J. David Ake/Getty Images

A federal appeals court panel ruled on Tuesday that the Trump administration illegally fired the head of Voice of America (VOA), Michael Abramowitz, last year. Earlier this year, a federal judge also revoked the firing of more than 1,000 journalists at VOA and voided Trump’s installment of his ally to serve as the interim chief of the United States Agency for Global Media, which is the parent agency of VOA. In a statement, Abramowitz said, “There is no longer any reason for the government to prevent me from doing the job for which I was legally installed on a bipartisan basis more than two years ago.”

Greta Thunberg Attends U.N. Climate Summit for the First Time Since 2021

Nov 11, 2026

As world leaders and delegates from over 190 nations kicked off the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, this week, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan took the opportunity to celebrate the discovery of two new oil fields in the Gabar Mountains and the possibility of future fossil fuel projects. Phasing out fossil fuels has been a central proposal at the annual climate talks pushed by Indigenous and environmental activists who are again demanding urgent climate solutions.

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg arrived at COP31 on Tuesday. It is the first time she is attending the climate summit since 2021.

Greta Thunberg: “In all the catastrophes we are facing, it is scientific fact that if we continue like now, things like food, clean water, functioning infrastructure will become luxury.”

Thousands of Protesters Rally in Indonesia over Government’s Response to Fires

Nov 11, 2026

In Indonesia, thousands of students and activists rallied across the country on Tuesday over the government’s inadequate response to forest and land fires. They demanded that the government declare a national disaster and punish those responsible for the blazes. The protesters also called for more jobs and economic relief.

Faturrohman Jaguna: “We call on the local government and the Yogyakarta Regional House of Representatives to improve the welfare of small and medium-sized enterprises, pedicab drivers and all the people of Yogyakarta who today are facing hardships from a weakening economy. Therefore, we urge the government to restore the people’s economy in Yogyakarta and across Indonesia.”

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: A Sampling of Barbershops
World.content:
My barber’s tools.

By Erick Hernandez

HAVANA TIMES – Not all barbers are alike. Some keep their work areas organized and spotless, while others leave their tools scattered around as they use them. Some sweep the hair off the floor after every haircut, while others do it only at the end of the day. And it’s not simply a matter of one group or the other, or even two different ways of doing things. The reality is more complex, and the messiest barbershop may be precisely the only one that uses aftershave, for example.

Ultimately, many factors determine whether a customer stays or leaves. There are places where a customer simply doesn’t fit in and looks for somewhere else. Barbershops reflect their owners, and if a barber and a customer would have little in common in their social lives, making friendship unlikely, the customer will eventually look for another barber with whom they feel more comfortable.

Every barbershop is shaped by its surroundings, by the neighborhood where it is located. Thus, a particularly flashy barbershop in one of the city’s poorest, most working-class neighborhoods resembles those found in United States ghettos, with graffiti on the walls, classic hip-hop playing through the speakers, and barbers sporting a distinctly urban style.

Businesses in wealthier areas tend to be cleaner, have air conditioning, and operate by appointment. But all these establishments here share the same tormentor: power outages. It has become standard for all barbers to have cordless, battery-powered clippers because of the constant electricity cuts. If they used traditional clippers plugged into an outlet, they would only be able to work three or four hours a day, without even knowing when those hours would be.

That’s where another type of barbershop comes in, exclusive simply because there are so few of them: those located on protected electrical circuits. The atmosphere in these shops is completely different. If it weren’t for the prices, anyone might think it was still 2015. The clippers they use have cords, and they’re heavy and powerful. There’s always a light on the wall illuminating the work area, and a speaker on the floor playing music nonstop. Depending on the place, you might see extension cords where customers plug in their cell phones to charge. A fan is never missing from those barbershops. But even those barbers have cordless clippers, “just in case.”

Being young makes me the perfect target for advice and suggestions from older people, but it also gives me the opportunity to surprise them and show them new things. During my first few months, whenever a new adult customer came in, he would ask me things like how I had managed to build that barber’s chair using a wheel from an agricultural plow, and many other questions.

One thing that always came up in those conversations was how long the clippers’ battery lasted and how long it took to recharge. If the customers were particularly elderly, they would sometimes bring in a pair of clippers that a son in the United States had sent them, but without the charger. Then they would ask whether I knew where they could find one.

Beyond the small details that distinguish us, there are other aspects that are common everywhere. The trust that loyal customers place in their barbers, and the barbers’ discretion regarding the compromising secrets they hear; the reduced prices offered to an elderly person who cannot afford to pay what everyone else does; the good spirits and willingness to help.

Whenever a customer told me, halfway through a haircut, that he was also a barber, I would tense up and feel as though I were being evaluated. But after that initial seriousness, a sense of camaraderie and advice would always follow. We understood each other, as all human beings should, because we practiced the same trade.

Read more from the diary of Erick Hernandez here on Havana Times.

World.title: Sunrise Movement Co-Founder Elected to Congress on Anti-Data Center Platform
World.content:
By Democracy Now

HAVANA TIMES – Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech.

“I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’”

Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.

Transcript

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan Gonzalez.

In Michigan, progressive candidate Will Lawrence has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence is the co-founder of the youth-led climate group the Sunrise Movement. He ran a grassroots campaign focused on lowering the cost of housing and healthcare, opposing the war in Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech.

One of the central issues of Lawrence’s campaign was opposition to artificial intelligence, AI, data centers. He called for a pause on the construction of new centers, joining residents’ concerns about their impact on Michigan’s water, electricity bills, quality of life, including noise pollution. Three hyperscale data centers have been proposed in different parts of the district. Lawrence also campaigned against Flock surveillance cameras and called for tighter restrictions on AI overall.

The race was one of the most expensive House contests in the country, $66 million spent on political advertising.

But Will Lawrence is now in Washington, D.C. The congressmember-elect is there for orientation.

Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence, welcome to Democracy Now! If you can start off by —

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN: — talking about what you’re planning to bring to Congress, and then respond to what’s happening? The House leader race is underway. There’s going to be an internal vote, I think, next week, with Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries as the House speaker. But there are those who are questioning that leadership. I’m wondering if you can talk about that, as well.

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Thank you, Amy. It’s a real honor to be here. Longtime fan of the show.

You know, I’m just thrilled to be here to offer independent-minded representation for my district. People voted to get Big Money out of politics, to hold Big Tech accountable, to stop these endless wars around the world and to bring our money home to invest in first things first, good jobs and education, housing and healthcare, so that we can all look forward to the future again. And I just couldn’t be more honored to represent the people of my district.

And, you know, I’ve been getting the correspondence from my constituents over the last number of days, you know, expressing concern about who the next speaker is going to be. And I do want to make clear that I’ve said since July that I will support Hakeem for speaker. I’m a man of my word, and I intend to keep that word. But the correspondence is very important, not just in my district, but I’m hearing from all my other incoming freshmen here that they’re also hearing the same thing. And it reflects the anxiety that people feel that this election, which was clearly about change and a repudiation of the status quo, could result in more of the same. And they’re hungry to know that it’s going to be different and the Democratic Party is truly going to fight for real reform in our economy and our democracy. And people doubt that that will happen because of leadership’s well-documented ties to Big Money, including weapons manufacturers and health insurance CEOs and AIPAC and many others.

And so, I’m going to push Leader Jeffries publicly, and I will push him privately, to hear those concerns and commit to giving voice to the American people by putting votes on the floor that reflect the issues that I and people across the country campaigned on. We need to have a vote to block the bombs to Israel. We need to have a vote to guarantee healthcare to every person in my district. And we need to have a vote to get Big Money out of politics and ban super PACs, because people deserve to know that their representatives actually represent them rather than the wealthy elite. And as long as we have this Big Money in politics, they will never be able to be confident in that knowledge. So, regardless of the speaker’s own positions on those issues, he can give voice to the American people by putting those votes on the floor and letting us have those votes, regardless of where he personally comes down on the issue. And I’m going to be pushing hard to ensure that that happens.

JUAN GONZALEZ: Well, Will Lawrence, one of the big planks of your campaign was your opposition to these data centers and AI regulation, Flock cameras. Now that you are — will be in Congress, and I expect, if history is any lesson at all, the tech industry will start shifting more money to Democrats, hoping to peel people off and be able to neutralize any major legislation, what are your red lines, and what are you expecting to be able to accomplish when it comes to AI regulation, these data centers and Flock cameras?

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Well, what I hear from residents across my district is that this is out of control, it’s moving too fast, and we need to slow it down. And they’re fighting on a playing field that is fundamentally rigged to the benefit of these billion-, soon to be trillion-dollar corporations in Silicon Valley and leaves local communities behind.

So, I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development. I mean, these developers come into small towns, and they say, you know, “We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.” I mean, what are we talking about? What are we talking about? Why have we allowed these clearly reckless individuals, who do not share the values and aspirations of my constituents in Michigan, to determine the future of our entire economy?

You know, I believe that AI could be used for the benefit of humanity, but right now it’s on track to make the already rich and powerful even richer and more powerful. And that’s why there is such a bottom-up grassroots rebellion happening, not just in my district, but around the country. And it’s uniting Democrats and Republicans from the bottom up who do not trust Big Tech to write the future of our communities and our entire economy.

JUAN GONZALEZ: And could you comment about what made it possible, despite all this money poured into the — into your district to defeat you, that you were able to emerge victorious?

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Well, we had an unprecedented ground game. You know, I’m an organizer by trade. I was a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement. I’ve been an organizer fighting alongside renters and tenants to assert our rights and prevent homelessness in my area. And we built a ground game that knocked on 350,000 doors between the primary and the general election. And when there were so many negative ads on TV, so many lies and so many smears, it was those face-to-face conversations, eye contact, a handshake, a real human being coming to you and talking about the values that we share and the future we can build together, that cut through all the noise. And that’s what allowed us to win this election. And I’m just tremendously proud of all the volunteers, the whole team, everybody who poured into the movement. It was a true team effort, and I couldn’t be more honored to be representing that movement here in Congress.

AMY GOODMAN: Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence of Michigan, thank you so much for being with us as you stand there in Washington at orientation for new congressmembers. He defeated incumbent Republican Congressmember Tom Barrett in one of the most competitive swing House races these midterms, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement.

Read more interviews here on Havana Times.

World.title: Sheinbaum calls NYT report on CIA’s alleged bargain with Chihuahua prosecutor ‘very interesting’: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📰 NYT report spotlights ex-prosecutor who allegedly partnered with CIA: Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany.

Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany. ⚖️ “ It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law”: Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.”

Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.” 🏥 IMSS Bienestar doctor’s appointments up 55% since 2023: Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%.

Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%. 📈 Opposition-governed states lag: Svarch said “general consultations” rose just 4% between 2023 and 2026 in the eight states that haven’t joined IMSS Bienestar, which operates in 24 of 32 federal entities, while specialist appointments are forecast to rise 27%. “It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” he said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum responded to a New York Times report headlined “The Man Who Helped the C.I.A. Secretly Operate in Mexico.”

Published on Tuesday, the article focuses on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, the state where U.S. Central Intelligence Agency officers allegedly participated in a drug lab raid in April without the authorization or knowledge of the Mexican government. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua police officials died in a car accident after the raid, a tragedy that helped bring the CIA’s presence in the state to light.

The New York Times report states that “[w]hen the Central Intelligence Agency was looking to quietly expand its operations in Mexico last year, it found an especially useful partner.”

“… To the C.I.A., Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a prosecutor and former police commander in the border state of Chihuahua, offered a different kind of partnership,” the report says.

“He could pair C.I.A. officers with Mexican police units on counter-cartel operations — and he was in a bind that made him uniquely cooperative, Mexican and U.S. officials said.”

That bind, according to the Times, was that Zuany’s U.S. visa had been revoked “because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out.”

The Times reported that Zuany’s visa was reinstated after he “shepherded C.I.A. officers as they trained Chihuahua State forces, joined those forces on certain missions and provided expertise during ground operations” during a period of more than six months.

Beyond Sheinbaum’s response to the New York Times report, another notable topic at today’s mañanera was the performance of IMSS Bienestar, Mexico’s public healthcare service for people without social security coverage through institutions such as the Mexican Social Security Institute, or IMSS, and the State Workers’ Social Security Institute, or ISSSTE.

The IMSS Bienestar scheme was established by the previous federal government and now operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities. Eight states have opted against signing onto the scheme. Those states — Nuevo León, Coahuila, Durango, Jalisco, Querétaro, Aguascalientes, Chihuahua and Guanajuato — are all governed by opposition parties, rather than by Morena, Mexico’s ruling party.

NYT report ‘very interesting,’ says Sheinbaum

A reporter raised the New York Times report about Zuany, noting that it quotes the former prosecutor as saying that Chihuahua Governor Maru Campos was aware of the CIA’s presence in the northern border state, something that Campos denies.

Sheinbaum, who has previously been critical of the Times’ reporting on Mexico, said she read the report and described it as “very interesting.”

🇲🇽#México | Claudia Sheinbaum se refirió al reportaje de The New York Times sobre la presunta facilitación de operaciones de la CIA por parte de Guillermo Zuany, fiscal especializado de Chihuahua. La presidenta calificó la publicación como “muy interesante” y sostuvo que los agentes estadounidenses deben apegarse a la Ley de Seguridad Nacional. “En este caso no se respetó”, afirmó. #ClaudiaSheinbaum #Chihuahua #CIA #SeguridadNacional 🌐 Consulta #ElPortalDeÁngulo7

➡️ https://t.co/14SVC19UGG — Ángulo7 Noticias (@angulosiete) November 11, 2026

She subsequently noted that the former attorney general of Chihuahua, César Jáuregui, was arrested in connection with the CIA’s presence in the state. Jáuregui, who was detained by federal authorities on a treason charge last month, is accused of allowing CIA officers to participate in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without authorization from the Mexican government.

Sheinbaum said that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) has to continue its investigation of the case. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said on Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding warrants for the arrest of Zuany.

Sheinbaum said that Zuany’s alleged conduct is “very relevant” to investigations into the CIA’s presence in Chihuahua.

“It’s worth learning about who this person is and how he collaborated with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said.

Although the New York Times report states that CIA officers joined Chihuahua state forces “on certain missions” and that the CIA “began working” with Zuany “around 2025,” Sheinbaum asserted that “the article doesn’t say that there were operations [with the CIA] since 2025.”

“It says there was [CIA] presence,” she said.

Sheinbaum highlighted that her government pointed out that the CIA’s participation in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua was illegal as soon as it found out about it.

“It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law,” she said.

“And the Federal Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation,” Sheinbaum added.

“Today, the [former] attorney general of Chihuahua is detained for this reason. The important thing is that … any collaboration [with foreign authorities] has to guarantee respect for the [Mexican] Constitution and the National Security Law,” she said.

“Any agent from a U.S. agency in Mexico has to comply with the National Security Law,” Sheinbaum said.

“In this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed,” she said.

IMSS Bienestar chief reports sharp increase in doctor’s appointments

At the start of his presentation, IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch said that “for decades, where a person was born and the job they held determined the range of medical care they were able to receive.”

“Three years ago, IMSS Bienestar began transforming this reality,” he said.

“Today we are the largest network of public health services in our country and above all we’re an institute that is achieving results,” Svarch said.

He went on to report that the number of medical consultations provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to increase 55% this year compared to 2023. IMSS Bienestar is on track to provide 58.3 million free doctor’s appointments this year, according to the data presented by Svarch, up from 37.3 million in 2023.

“That’s why we say the model works. The results are clear and compelling,” the IMSS Bienestar chief said.

Svarch noted that IMSS Bienestar operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, while eight states have their own public healthcare systems for people without social security coverage.

He reported that “general consultations” increased just 4% this year compared to 2023 in the eight states that haven’t signed on to IMSS Bienestar.

“It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” Svarch said.

He also reported that the number of specialist doctor’s appointments provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to rise 105% this year compared to 2023, while the increase over the same period in states where IMSS Bienestar doesn’t operate is forecast to be 27%.

“These results are not the product of chance,” Svarch said.

“They are the product of actions and a very specific implementation plan,” he said.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Eat, dance, swim, run, repeat!
World.content:
One of the things I love most about living in Puerto Vallarta is the variety of entertainment and activities on offer. Case in point, this month you can 1) taste cuisine from some of Mexico’s top chefs at the 31st International Gourmet Festival; 2) listen to live jazz, rock and mariachi at one of Vallarta’s many great music venues; 3) compete in an open-water swimming race; or 4) run a half-marathon. OK, so the last two might not be for everyone, but you can cheer on the racers instead.

Read on to learn more about these exciting events.

31st International Gourmet Festival

Puerto Vallarta’s reputation as a culinary destination is on the rise. Earlier this year, two local restaurants, Icú and Pancho’s Takos, earned spots on the prestigious Michelin Guide’s recommended list, a first for the city. This month, Vallarta will host the 31st International Gourmet Festival from Nov. 12-22. The festival brings some of the most celebrated Mexican chefs together for 11 days of culinary events at more than 25 top-rated restaurants in Puerto Vallarta, Riviera Nayarit and Tepic.

Events include tasting experiences featuring food and wine from more than a dozen restaurants, dining “safaris” where you travel to a few selected restaurants in one night, multicourse fine dining at single restaurants featuring guest chefs and even a drag brunch.

On Nov. 17, the Technological University of Bahía de Banderas (UTBB) will host a panel of chefs who will discuss the latest trends shaping the culinary scene in Mexico. The panel discussion is free and open to the public. Tickets for the dining experiences are available for purchase on the festival website.

Live music up close and personal

I love listening to live music, especially in intimate settings where I can watch the performers up close. In my last events roundup, I promised to share some of my favorite venues. True to my word, here you go:

The Social Club: The Social Club is a modern-day speakeasy located at 447 Basilio Badillo in the Romantic Zone. Just a narrow black door marks its spot. If you’ve never been before, you could easily miss it. I feel transported to another era every time I visit. After entering the front door, you climb up a narrow staircase, pass through red velvet curtains and enter a small parlor-style room with tiny tables lit by tiny lamps. The “stage” is at the back of the room, just a few feet from the tables. Waiters clad in Prohibition-era outfits serve bespoke and classic cocktails. Doors open at 9 p.m., and music starts around 10 p.m., featuring many of the best local jazz musicians and many special events. This is one of our favorite date-night spots in all of Vallarta.

Aquí Nomás: In the mood for a Mexican folk music singalong? Then you want to go to Aquí Nomás in Versalles. On Friday and Saturday nights, the neighborhood cantina hosts a live mariachi band that plays all the classic songs that Mexicans seem to know by heart. On our first visit in early October, we had only planned on staying for dinner and venturing someplace for music. But, being early season, the other venues in Versalles were closed. Our waitress convinced us to stay, and we’re so glad we did. Around 10:30 in the evening, the band showed up — a full 10-person mariachi ensemble — and the tables filled up, too. Pretty soon, the band was passing the mic, and everyone was singing along. It was such a friendly, local vibe; we are looking forward to returning soon with the whole family.

Casita & Garden: Casita & Garden in the Romantic Zone offers a variety of live music from jazz to funk to rock and pop every night of the week except Sundays. Shows are held in its lovely outdoor courtyard during the winter season starting at 7 p.m. In addition to live music, you can sample wine and sake selected by their in-house sake sommelier, and fill up on sushi and wood-fired pizza. The venue also hosts private dinners and wine tastings, but they are popular, so it’s best to reserve well ahead of time.

For the sporting type

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CRUCE VALLARTA (@crucevallarta)

Coming from Boulder, Colorado — arguably the sporting capital of the United States — where every summer weekend is packed with running, biking and triathlon events, I was astounded to find a similar enthusiasm for sports in Puerto Vallarta. It seems there is a race of some sort every weekend. Yet I’ve found the events way more chill and the athletes much friendlier than in Colorado. (Even though they still crush the course.)

Since moving to Mexico, I’ve become an avid open-water swimmer, and recently joined a local swimming group. They convinced me to 

If running is more your speed, the next day, on Nov. 15, Puerto Vallarta is hosting its 22nd Annual Half Marathon. The 21-km run is a grand tour of the hotel zone and the Marina, starting at the Sheraton and heading north along Av. Francisco Medina Ascencio (aka the 200), winding through the Marina and returning to the Sheraton via Av. Francisco Medina Ascencio. There is also a 5 km distance. You can register for either distance online.

I hope to see you out there, enjoying great food, good music and fun sports.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: The MND Sheinbaum Index™ for September 2026: Jobs and economic growth boost president’s rating
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND SHEINBAUM INDEX™

Measuring Mexico’s president beyond the polls

MND Intelligence · Seventh edition

Welcome to the seventh edition of the MND Sheinbaum Index™, an eight-pillar index designed to give our readers balanced, data-driven insight into the current situation in Mexico across a range of areas under the leadership of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

In this edition of the index — which mainly uses data from the month of September — the headline number is 71.5, representing an increase of 3.6 points compared to the previous score. This is the highest MND Sheinbaum Index™ score to date and the first time it has exceeded 70.

WHAT DROVE THE INCREASE?

Higher economic growth and improvements in employment data were the main drivers of the increase in the MND Sheinbaum Index™ score in September.

Sheinbaum has said that the construction of public infrastructure projects has helped to spur stronger economic growth in recent months.

A slight increase in the president’s approval rating and a modest improvement in Mexico’s business confidence score also helped lift the MND Sheinbaum Index™ score in September.

A detailed summary of the latest index results appears below.

Before we look at the results and present the index trend during Sheinbaum’s administration, here is a short guide to the significance of an MND Sheinbaum Index™ score:

85–100: Exceptional — administration performing at a high level across nearly all indicators.

— administration performing at a high level across nearly all indicators. 75–84: Excellent — administration performing well across most indicators.

— administration performing well across most indicators. 60–75: Quite good, but room for improvement — meaningful strengths, some areas of concern.

— meaningful strengths, some areas of concern. 50–60: Mixed — passing marks overall.

— passing marks overall. Below 50: Broad underperformance — more indicators below benchmark than above.

MND Sheinbaum Index™ pillars for September 2026

Each pillar is given a stoplight color indicating a strong performance (green: a score above 9.4 out of 12.5), an average performance (yellow: 6.2-9.4) or a poor performance (red: below 6.2).

An upward-pointing arrow ⬆️ indicates that the pillar score improved compared to August. A downward-pointing arrow ⬇️ indicates a deterioration in the pillar score. A pause icon ⏸️ means there was no change in the pillar score compared to the previous month.

As you’ll see below, scores for four of the eight pillars increased in September compared to August. The score for three pillars declined, while the score for one pillar was unchanged.

🟢 ⬆️ ECONOMIC GROWTH (11.75 out of 12.5)

For the first time, the economic growth pillar is the top contributor to the overall MND Sheinbaum Index™ score.

Year-over-year economic growth was 3.7% in September, according to preliminary data from INEGI — a significant increase compared to August’s 2.5% reading.

(Annual economic growth in August was subsequently upgraded to 3.5% in revised final data.)

As a result of the higher economic growth in September, the pillar score increased to 11.75 from 8.75 in August.

🟢 ⬇️ INFLATION (11.38 out of 12.5)

After four consecutive months as the top contributor to the MND Sheinbaum Index™ score, the inflation pillar was relegated to second place in September.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate rose to 3.45% in September, up from 3.26% in August. The rate remains relatively close to the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target, but its upward trend is a concern for President Sheinbaum and the federal government, if not for the central bank itself, which cut its benchmark interest rate last week.

Due to the uptick in the headline rate, the inflation pillar score declined to 11.38 in September from 11.85 in August.

🟢 ⏸️ LABOR POVERTY (10.25 out of 12.5)

There is no change to the labor poverty pillar score in this edition of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ as the most recent data remains that published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Aug. 26.

Based on that data, the labor poverty pillar score is 10.25.

The labor poverty rate was 31.9% in the second quarter of 2026, an annual decline of 3.2 percentage points.

In the second quarter of 2026, real incomes rose 8% annually.

🟡 ⬇️ SECURITY (9.11 out of 12.5)

The pace of homicide reduction declined in September for a second consecutive month. The year-over-year decline in homicides was 30.6% in September, per data presented at Sheinbaum’s Oct. 13 press conference, down from a 32.1% reduction in August.

The security pillar score consequently declined to 9.11 from 9.37 in August.

A perfect score requires a 50% year-over-year decline in homicides.

🟡 ⬆️ APPROVAL RATING (8.81 out of 12.5)

Sheinbaum’s average approval rating was 70.5% in September, up two percentage points from August. Thus, the approval rating pillar score increased to 8.81 from 8.56 in August.

Per El Financiero’s September poll, Sheinbaum’s approval rating was 70%, an increase of two points compared to August.

A Sept. 28-Oct.1 poll conducted by QM Estudios de Opinión for the newspaper El Heraldo de México yielded a 71% approval rating for the president.

🟡 ⬆️ EMPLOYMENT (8.13 out of 12.5)

Mexico’s unemployment rate was 2.8% in September, below the 3% neutral benchmark, and down 0.2 percentage points from August.

The informality rate decreased 0.6 percentage points year over year in September, whereas the rate increased 0.2 percentage points in August. Despite the decline, Mexico’s informality rate in September remained very high at 54.3%.

The decrease in the unemployment rate and the informality rate meant that the scores for both components of this pillar increased in September.

The overall score of 8.13 is 1.5 percentage points higher than the score in August.

🟡 ⬇️ TOURISM (6.66 out of 12.5 — This pillar has a one-month lag)

International arrivals increased 1.3% year over year in August, the data period used for this index, down from 2.9% growth in July.

Thus, the tourism pillar score fell to 6.66 from 7.16 a month earlier.

🔴 ⬆️ BUSINESS CONFIDENCE (5.39 out of 12.5)

Mexico’s business confidence score, as measured by a monthly INEGI survey, was 48.4 in September, up 0.2 points from August. The score remains below the neutral benchmark of 50. In late 2024, when Sheinbaum was at the start of her six-year term, the business confidence score was around 52.

In September, the score for the foreign direct investment component of the pillar remained steady as the most recent data was once again that published by the Economy Ministry on Aug. 24.

According to that data, FDI in Mexico in the first six months of 2026 increased 2.1% annually, a much slower pace of growth compared with the 10.4% year-over-year gain in the first quarter of the year.

The slight improvement in the business confidence score led to an increase of 0.06 points in the overall pillar score. Nevertheless, the business confidence pillar remained in red light territory.

The MND Sheinbaum Index™ trend

In the graph below, you can see how the MND Sheinbaum Index™ score has changed over time.

We have now calculated a total of 12 index scores in a period spanning two years between September 2024 (the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency) and September 2026.

The difference between the lowest score (54.5 in March 2025 — predating the publication of the first MND Sheinbaum Index™ article) and the highest (71.5 in September 2026) is 17 points. The index results clearly show that Mexico — under Sheinbaum’s leadership — was doing significantly better in September than in earlier stages of the current federal administration.

What to watch

The next MND Sheinbaum Index™ will focus on the month of October.

Here are three things to look out for in the October Index:

Labor Poverty: INEGI will publish third-quarter data on labor poverty and real wages on Nov. 26. Therefore, the labor poverty pillar score will likely change in the next MND Sheinbaum Index™ .

INEGI will publish third-quarter data on labor poverty and real wages on Nov. 26. Therefore, the labor poverty pillar score will likely change in the next . Inflation: The inflation pillar score will decline again in the next MND Sheinbaum Index™ as Mexico’s headline inflation rate rose for a third consecutive month in October to reach 3.75% .

The inflation pillar score will decline again in the next as . Security: The security pillar score will also decline as the pace of homicide reduction slowed again in October. The year-over-year reduction was 22.9%, according to federal government data , down from a 30.6% decline in September.

MND Intelligence

* MND acknowledges that President Sheinbaum does not directly control outcomes in all eight pillars. For example, global commodity prices and tariff decisions in Washington can affect Mexico’s inflation and growth rates. The Index measures what is happening in Mexico on Sheinbaum’s watch.

World.title: For second year in a row, central Mexico’s reservoirs are above 95% full
World.content:
The Cutzamala System, which supplies one in every five liters of drinking water to the Valley of Mexico, has reached one of its best storage levels in the last decade, bolstered by seasonal rainfall and runoff.

According to the National Water Commission’s (Conagua) latest report on reservoir storage levels, the Cutzamala System reached a storage volume of 750.286 million cubic meters of water, equivalent to 95.88% of its capacity.

This figure exceeded the level recorded at the end of October, when reserves totaled 749.336 million cubic meters, representing 95.76% of capacity.

Conagua also reported that as of Nov. 9, the three reservoirs that make up the system were nearing full capacity: Villa Victoria stood at 87.44%, with 162.3 million cubic meters; Valle de Bravo at 99.14%, holding 390.9 million cubic meters; and El Bosque at 97.29%, with 196.9 million cubic meters.

The system’s current status contrasts greatly with the 2024 water crisis, when reserves in the Cutzamala system fell to around 26% of their capacity mid-year, largely due to extreme drought. Compared to 2025 at this time, however, the Cutzamala’s water volume is slightly lower.

Threats to the Cutzamala system

Despite the reservoirs’ staggering recovery over the past two years, a report by the news outlet Excélsior revealed that water supply remains threatened by illegal activities and pollution.

In the Valle de Bravo region, more than 27 unauthorized private dams have been identified, in addition to clandestine wells used for water extraction.

Furthermore, Excélsior revealed in June 2024 that, according to satellite imagery, the number of illegally constructed bodies of water increased from 400 to 600 between 2017 and 2024 in the Valle de Bravo-Amanalco area in México state.

According to the news outlet, this infrastructure serves as a supplementary irrigation source for corn or oat crops. However, it said the vast majority are intended for ornamental or landscaping purposes, for the enjoyment of the ranch owners.

Meanwhile, on the Michoacán side — within the Cutzamala River sub-basin — thousands of clandestine water extraction points have been detected, used for large-scale crop irrigation, including avocados and guavas.

Beyond clandestine wells, the system faces another threat: the pollution of the Valle de Bravo reservoir caused by the discharge of untreated wastewater, which is exacerbated by deficiencies in sanitation infrastructure.

With reports from Excélsior and Imagen TV

World.title: Aeroméxico announces 6 new non-stop flights to US, Puerto Rico starting in 2027
World.content:
Aeroméxico has announced it will expand its offerings from Mexico City International Airport in 2027 with six new routes to the United States and Puerto Rico, as part of its commercial alliance with Delta Airlines.

The expansion includes Nashville, New Orleans and San Juan, with flights beginning in June. Aeroméxico will operate four weekly frequencies on each route, becoming the only carrier offering non-stop flights to those destinations.

CDMX-Nashville will begin operations on June 13; CDMX-New Orleans, on the 17th; and CDMX-San Juan, on the 24th.

The Nashville and New Orleans routes will use 99-seat Embraer 190s, while the San Juan route will use a 166-seat Boeing 737-8.

“The addition of Nashville, New Orleans and San Juan to our network will allow us to offer greater connectivity options, bringing passengers closer to destinations with unique identities and major attractions,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, vice president of sales at Aeroméxico, said.

Beyond the new routes, the airline will add a second daily flight between Austin, Texas, and CDMX, starting June 3, 2027. With existing routes to Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and San Antonio, the additional service will give Aeroméxico six daily departures from Mexico City to Texas.

The airline’s expansion follows the recent announcement of daily services between Mexico City and Orange County, California; Fort Lauderdale, Florida; and Portland, Oregon starting in January 2027. All three flights will operate year-round using a Boeing 737-8 aircraft.

The move addresses an increasing demand for these destinations. Data from Sabre Market Intelligence, cited by Aviation Week, indicate that Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan accounted for approximately 101,600 passengers traveling to and from Mexico City in 2025 — a combined growth of 19% compared to the previous year.

San Juan accounted for approximately 52,800 passengers, followed by Nashville with 27,900 and New Orleans with 20,900.

With reports from Aviation Week and SPD Noticias

World.title: Inside the Otomí takeover of Mexico’s Indigenous affairs headquarters
World.content:
At 18, Anselma Margarito had spent her entire life waiting outside government offices.

Her Otomí family, originally from Santiago Mexquititlán, Querétaro, lived in one of several precarious properties occupied by Indigenous migrants in central Mexico City. Their home was made of corrugated metal sheets riddled with holes.

“When it rained, we had to cover our blankets,” she recalled. “We had to put buckets all over our little house so we wouldn’t get wet.”

For years, community members petitioned authorities for decent housing. They brought documents to the headquarters of the National Institute of Indigenous Peoples, or INPI, the federal agency charged with defending their rights.

“Only the document went inside,” Margarito said. “You stayed outside.”

On Oct. 12, 2020, they decided to go inside too.

At about 8 a.m., roughly 100 members of the Otomí community gathered near the INPI’s headquarters on Avenida México-Coyoacán. Margarito remembers being terrified.

“We could face repression. They could beat us. They could throw us out however they wanted,” she said.

The children entered first, followed by the women and then the men. With the pandemic keeping many federal employees home, Margarito said, there were relatively few workers inside. The community asked them to leave.

“The takeover of the INPI was peaceful,” she said. “We never hit any worker here.”

They expected to stay a week.

Six years later, they are still there.

A federal office becomes an autonomous home

What began as an audacious protest over housing has transformed a six-story federal office building into something neither the government nor its occupiers apparently anticipated: a home, autonomous school, communal kitchen, cultural center and organizing hub for Indigenous peoples and social movements from across Mexico.

The former INPI headquarters is now called the Casa de los Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas “Samir Flores Soberanes,” honoring the Indigenous land and water defender assassinated in Morelos in 2019.

Its transformation was on display last month when more than 600 Indigenous delegates and invited allies from across Mexico and beyond gathered there for the 30th anniversary of the Congreso Nacional Indígena, or CNI. Otomí women cooked for hundreds in a former parking garage converted into a colorful dining hall adorned with resistance-themed murals, while delegates gathered under a gigantic tent outside, taking over a section of Avenida México-Coyoacán, a major city thoroughfare that had been blocked off for the event.

From Santiago to Mexico City

For Isabel Valencia, 59, the story of how the community arrived here began more than half a century ago.

Valencia was born in Santiago Mexquititlán and came to Mexico City as a small child. Her memories are fragmentary: traveling back and forth between the city and the village, and eventually a camp of Otomí families in Mexico City. They settled in Pedregal de Santo Domingo, a lava-rock expanse on the edge of Coyoacán that was occupied by landless families in the 1970s and gradually built into a working-class neighborhood.

Her parents, she said, came looking for work.

“Everyone who is in the city is here in the same way,” Valencia said. “To survive because there is no work in the communities.”

The migration had deeper roots. Researchers trace a major exodus from Santiago Mexquititlán to the 1940s, when the community lost much of the irrigation water that had supported subsistence farming. Anthropologists Regina Martínez Casas and Guillermo de la Peña link that loss to the canalization of the Lerma River toward regional reservoirs, particularly the Solís dam in Guanajuato.

Valencia remembers elders saying that “they stole our water,” and recalling a time when the Lerma ran clean enough to irrigate crops.

In Mexico City, her family did not find stability.

Valencia’s memories of Pedregal de Santo Domingo are harsh. “There was no water, there was no electricity; it was pure stone,” she recalled. Her parents constructed “a little house of cardboard, black cardboard sheets,” where the family lived for years.

As Valencia’s generation grew up and started families of its own, space ran out.

After the 1985 earthquake, Otomí families began occupying damaged or abandoned properties in Roma and Juárez, central neighborhoods that would later become some of Mexico City’s most heavily gentrified.

At Zacatecas 74, where Valencia lived, almost nothing remained but rubble.

“We went in looking for a place to stay, somewhere we wouldn’t get wet,” she said. They sheltered with cardboard, plastic sheets and whatever materials they could find. Later they received recycled galvanized sheets that rusted and developed holes.

“In the cold, the sheets absorb all the cold. It’s like a refrigerator,” Valencia said. “And when it’s hot … it’s like an oven.”

Other community families faced eviction. Margarito recalled residents of Roma 18 being forced out while their clothing, identification and other possessions remained inside. When officials later demanded documents from them to access services, she said, the contradiction was infuriating: their papers had been lost in the eviction itself.

Housing was not the only grievance.

Over time, members of the community and their allies in the CNI increasingly came to see the INPI as aligned with a federal government pushing megaprojects through Indigenous territories.

Particularly painful was the role of then-INPI director Adelfo Regino, who had emerged from Indigenous organizing circles but now represented an administration defending projects fiercely opposed by the CNI.

At a press conference shortly after the occupation, Valencia put the break bluntly: “This institute does not represent us.”

25 years knocking on doors

By 2020, the housing struggle itself had already stretched across decades.

Valencia says her community spent 25 years “knocking on doors,” fulfilling requirements and pursuing the expropriation of Zacatecas 74.

They went from one agency to another.

“In the end, we realized they were just passing the buck,” she said. “Go there; it’s not my responsibility anymore.”

Some documents had expiration dates. As the years passed, Valencia feared the community would be forced to start the entire process again.

“We went to every government office that corresponded to an expropriation,” she said. “We never skipped an agency. But in the end they never paid attention to us.”

The government’s response after the takeover was more complicated than simple confrontation.

Three days later, the INPI announced that it would seek dialogue, saying the federal government was committed to addressing Indigenous peoples’ “legitimate aspirations.” Regino and Mexico City officials later met with community representatives and recognized their demand for dignified housing as legitimate.

But negotiations did not end the occupation.

By February 2022, the INPI and Mexico City government were publicly asking the community to vacate the building, arguing that the takeover impeded services to Indigenous people nationwide and threatened the institute’s 23,000-piece Indigenous art collection, one of the country’s most important of its kind. Regino also filed a complaint over possible damage to the property and collection.

From occupation to Casa de los Pueblos

Meanwhile, life inside the building took on a momentum of its own.

When authorities did not quickly remove them, the Otomí families created committees for food, security, cleaning and communications. Supporters brought rice and beans. Eventually they opened the space to other Indigenous peoples.

“We saw that our struggle, our demands, were the same as those of other peoples,” Valencia said.

They began inviting communities to hold meetings and conferences there, she said, “to make use of this building, to give the information that this building never gave.”

That evolution gave birth to the Casa de los Pueblos.

An autonomous school followed, along with spaces for visiting delegates, artists, organizers and social movements.

‘A living example of dignity’

By the sixth anniversary this October, the occupation had acquired a meaning far beyond housing.

Carlos González, an Indigenous-rights attorney and CNI founding member, recalled the Otomí families sleeping on sidewalks after the 2017 earthquake.

They had migrated from Santiago Mexquititlán “to seek the life that was denied to them there,” he told the anniversary gathering, only to encounter more poverty and rights violations in Mexico City.

In taking over the building, González said, they were exercising fundamental rights. He called the six-year occupation “a living example of dignity” and praised the community for filling the former bureaucracy “with color, voices and dignity.”

María de Jesús Patricio Martínez, better known as Marichuy, the CNI spokeswoman and first Indigenous woman to seek Mexico’s presidency, praised the community’s “resistance, organization and permanence,” particularly in the face of repeated pressures and attempts to remove them.

“They have shown us, with organization and courage, how to defend dignity as a people, as an autonomous community,” she said.

The occupation has produced one concrete housing victory.

Mexico City expropriated Zacatecas 74 in 2021 after community members staged another protest, this time occupying Avenida México-Coyoacán around the clock for seven days. Housing is now under construction there, and Valencia says residents have been told the apartments could be ready by March.

After roughly 30 years of struggle, however, she finds the prospect bittersweet.

“I expected it 25 years ago,” she said. She is approaching 60 now, her children already grown.

1 of 3

“I’m going to accept it because it is my struggle, because I have fought for it for 30 years,” she said. But the proposed apartment, at roughly 41 or 42 square meters, still does not represent dignified housing to her.

“No one asked us, as Indigenous peoples, what dignified housing is or what we need.”

She paused over what those decades had cost. Her children had already grown up in the conditions she had spent her adult life trying to change.

“That can’t be recovered,” she said.

1 of 2

For Margarito, now 24, another generation is already being shaped inside the struggle.

She speaks of children who have grown up attending demonstrations, witnessing confrontation and watching their parents organize.

“They too have resisted these six years,” she said. “Our children are the strength that allows us to keep holding on.”

On Oct. 12, six years to the day after walking into the INPI, the Otomí community made its boldest declaration yet.

The Casa de los Pueblos, Margarito announced, would become patrimony of the CNI and the Zapatista Army of National Liberation.

Thirty years after Comandanta Ramona came to Mexico City demanding “never again a Mexico without us,” Indigenous activists had turned the headquarters of the federal agency created to serve them into something of their own.

For Margarito, it is no longer primarily a government building under occupation.

It is the place where, she says, Indigenous people stopped waiting outside.

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: Aguascalientes students take top prizes at international robotics competition
World.content:
Student teams from the north-central Mexican state of Aguascalientes earned three awards at an international robotics competition in Germany over the weekend.

The Aguascalientes team, nicknamed Lanceros Overclock, won the high school division (ages 14 to 20) of Robo Shuttle at ROBOchæmpions, held Saturday and Sunday in the city of Lörrach.

Robo Shuttle is an event in which the budding scientists build and program autonomous robots to follow a marked course while transporting pingpong balls.

The team NexumAMG finished second in the same event and division, while the MagiBot squad took second in the middle school division (ages 11 to 14) of Robo Clash — in which team-built robots face off in a battle arena.

Competition rules required teams of two to four students.

Separately, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum honored students from Aguascalientes on Tuesday for an earlier victory in Japan, according to the state government.

In August, students from José Guadalupe Posada General Secondary School No. 6 won the FastBot Middle School division at the RoboRAVE world championship in Osaka. Next year’s RoboRAVE world championship is set for Houston.

Tuesday’s presidential recognition came during the National Meeting of Students in Science at the federal Education Ministry in Mexico City. The gathering recognized young people’s international achievements in science, mathematics, robotics and technology.

In Germany, Mexico’s winning teams represented three schools: Lanceros Overclock from the Lanceros de Aguascalientes state civic high school; NexumAMG from José Guadalupe Posada; and MagiBot from Magisterio Nacional Elementary School.

Overall, 16 students from Aguascalientes competed, but the names of the winners were not included in official results.

According to organizer Phaenovum — a student research center in Lörrach, Germany — the inaugural competition hosted teams from Mexico and Egypt in addition to regional competitors. It succeeded RoboRAVE Germany, a previous local version of RoboRAVE.

The organizer published results in five categories spanning races, robot duels, transport tasks and autonomous firefighting.

One challenge required robots to extinguish a candle flame autonomously.

Teams prepared and tested their robots Saturday before Sunday’s judging, awards ceremony and public demonstrations.

Aguascalientes students have also earned recognition elsewhere: José Guadalupe Posada students won two third-place awards at RoboRAVE in Silicon Valley in July 2025, while a Panamerican University team from the state finished sixth at RoboCup in Brazil that year with a search-and-rescue robot, according to the state government.

With reports from Futuro Bajío and Phaenovum

World.title: Auto parts sector posts best month on record
World.content:
The value of auto parts production in Mexico increased 9.1% year over year in August to reach US $11.118 billion, according to the National Auto Parts Industry (INA), a trade association.

That is the highest monthly production value on record for Mexico’s auto parts industry. A wide range of auto parts are made in Mexico, including electrical components, transmissions, engine parts, suspension components and clutches.

In the first eight months of 2026, the value of auto parts production in Mexico was $85.8 billion, according to INA, an increase of more than 8% compared to the same period of last year. Coahuila is Mexico’s top auto parts manufacturer, followed by Guanajuato and Nuevo León.

Presenting the latest data on auto parts production on Monday, INA’s head of economic studies, Julio Galván, said that Mexico’s auto parts sector is benefiting from the development of North American supply chains and the replacement of Asian imports with locally manufactured components.

Galván said that Mexico plays a “strategic role” in the North American supply chain. Unlike Mexican vehicles, auto parts made in Mexico can enter the United States tariff-free provided they comply with United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) rules. INA said last year that only about 8% of the nation’s parts manufacturers are not in compliance with USMCA regulations.

INA: Mexico’s auto parts exports exceeded $74 billion between January and August

INA reported that Mexico’s auto parts exports were worth $74.32 billion in the first eight months of 2026. Almost three-quarters of that total came from shipments to the United States.

Mexico imported auto parts worth $49.77 billion between January and August, leaving it with an auto parts trade surplus of $24.56 billion.

Galván said that Mexico and the United States have a “very strong” relationship in the auto parts trade, meeting each other’s needs in the automotive sector. However, the United States’ auto parts imports from Mexico decreased 1% in value year over year in the first eight months of the year to $54.35 billion, according to INA.

Despite that, Mexico remains the world’s top supplier of auto parts to the U.S., capturing almost 45% of that country’s total market for auto parts imports between January and August.

INA estimates that the total value of auto parts production in Mexico this year will be around $126 billion. The industry group predicts that Mexico’s 2026 auto parts exports will total $109 billion.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: F1 Champion Antonelli Penalised in Brazil
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli’s Mercedes at the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix. A file photo from 4 October: it does not show the Austin race. Photo: Liauzh / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Key Facts Who. Kimi Antonelli, 20, Mercedes driver and the 2026 Formula One champion, received a five-second penalty.

Why. Stewards, the FIA officials who rule on race incidents, found he was released unsafely from the pit lane.

Effect. None on the result. He stays fifth at the Brazilian Grand Prix on Sunday, 8 November 2026.

Next. Las Vegas Grand Prix, Saturday, 21 November, 8 p.m. local time (11 p.m. ET).

Kimi Antonelli, the youngest Formula One champion in history, picked up a five-second penalty at Interlagos, the São Paulo circuit, but it cost him nothing. His fifth place at the São Paulo Grand Prix 2026 stands.

For readers in the United States, the story matters because the championship now moves to Las Vegas on 21 November. Mercedes arrives there with both titles already decided.

Why the Stewards Stepped In

The stewards ruled after the race on Sunday, 8 November. They found that Antonelli’s car, number 12, was released into the pit lane in an unsafe manner while Franco Colapinto’s Alpine, car number 43, was approaching in the fast lane.

An unsafe release means a car is sent out of its pit box into traffic. Mercedes told the stewards the release could have been handled better and in a safer manner, and the five seconds were added to Antonelli’s race time.

Why Fifth Place Did Not Move

Antonelli finished 7.0 seconds behind his teammate George Russell in fourth. He was about 15.5 seconds ahead of McLaren’s Oscar Piastri in sixth, so the penalty changed no positions.

Late in the race Russell was told to swap places with Antonelli, and Antonelli obeyed. The official classification still has Russell ahead.

A Wet Day That Mercedes Will Remember

Lando Norris of McLaren won in the rain, his third victory of the season, 14.6 seconds ahead of Max Verstappen of Red Bull. Mercedes clinched the constructors’ title, the prize for the best team, in São Paulo.

Antonelli had led after passing Norris at the start, then spun at Turn 1 around lap 20 and handed the lead back. He said on the team radio that the car was pulling to one side under acceleration.

Russell also spun on the pit exit after switching to slicks, the tyres for dry tracks. He recovered to take fourth.

The Title Picture With Three Rounds Left

Antonelli clinched the drivers’ title in Mexico City on 1 November, aged 20 years and 68 days, with four rounds still to run. He leads the standings on 390 points.

The fight that remains is for second place. Verstappen has 279 points and Russell 262, a gap of 17.

Las Vegas Is Next

The Las Vegas Grand Prix starts on Saturday, 21 November, at 8 p.m. local time, which is 11 p.m. on the US East Coast. After that come Qatar on 29 November and the season finale in Abu Dhabi on 6 December.

Viewers on the East Coast will watch late on a Saturday night.

What It Means for US Readers

With the champion already crowned, the interest shifts to the contest for second place and to how Mercedes handles pit-lane discipline after this warning.A penalty without a consequence is a reminder that small procedural errors can decide a tight race.

Next time the margin may not be seven seconds.

What Is Not Known

We found no sign that Mercedes has appealed the ruling, and none is expected given that the result did not change. The exact cause of Antonelli’s spin has not been explained beyond his radio remarks.

No prediction market lists an active contract on this topic. We will update this story if the stewards or the team add anything.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the penalty change Kimi Antonelli’s result in Brazil?

No. He remains fifth, about seven seconds behind George Russell and 15.5 seconds ahead of Oscar Piastri.

When is the next Formula One race?

The Las Vegas Grand Prix is on Saturday, 21 November, at 8 p.m. local time, or 11 p.m. ET. Qatar and Abu Dhabi follow.

Which 2026 titles are already decided?

Antonelli clinched the drivers’ title in Mexico City on 1 November. Mercedes clinched the constructors’ title in São Paulo on 8 November.

World.title: Kenya’s Co-op Bank Lifts Dividend by 50%
World.content:
KENYA · BANKING

Kenya’s Co-operative Bank has given its shareholders a clear raise: Co-operative Bank of Kenya (Co-op Bank), listed in Nairobi, will pay an interim dividend of 1.50 Kenyan shillings (KSh) a share (about 1.2 US cents) on 4 December 2026. That is 50% more than the KSh1.00 (about 0.8 US cents) it paid a year ago.

The Nairobi bank said on Wednesday 11 November 2026 that Co-op Bank Group’s profit before tax for the nine months to 30 September rose 19.6% to KSh35.9 billion (about US$276 million). Investors in Nairobi-listed bank shares, and Kenyans who borrow from or save with the bank, are the people most affected.

Loans Group net loans KSh496.9 billion (about US$3.8 billion), up 22.2%; deposits up 14.8%.

The group grew profit faster than its costs and cleaned up its loan book. It shared the gain with shareholders through a 50% bigger interim dividend.
