Where the Profit Came From

The group’s profit before tax reached KSh35.9 billion in the nine months to 30 September 2026, against KSh30.0 billion (about US$231 million) a year earlier. Profit after tax grew faster, up 27.2% to KSh27.4 billion (about US$211 million) from KSh21.6 billion (about US$166 million).

Net interest income, the gap between what the group earns on loans and pays on deposits, grew 12.7% to KSh51.0 billion (about US$393 million). Total operating income rose 11.6% to KSh75.2 billion (about US$579 million).

Operating expenses grew only 5.3%. Cost of risk, a measure of loan losses against the loan book, fell to 1.4% from 2.5%.

Kenyatta Avenue in central Nairobi, August 2025. Photo: Bahnfrend / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

A Bigger, Cleaner Loan Book

The group’s net loans and advances climbed 22.2% to KSh496.9 billion (about US$3.8 billion), and customer deposits rose 14.8% to KSh642.5 billion (about US$4.9 billion). Total assets grew 11.3% to KSh907.4 billion (about US$7.0 billion) from KSh815.3 billion (about US$6.3 billion).

The group’s share of loans that borrowers have stopped repaying, known as the non-performing loan ratio, fell to 12.9% from 17.1% a year earlier. The group’s cost of risk, noted above, was 1.4% against 2.5% a year earlier.

Return on average equity, a gauge of profit earned on shareholders’ money, rose to 21.3% from 19.4%. The cost-to-income ratio before provisions stood at 46.4%.

Why It Matters

The 50% dividend rise turns a profit gain into cash. Based on the 5,867,174,695 shares on the bank’s register at 30 April 2026, the KSh1.50 payout comes to about KSh8.8 billion (about US$68 million), or roughly 32% of nine-month profit after tax by our calculation.

Co-op Holdings Co-operative Society, a member-owned society that is the bank’s largest shareholder, held 64.56% of the shares on that register. On the same arithmetic it would receive about KSh5.7 billion (about US$44 million), so most of the dividend goes to that one society.

What to Watch Next

Shareholders on the register at the close of business on Wednesday 25 November 2026 qualify for the interim dividend, which is paid on Friday 4 December 2026. The bank’s next set of full-year results will show whether the nine-month pace holds.

Kingdom Bank, a Kenyan subsidiary of Co-op Bank, completed its upgrade of Finacle, a core banking software system, in October 2026, after earlier rollouts at Co-operative Bank of Kenya and Co-op Bank of South Sudan Ltd. Our Kenya coverage page tracks the wider story, and our report on the US$50 million currency swap with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the first use of a US$100 million facility covers its recent funding deal.

What It Means for You

For investors who hold Nairobi-listed bank shares, the result shows a lender growing loans by more than a fifth while bad debts shrink. Dividends are paid in Kenyan shillings, so returns for a US holder also depend on the exchange rate, which stood near KSh129.85 to the dollar on 11 November 2026.

For Kenyan micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), the bank is lending more. Co-op Bank Group said 273,783 small businesses were onboarded to its tailored packages and that MSMEs make up 16.7% of its loan book.

What Is Not Known

The bank has not said whether the interim payout signals a higher full-year dividend. It has also not published a profit figure for the third quarter alone in its press release.

In Plain English An interim dividend is a payout to shareholders before the year ends. Profit before tax is earnings before the tax bill; profit after tax is what remains. A co-operative society is a member-owned organisation. Here, one such society, Co-op Holdings, owns most of the bank.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Co-op Bank’s interim dividend?

The board approved KSh1.50 a share, up 50% from KSh1.00 (about 0.8 US cents) last year. It goes to shareholders on the register at the close of business on 25 November 2026 and is paid on 4 December 2026.

How much profit did Co-op Bank make?

Group profit before tax was KSh35.9 billion (about US$276 million) for the nine months to 30 September 2026, up 19.6%. Profit after tax was KSh27.4 billion (about US$211 million), up 27.2%.

Is Co-op Bank’s loan quality improving?

Yes. The group’s non-performing loan ratio fell to 12.9% from 17.1% a year earlier, and the cost of risk dropped to 1.4% from 2.5%.

Who owns Co-op Bank of Kenya?

Co-op Holdings Co-operative Society held 64.56% of the shares at 30 April 2026, according to the bank’s shareholder profile. The register listed 112,434 shareholders in total.

Sources: Co-operative Bank of Kenya, Q3 2026 financials press release, 11 November 2026 (https://www.co-opbank.co.ke/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Press-Release-Coop-Bank-Q3-2026-Financials.pdf); Co-operative Bank of Kenya, shareholder profile as at 30 April 2026 (https://www.co-opbank.co.ke/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CO-OPERATIVE-BANK-LIMITED-SHAREHOLDER-PROFILE-AS-AT-30.04.2026-1.pdf); exchange rate from RT market data, USD/KES 129.85, 11 November 2026.

World.title: Belize Says Mexico Will Keep Power Flowing
World.content:
File photo, 2024. A Belize Electricity Limited high-voltage substation; the sign on the gate reads Lake Independence Substation. (Photo: Vasnihpech, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

BELIZE · ELECTRICITY

Belize’s Minister of Public Utilities, Michel Chebat, said Mexico will keep supplying his country with electricity. He spoke after meeting Emilia Esther Calleja Alor, head of CFE (Comisión Federal de Electricidad), Mexico’s state power company.

For travellers, expatriates and US readers with property or tourism plans in Belize, steady power is a basic comfort. It is also a matter of money, because Belize Electricity Limited (BEL, the main power distributor) owes CFE for past supplies.

Key Facts Who Belize’s Minister of Public Utilities, Michel Chebat, said he met the head of CFE, Mexico’s state power company.

Promise Chebat said Belize gets 55 megawatts (a unit of electricity capacity) from CFE now and that this will continue.

Debt Lynn Young, executive chairman of Belize Electricity Limited (BEL, the main power distributor), put overdue CFE bills at about BZ$20 million (US$10 million).

Next Chebat said a technical group is being set up to keep both sides talking.

Unknown Contract price, length and the payment terms were not disclosed.

Belize’s utilities minister says Mexico’s CFE will keep sending 55 megawatts, while the two sides talk about more power and unpaid bills.

What Chebat Said After the Meeting

Chebat said: “we are currently getting 55 megawatts from them, and that will absolutely continue.” He also said he met CFE staff and officials from Mexico’s Energy Ministry.

Chebat said Belize is setting up a technical group so the two utilities can stay in constant conversation. He said CFE is thinking about new generation plants in southern Mexico by 2028.

The Unpaid Bills

On Wednesday 28 October, BEL executive chairman Lynn Young put BEL’s overdue bills to CFE at roughly BZ$20 million (about US$10 million, at the fixed two-to-one Belize dollar peg). Young said BEL had Belize dollars for some bills but struggled to find the US dollars needed to pay CFE.

Chebat said the debt is a separate matter from supply. He said CFE has a payment mechanism for the money, and he did not describe it.

Why It Matters

If Chebat is right, households and businesses in Belize can expect the Mexican power they rely on to keep flowing. A cut would be felt first in homes, hotels and shops.

Mexico is also busy at home, as our earlier report on CFE grid financing shows. For wider context see our guide to Belize’s economy and its key players.

What to Watch Next

The technical group still has to be formed and meet. Talks on a possible increase in supply have opened.

What It Means for You

Visitors should not expect a sudden change in power supply on the strength of these statements alone. Anyone with power-dependent plans in Belize, such as rentals or remote work, should still keep a back-up.

What Is Not Known

No price, contract length or payment schedule has been published. We found no statement from CFE on the meeting.

It is also unclear how much extra power CFE could offer, or when. The statements come from Belize’s side only.

In Plain English A megawatt is one million watts, a unit of electrical power. Arrears are bills that are overdue. CFE is Mexico’s state power company. BEL (Belize Electricity Limited) is Belize’s main power distributor.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will Belize keep getting Mexican electricity?

Minister Michel Chebat said Belize now gets 55 megawatts from CFE and that this will continue. He said the overdue bills have nothing to do with supply.

How much does Belize owe CFE?

Lynn Young, executive chairman of Belize Electricity Limited, put overdue bills at about BZ$20 million (about US$10 million) on Wednesday 28 October. The Belize dollar is fixed at two to one against the US dollar.

Could Belize get more Mexican power?

Chebat said CFE is thinking about new plants in southern Mexico by 2028. No volume or date has been agreed.

Sources: the statements of Belize’s Minister Michel Chebat and BEL’s executive chairman Lynn Young as relayed by the Embassy of Belize in Mexico (primary actors), 10 November 2026.

World.title: Uruguay Factory Output Up 7.7% in September
World.content:
File photo of visitors at a UPM pulp mill in western Uruguay during a US Embassy tour, September 2020. (Photo: U.S. Embassy in Uruguay, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

URUGUAY · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Uruguay is a small South American country between Argentina and Brazil.

What happened Uruguay’s factory output rose 7.7% in September from a year earlier.

The catch One oil refinery restarting after repairs added 5.9 percentage points of the 7.7% growth; without it, output rose 1.8%.

The workers Hours worked in factories fell 2.9% and jobs fell 2.8%.

Power Index Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 45.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Uruguay’s factories made 7.7% more in September than a year earlier, the National Statistics Institute (INE) said on Wednesday 11 November 2026. The headline looks strong, but most of the jump comes from one oil refinery that was switched off a year ago.

For US readers, the number is a lesson in reading base effects: a weak month last year makes this year look better. Our earlier look at August’s industrial output showed a 4.8% rise that the refinery also lifted, so September is not a clean break.

What Happened

INE publishes a monthly index of the physical volume of manufacturing, called IVFIM in Spanish. It counts how much factories produce, not how much money they earn, measured against a base period set to 100.

The September reading was 121.4, which is 7.7% above September 2025. Compared with August, and after removing normal seasonal swings, output actually slipped 0.4%.

Why the Refinery Matters

The biggest single push came from the refining of petroleum products, which INE counts as its own division of industry. ANCAP, Uruguay’s state oil company, had its refinery out of production in September 2025 while crews repaired an offshore oil buoy at José Ignacio, a coastal site.

Because the refinery produced almost nothing a year ago, its output this September is up by an enormous percentage. INE says that single division added 5.9 percentage points to the 7.7% total.

Without the refinery, the index stood at 122.1 and grew 1.8% from a year earlier. That is the better guide to the everyday strength of Uruguayan industry.

Winners and Losers Inside Industry

Food production rose 3.3% in September and added 1.4 points to the total. Paper and paper products rose 3.1%, adding 0.4 points.

Beverages fell 17.0%, which cut 1.1 percentage points from the total, and printing fell 22.8%. INE also reports a 2.5% drop in pharmaceuticals.

Over the first nine months of 2026, factory output averaged 3.8% more than a year earlier. Over the latest 12 months, the average gain is 2.9%, and food is the largest contributor to both.

The Job Picture

Hours worked by factory workers fell 2.9% from a year earlier, and the number of people employed in industry fell 2.8%. Food production accounts for the largest share of the lost hours and jobs.

Hours and employment fell even as output rose. INE does not give a reason for the gap.

How September Compares With August

August’s 4.8% rise was also lifted by the refinery, which added 3.8 percentage points. Without it, output grew only 1.0% in August.

The measure without the refinery therefore picked up from 1.0% in August to 1.8% in September. That is a modest improvement, not a surge.

A percentage point here means one point of the overall growth rate, so a division adding 5.9 points supplies 5.9 of the 7.7 percentage points. The other divisions together supplied the remaining 1.8 points.

What It Means for You

If you follow Uruguay through a US fund or a bond, read 7.7% as a figure flattered by a one-off repair a year ago. The 1.8% growth without the refinery and the 0.4% monthly dip give a more modest picture of the underlying pace.

Readers tracking the wider economy can also see our reports on Uruguay’s October inflation and the September unemployment rate. Both give context for how Uruguay’s households and firms are doing.

What Is Not Known

INE does not say how much the refinery will add or subtract in coming months. The INE release does not say what caused the 17.0% fall in beverages.

The data also does not show profits or exports, so it cannot say whether companies are earning more. A single month with a one-off distortion cannot settle the trend.

More: Uruguay news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How Much Did Uruguay’s Factory Output Rise in September?

Output rose 7.7% from September 2025, according to INE, the national statistics office. Without the oil refinery, the rise was 1.8%.

Why Is the 7.7% Figure Flattered?

Uruguay’s state refinery was shut for repairs in September 2025, so its output this year looks huge by comparison. That one division added 5.9 points to the total.

Did Factory Jobs Grow in Uruguay?

No. Hours worked by factory workers fell 2.9% and employment fell 2.8% from a year earlier.

What Happened to Output From August?

After seasonal adjustment, September output was 0.4% lower than August. In August, output had risen 4.8% from a year earlier.

Sources: National Statistics Institute of Uruguay (INE), Physical Volume Index of Manufacturing (IVFIM), September 2026, 11 November 2026.

World.title: Sasol and Mozambique Sign LNG Terminal Study
World.content:
Africa · Energy

Sasol, the South African energy and chemicals group, and ENH, Mozambique’s state oil and gas company, signed a memorandum of understanding on Wednesday 11 November 2026 to assess whether a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal linking Inhassoro and Beira is feasible. Sasol Moçambique, the group’s local arm, and ENH both described the plan, but Sasol Moçambique’s statement gave no cost, capacity or date.

The signing took place in Maputo on the sidelines of the Africa Gas & LNG Summit 2026, a gas industry conference held at the Joaquim Chissano International Conference Centre. Maria Benvinda Levi, Mozambique’s prime minister, attended the summit and visited its exhibition, where she learned about Sasol’s operations, according to Sasol Moçambique.

Key Facts —Who. Sasol, a South African energy group, and ENH, the Mozambican state hydrocarbon company. —What. A memorandum of understanding to study an Inhassoro-Beira LNG terminal and gas link. —When. Wednesday 11 November 2026, at the Africa Gas & LNG Summit 2026. —Terms. Sasol’s statement gave no cost, capacity or date. —Link. Sasol holds 20% of the company running the pipeline that carries Mozambican gas to South Africa.

What We Know

ENH’s Director of New Business, Rijcard Manuel, said the aim is to bring gas from the Rovuma Basin, the offshore gas fields in the far north, to consumers in the centre and south of Mozambique. He said the north lacks the infrastructure to move that gas, and that ENH wants to use Sasol’s experience.

The plan, as described by ENH, uses a floating storage and regasification unit, a ship that turns LNG back into gas, anchored near Inhassoro. It would supply the Beira region by ship and connect to Inhassoro by a pipeline of about 135 kilometres, as ENH described it at the summit.

Sasol would provide technical help and specialist staff during development. The work should start with feasibility studies, followed by environmental and social studies and then engineering, according to ENH.

Sasol and ENH have been partners for more than two decades, since they signed gas agreements in 2000, according to Sasol Moçambique. Sasol has produced gas in Mozambique since 2004.

An LNG carrier, the Gulf Energy, at Avaldsnes, Norway, in June 2021. Photo: Christoffer Hjeltnes Støle, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Why It Matters

In November 2025 the Mozambican government gave ENH and three other state companies a 30-year concession to build and run gas facilities at the Port of Beira and at Inhassoro. The other three are the ports and railways company CFM, the power utility EDM and the Cahora Bassa hydropower company HCB.

The national petroleum regulator, the National Petroleum Institute (INP), said then that the project rests on a floating storage and regasification unit anchored at Beira and in Inhambane province. Sasol also holds 20% of ROMPCO, the Mozambique-South Africa pipeline company behind the 865-kilometre line that carries Mozambican gas to South Africa, while the Mozambican and South African sides hold 40% each.

A feasibility study is not an investment decision, and before the signing ENH had pointed to 2030 or 2031 for its planned gas infrastructure. Those northern projects include Rovuma LNG and Mozambique LNG.

What Is Not Known

No budget, capacity or financing plan has been published, and the individual signatories were not named. The Rio Times has not seen the memorandum itself, and the two accounts differ in emphasis: Sasol Moçambique speaks of a terminal feasibility study, ENH of a wider gas transport project.

What It Means for You

For readers following African gas, this is a study agreement, and no change in supply or prices was announced. The next signal to watch is a published scope of work or a named financing partner, as covered on our Mozambique page.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Sasol and ENH sign?

They signed a memorandum of understanding on 11 November 2026 to assess the feasibility of an Inhassoro-Beira LNG terminal. Sasol Moçambique gave no cost or date.

What is ENH?

ENH is Mozambique’s state-owned National Hydrocarbon Company. Sasol Moçambique says the two have worked together since 2000.

Where are Inhassoro and Beira?

Inhassoro is a coastal district in Inhambane province in southern Mozambique. Beira is the main port city of Sofala province in the centre of the country.

Sources: Sasol Moçambique announcement, 11 November 2026; ENH statements at the Africa Gas & LNG Summit, Maputo, 11 November 2026; National Petroleum Institute (INP), Mozambique, statement on the Beira and Inhassoro concession, November 2025.

World.title: Dubai Park Owner Lists After US$529M IPO
World.content:
The Dubai skyline at sunrise, with the Burj Khalifa tower at right. File photo, not linked to the story. (Photo: Rio Times library)

UAE · MARKETS · IPO

DIP Holding, which owns the operator of Dubai Investments Park, began trading on the Dubai Financial Market, the emirate’s stock exchange, on Wednesday 11 November 2026. It followed the UAE’s first initial public offering (IPO) of 2026, meaning a company’s first sale of shares to the public.

The sale of 20% of the company was priced at AED1.12 (UAE dirham) a share, about US$0.30, for a total of AED1.94 billion (about US$529 million). EFG Hermes, the investment bank of Egypt’s EFG Holding, said it completed its role as joint bookrunner, one of the banks that organise and sell such an offer.

Key Facts Deal 20% of DIP Holding sold at AED1.12 a share, worth AED1.94 billion (about US$529 million).

Seller Its parent company, Dubai Investments, sold the shares and keeps 80%; DIP Holding gets no proceeds.

Value Stock-market value of about AED9.7 billion (US$2.64 billion) at the offer price.

Debut Shares rose as much as 6% in early trading on 11 November 2026.

Asset Dubai Investments Park, a 23 million square metre mixed-use zone in southern Dubai.

What Was Sold

The offer covered about 1.74 billion existing shares, which are 20% of DIP Holding’s capital, and the price sat near the middle of its marketed range. At that price the company is worth about AED9.7 billion (US$2.64 billion), converted at the dirham’s fixed rate of about 3.67 per US dollar.

EFG Hermes said professional and institutional investors took 92% of the offering. The rest went to retail investors, employees and eligible shareholders of the parent, Dubai Investments.

Who Gets the Money

No new shares were issued, so the proceeds go to the seller, Dubai Investments, and DIP Holding itself receives none. Dubai Investments keeps an 80% stake.

DIP Holding plans annualised cash dividends, subject to approvals, of AED700 million (about US$191 million) for 2026, AED725 million (about US$197 million) for 2027 and AED750 million (about US$204 million) for 2028. The first payment after listing, AED350 million (about US$95 million) for the second half of 2026, is expected in April 2027.

A large UAE flag carried through Downtown Dubai, with the Burj Khalifa tower at left. File photo, not linked to the story. (Photo: Rio Times library)

What DIP Holding Owns

DIP Holding owns the company that operates Dubai Investments Park, a mixed-use development of 23 million square metres (about 8.9 square miles) between Jebel Ali Port and Al Maktoum International Airport. The park has about 1,000 tenants, about 5,700 sub-leases and more than 150,000 residents.

Occupancy of its ground leases, meaning land rented to tenants, was 99.9% at 30 June 2026, according to the company. Dubai Investments Park spans industrial, logistics, commercial and residential uses.

What It Means for You

The listing is the UAE’s first IPO of the year, and EFG Hermes said further IPOs it advises are lined up before the end of 2026 and in early 2027. Christopher Laing, head of equity capital markets at EFG Hermes, said the deal “provides a valuable reference point” for regional companies weighing a share sale.

For readers following Africa’s markets, it shows an Egyptian investment bank at work in the Gulf, after its role in the debut of Banque du Caire, an Egyptian state lender. Dubai is also a venue for African finance, as the Republic of the Congo’s US$1.55 billion bonds listed in Dubai show.

What Is Not Known

We have not confirmed the official closing price of DIP Holding’s first day, only its move in early trading. EFG Hermes’ statement does not name the other banks that ran the offer.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is DIP Holding?

DIP Holding owns the company that operates Dubai Investments Park, a 23 million square metre mixed-use development in southern Dubai. Its parent, Dubai Investments, keeps 80% after the IPO.

When did DIP Holding start trading?

Shares began trading on the Dubai Financial Market on Wednesday 11 November 2026. They rose as much as 6% in early trading.

How much was the IPO worth, and who gets the money?

The offer was worth AED1.94 billion (about US$529 million) at AED1.12 a share. The seller, Dubai Investments, receives the proceeds because no new shares were issued.

What was EFG Hermes’ role?

EFG Hermes, the investment bank of Egypt’s EFG Holding, said it completed its role as joint bookrunner. A bookrunner helps organise and sell the offer to investors.

Sources: Dubai Financial Market listing and offer announcements, October to 11 November 2026; EFG Hermes statement on the offering, 11 November 2026.

World.title: Nigeria’s Alt Bank Names Gul Khan New CEO
World.content:
Office towers in the Marina business district of Lagos, Nigeria. File photo, not linked to the story. (Photo: Rio Times library)

NIGERIA · BANKING · APPOINTMENTS

Nigeria’s Alternative Bank, known as Alt Bank, has named Gul Khan as its managing director and chief executive. The appointment follows approval from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), the country’s banking regulator, and became public in November 2026.

Khan most recently led the Kenyan lender I&M Bank and succeeds Hassan Yusuf, the bank’s founding managing director. Alt Bank is the non-interest (interest-free) banking arm of Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc, a financial group listed on the Nigerian Exchange, the stock market in Lagos.

Who Is Gul Khan?

Alt Bank’s announcement says Khan has more than 25 years of banking experience across Africa, Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Middle East. He most recently served as chief executive and board director of I&M Bank in Kenya.

What Alt Bank Said

Non-interest banking is banking that avoids charging or paying interest. Muhtar Bakare, Alt Bank’s chairman, said Khan’s “expertise in non-interest banking and his leadership experience across African financial services position him well” for the job.

Khan said the opportunity is to “make Alt Bank the preferred choice for consumers and businesses in Nigeria.” The bank also said it met the CBN’s revised minimum capital requirement for national non-interest banks well ahead of the regulatory deadline.

The city gate of Abuja, Nigeria’s capital and the seat of its financial regulators. File photo, not linked to the story. (Photo: Rio Times library)

The Group Behind the Bank

Sterling Financial Holdings, which also owns Sterling Bank, the group’s other lender, reported a 37.1% rise in nine-month profit before tax, as our earlier report on the results shows. Alt Bank has said it also moved to MIZAN, a core banking platform built for non-interest institutions.

The bank says its aim is to expand access to non-interest financial solutions for individuals and businesses across Nigeria. For another Nigerian lender’s push into new payments, see our report on Stanbic IBTC’s naira-to-yuan payment service.

What It Means for You

For investors in Sterling Financial Holdings, this is a leadership change at one subsidiary, not at the group. The appointment changes the bank’s leadership, not its ownership.

For US readers tracking Nigerian banks, the practical point is that the regulator has already cleared the appointment. Results in the coming quarters will show whether the change pays off.

What Is Not Known

The bank has not said how long Khan’s term runs, what his first priorities will be or when exactly he starts. We could not confirm the exact date of the announcement from the bank itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Gul Khan?

He is the new managing director and chief executive of Nigeria’s Alternative Bank. He most recently led I&M Bank in Kenya and has more than 25 years of banking experience.

Who did Gul Khan replace at Alt Bank?

He succeeds Hassan Yusuf, who was the bank’s founding managing director. The bank has not said how long Khan’s term runs.

What is Alt Bank?

The Alternative Bank Limited is the non-interest banking subsidiary of Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc. Non-interest banking avoids charging or paying interest.

Did the regulator approve the appointment?

Yes. Alt Bank said it appointed Khan following approval by the Central Bank of Nigeria.

Sources: Alternative Bank Limited announcement, November 2026; Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc nine-month results, 2026.

World.title: Afreximbank Backs Nigerian Firms With US$75M
World.content:
File photo. Central Lagos seen from above, September 2018. Photo: Subomi07, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

NIGERIA · BANKING · SMALL BUSINESS

Afreximbank, the Cairo-based pan-African trade bank, has committed a US$75 million finance facility to the Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN) to lend to small and medium-sized businesses. The agreements were signed at the opening of CANEX WKND 2026, Afreximbank’s Creative Africa Nexus event for creative industries in Lagos (5 to 8 November), and the press release followed on Wednesday 11 November 2026.

DBN will pass the money to eligible firms through its partner financial institutions, including businesses in fashion, film and music. For US readers, it shows a pan-African lender backing small firms in Nigeria, including creative businesses that want to export.

Afreximbank said the facility will widen access to finance for Nigerian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including eligible businesses in the creative economy. Who the Two Lenders Are

Afreximbank describes itself as a pan-African multilateral bank mandated to finance and promote trade within and beyond Africa. It reports total assets and contingencies of more than US$48.5 billion at the end of December 2025.

DBN describes itself as a wholesale development finance institution, which means it lends through other banks rather than directly to firms. It offers long-term financing and risk-sharing support to address the financing limits that micro, small and medium-sized firms face.

Awani said the aim is to “help Nigerian SMEs build productive capacity, strengthen their competitiveness and make the transition from promising local businesses to sustainable exporters.” Okpanachi said the capacity-building and market-access parts of the deal are “particularly important to us.”

The deal shows Afreximbank channelling money into Nigeria’s creative economy through its Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) programme, which our earlier report on its US$1 billion creative-deals goal covers. For investors and trade watchers, the facility is one visible example of that creative-economy push.

Loans of this kind reach businesses through banks, so the effect on any single firm depends on those banks’ own lending decisions. Firms in fashion, film, music and design are among the intended beneficiaries.

Neither institution has published the interest rate, repayment period or disbursement date. They have also not said how many firms will benefit or which partner banks will lend the money.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Dollar Slides Back Toward Its Record Low
World.content:
The dollar has fallen back to within two colones of its all-time low in Costa Rica, erasing most of the rebound it had in early October. The average price on Monex, the wholesale market where banks and other authorized institutions trade dollars, closed yesterday at 448.43 colones, according to Central Bank data. That was the lowest close since Sept. 18 and 1.63 colones above the record of 446.80 set on Sept. 17.

For anyone here paid in dollars, the gap with January keeps widening. On Jan. 2, the first trading day of the year, the Monex average was 497.07 colones, and the dollar exchange rate in Costa Rica has trended lower for most of the months since. At Tuesday’s average, $1,000 converts to 448,430 colones. That is 48,640 colones less than on Jan. 2, a drop of about 9.8% in just over 10 months.

The decline resumed after a brief reversal. Following the September low, the rate climbed to 460.45 colones on Oct. 1, eased through the rest of October and has fallen in each of the last five sessions. The Central Bank has been buying dollars to slow the fall. It purchased $9 million on Friday, Nov. 6, its second consecutive day in the market, bringing its stabilization purchases over the two sessions to $24 million.

The Central Bank’s dollar trading on Monex this year total $2.004 billion, of which $1.288 billion were stabilization operations. The bank says those operations are meant to moderate abrupt swings in the price of the dollar, not to set a fixed exchange rate. Carlos Valerin, an exchange-market specialist, said the October rebound was driven mainly by a 25-basis-point rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, while the Central Bank kept its own policy rate unchanged.

Valerin also pointed to the calendar. November brings aguinaldo payments, the year-end bonus required under Costa Rican law, and transnational companies typically pay the second half of December salaries early, he said. Both concentrate dollar conversions into a few weeks.

Central Bank President Róger Madrigal has described a risk running the other way. He said the gap between Costa Rican and US interest rates is likely to widen, which could encourage saving in foreign currency and capital outflows. When interest rates favor a foreign currency, Madrigal said, demand for that currency rises, which in principle should push the exchange rate up. He said the bank is monitoring the situation closely.

The strong colón has squeezed businesses that earn in dollars and pay their costs in colones, from coffee growers to medical tourism providers. It has also cut the purchasing power of residents who live on pensions or other income from abroad. Monex is a wholesale market, so the rates offered at bank windows differ from its daily average. Banks add a margin when they buy and sell dollars, and that margin varies from one institution to another.

The rate now sits closer to its record than at any point since September, and the next few days will show whether the year-end flow of dollars pushes it through.

World.title: Costa Rica Mourns Actor and TV Host Leonardo Perucci, Dead at 87
World.content:
Leonardo Perucci, the Chilean-born actor, director and television host who became one of the most familiar faces on Costa Rican screens and stages, died Tuesday, Nov. 10, at age 87. His daughter, Valeria Perucci, confirmed his death. For a generation of Costa Ricans, Perucci was the host of Fantástico, the Channel 7 variety program that aired from 1985 to 1995. He also appeared on Fabulosos Sábados and later co-hosted the morning show Giros on Repretel.

Perucci had undergone a heart procedure on Monday to treat a blocked coronary artery, according to local reports. His family has not released an official cause of death. Born in Antofagasta, Chile, on Dec. 13, 1938, Perucci began acting professionally in the early 1960s. In 1967 he starred in Los Días Jóvenes, widely regarded as Chile’s first telenovela, and went on to appear in 14 Chilean soap operas.

After the 1973 military coup in Chile, he went into exile in Cuba, where he spent about five years working as an actor, director and playwright. He arrived in Costa Rica in 1979 and never left. Within two weeks of his arrival he was on stage in Fuenteovejuna, directed by Atahualpa del Cioppo. As a member of the National Theater Company, he went on to perform in productions including Pedro y el capitán and La visita de la vieja dama, becoming part of Costa Rica’s long theater tradition.

He also worked extensively behind the scenes, directing plays and training young actors in university classrooms. On screen, he appeared in Costa Rican films including Caribe and Buscando a Marcos Ramírez. In 2004 he returned to Chilean television for a new run of telenovelas, among them Brujas, Descarado and Papi Ricky. The roles introduced him to a new generation of viewers in the country where his career began.

The Universidad Nacional (UNA) honored Perucci with the Universidad Nacional Medal, its highest institutional distinction, which he received alongside his wife, the writer and actress Arabella Salaverry. Culture and Youth Minister Jorge Rodríguez said he had just learned of the death of a leading figure of Costa Rican theater and television. He extended his condolences to Perucci’s family, friends and the country’s arts community.

A wake is scheduled for today from 4 p.m. at the Funeraria del Magisterio, with a memorial Mass planned for Thursday at the San Juan Bosco church, according to arrangements announced by his family. The time of the Mass had not yet been confirmed. Reflecting on his life in Costa Rica in a past interview, Perucci said he would run out of years before he could fully thank Costa Rica for everything it had given him, as an artist and as a person.

World.title: Women in Costa Rica Can Now Choose a Female Uber Driver
World.content:
Women who use Uber in Costa Rica can now ask to be driven by another woman. The company launched the option, called Uber Mujeres, yesterday. It is rolling out gradually across the Greater Metropolitan Area this week and works only with UberX for now. If you don’t see it in your app yet, that’s why.

There is a catch since Uber says availability depends on how many women drivers are connected when you make your request, so a match isn’t guaranteed. You can use the option in three ways. Choose Uber Mujeres when you request a ride right away, if it appears in your app. Book a trip in advance through the app’s reservation feature, or set it as your default so the app prioritizes women drivers on future trips.

To set it as your default, open the app, go to Account and scroll to your ride preferences. In the Spanish-language version of the app, the setting reads “Prefiero viaje con socias colaboradoras,” meaning you prefer trips with women drivers. The size of the pool is the real limit. Women make up more than 10% of Uber’s active drivers in Costa Rica, according to the company, and its press office puts their number at roughly 3,400 to 4,000.

Uber says the number of active women drivers has grown more than 272% over the past five years. Even so, most people driving for the platform in Latin America are men. Laura Santillán, Uber’s general manager for Costa Rica, Panama and the Caribbean, said in an interview that the company aims to raise the share of women drivers to 20% within five years.

The company says the idea grew out of Uber Ellas, a feature launched in 2020 that lets women drivers choose to take trips only with women passengers. Santillán said that experience, along with feedback from riders, led Uber to give women passengers the same choice. Before the launch, Uber surveyed a group of its women users in Costa Rica. According to the company, 90% said a woman-driver option was very or somewhat important, and 95% said offering it showed Uber was listening to women’s needs.

Respondents said they would be most likely to use it for trips at night, when traveling alone and on longer rides. Uber has not published the survey’s sample size or methodology. Costa Rica is the sixth country in Latin America to get Uber Mujeres, the company said. It is the latest addition to an app that already lets you book Costa Rica’s red taxis.

Ride-hailing apps still operate in Costa Rica without a law written specifically for them. A bill to regulate platforms such as Uber and DiDi remains before the Legislative Assembly, years after the apps reshaped the taxi market. Uber has not said when Uber Mujeres will reach areas outside the Greater Metropolitan Area or other ride types beyond UberX.

World.title: Teachers Strike Today as 11 Groups March Through Downtown San José
World.content:
If you plan to drive, ride a bus or walk through downtown San José this morning, expect delays. Teachers’ unions and public universities are holding a one-day strike today with a march from Parque La Merced to the Legislative Assembly. The march is set to leave La Merced at 9 a.m., according to the Ministry of Public Education (MEP) and several of the organizing groups. One union call puts the gathering at 10 a.m., so crowds may build over the whole morning.

The route crosses the city center to the Plaza de la Democracia, in front of Congress. No official road closures had been announced by early Wednesday. Plan for slow traffic on the main avenues through the center and around the Plaza de la Democracia from mid-morning until the crowd disperses. If you can, avoid the area or give yourself extra time, much as you would have during last month’s university march.

Eleven unions and education groups have backed the strike, including the main teachers’ unions ANDE, APSE and SEC, university staff unions and the teachers’ professional association, Colypro. The University of Costa Rica and the National University (UNA) have authorized staff and students to take part. The National Technical University (UTN) has called on its students and staff to join.

Organizers say the 2027 budget falls far short of the constitutional target of 8% of GDP for education. APSE puts next year’s education spending at 4.9% of GDP. Unions are also demanding unpaid salary adjustments and payment of what the state owes the teachers’ pension fund, Jupema.

APSE says that pension debt still tops 44,000 million colones (about $97.6 million), even after a 30,000 million colón payment (about $66.5 million) announced by the MEP. The union also says about 50,000 million colones ($110.9 million) is missing from the 2027 budget to cover pension obligations.

Universities have their own grievance. Lawmakers approved a cut of 8,048 million colones (about $17.8 million) to the Special Fund for Higher Education (FEES) for 2027, part of the dispute that drove thousands into the streets in October. The National Rectors’ Council (CONARE) and the public universities say that money is part of 62,590 million colones (about $138.8 million) postponed in 2020 and 2021 that the government agreed to repay in installments, and that the first installment has not been paid.

University budgets also pay for public services outside the classroom, such as round-the-clock tsunami monitoring. Education Minister Leonardo Sánchez has rejected the unions’ arguments, saying their motives are more political than technical. He said that if classes are suspended, the ministry will ask the Attorney General’s Office (PGR) within 24 hours to seek a court ruling on whether the strike is legal.

If you have children in public school, the MEP has ordered all schools to stay open today. Schools must keep cleaning and security staff on duty and continue serving meals and special-education services, the ministry said. Whether your child’s teacher works depends on the school, so check with the school directly.

The strike comes as the government looks for savings across the board, with a revenue shortfall of $882 million squeezing courts, police and schools. Public schools have also lost 180,000 students in five years. The fight now moves to the final vote on the 2027 budget, which the Constitutional Chamber has barred lawmakers from approving in second debate before Nov. 29. Whatever happens on the streets today, that vote will decide how much money schools, universities and courts have to work with next year.

World.title: A Quiet Island Escape in Costa Rica’s Gulf of Nicoya
World.content:
A three-hour journey and a short boat ride from my home in Costa Rica took me somewhere that felt much farther away. Isla Jesusita sits in the Gulf of Nicoya near Paquera, surrounded by forested hills, calm water and small islands crowded with birds. I went there for two nights at Isla Chiquita Glamping Hotel, expecting a comfortable little escape.

What I found was one of those places where the surroundings quickly became more important than the accommodation.My arrival was gray, misty and cooler than I expected. I had pictured bright tropical sunshine, but the hills were wrapped in clouds and the Gulf had an almost rainforest feel. I immediately wished I had packed a light jacket.

A few hours later, the rain stopped and the sky produced one of the most beautiful sunsets I have seen in Costa Rica. By the next morning, the water was calm and the sun was shining. I liked the changeability of it. Nothing felt staged. The island seemed to shift with the weather.

The setting reminded me of Tsowa Safari Island, a tented camp where I stayed on the Zambezi River near Victoria Falls. Obviously, the Gulf of Nicoya is very different from the Zambezi, but the feeling was remarkably similar. In both places, I felt as though I was staying inside the landscape rather than looking at it from a conventional hotel.

My air-conditioned canvas tent was comfortable without separating me from what was happening outside. I could hear the sounds of the island, walk down to the water within minutes and spend much of the day outdoors. The property is small enough that it never felt crowded during my stay, which became one of the things I appreciated most.

The beach itself is not the kind of broad white-sand beach people often picture when they think about Costa Rica. It is smaller and quieter, and I found myself paying attention to things I might normally have walked past. At low tide, for example, the wet sand was covered with elaborate flower- and fern-like patterns created by tiny crabs feeding beneath the surface. At first, I wasn’t quite sure what I was looking at. Once I realized what was making them, I kept stopping to examine the patterns.

There is also a forest trail through the island. I had intended to explore it, but after the rain, I took one look at the mud, exposed roots and steeper sections and reconsidered. I had brought water shoes rather than proper walking shoes, so the beach won. It was a good reminder that glamping does not necessarily mean every part of the experience is manicured.

One of my favorite parts of the stay was actually how little I felt I needed to do. I slept incredibly well. One morning, I woke around five to the sound of howler monkeys somewhere in the distance and stayed in bed listening to them for a while. Eventually, I wandered down for breakfast and spent much of the morning simply enjoying the water and the quiet.

That pace worked particularly well for me as a solo traveler. There was enough privacy that I could disappear with a book or walk by myself, but I never felt isolated. The excursions provided natural opportunities to meet other people without requiring me to organize my trip around a group.

I met a couple from Austin on a sunset cruise through the Gulf. As we traveled among the small islands and rocky shoreline, we watched frigatebirds circling overhead, large groups of birds filling the trees and bright red crabs clinging to the rocks. Then the sky began to change. Orange, pink and lavender spread across the water while the islands became dark silhouettes. Every few minutes, the colors shifted again. I have lived in Costa Rica long enough to know that the country does spectacular sunsets very well, but this one was exceptional.

Later that evening, we went back onto the water for a bioluminescence excursion. We were given nets to move through the water, triggering flashes of light from the tiny organisms below the surface. The glowing water was fascinating, but what surprised me just as much was the sky. Away from the brighter lights, the stars were spectacular. For a few minutes, there was light above me and light below me.

That was probably my favorite moment of the trip. The Gulf of Nicoya does not always get the attention given to Costa Rica’s more famous beach destinations. That may be part of its appeal. From the water, the landscape feels less like a beach resort corridor and more like a collection of islands, forest, fishing communities and stretches of undeveloped coastline.

It also felt refreshingly uncrowded. There were no lines, no packed beaches and none of the sense that everyone was competing for the same photograph. The experience was quieter and more intimate than that. For travelers interested in making a similar trip, Isla Chiquita is located on Isla Jesusita near Paquera. Guests arriving from the Guanacaste side travel by road to a mainland meeting point at Punta Cuchillos, where a small hotel boat provides the final transfer to the island. The boat ride is short, but it creates a definite psychological break between the mainland and the stay.

My two-night air-conditioned tent stay, including breakfast, cost $460. My share of the sunset cruise and bioluminescence excursion brought my accommodation-and-activity total to a little over $556 before additional meals, drinks and incidentals. Those were the prices during my November 2026 visit and should be checked directly before planning a trip.

I would also pack differently next time. Comfortable walking shoes would make the forest trail much more practical, particularly during the rainy season, and I would bring a light sweater or jacket. Costa Rica may be tropical, but an evening on the water after rain can feel surprisingly cool.

I would return, but not because Isla Jesusita offers a checklist of things to do. In fact, almost the opposite was true. What I enjoyed was waking to monkeys, watching the tide expose tiny signs of life on the beach, seeing islands filled with birds and sitting on the water as the sky changed color. It gave me the scenery and solitude I wanted, but enough interaction with other travelers that being there alone never felt lonely.

Sometimes a short trip does not need to be packed with activities to feel like an adventure. Sometimes it is enough to go somewhere quiet and pay attention.

About the Author

Jennifer Pietrzak-Wahl is a retired technology executive and solo traveler living in Costa Rica. She writes about independent travel, immersive experiences and the practical realities of exploring the world later in life. Her travels have taken her from safari camps in Africa to the Scottish Highlands and islands throughout the Caribbean, with a particular interest in experiences that combine culture, nature and a strong sense of place.

World.title: Costa Rica Has Seized 74 Tons of Drugs This Year, a Total the US Calls Historic
World.content:
Costa Rican police have seized more than 74 metric tons of drugs so far in 2026, according to the government, a total the United States Embassy described as historic and higher than in previous years. The figure was released Monday after President Laura Fernández held a security meeting at the US Embassy in Pavas, in western San José, with Ambassador Melinda Hildebrand, embassy political and counternarcotics officials, and representatives of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

The session resumed the meetings of what the Presidency calls its “Fuerza Élite,” a group of senior security officials that the president convenes weekly to review the country’s security situation. According to the Presidency, the discussion covered drug seizures, coordinated operations against drug trafficking and strategies to dismantle transnational criminal groups.

Photos released by the Presidency showed Foreign Minister Ana Elena Pinto, Public Security Minister Gerald Campos, Justice and Peace Minister Gabriel Aguilar and Communication Minister Arnold Zamora at the meeting. The government did not announce any new operations, agreements or funding.

The US Embassy credited Costa Rican police and security forces for the seizures and said Washington would keep supporting the country, adding that neither side could afford to let its guard down. The government linked the results to Costa Rica’s participation in the Coalition Against Cartels of the Americas and the Shield of the Americas, two regional security frameworks it joined this year.

Costa Rica backed a regional security declaration in March and a multilateral declaration in September that included migration restrictions and mechanisms to freeze criminal assets, according to the government.

The meeting followed the interception of a fast boat in the South Pacific on Sunday night. The Ministry of Public Security said officers from its Special Operations Group and the Coast Guard, supported by a US aircraft, stopped the vessel about 41 nautical miles (76 kilometers or 47 miles) southwest of Sierpe de Osa.

Two Colombian men, aged 55 and 52, and a 38-year-old Ecuadorian man were detained, according to the ministry. The unflagged boat, about 9.75 meters (32 feet) long with two outboard motors and satellite communications equipment, was taken to Golfito. The Drug Control Police will determine the type and quantity of the suspected cargo, and the ministry has not said what legal measures it will seek against the suspects.

Days earlier, authorities seized marijuana off Punta Burica, near the Panama border, and detained two Ecuadorian nationals. The growing volume has also strained the country’s ability to dispose of what it seizes. In late September, the two governments announced that a US military plane would carry 45 tons of seized drugs to the United States for destruction because the country lacked the capacity to incinerate them.

Security cooperation with Washington has deepened under the Fernández administration. The president has said that US ground operations would benefit national security. Hildebrand, who arrived in Costa Rica as ambassador in January, hosted Monday’s session. Officials have presented the record seizures as evidence that joint operations are working. The larger figure also reflects how much cocaine continues to move along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast toward North American and European markets, a flow authorities have tied to much of the country’s violence in recent years.

World.title: Costa Rica Can’t Build Its Way Out of Traffic, Public Works Minister Says
World.content:
Costa Rica has spent decades underinvesting in its road network, and the gap has pushed Costa Rica’s traffic problems well beyond long commutes, Public Works and Transport Minister Efraím Zeledón said this week. Zeledón acknowledged that Costa Rica has not put enough money into roads to keep pace with the growth in vehicles, leaving a deficit that has built up over several decades. He argued, however, that wider highways alone will not solve the problem.

No country has managed to end its congestion by adding lanes, the minister said, because more road capacity draws more drivers. Transport planners call this induced demand, and Zeledón cited it as the reason the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) is betting on trains, buses and digital mobility platforms rather than road expansion alone.

He also pointed to a newer pressure on the network. The exchange rate has pushed vehicle prices down sharply, Zeledón said, making it easy for more people to buy a car or motorcycle and adding traffic to roads that were already over capacity. The cost of congestion is showing up in the workplace. A recent study by the Federation of Chambers of Commerce of the Central American Isthmus (FECAMCO), based on consultations in five cities across the region, found that 60% of workers said a company’s location influences whether they accept or keep a job. About one in four, or 24%, had considered changing jobs because of commuting problems.

Employers described similar strain. Half of the business owners consulted said mobility conditions or their company’s location had made it harder to attract or retain staff, and eight in ten identified added costs tied to those problems. Seven in ten participants overall reported a moderate or high impact on their family, personal or rest time. In the Greater Metropolitan Area, where daily commutes link San José, Heredia, Alajuela and Cartago, those hours on the road come directly out of time for work, study and family.

The government’s main bet is the electric passenger train known as Tibi, which Zeledón has described as the backbone of a future public transport network and which authorities aim to have 80% complete by 2030. The project still faces hurdles, including more than 400 buildings that sit in its right of way.

MOPT is also exploring a cable car that would connect southern San José areas such as Desamparados and Aserrí with the future train. Zeledón has said the ministry is seeking financing for the prefeasibility and pre-investment studies needed to determine whether the project is viable. The minister framed the task ahead as recovering years of lost investment while building a public transport system reliable enough that commuters choose it over their own vehicles.

World.title: ATP Finals 2026 Set for Turin Without Sinner as Four Newcomers Join Field
World.content:
The 2026 ATP Finals will begin Sunday, November 15, with a different look from recent years. World No. 1 Alexander Zverev leads an eight-player field that includes Carlos Alcaraz, two Americans and four first-time qualifiers, while defending champion Jannik Sinner will miss the season-ending tournament because of a knee injury.

The tournament runs through November 22 at the Inalpi Arena in Turin, bringing together the season’s leading players for one of the most prestigious titles outside the Grand Slams. With the field now confirmed, attention turns to Thursday’s group draw and the opening matches this weekend.

Sinner’s absence is the biggest change. The Italian, who won the ATP Finals in 2024 and 2025, has not competed since capturing his fifth Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in July. Speaking at a press conference in Milan on Tuesday, November 10, Sinner said he hopes to return for the 2027 Australian Open but will not rush his recovery. He is following medical advice and wants to protect his long-term career rather than risk returning too soon. His withdrawal means Turin will crown a different champion this year and removes one of the tournament’s leading attractions, particularly for Italian fans.

Zverev enters as the highest-ranked player and one of the most experienced competitors in the field. The German has won the ATP Finals twice, in 2018 and 2021, and will be making his ninth appearance at the year-end championships. Alcaraz arrives with renewed confidence after defeating Ben Shelton in Sunday’s Paris Masters final. The Spaniard, who reached the ATP Finals championship match in 2025, is still chasing his first title at the event.

Daniil Medvedev, the 2020 champion, is the other former winner competing this year. For American tennis, the tournament offers another opportunity to end a long wait for a champion. Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will both compete in Turin, marking the second consecutive season that two Americans have qualified.

Shelton returns for his second appearance, while the 28-year-old Tiafoe makes his debut. No American has won the singles championship since Pete Sampras in 1999. The remaining newcomers bring several compelling stories. Italy’s Flavio Cobolli will make his first ATP Finals appearance in front of a home crowd after a breakthrough season that included reaching the French Open final.

France’s Arthur Fils becomes the first Frenchman to qualify for the tournament since Gael Monfils in 2016. Fils won titles in Barcelona and Cincinnati during a season that established him among the leading young players on the ATP Tour. Perhaps the most unexpected qualifier is Spain’s Rafael Jodar, who was still playing college tennis at the University of Virginia a year ago.

Jodar, 20, began the season outside the established elite but climbed high enough in the ATP Race to secure the final position in Turin. He follows Alcaraz in progressing from the Next Gen ATP Finals to the season-ending championship the following year. The ATP Finals use a format different from regular tournaments. The eight singles players are divided into two groups of four, with each competitor playing three round-robin matches. The top two players from each group advance to the semifinals.

The format allows a player to lose a match during the group stage and still compete for the championship. There is also considerable prize money at stake. The tournament carries a total purse of $15.75 million, with an undefeated singles champion eligible to earn $5.171 million. The group draw is scheduled for Thursday, November 12, and will determine the opening matchups. Round-robin play begins Sunday, November 15, followed by the semifinals on November 21 and the championship match on November 22.

With Sinner sidelined, Zverev seeking a third title, Alcaraz chasing his first and half the field making its debut, this year’s ATP Finals offer a different mix of established champions and emerging contenders.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard stands ground as Guatemalan military presence reported in Sarstoon
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard stands ground as Guatemalan military presence reported in Sarstoon

By Zoila Palma: New footage obtained by Breaking Belize News reportedly shows several Belize Coast Guard vessels facing off with Guatemalan Armed Forces (GAF) personnel in the Sarstoon River this morning.

The footage shows Belize Coast Guard vessels operating in close proximity to an apparent Guatemalan military vessel, with Belize appearing to have a significantly larger security presence on the water. The reported encounter comes amid heightened tensions following Saturday’s confrontation between Belizean and Guatemalan military personnel.

The latest development comes just one day after Belize Coast Guard Commandant Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis delivered a stern message to Coast Guard personnel, emphasizing that Belize’s sovereignty must be defended. “Any belligerent force that threatens Belize’s sovereignty will be confronted with military professionalism, courage, discipline, and absolutely no fear,” Soberanis declared. He further assured personnel, “We will stand firm, united, and resolute in the defence of our nation and its sovereign interests.”

The increased security presence follows Saturday’s confrontation, during which Guatemalan military personnel reportedly rammed a vessel carrying Belize Defence Force (BDF) soldiers.

The incident prompted Belize to reinforce its security presence in the Sarstoon. National Security Chief Executive Officer Retired Major Francis Usher confirmed on Tuesday that additional Coast Guard and BDF vessels and personnel remained deployed in the area, with further reinforcements positioned nearby.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has reiterated that Belize’s sovereignty and territorial integrity must be protected.

World.title: International News: El Salvador’s military destroys headquarters of major Haitian gang in anti-crime operation
World.content:
International News: El Salvador’s military destroys headquarters of major Haitian gang in anti-crime operation

By Zoila Palma: El Salvador’s military has helped destroy the reported headquarters of one of Haiti’s largest criminal gangs during an operation in Port-au-Prince, according to Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele.

The target was a two-storey property allegedly connected to the 400 Mawozo gang, a notorious criminal organization known for mass kidnappings and extortion, The Telegraph reports.

Bukele confirmed the attack in a post on X, stating, “We destroyed the house of Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang’s headquarters.” He also shared video footage showing helicopters striking a large compound in the Croix-des-Bouquets suburb, considered a stronghold of the gang.

The operation follows El Salvador’s deployment of more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti last month as part of efforts to support the fight against escalating gang violence. The deployment was initially linked to a mission to rescue four kidnapped Salvadoran Air Force personnel who were part of the United Nations-approved Gang Suppression Force (GSF).

According to reports, the attack took place on Sunday and was carried out by a Haitian police task force supported by Salvadoran troops.

Footage shared by Bukele showed individuals fleeing the compound on foot and motorcycles as helicopters circled overhead. The Salvadoran president criticized those who fled, calling them “cowards” for not “even trying to fight.”

The gang’s leader, Wilson Joseph, known by the alias “Lanmò Sanjou,” was reportedly not present at the property during the operation.

Joseph is under United States and United Nations sanctions over alleged human rights abuses, including disrupting humanitarian aid, sexual violence and recruiting children.

The 400 Mawozo gang gained international attention in 2021 after abducting 16 American missionaries and a Canadian national, including children, who were eventually released unharmed after a ransom was reportedly paid.

Haiti’s Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé praised Bukele and the Salvadoran forces for their support in the campaign against criminal gangs. “Hats off to President Nayib Bukele… for your support and commitment to the national fight against gangs,” he wrote on X.

World.title: Belize and European Union explore new investment and development opportunities
World.content:
Belize and European Union explore new investment and development opportunities

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Economic Transformation Dr. Osmond Martinez met with representatives of the European Union (EU) to discuss ongoing cooperation and explore opportunities to support Belize’s national development priorities. The meeting focused on strengthening bilateral relations, mobilizing development financing and identifying initiatives that can contribute to sustainable economic growth and climate resilience.

The EU delegation included Valerio Diaz Martin, Head of Partnerships at the Delegation of the European Union to Jamaica, Belize and The Bahamas, and Elizabeth Mary Lanzi Mazzochini, Head of Office in Belize.

Also participating were Karlene McSweeney, Acting Director of the Climate Finance Unit (EU and Other Grants), and Jason Middleton, Senior Project Officer.

Among the key matters discussed was the EU’s operational reorganization, including the establishment of the Barbados Hub to support projects in Belize, while the EU Delegation in Jamaica will continue serving as the focal point for Belize-EU cooperation.

Discussions also addressed the EU’s electric bus proposal and potential investment and financing opportunities through the Global Gateway initiative and the European Investment Bank (EIB).

The meeting further examined the programming of the second tranche of funding for 2025–2027 under the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI) 2021–2027.

World.title: A lifeline for wildlife: Belize completes Maya Forest Corridor with 3,500+ acres
World.content:
A lifeline for wildlife: Belize completes Maya Forest Corridor with 3,500+ acres

By Zoila Palma: Belize has reached a historic milestone in its forest conservation efforts with the addition of more than 3,500 acres of land to the Belize Maya Forest Corridor Trust, completing a protected connection between important wildlife habitats in Central Belize.

The achievement was announced on November 6, 2026, by the Ministry of Natural Resources, Petroleum and Mining, in partnership with the Belize Maya Forest Corridor Trust. The newly incorporated lands connect the Labouring Creek Jaguar Corridor Wildlife Sanctuary with the Manatee Forest Reserve, strengthening the Maya Forest Corridor and providing a more continuous protected landscape for wildlife.

The milestone represents years of collaboration among the Government of Belize, conservation organizations, landowners and local communities to safeguard the country’s natural heritage.

Minister of Sustainable Development Orlando Habet highlighted the regional significance of the corridor, noting that it contributes to a wider conservation vision shared by Belize, Guatemala and Mexico under the Calakmul Biocultural Declaration. “Beyond our national commitments, the Maya Forest Corridor contributes to our shared regional vision under the Calakmul Biocultural Declaration,” Habet said. He emphasized the importance of cooperation across borders, stating, “Forests do not recognize political boundaries.” Habet added, “The Maya Forest Corridor demonstrates that conservation and sustainable development can advance together.” He also stressed the importance of ensuring local participation, saying, “Communities must be recognized as partners in the corridor’s management and governance, with meaningful opportunities to participate in decisions and benefit from its conservation.”

Minister of Natural Resources Cordel Hyde also expressed pride in the achievement, pointing to the importance of protecting Belize’s forests at a time when conservation commitments are facing challenges globally. “All over the world, developed countries are failing to deliver on their conservation commitments,” Hyde said. He added, “So I’m mighty proud of this that is happening today and to be a part of this initiative to do our small part.” Reflecting on the significance of completing the protected connection, Hyde stated, “To finally connect this corridor and make it complete and in this process honor our ancestors.”

He further explained the purpose of the land arrangement, emphasizing, “This is not a sale, this is a vesting for conservation purposes.” Hyde explained that the newly incorporated lands are being secured on behalf of the people of Belize to prevent future governments or ministers from alienating them for other purposes, as has happened in the past.

Celso Poot, Managing Director of TBZ, described the corridor as critical to the survival and movement of wildlife in Central Belize. “The Maya Forest Corridor is the last hope. It is the last piece of forested area in Central Belize where animals are moving safely.” He explained that the corridor consists of different land uses and human activities, making connectivity particularly important for wildlife. “The Maya Forest Corridor is a mixed landscape. We have agriculture, we have protected forests, we have savannah, we have resources, we have roads, we have communities. What we know and what we see is that animals avoid people, avoid disturbances in space and in time.”

Dr. Elma Kay, Chairman of the Maya Forest Corridor Trust Board, recalled that growing land clearing and changes to the landscape prompted increased research into whether the natural connection remained intact. “What we started seeing at the time, I would say about 2012, 2010, was that there was a lot of clearing that was happening, a lot of transformation of the area, and so this triggered more and more research in the area to try and understand whether the connection was still intact.” She also highlighted the importance of wildlife to Belize’s identity and tourism industry, stating, “Many of the animals of the corridor are part of Belize’s iconic biodiversity, but they are also symbols of our natural heritage, and they are part of what feeds our tourism industry because people come to see those animals.”

Prime Minister John Briceño noted that the development of the Maya Forest Corridor is linked to Belize’s broader efforts to strengthen its protected areas network. “We came up with the National Protected Areas Policy and System Plan, and from that plan we realized there has to be some kind of corridor that connects the north to the west and to the south to be able to have this connectivity within our protected areas.”

Deputy Prime Minister Cordel Hyde also reflected on the responsibility to preserve the country’s natural resources for future generations. “They say every generation has a responsibility to make life better for the generation that comes after, and so this initiative excites me. The benefits of this is that we get an opportunity to leave something intact, preserve something for future generations-for our children and their children and their children.”

The Belize Maya Forest Corridor Trust includes the Belize Zoo and Tropical Education Center, WCS Belize, the Foundation for Wildlife Conservation and the Environmental Research Institute of the University of Belize.

World.title: Attorney Smith says Belize should switch since China poised to overtake the U.S. as economic giant
World.content:
Attorney Smith says Belize should switch since China poised to overtake the U.S. as economic giant

By Zoila Palma: Following the revocation of his U.S. visa, Attorney Godfrey Smith said that he believes his U.S. visa was cancelled due to his ties with China.

Smith said that he had met with officials of China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and arranged a visitor programs for Belizean journalists and academia professionals.

During an interview with 7news Belize, Smith said that he believes Belize should switch diplomatic relations from Taiwan to China because he says China is poised to overtake the U.S. as an economic giant.

“And may I just at this point, too-because I know what social media is like-I do not get paid by the Chinese government to do this. So this is strictly out of belief, policy belief, philosophical belief, ideological belief that this is the way to go, and people should come… Belizeans should be aware of what China means and represents.

Why have diplomatic relations with a little district or a province of a giant superpower poised to overtake the United States as the economic and military giant in the future, if not already?,” Smith said.

Smith has indicated that he does not intend to reapply for a U.S. visa.

World.title: Ministry of Health and Wellness urges vaccination to protect against Measles
World.content:
Ministry of Health and Wellness urges vaccination to protect against Measles

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health and Wellness is urging everyone to take the necessary steps to protect themselves, their families, and their communities from measles through vaccination and early medical care.

As of November 2, 2026, the Ministry reported 19 cases of Measles with 4 being in the Cayo District in October.

“Measles is highly contagious and can spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.

Vaccination is the best protection against measles. Ensure you and your family are up to date with your vaccinations.

Protect yourself. Protect your family. Protect Belize,” the Ministry said.

Symptoms usually start between 7 and 21 days after contact with an infected person. The illness begins with high fever, runny nose, red eyes, and a rash that starts at the hairline, spreads down to the chest, back, and limbs, and then to the rest of the body. Persons are contagious 4 days before and 4 days after the rash appears.

Measles is preventable through the Measles, Mumps and Rubella (MMR) vaccination.

The Ministry says that the MMR vaccine is safe and highly effective, with two doses providing lifetime immunity.

World.title: Halo BPO is hiring Belize’s best talkers
World.content:
Halo BPO is hiring Belize’s best talkers

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Some people can talk to anyone. They walk into a room full of strangers and leave with three new friends. If that sounds like you, Halo BPO wants to hear from you.

The company is expanding its Belize operation and recruiting remote sales agents for its newest campaign. It says the quality it screens hardest for is one that never shows up on a resume.

“The product we can teach you in a week,” the company said. “What we cannot teach you is what happens in the first ten seconds of a call. You either have that or you don’t.”

Halo BPO is looking for people with vibrant personalities who can sell confidently over the phone. That means agents who are remembered after one conversation, who can hear the word no without losing their footing, and who can make a stranger laugh before making an offer.

Experience still matters. Candidates need at least two years in sales. Credit repair experience is an asset, and applicants who have handled complex customer service and sales campaigns are strongly encouraged to apply.

The role is fully remote. Pay is $9.00 BZD per hour, plus commissions and performance bonuses, paid weekly.

To apply, email your resume to [email protected] with your full name in the subject line.

World.title: Belize pushes for climate finance at COP31 in Türkiye
World.content:
Belize pushes for climate finance at COP31 in Türkiye

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize is making its case for better access to climate funding at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye.

Leroy Martinez, Director of the Climate Finance Unit in the Ministry of Economic Transformation, is attending as part of Belize’s official delegation.

At the conference, Martinez is following negotiations on climate finance, with a focus on helping Belize access and mobilize the resources it needs to carry out its national development and climate priorities.

The Ministry said his participation will stress the importance of accessible, adequate and predictable climate finance to advance the priorities in Plan Belize 2.0, along with Belize’s other national climate change policies, plans and strategies.

Martinez will also hold bilateral meetings with development partners and climate finance stakeholders, and will take part in a panel discussion on opportunities for greater collaboration and climate finance mobilization.

World.title: You said it’: Cardi B calls out Ryan Burke, apologises to Jamaican gov’t
World.content:
Cardi B (Photo: billboard.com)

American rapper Cardi B has apologised to the Jamaican Government after making claims that it had offered to cover the outstanding balance of her performance fee for BZR WKND, which was scheduled to take place from October 16 to 18.

During an Instagram live on Tuesday, the Grammy-winning artiste claimed that event organiser Ryan Burke had sent an email indicating that the Jamaican Government had invested in the festival.

“I want to apologise to the Government of Jamaica… Motherf***s was putting y’all name in the finesse. I got text messages…And in two hours from now, I challenge a motherf**** to call my bluff. Call my bluff. Cause I’m gonna post this email and I’m gonna post this text message where you, Ryan…I got an email from you telling my people, you said it, that the Government invested in the festival, you said it. Now, I dont know if that’s true or not cause like I said, everything was a finesse,” the rapper said.

“It was a finesse from the beginning because you presented the show as a festival and then you presented it as a Cardi B concert cause you was expecting me to pay for the production for the whole festival. You sent an email saying that the Government, you sent it. You did!” she continued.

Cardi B added, “I give you two hours to call my bluff, cause now y’all p*ssing me off.”

Her apology follows a statement from the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport denying any financial involvement in the proposed concert.

The ministry clarified that it had made no commitment or payment towards Cardi B’s appearance fee or any other expenses associated with the event. It further emphasised that BZR WKND was a private commercial engagement in which the Government had no involvement.

The development comes amid an escalating dispute between the Bodak Yellow rapper and the festival’s organisers following her withdrawal from the event.

On Monday, Cardi B threatened legal action against the organisers after reports emerged that they intended to sue her over her cancellation.

BZR WKND Chief Executive Officer Ryan Burke disclosed the organisers’ intention to pursue legal action during an interview this week with CVM News.

The controversy has since intensified, with both parties publicly disputing the circumstances surrounding the rapper’s cancelled performance.

READ: No gov’t funds committed to proposed Cardi B concert, says Ministry

World.title: Stabbed, robbed student loses case against UWI
World.content:
The main entrance to The University of the West Indies, Mona campus. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)
