A student who sued The University of the West Indies (The UWI) for negligence after being robbed and stabbed while studying on the Mona campus 11 years ago, lost his case after a Supreme Court judge found that he failed to provide sufficient evidence that the institution had breached its duty of care or been lax in its security obligations.

According to the evidence in the case, the student was studying at a gazebo between the Confucius Institute and the Carimac Annex Lab on June 29, 2015, when two men came up to him and stole his laptop. They stabbed him twice in his chest and once in his abdomen, about 100 metres from a manned security booth at the campus’s post office entrance which, the student said, was within his line of sight. He said that before he was cut, he was not aware that the attackers were armed.

According to the account of another student, who was a witness in the matter, the two men had first appeared on bikes and called out to them “asking for free Wi-Fi”. She said her colleague responded and the two men rode away but returned on foot some moments later and sat in front of them. She said one of the men then demanded the male student’s laptop. She said when he reached for the laptop to secure it, the man pulled a knife and cut him on his arm while the other man attacked her.

According to her, their attackers then ran. They gave chase. She said while running she saw a friend and “called out to him”. She said they both helped her injured colleague to a vehicle and took him to hospital.

According to the injured male student, he chased the men because the weapon fell and he thought he was out of danger. He further said he did not call out to the security guard stationed at the post office gate, so that individual was unaware of what had transpired.

In his suit, the male student sought to recover damages on the basis that the university did not provide adequate security for its students.

Supreme Court judge Justice Tara Carr, who heard the matter in open court on three dates between June and early November this year, said the issues for determination were whether the university owed a duty of care to the student, either by virtue of statute or at common law in negligence and, if so, whether it breached that duty resulting in injury, loss, or damage to him and whether he was entitled to damages.

The student, in his defence, also relied on a letter from the campus registrar which stated, “As a result of this incident we have revisited and changed the protocols surrounding visitors to the campus who travel on motor bikes. We believe that this will go a far way in preventing incidents of this nature in the future.”

According to Justice Carr, this “tacit admission” was the lynchpin of the case for the student whose attorney argued that “this is sufficient for the court to find that the university did not do all that it could have to prevent the unfortunate incident which occurred”.

However, the university, in its defence, stated that it took reasonable care to ensure the safety of the student by implementing adequate and appropriate security measures.

An expert report and answers to questions posed from criminologist Dr Jason McKay formed a part of the evidence on behalf of the university. In his expert report, McKay stated that the university’s property is approximately 650 acres, with 67 security guards deployed at night on the campus which, he said, was, by any standard, a generous allocation of security personnel. McKay said he found that the property was secure and had security personnel posted at the entrances while noting that a property of this nature and size cannot facilitate a close protection security detail. He opined that the security arrangements at the university on the date of the incident were adequate and could be functional if all persons adhered to the directives as stated in the handbook.

Meanwhile, retired Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Marlon Nesbeth, who is campus security manager, in his evidence, outlined that the university maintains a structured security system tailored to ensure the safety of all staff, students, and visitors to the campus. He said at the time of the incident the security team was comprised of 20 cops at the Mona Police Post and 200 security guards strategically stationed around the campus.

Furthermore, he said the university has designated areas for students outside of the operational hours of the campus, which are equipped with surveillance cameras and are well-lit. He also noted that the faculties have a security presence until 10:00 pm and the main library has 24-hour security.

Said Justice Carr: “There is no allegation that the physical conditions of the university caused the incident; neither can it be said that the university failed in its duty, whether by things done or undone, to provide a safe environment for all students to include [the student who was robbed and stabbed].”

“It is fair to say, based on the evidence, that the university provided spaces that were secure and safe for students to study throughout the day and night. The deployment of security guards and the erection of security posts over a 24-hour period is also accepted. The evidence [of the student] confirmed that there was a patrol that passed shortly before the incident. There is no evidence that contradicts these factual findings. Nor is there any evidence to suggest that the arrangements made by the university are insufficient or inadequate,” she noted further.

In disposing of the matter, Justice Carr said: “There is evidence to suggest… that the university employed several strategies to combat the rising level of crime on the Mona campus.”

Pointing out that it was the duty of the student’s attorneys to “put forward evidence to contradict this, or at the very least, to suggest that there were alternative options or arrangements that would have increased the security measures on the campus”, she said the claimant “did not provide the court with any evidence to support his case that the university did not do all that was reasonable in the circumstances to secure the campus and to provide a safe environment for all students”.

Said Justice Carr, in ruling in favour of the university, “The combination of the security measures outlined by Mr Nesbeth, the student handbook, and the warnings given are reasonable methods to prevent criminal activity at the university. [This student’s] injuries are a direct result of criminal conduct which, in our society, unfortunately is far too commonplace. I cannot say, however, that, based on the evidence as presented, the university was negligent or that they breached their statutory duty under the Act. In the round, therefore, I find that the claim has not been proved to the requisite standard and judgment is entered for the defendant.”

World.title: Swaby hits back
World.content:
SWABY... I have observed that Minister of Works Robert Nesta Morgan has developed what appears to be a rather special interest in the affairs of the KSAMC, and in me personally.

KINGSTON Mayor Andrew Swaby has challenged Works Minister Robert Morgan to acknowledge the funding challenges facing municipal corporations across Jamaica, arguing that the deteriorating state of the country’s roads cannot be blamed on local authorities without recognising the inadequate resources available to them.

Swaby, speaking at Tuesday’s sitting of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation monthly meeting, continued his public joust with Morgan, accusing him of singling out the Opposition-led corporation for criticism while appearing to overlook similar difficulties facing municipalities controlled by the governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP).

“I have observed that Minister of Works Robert Nesta Morgan has developed what appears to be a rather special interest in the affairs of the KSAMC, and in me personally. Judging from how frequently he speaks about the KSAMC, one would assume that he was given the responsibility for local government. I trust that Minister [of Local Government Desmond] McKenzie has been advised of this apparent expansion of his colleague’s responsibility,” Swaby commented, drawing murmurs of agreement and chuckles from councillors within the chamber.

“What I find particularly interesting, however, is that I have heard little from Minister Morgan about the challenges facing municipal corporations led by his own party,” he continued.

Swaby’s scrutiny comes as a direct response to Morgan’s September media comments, in which the works minister claimed the KSAMC was not doing enough to effect change on municipal roads.

At the time, Morgan admitted that several major thoroughfares in the Corporate Area were in need of repair but argued that many, including South Avenue, Lindsay Crescent and Beechwood Avenue, are municipal corporation roads and are to be fixed by the KSAMC.

“For example, most of the roads that the Government has fixed in Kingston and St Andrew are not NWA (National Works Agency) roads, they are KSAMC (Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation) roads, and before this new mayor [Andrew Swaby] came in, the Parochial Revenue Fund was about $700 million a year; it is now over $1 billion, and we have not seen a commensurate increase in the allocation for repairing roads,” Morgan told the Jamaica Observer.

But on Tuesday, Swaby argued that the challenges facing the KSAMC were not unique, pointing out that discussions with JLP mayors and councillors had revealed widespread concerns about insufficient funding for road maintenance and other necessary services.

“They too are struggling with inadequate resources to maintain roads and provide essential services to their municipalities. Some may not enjoy the same freedom to speak publicly about these difficulties, but their silence should not be mistaken for the absence of concern. So I would encourage Minister Morgan to turn some of his attention to those municipalities. He may discover that the concerns I have raised are shared by many of my colleagues on his side,” urged Swaby.

The mayor further questioned how Morgan could expect the KSAMC to adequately address its decrepit road network when the Government’s $40-billion Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to our Road Network (SPARK) programme was insufficient to rehabilitate all roads requiring attention nationally.

“Nobody expects the SPARK programme to fix every road in Jamaica. So if $40 billion cannot address all our road rehabilitation needs, how does Minister Morgan expect the KSAMC to do so with the meagre resources at his disposal?” he asked.

The mayor explained that during the 2025-2026 financial year, the corporation received an average $85 million monthly from the parochial revenue fund (PRF) which must finance not only road maintenance but also drain cleaning, and de-bushing across its 40 divisions.

According to Swaby, rehabilitating a single kilometre of parochial road, approximately 6.5 metres wide, costs about $40 million.

With more than 100 kilometres of roads requiring attention across Kingston and St Andrew, Swaby said a project of that magnitude would require at the very least a supportive budget of $4 billion.

“If that programme were to be undertaken in over 12 months, it would require an expenditure of an average of $333 million every month. Compare that with $85 million we received monthly from the Parochial Revenue Fund in the last financial year, which must also cover drain cleaning, de-bushing and other things. The difference is substantial. It illustrates the inadequacy of the present financial arena,” remarked Swaby.

He maintained that no amount of administrative efficiency could overcome the existing funding shortfall, stressing that the core issue remains an inadequate budget.

“We can establish a new authority, reorganise existing agencies, and change administrative arrangements under which roads are managed. But unless we confront the underlying financial problem, we risk transferring responsibility for deteriorating roads from one institution to another without providing the resources necessary to improve them. That would hardly constitute meaningful reform,” charged Swaby.

World.title: Brick & Lace lands silver in UK
World.content:
TWENTY-TWO years ago, when they recorded the song Love is Wicked, the members of the sister duo Brick & Lace knew they had a hit on their hands.

Last Friday the song, which blew up on social media platform over the past year thanks to a dance challenge, was certified silver in the United Kingdom by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) for sales and streaming equivalent of 200,000 units.

Love is Wicked is included on the duo’s album of the same name, which was released in 2007 via Geffen Records/180 Entertainment/Kon Live. Nailah “Nyla” Thorbourne of Brick & Lace was unaware of the song’s latest achievement when the Jamaica Observer contacted her on the weekend.

“I feel happy about it. For a long time Love is Wicked never really caught on in the UK the same way it did in certain territories, like France or Sweden, but to know it’s getting its due now in such a big way is very gratifying,” Nyla told the Observer.

Written by Nyla and her siblings Nyanda and Tasha Thorbourne, Love is Wicked was first recorded in 2004 and was featured on Steven “Lenky” Marsden’s inescapable Diwali rhythm.

Three years later, after the duo signed to Geffen, the song was re-recorded and re-released.

“The original version of the song was recorded in Canada but then we re-recorded it in Los Angeles. Lenky Marsden did the original production of the song. Ron Fair [former chairman of Geffen Records], who was head at Geffen at the time when we were signed, took the track and revamped or revised it a bit. We knew the song was special and it was one we always championed for at label,” Nyla explained.

Love is Wicked was a hit locally and earned the duo several awards at the then Youth View Awards, held at the National Indoor Sports Arena.

The song wasn’t a hit in the United States, but it scaled several charts in Europe, including #37 in Belgium, #6 in Finland, #4 in France, #13 in Norway, #27 in Sweden, #63 in Switzerland, and #13 on the Billboard European Hot 100 chart.

“I think we were surprised how big it got in Africa. We knew the song had the makings of a hit record we just didn’t know how big it would spread around the world. The success of the song gave us the opportunity to travel and perform in so many different countries around the world.

We have met prime ministers and have been in the homes of dignitaries,” Nyla recalled.

Love is Wicked has to date sold more than 120,000 units in France.

The song is featured on the Bratz: Motion Picture Soundtrack which was released by Geffen Records. It previously earned gold certifications in France and Portugal.

After Brick & Lace went in hiatus in 2013, the sisters focused on solo projects. Nyanda is in real estate and Nyla is promoting her shapewear line Vlair Shapewear.

Now residing in Florida, Nyla was on the island last week for the coronation of the 2026 Miss Jamaica World pageant. One of the contestants, Skye Gibson Moo Young wore the sash Miss Vlair Shapewear.

Nyla says the duo has reunited and will be releasing new music early next year.

“We are looking to put out some Brick & Lace records probably at the top of the year. For now, I have been mainly focused on promoting my shapewear line Vlair Shapewear and Nyanda has been focused on her real estate. The fans will just have to hear when it comes out. Just know whatever we do it always has that global appeal,” she shared.

World.title: REIT reform gets PM’s ear
World.content:
From left, Kingston Properties CEO Kevin Richards and Chairman Garfield Sinclair greet Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness ahead of Tuesday’s launch of the Rousseau Road Commercial Complex. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

PRIME Minister Dr Andrew Holness says the Government is open to drafting a law for real estate investment trusts (REITs), but any tax breaks would have to generate enough new revenue to offset what the Treasury gives up over the long term.

Holness was responding to a call from Kingston Properties Limited (KPREIT) for a legal framework that would make it easier for pension funds and individual investors to put money into income-producing property. The company made its case on Tuesday at the opening of its Rousseau Road Commercial Complex in Kingston, its first development built from the ground up.

“…at this time you would have to be very careful how we give up certain tax revenues. Not that we wouldn’t create fiscal incentives for it, but we would have to have a very strong guarantee that whatever fiscal incentive regime we create, it is going to be offset by revenues that are coming in,” Holness said, adding that the gains would have to hold over the long term.

“So that is something that we will consider. And I want to give you the assurance that the government is not opposed to setting up, as the leader of the Opposition calls it, bespoke legislation for REITs. Nevertheless, I do believe that there are improvements in the current regulatory environment that can be quickly implemented that would assist real estate development on a large scale,” he continued.

A REIT gives investors a share of the income from properties such as warehouses and offices without having to buy a building themselves.

Kingston Properties already offers that exposure through its listed shares, but Chairman Garfield Sinclair said the company operates under general company and securities laws that were never designed for businesses set up to hold property and distribute the income to thousands of investors.

Sinclair wants a law that would require REITs to pay out most of their income and have that income taxed once, in the hands of investors. He also called for standards on governance, property valuations, borrowing and disclosure, arguing that a regulated source of long-term capital could make clean titles, planning approvals and adequate insurance conditions for financing.

“When development is financed through regulated vehicles, compliance becomes a condition of funding rather than an afterthought. Legislation is therefore not only a capital markets reform, it’s a lever for more compliant and resilient development across Jamaica,” Sinclair said.

“I want to be clear, however, this is not a request just on behalf of Kingston Properties. A proper framework would invite new competitors and we would welcome that. It is a request on behalf of the entire market and of every Jamaican who should be able to own a share of this country’s real estate. We, together with our colleagues right across the industry, stand ready to work with the ministry, Financial Services Commission, and all of the Government members in order to get this done. And I implore you to give us a shot at helping you do this,” he added.

Opposition Leader Mark Golding also made a case for taxing investment income once, though he pointed to a different approach. He cited the Caricom tax agreement as a model under which income is taxed where the enterprise earns it, with shareholders in other member states receiving the distribution without a further layer of tax. Golding said Jamaica should look at such changes over the medium term to improve its competitiveness, while acknowledging that the fallout from Hurricane Melissa and successive quarters of economic contraction make it a difficult time to give up revenue.

Meanwhile, Holness said Jamaica’s existing securities framework already accommodates instruments backed by real estate and that some regulatory changes could be made more quickly. He raised the possibility of requiring REITs to distribute 90 per cent of their profits and said he would consider how those distributions are taxed where the trusts invest in areas of strategic national interest, such as logistics facilities that support the port.

The Prime Minister also suggested that REITs could give owners of idle land a way to retain a financial stake while making the property available for development. An owner could take shares in a trust, he said, and earn a share of the income once the land is put to use. Holness linked that idea to separate plans for legislation to designate business development districts, including tourism districts.

At 11 Rousseau Road, Kingston Properties has built 14 modular units, each with ground-floor warehouse space and an office. The company designed the complex for businesses such as wholesalers, distributors, small manufacturers and courier operators that need to store stock and run their offices from the same address.

Rousseau Road gives Kingston Properties a new way to grow its rental income. The company has typically bought existing buildings, then raised rents, refurbished space or brought in new tenants. At Rousseau Road, it took a greenfield project and built 14 units it can now bring to the leasing market. The company identified spending on the development as one of the reasons group assets rose to US$98.17 million at June 30, up from US$88.84 million a year earlier.

Jamaica remained the largest source of rental income, contributing US$1.66 million, or about 45 per cent of the group total, in the first half of 2026. The Cayman Islands contributed US$1.27 million, while rental income from the United Kingdom rose 78.5 per cent to US$791,394 as properties acquired in 2025 began contributing more. The December purchase of a property in Dartford, England, together with rent increases in Jamaica, helped lift June-quarter rental income by 15.3 per cent to US$1.90 million.

Borrowing has also risen as the portfolio has expanded. Loans payable reached US$39.78 million at June 30, up from US$33.84 million a year earlier, and net finance costs for the first half increased to US$1.13 million from US$941,010. Over the same six months, operating income before other gains rose 28.8 per cent to US$2.61 million, while total comprehensive income fell about 10 per cent to US$1.47 million. The prior-year period benefited from property valuation and disposal gains, and the group recorded a tax charge this year after receiving a tax credit in the comparable period.

— Adittional reporting by Billeane Williams

World.title: Pride over pocket
World.content:
West Indies’ Roston Chase (third left) celebrates with teammates after taking the wicket of India’s Captain Shreyas Lyer (not in picture) during the third T20 international cricket match between India and West Indies at Holkar Cricket Stadium in Indore on October 11. (Photo: AFP)

FORMER West Indies and Jamaica bowlers Daren Powell and Nehemiah Perry believe the current Caribbean players should not allow reduced earnings to negatively affect their performances going forward.

Cricket West Indies’ (CWI) decision to cut the salaries of its men’s and women’s players by 25 per cent officially took effect following the announcement of the proposal in September. The move is one of several initiatives introduced by CWI to address its financial crisis.

As reported by the Jamaica Observer last month, Jamaicans Rovman Powell, John Campbell, Vitel Lawes, Stafanie Taylor, Chinelle Henry are among the 33 players who accepted CWI’s international retainer contracts, which run until September 2027.

There have been suggestions that players could lose form or lose motivation playing for the Caribbean team, given they’ll be earning less.

However, former fast bowler Powell, who picked up over 150 wickets in 92 caps for the Windies, says salaries shouldn’t determine the standard of their performances, pointing to his own experience.

“When I started playing, I can remember, we had no contracts. I was earning less than [US]$200 per game. When you got into the West Indies team at the time, my highest pay was $1,500. We had a whole lot of arguments about pay cuts at that time, players not fit, and all sorts of things, why we weren’t winning cricket,” he told the Observer.

“We weren’t playing that bad, we were winning here and there. I think we were the only Test team until this date, who won a Test match in South Africa and look how many greats played before us and didn’t do that. So I don’t think it’s necessarily about a salary thing that causes players not to perform.”

Powell believes the increased earnings and lifestyle distractions have contributed to the decline of West Indies cricket.

“What has happened over the years is we have players who have been earning more, doing more carelessness with their time, other than focusing on what they do to enhance their talent for them to become better players to compete against those who modelled a programme against the era of West Indies cricket when we were dominant, to beat us,” he said. “We earn money, we buy cars, we drink rum and we find more women, other than focusing on a better way to grow as a player and it went through a crack, until the crack became a hole, until the hole became a big open space, then we started realising that we need to start doing things differently.”

Former offspinner Perry, who represented the Windies 25 times across Tests and ODIs, believes pride should take precedence when playing for the regional team.

“The game itself is what’s going to make your name, it’s going to keep you relevant, it’s going to make you money down the road,” he told the Observer. “You must go out there and play with that same passion and pride. The driving force should not be money.

“Yes, money is important, and we’re not saying you must play cricket without pay, it is hard, if that’s what you do for a living, because you have your family to take care of, you have your bills to deal with, and so forth. But we have to now balance it and have that sit-down and that frank conversation as to where we are financially, and how you guys can help us out of this situation.”

Perry says players should recognise that the current salary situation is not necessarily permanent.

“Once funds start to flow back into the coffers of the West Indies Cricket Board, then we will go back to some sort of normalcy,” he said. “I don’t think the players should really take it as a long-term fix, but certainly they have to be mindful as well that the board is in a situation and at the end of the day … We are in a situation, and we have to work together as a team, and that will come out in a balanced situation.”

Powell believes the salary cut could be a blessing in disguise to help improve the players’ performances.

“This is forcing them now to really realise and wake up that what they are doing is way behind,” he said. “No wealthy guy plays sport in the region. If you check their background, if you check their history, they’re coming from poor families. This is an avenue for them to better themselves. You see all these millions going around and you have your God-given talent and because of a pay cut, you’re going to [decline]? That will never happen.”

“The ICC has been putting money in the big three — Australia, England and India and the other nations are suffering. So this was one of the avenues, again, to send another signal to the cricketing heads that we need help. But the players themselves need to do the right thing to make sure they can put themselves onto the bargaining table.”

World.title: Business groups push back against EXIM/DBJ merger as talks resurface
World.content:
Renewed discussions about a possible merger between the Development Bank of Jamaica (DBJ) and EXIM Bank have drawn opposition from business groups concerned about the potential impact on financing options for small businesses.

AS discussions surrounding a possible merger of the National Export-Import Bank of Jamaica (EXIM Bank) and the Development Bank of Jamaica (DBJ) resurface, business groups have renewed calls for Government to abandon the proposal, warning that such a move could undermine specialised financing support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs).

The Small Business Association of Jamaica (SBAJ), through its president Garnett Reid, reignited the debate late last week following a meeting at which he said the proposed merger was raised as an option still under consideration.

Categorically rejecting the proposal, Reid said the SBAJ, which represents more than 700 members, remains firmly opposed to any move that seeks to close the EXIM Bank or subsume its functions into another institution.

In a media release, the association argued that the two institutions serve distinct but complementary roles in Jamaica’s development financing landscape, offering different products, financing arrangements and areas of support.

To this end, it warned that any plans to merge them could erode specialised services and narrow the financing options available to businesses.

“Rather than considering the closure or merger of EXIM Bank, I am calling on the Government of Jamaica to invest more resources into the institution. The Government should be pumping more money into EXIM Bank so that it can expand its lending capacity, provide greater access to affordable financing and reach more MSMEs across the island. Our small businesses need more financial support at this time — not fewer financing option,” Reid said.

Established in May 1986, the EXIM Bank focuses on trade and business financing, particularly for local exporters, manufacturers and other businesses involved in international trade or export-related activities. Its specialised offerings include letters of credit, bank guarantees and working-capital facilities to support imports, exports, cash-flow management and business expansion.

The DBJ, formed in 2000 through the merger of the Agricultural Credit Bank of Jamaica Limited and the National Development Bank of Jamaica Limited, on the other hand supports broader economic development, with financing directed towards MSME growth, energy, agribusiness and other productive activities. It primarily channels its funding through approved financial institutions (AFIs), including commercial banks and microfinance institutions.

While acknowledging the need to improve operational efficiency, the SBAJ head argued that sharing facilities and other resources would be a more practical alternative to merging.

He also cautioned against pursuing consolidation at a time when small businesses are still grappling with economic pressures and seeking to rebuild and expand their operations post-Hurricane Melissa and other economic shocks.

“At a time when Jamaica’s MSME sector is facing significant economic challenges and businesses are working to recover, expand and become more competitive, we should be strengthening our development financing institutions — not reducing the options available to entrepreneurs,” Reid said.

“Our position is clear: Jamaica needs more accessible and affordable financing options for its small businesses — not fewer. An institution providing financing at interest rates as low as 4.2 per cent is an invaluable resource to the MSME sector and as such… the EXIM Bank must be preserved, adequately funded and strengthened to ensure that businesses can continue to have access to the specialised financial products they need to survive, grow and contribute to national development,” he added.

Meanwhile, president of the Young Entrepreneurs’ Association of Jamaica (YEA) Cordell Williams said any consideration of a merger must be driven primarily by the interests of the businesses the institutions were established to serve.

“While we recognise the potential benefits of greater operational efficiencies, improved coordination, economies of scale and reduced administrative costs… we must also ensure that in pursuing these objectives we do not inadvertently restrict access to financing for the very businesses that will need it most,” she told the Jamaica Observer this week in response to the renewed merger discussions.

Noting that the DBJ primarily provides wholesale financing through AFIs, which subsequently lend to businesses, while the EXIM Bank offers direct financing alongside specialised products and services, Williams said the distinction was particularly important for MSMEs — which often struggle to secure funding through traditional commercial lending channels.

“The Government should consider whether a merger is necessarily the best approach or whether greater collaboration, integration of products and services and streamlined processes could achieve similar efficiencies while preserving the specialised capabilities of both institutions. The entrepreneurial community, including the YEA and other MSME stakeholders, should be meaningfully consulted before any final decisions are made,” Williams said.

She argued that the success of any restructuring should not be measured simply by the consolidation of two institutions, but by whether it improves businesses’ access to capital and puts them in a stronger position to grow, create jobs, compete and export.

“If a merger can deliver these outcomes, then it is certainly worth considering. However, if the result is simply a consolidation of institutions without addressing the fundamental financing challenges facing entrepreneurs, then we would have missed an important opportunity. The YEA’s position is that Jamaica does not simply need fewer development financing institutions; it needs a better development financing system and as such any restructuring must leave entrepreneurs better served — not worse off,” she said.

The Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association which also raised concerns when the merger proposal surfaced in 2022 described it at the time as a “bad move” that would narrow financing channels for businesses in the productive sector.

Past president John Mahfood called for greater clarity on the proposal and a clear explanation of how the merger would benefit local manufacturers — particularly smaller operators. Executive Director Kamesha Blake, who also argued that both institutions were needed, stressed the importance of consulting key players before any final decision is taken.

Talks about merging the entities have been ongoing for several years, but to date no formal announcement has been made. However, stakeholders close to the issue have indicated that recent discussions suggest that the proposal remains active.

When contacted on Monday for an update, an EXIM Bank official referred the Business Observer to its parent ministry, the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce, advising that queries be directed to the minister or permanent secretary, as the bank was not authorised to comment on the matter.

Attempts to reach portfolio minister Aubyn Hill were unsuccessful up to press time. The minster in previous communications has, however, maintained that no official decision has been taken.

Meanwhile, the DBJ in responding to queries from the Business Observer said the proposed merger forms part of an optimisation strategy as government continue efforts to improve efficiencies across the public sector.

“The focus is on leveraging the strengths of both organisations to better serve Jamaica’s wider business community, including MSMEs and improve access to capital solutions,” the institution said.

World.title: No relief in sight for Spring Mount road woes
World.content:
The badly damaged section of the Spring Mount road in St James

MONTEGO BAY, St James — It appears any hopes held by residents to have a collapsed section of the Spring Mount main road in St James repaired any time soon have been dashed. The Government has revealed that a fix — which could cost US$200 to 300 million — would likely erode within five years due to unstable soil in the area.

Options now being explored include purchasing nearby land so the road can be realigned, or using the much longer route through Anchovy.

“The dilemma that we face at Spring Mount is that if we fix Spring Mount, it’s going to go again in five years because of the type of soil that is there and that the hillside consistently is moving,” stated minister without portfolio with responsibility for works Robert Nesta Morgan.

He was responding to queries from the Jamaica Observer during a water and road projects stakeholder engagement meeting held at Pier 1 in Montego Bay, St James, on Tuesday afternoon.

The massive breakaway near the Spring Mount Police Station, caused by Hurricane Melissa last year October, has reduced passage to a narrow footpath, cutting off vehicular traffic.

The situation has sparked frustration among residents and transport operators, who have staged roadblocks and protests to demand intervention. Member of Parliament

(MP) for St James South Nekeisha Burchell has also pressed Parliament and the National Works Agency (NWA) for a permanent fix as well as improvements to alternative routes.

Following initial assessments, the NWA previously informed residents that soil tests were being conducted to facilitate repairs. However, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness later said it would be more cost-effective to upgrade alternative routes instead.

On Tuesday, Morgan emphasised that the situation presents difficult questions regarding public expenditure.

“The question you have to ask yourself is, ‘What is a good spend for national resources?’ Do we continue fixing — because we fixed it already – do you continue fixing a hillside that is collapsing, or do you find another way for people to move around?” he asked.

The minister said the two main options currently on the table are: Upgrading a longer alternative route from Anchovy to Roehampton, or purchasing land above the breakaway to realign the road further up the hill.

Morgan acknowledged that relying on the Anchovy to Roehampton route would increase travel time for residents.

“That’s just the reality. A lot of people are uncomfortable with that because they’re saying,

‘Why don’t you give us back our road?’ Fixing the breakaway is going to cost US$200 to 300 million, or buying the land above it. But the reality is that the road is not a safe road to continue using at that point,” said the minister.

“We’ve had consultations with the prime minister, and we’re going to have to make a decision whether we’re going to buy the land above the road and buy the houses, or we’re going to continue with the rehabilitation of the Roehampton route. But it’s not finalised yet,” he added.

World.title: ‘The only way to get this done’: Why the US wants Europe at Ukraine talks next time
World.content:
The mood cooled from the first day to the second. On Tuesday, with negotiations lasting four and a half hours, officials on the ground in Abu Dhabi who were familiar with the talks described them as “constructive.” The best they could muster on Wednesday, when the session broke up after just two hours, was that the exchange had been “neutral.”

In truth, few on the Ukrainian side ever believed this week’s resumption of face-to-face negotiations would deliver a breakthrough. The biggest announcement concerned the non-trivial matter of a planned prisoner exchange — which Kushner said would be the biggest in the war so far, but on even this they failed to announce the final agreed numbers.

Yet despite the muted rhetoric, the meeting in the air-conditioned environs of a secure government guest house — where staff were constantly on hand to provide coffee, sandwiches and even pizza — was nevertheless a significant moment in the stop-start journey toward peace after nearly five years of war.

Here’s what you need to know about where things stand.

What did they discuss?

Everything. According to Kushner, there was no significant topic that was not raised over the two days. The question of territory, he said, would clearly be “the hardest” to resolve. According to Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Kyiv’s negotiators scored a major win on day one by convincing the Americans to accept their analysis of where the front line stands, and just how much less Ukrainian territory Russia has conquered than Moscow claims.

It’s hard to see a quick resolution on that issue, although privately U.S. officials say both sides have shown some flexibility on how to settle territorial claims. Zelenskyy still insists, and it seems the American mediators agree, that matters relating to the fate of Ukrainian land can only be discussed at the level of leaders. That kind of meeting is still very far away. “Clearly, there’s not great trust or love between the leaders,” Kushner said.

World.title: Lagarde would equal any other centrist in Elysée run, poll shows
World.content:
In a highly unlikely scenario in which Lagarde runs next to Philippe and multiple recently declared candidates, including Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner and columnist Natasha Polony, she would also rival President Emmanuel Macron’s former prime minister with 8% support.

In both cases, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen and leftist hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon are projected to finish first and second, respectively, which would qualify them for next May’s runoff round.

Cluster17’s survey, the first public poll to test a Lagarde candidacy, shows the centrist vote is “very fluid,” according to the institute’s president, Jean-Yves Dormagen. “At this stage there is a patent lack of leadership in the moderate and centrist space.”

The centrist camp is grappling with an internal conflict between Philippe and Gabriel Attal, another former prime minister. Philippe, who was once a favorite to face Le Pen in the second round, has struggled to gain traction despite months of campaigning, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls show.

Conservative Bruno Retailleau, who served as interior minister under Macron, is also a candidate along with right-wing Cannes Mayor David Lisnard and center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann. All hope to defy the increasing odds of a Le Pen-Mélenchon runoff.

Lagarde previously dismissed her candidacy as “not a good idea at all,” but since announcing her early exit from the ECB on Oct. 29 she has avoided answering the question directly.

Asked by POLITICO whether she was still ruling out running during a panel at the Paris Peace Forum on Wednesday, Lagarde stuck to her guns: “I said I want to recover my freedom to speak, my freedom to engage in matters that are not monetary policy, and that’s what I want to do.”

Lagarde will leave her ECB post on Feb. 7 next year, about a month before presidential hopefuls must formally apply to run.

World.title: SONDAGE EXCLUSIF 2027. Christine Lagarde “bien accueillie” par les électeurs du centre
World.content:
Mais ils sont nombreux dans l'écosystème politique, économique et médiatique, à rêver de voir cette "grande dame" (dixit un communicant qui lui est proche) se présenter à l'élection présidentielle, pour redonner espoir à un camp central en plein doute – son candidat le mieux placé, l'ancien Premier ministre Edouard Philippe, étant en perte de vitesse dans les sondages et désormais loin de la barre de qualification pour le second tour.

Ceux-là ne peuvent s'empêcher de remarquer que Christine Lagarde n'est pas toujours aussi claire qu'elle l'a été au mois de septembre et élude même quelques fois la question. Interviewée ce lundi matin par POLITICO lors d'une table ronde à l'occasion du Forum de la Paix à Paris, celle qui doit publier son autobiographie au mois de février, intitulée "Lady First" (éditions de l'Observatoire), répondait ainsi, à une question sur ses intentions : "J'ai dit que je voulais retrouver ma liberté de parole, ma liberté d'action (...) et c'est ce que je ferai !"

L'institut Cluster 17 a testé* l'hypothèse d'une candidature de l'ancienne ministre de Nicolas Sarkozy. Dans le premier scénario, elle serait candidate en lieu et place d'Edouard Philippe, le président de LR Bruno Retailleau maintenant sa candidature, tout comme celui de Nouvelle Energie, David Lisnard, actuellement en dynamique dans les sondages. Le résultat est saisissant : selon l'institut, Lagarde ferait jeu égal d'entrée de jeu, voire un poil mieux que le président de Horizons, avec 14% d'intentions de vote, contre 13,5% pour le Havrais dans la même configuration.

"Elle est plutôt bien accueillie par les électeurs du centre", note donc Jean-Yves Dormagen, président de l'institut Cluster 17. Il précise toutefois : "Tout cela confirme la très forte liquidité de l'espace central". Dans le détail, Lagarde rassemblerait notamment 55% des électeurs "libéraux" et 59% des "centristes", ainsi que 23% des "modérés", selon la méthode de classification de l'institut, qui se tournerait alors légèrement moins vers le candidat du Parti socialiste et de Place publique Raphaël Glucksmann.

A noter : au mois d'octobre, Edouard Philippe, déjà en perte de vitesse, récoltait 16% d'intentions de vote dans notre sondage, dans un scénario sans la candidature de David Lisnard, le maire de Cannes. Cette fois bien testé, celui-ci récolte le score non négligeable de 10% d'intentions de vote, qu'il soit face à Christine Lagarde, Edouard Philippe ou même Gabriel Attal (qui obtiendrait quant à lui 11% des voix lorsqu'il est testé à la place d'Edouard Philippe comme candidat). Dépassé, le président des Républicains Bruno Retailleau se maintient quant à lui entre 5 et 6 points d'intentions de vote, dans les trois hypothèses.

Dans un troisième scénario, certes hautement improbable, Christine Lagarde ferait face à une kyrielle de candidats déclarés ou en passe de l'être : Dominique de Villepin, Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, Natacha Polony, David Lisnard et Teddy Riner, notamment. Et le rapport de forces est là encore intéressant, puisqu'elle fait de nouveau jeu égal avec Edouard Philippe, tandis que Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon continuent de caracoler en tête (avec respectivement 27% et 19% d'intentions de vote). Surtout, note Jean-Yves Dormagen, "tout le monde est en dessous de 10, ce qui est montre que personne n'a de socle large à ce stade".

World.title: Bomb threats hit hundreds of schools in Italy, Ireland and UK
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on Facebook that the country was “doing everything necessary to ensure the safety of citizens.”

“At the moment, from the investigations carried out, there is no element that makes a concrete danger seem to be persistent,” she added.

Similar threats were received by schools in the U.K. and Ireland, with more than 270 Scottish schools and over 300 schools in Northern Ireland targeted. Some schools in England and the Republic of Ireland also received emails. Irish Education Minister Hildegarde Naughton said that police assessed the emails as “not credible” and that “there is no need for schools to evacuate.”

The latest threats come after several of Ireland’s top media outlets and at least 18 European flights were targeted last Friday, with at least 22 flights disrupted the day before, forcing some to divert or make emergency landings and prompting fighter-jet escorts. Authorities found no explosives on board the aircraft.

ANSA reported that the threats against flights were signed “Fighters of the Male State” — a reference to a Russian ultranationalist, misogynistic movement which Moscow banned in 2021. The group’s founder denied involvement.

World.title: EU needs a system to respond to AI incidents, Finland and Estonia say
World.content:
AI safety and security are on Friday's agenda of the first-ever European Council meeting devoted to the revolutionary new technology.

Concerns about whether Europe is prepared to respond to AI-powered threats have been picking up steam since a series of incidents this summer in which AI agents went rogue and hacked into other companies. Recent cyberattacks and revelations of coding vulnerabilities have also raised concerns that security systems must be better equipped for the arrival of artificial intelligence.

Hungary pushed for a network of national contact points in case AI model providers lose control of their models, in an October paper seen by POLITICO. The country also pushed for a team of "pre-vetted, security-cleared" independent evaluators who can be ahead of incidents.

The letter from Finland and Estonia called for investment in European frontier AI models "as an economic priority and as a foundation for Europe's influence on the future of AI."

The countries warn that Europe requires "independent capacity to evaluate the most advanced models and their safety and security risks."

World.title: European gaming firms say new EU consumer rules will ‘cripple’ the industry
World.content:
The Commission says these practices encourage overspending, which is especially dangerous for vulnerable consumers like kids. Violating the rules can lead to fines of up to 6% of global revenue in cases that affect more than two-thirds of the EU population.

“We want the European gaming industry to continue to thrive,” said Michael McGrath, the commissioner for consumer protection, announcing the measures. But competition, McGrath added, should be based “on creativity, innovation, and quality, and not on practices that exploit consumers.”

In a joint statement, the European Game Developer Federation, an association representing EU firms, and Video Games Europe, which includes global juggernauts like Sony and Epic Games, say that the proposed definition of pay-to-win is “fundamentally flawed, lacks clear definitions and would create huge confusion for players and developers alike” since it could cover “any purchase.”

Angry Birds & friends

While Europe has struggled to keep up with the U.S. and China in several tech sectors as AI and social media, the bloc is home to developers of some of the world’s most popular games such as Angry Birds and The Witcher. Video game spending in the bloc topped €27 billion, accounting for 17% of the global market, last year, according to the European Audiovisual Observatory.

The gaming groups argue that the industry already does a good job regulating itself with parental controls and the content rating system PEGI, which the DFA doesn’t take into account.

“Effectively, the DFA moves all decisions from parents and children to the Commission,” they wrote.

The DFA aims to regulate a slew of other industries, cracking down on manipulative practices in online commerce such as addictive design, dynamic pricing and making it difficult to unsubscribe from a digital subscription.

World.title: ‘Systemic’ sexual misconduct in German armed forces, study finds
World.content:
That includes unwanted sexual comments, sexual images, unwanted touching and sexual violence. Over the same period, 2% of both women and men reported experiencing sexual violence.

More than 8,100 soldiers completed the July 13 to Aug. 27 anonymous survey, about 18% of those contacted. The researchers said they had adjusted the results to reflect the makeup of the military.

The study found that only one-sixth to one-third of sexual incidents were reported, depending on the type of misconduct, with many victims saying they didn’t want to draw attention to themselves. Others feared consequences or doubted that reporting an incident would lead to action.

Pistorius presented the findings to the defense committee in the country’s parliament alongside Germany’s top military officer, Carsten Breuer. Speaking afterward, he promised “zero tolerance” for sexual misconduct.

Pistorius called the handling of complaints a “systemic problem.” He said military structures and the traditional responses of some commanders to complaints were partly to blame.

He announced a 34-point plan to improve protection for victims and make it easier to report incidents, including a new advice service outside the usual military chain of command. The service is currently available daily but is expected to become available around the clock.

World.title: Tino Chrupallas Alleingang
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Ein Video über Donald Trump bringt Tino Chrupalla in der eigenen Partei massiv unter Druck. Weil der AfD-Chef die US-Migrationspolitik als zu hart kritisiert, erntet er offenen Widerspruch von Alice Weidel und einen Richtungsstreit in der Fraktion.

Exklusive Einblicke in geleakte Austritts-Mails zeigen zudem, warum einst loyale Mitglieder der Partei frustriert den Rücken kehren. Die internen Dokumente offenbaren eine tiefe Entfremdung. Es geht um zunehmende Radikalisierung, Intrigen und einen pro-russischen Kurs, der langjährige Unterstützer abschreckt. Der Blick in die Postfächer zeigt schonungslos, wo die rote Linie für viele an der Basis verläuft.

Außerdem gibt es eine überraschende taktische Wende in Sachsen-Anhalt: Der AfD-Kandidat Ulrich Siegmund würde bei der Ministerpräsidentenwahl womöglich doch mehrfach antreten. Welche Rolle die CDU bei diesem Manöver spielt und was das für die künftigen Machtverhältnisse bedeutet, ordnet diese Folge präzise ein.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: German tech company signs €60 million contract with Elon Musk for satellite solar cell supply
World.content:
Elon Musk signed a major order on Wednesday with a medium-sized German tech company, Singulus Technologies, to supply solar cells for his new line of satellites, Starmind.

 

The €60 million major order is the first of many, according to a statement from SpaceX founder Elon Musk on X.

Following the deal, the company's stock temporarily spiked by 65% to 80%, which valued the firm at around €73 million. A groundbreaking rise as the company's annual revenue in 2025 was only €48.3 million.

As part of a strategic partnership, further facilities and production lines are planned to be created for a solar power production capacity of 100 gigawatts, the equivalent of the annual production of ten large nuclear reactors.

'Next-generation solar cell technology'

The company, based in Kahl am Main in Bavaria, manufactures "heterojunction solar cells" that are particularly suitable for space applications, according to Business Insider.

"The strategic partnership with SpaceX allows us to further industrialise these capabilities at a meaningful scale and solidify our position as a leading Western provider of next-generation solar cell technology," Lars Lieberwirth, Member of the Executive Board of SINGULUS, said in a statement.

"The combination of their process expertise and our long-term commitment creates a durable option for scaling solar production," said Mike Nicolls, SpaceX’s Senior Vice President of Starlink.

Singulus develops and assembles machines used in the "Photovoltaics, Semiconductor, Medical Technology, Packaging, Glass and Automotive, as well as Battery and Hydrogen markets."

'Sentient sun' project

The order will supply the solar cells for the SpaceX Starmind satellites manufacturing site in Texas in early 2027.

The Starmind project aims to produce satellites that will serve as AI data centres in space, a way to create a "sentient sun", as Musk said.

Equipped with huge power-generating solar wings that will measure 75 meters long, the Starmind satellite constellation is intended to compute AI data in space and send it to Earth via laser, acting as a large computer.

"By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centres," Elon Musk said in a filing at the Federal Communications Commission.

Even though Musk's claim to launch 1 million satellites to orbit Earth as part of this new project is unlikely, satellite operators often request approval for a higher number to buy design flexibility.

As of today, only 15,000 satellites exist, and Musk's Starlink constellation accounts for 9,500 of them.

While the technology hasn't proven itself, Google has similar plans to use satellites as computing units for AI calculations, harnessing the sun to power them.

World.title: Russian ambassador to the US dies, Russia's foreign ministry announced
World.content:
Russia's ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died at the age of 66, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Wednesday.

 

He "passed away suddenly," said Russia's Foreign Ministry in a statement published on X without giving more details on the cause of his death.

"We have lost an outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader, a kind colleague and a mentor," Russia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

"We extend our deepest and most heartfelt condolences to Alexander Darchiev’s family and loved ones."

Darchiev held several positions within Russia’s Foreign Ministry before replacing Anatoly Antonov as ambassador to the US in early 2025, shortly after Donald Trump's election.

He previously served at Russia's embassy in Washington in the late 2000s and spent six years as Russia's ambassador to Canada between 2014 and 2021.

Veteran diplomat appointed by Vladimir Putin, Darchiev was known for his repeated condemnations of the West.

This death comes as Moscow and Washington struggle to restore deteriorated relations since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. At the time, Darchiev called the move a "necessary measure."

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 11th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Trinidad and Tobago highest court overturns gay sex ban
World.content:
A decade-long legal battle led by LGBT+ Trinidadian activists successfully ended as Trinidad and Tobago's highest court overturned a long-running law criminalising gay sex.

 

The UK-based final court of appeal for British dependencies and overseas territories issued a unanimous decision Tuesday that the 1986 Sexual Offences Act could not be used to prosecute private, consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex.

Seen as a landmark ruling for LGBT+ rights in the Caribbean, this law had previously carried sentences of two years for "serious indecency" and five years for "buggery".

"What I'm going to be doing in the coming months is very targeted activism about how the Caribbean, not just Trinidad and Tobago, deals with endemic homophobia," said LGBT+ Trinidadian activist Jason Jones after the verdict was read.

'Phenomenal victory for gay rights'

Freedom Law Chambers, the law firm that represented Jones, said in a statement that the judgement represented a "phenomenal victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which issued the decision, said constitutional rights must be interpreted in a way that makes them "practical and effective in the present day, not in the past."

The judgement was welcomed by UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk, who called it a significant milestone for rights and equality.

"I hope the judgment will help remove a longstanding source of stigma, exclusion, barriers and violence experienced by Trinidadians and Tobagonians based on sexual orientation and gender identity," Turk said.

World.title: Portugal closes all schools and non-essential services over Storm Charles
World.content:
Portugal closed all schools and shuttered non-essential public services on Wednesday as Storm Charles headed for the country’s mainland.

 

Streets were largely deserted ahead of the arrival of the major Atlantic storm, after the government told people to stay at home. Heavy rain and rough seas were expected to batter the Portuguese coast, with wind gusts of up to 140 kph.

It was the first time in living memory that Portugal’s roughly 8,000 schools had cancelled classes nationwide due to a forecast storm.

The bad weather has left part of the country on hold. One of the most heavily affected sectors is transport, with long-distance coach services halted, cuts and restrictions on rail and river links, flights cancelled and ships subject to restrictions in ports. On Tuesday, thousands of people suffered a power cut.

In the capital, Lisbon, buses drove through the city without passengers, and some streets flooded because of clogged drains. A national supermarket chain closed its stores.

A person sits at the Graca viewpoint overlooking downtown Lisbon under rain clouds, Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, as Portugal gets ready for the arrival of Storm Charles AP Photo

One of the main national retail chains, Pingo Doce, closed all its supermarkets, and even an international technology conference attended by around 70,000 people in Lisbon called off the day’s events. The Web Summit, being held in Lisbon, was scheduled for the second day of its event.

The government has ordered remote working in the civil service, while telecommunications operators and insurance companies have reinforced their response capacity. Assisted by the armed forces, the emergency services are on maximum alert in order to avoid a repeat of the tragedy caused by storm Kristin at the beginning of the year.

Storm Charles lost strength, forecasters say

Meanwhile, the latest forecasts suggest the storm’s impact will be milder than feared, because it has lost the "conditions needed to intensify."

Jorge Ponte, a meteorologist at the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA), said Charles split into two centres over the past few hours, a change he said "made all the difference."

Speaking to local broadcaster SIC, he said forecasters work with scenarios and probabilities, and most had pointed to a difficult situation on Wednesday. The storm then changed trajectory in a way the models had not predicted, significantly altering the outlook for the coming hours.

Passing further south of Madeira than first forecast, the depression’s centre moved out of reach of the jet stream linked to Storm Bruna, losing the conditions that would have let it intensify.

According to the latest forecasts, one of the storm’s centres will move inland along the Alentejo coast, south of Lisbon. The other is expected to head towards the Central region.

The change does not mean the earlier warnings about strong winds were misplaced, as winds will remain very strong, although some warnings have already been downgraded from red to orange.

Rainfall is also expected to stay intense, spreading gradually to the Central and Northern regions.

World.title: We should 'salute' Ukraine for military campaign against Russian diesel infrastructure
World.content:
As talks aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine continue, NATO has been represented by Dhabi by senior officials, including the alliance’s top military commander, Alexus Grynkewich.

 

Grynkewich is attending in his capacity as Commander of US European Command, “to provide advice for US leaders as they further President Trump’s efforts to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end”, NATO officials say.

Euronews NATO correspondent Shona Murray spoke to Deputy Supreme Allied Commander John Stringer at NATO headquarters. He said he “hoped” Russia was entering the talks in good faith, but pointed out there was little evidence President Vladimir Putin had moved away from his maximalist demands.

Stringer said Ukraine’s objectives in securing a ceasefire were “paramount” for NATO.

“Let’s see how serious Russia is here,” he told Europe Today.

“Let’s hope it’s not just, frankly, a restatement of demands that, as I said, go back to 2022,” he added, referring to Moscow’s original war aims, including the annexation of Ukrainian territory.

Asked about concerns that Ukraine could be pressured into accepting changes to its borders, including relinquishing control over parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, Stringer said Ukraine alone had the right to determine the future of its sovereign territory.

“In terms of territory, it’s absolutely one for the Ukrainians,” he said.

Stringer also praised successful Ukrainian operations targeting Russian diesel refineries.

US President Donald Trump called on Kyiv end military strategy, claiming that the strikes were responsible for rising energy prices.

But Stringer said Western allies should “salute” Ukraine’s success in “hurting Putin”.

“This is hurting Putin. He thought he was going to roll in, establish a new security architecture in Europe that started in Ukraine in early 22, and he’s been sorely disabused on that one,” Stringer said.

“What Ukraine has been able to do through imagination, innovation and will is quite incredible and we should salute it,” he added.

World.title: Finland approves Tesla assisted driving cars ahead of EU vote
World.content:
Tesla has received temporary approval to use its Assisted Driving system (TAD) on Finnish roads after making changes to the technology.

 

Finland's Transport and Communications Agency (Traficom) announced the decision on Wednesday, saying Tesla "can immediately start offering the system to its customers in Finland."

The technology allows cars to steer, accelerate and brake automatically, although drivers must remain in control and supervise its operation.

The system was renamed Tesla Assisted Driving from Full Self-Driving (FSD) Supervised to better describe what it does.

According to Traficom's Senior Specialist Jukka Juhola, the new name reflects the "true nature of the system" and distinguishes driver assistance technology from fully autonomous vehicles.

The approval comes as Europe continues to face regulatory challenges over automated driving technology.

The EU is stuck at a gridlock over rules that would permit driverless cars, prompting many firms to push ahead at regional and national level.

Yet differing national rules have complicated the roll-out of fully driverless vehicles, with companies having to seek approval from local and regional authorities in addition to national ones.

In Europe, the Netherlands authorised the system's use in April, followed by Estonia, Belgium, Lithuania and Denmark.

Tesla already offers the technology in the United States, Australia, Canada and South Korea.

World.title: EU targets subscription traps, addictive design and hidden fees with new digital rules
World.content:
From online subscriptions that are difficult to cancel to social media features designed to keep users scrolling, the EU says it wants to make the digital economy fairer for consumers.

 

The European Commission unveiled its proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) on Wednesday, setting out new rules to tackle manipulative online practices, improve price transparency and strengthen protections for children.

“We are tackling the new unfair commercial practices that distort consumers' choices and put pressure on them, undermining their ability to make informed choices,” said executive vice-president and EU tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen.

Among the measures presented in Brussels on Wednesday are a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, known as ‘dark patterns’; requirements for clear and transparent pricing; fairness by design for digital platforms and services; the option for consumers to disable addictive design features; and new rules for influencer marketing.

A revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation was presented alongside the DFA. It aims to grant the Commission stronger powers to investigate and issue fines directly in large-scale cases affecting consumers across multiple countries, such as the recently launched action against video game companies including Activision Blizzard.

“The Digital Fairness Act, together with the update to the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation, represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years,” said EU consumer protection commissioner Michael McGrath.

The proposals are the latest in a patchwork of EU laws being put forward in Brussels to regulate e-commerce and online consumer protection. They are also part of a wider push to rein in Big Tech companies.

The DFA would work alongside the recently proposed EU Kids Act, which aims to shift responsibility for protecting children online towards companies.

It would also complement the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act, which seek to make the online world safer, fairer and more transparent, as well as the AI Act, which governs the use of artificial intelligence.

Enforcement

The proposed revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation would give the European Commission direct powers to investigate large-scale cases with a major impact on consumers across multiple EU countries.

It would also speed up and improve coordination between national consumer authorities in cross-border cases, setting deadlines for key steps and improving how penalties are coordinated, for example when fines are collected in different jurisdictions.

Companies found to have violated consumer protection rules in these large-scale cases could face fines of up to 6% of their annual global turnover. The DMA already allows for fines of up to 10%, while the DSA provides for fines of up to 6%.

This approach has had mixed results in the EU. While some cases, such as Apple's €500 million fine in April last year, have brought about changes to its App Store policies, others, such as Google's antitrust cases, have had more limited results in changing behaviour.

Crucially for Big Tech, non-EU companies would be required to appoint a legal representative in the EU to cooperate with national authorities and the Commission.

Stronger consumer protections

The DFA introduces several proposed protections for consumers online, including a ban on ‘dark patterns’ – such as fake claims that a product is almost sold out to pressure consumers into making a purchase.

Consumers would be given the option to disable addictive design features such as endless scrolling and autoplay videos.

Pricing must be communicated clearly and transparently. This applies in several areas, including dynamic pricing for tickets to sporting or cultural events, where prices must be displayed in real time to show consumers what they may have to pay.

The rules also cover virtual currencies, where conversion rates are not always clear. This can be an issue on platforms such as video games, where players make purchases using in-game currency rather than real money.

The DFA would also restrict practices that encourage children to overspend in video games, including gambling-simulating loot boxes and mechanisms that pressure them to pay to progress.

Examples include wheels of fortune features such as FIFA Ultimate Team packs. The proposed restrictions would not apply in the same way to adult gamers, for whom loot boxes and streak mechanics would remain permitted.

Online subscriptions and contracts must also be easier to cancel. Consumers would receive reminders before free trials turn into paid subscriptions, while automatic renewals would require a conscious choice rather than being a forgotten obligation.

Online consumers would also be able to reach a human being in customer service rather than being left with a chatbot.

The DFA also proposes rules for influencers for the first time, requiring content creators to disclose commercial content and preventing them from exploiting children's trust.

It would also ban unfair personalised advertising and pricing that targets minors or exploits people's vulnerabilities.

“The DFA will make sure the digital economy works for consumers, not against them,” said McGrath. “Businesses that play by the rules should not lose out to those that cut corners.”

The Commission's impact assessment estimates that the rules would spare consumers €88.4 billion in financial losses between 2025 and 2035.

Including time lost to unfair practices, it puts the annual benefit at €13.7 billion, against recurring costs to businesses of €678 million a year, once overlaps between measures are accounted for.

Response

Tech leaders have cautiously welcomed the new rules, but some have raised concerns about mixed messages from Brussels.

While EU leaders have called for simpler rules across economic sectors since the European elections in 2024, this year has seen a glut of proposals, particularly concerning online platforms and services, raising concerns about potential overlap.

Isabelle Roccia, Managing Director for IAPP in Europe, told Euronews Next: “The rationale to update rules, some created 20 years ago, to digital economy makes sense, but there are rules already in place across consumer protection, privacy, platform regulation, AI, etc.

“Is the DFA introducing new tools that organisations, consumers and regulators don’t already have in their toolbox? Does it embrace the Commission’s simplification objective or unduly add to the complexity of online governance?”

Others feel the proposal is a good start, but that the devil will be in the detail.

Monika Zdzieborska, counsel in Clifford Chance's Tech/Digital practice, told Euronews Next: “The debate is likely to centre on three fault lines. The first is coherence: does the DFA fill genuine gaps, or does it add another layer on top of the DSA, AI Act, GDPR and Kids Act?

“The second is defaults: should consumers have to switch off features designed to keep them engaged, or should those features be off from the start?

“The third is proportionality: should a shopping site, a streaming service, a game and a social network be regulated in the same way, or should the law reflect their very different risks?

“With the Kids Act on a parallel track, the two files will be negotiated side by side. Decisions on one, particularly on minors, addictive design and age checks, are likely to influence the other.”

On consumer rights, Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, policy officer at European Digital Rights (EDRi), told Euronews that the organisation was concerned that the proposal’s rules on addictive design still relied too heavily on individuals finding the off switch, rather than requiring companies to prevent harmful practices.

“The Commission has spent years studying how companies manipulate us online. Now comes the uncomfortable part: telling those companies to stop. Parliament and Member States have plenty of work ahead to give this law the teeth it deserves.”

The proposal must now be examined by MEPs and national governments before passing into European law.

World.title: ‘Monstrous injustice’: King Charles condemns slavery as UK agrees to talks
World.content:
In this episode of Spotlight on Africa, we talked to scholars from the continent and the Caribbean about slavery reparations – a key topic discussed at this year’s Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

Advertising

The Commonwealth is a 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies, 21 of them in Africa. King Charles III remains head of state in 15 of them, including the UK.

Its biennial Heads of Government Meeting took place from 1 to 4 November 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda.

In a final communiqué issued on Wednesday, the group said the time had come for “meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation towards forging a common future based on equity”.

Timetable of talks

While no timetable for talks was announced, the group welcomed the United Kingdom’s willingness to engage “in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms”.

In his opening speech, King Charles III, who is politically neutral, called the slave trade “a monstrous injustice” that filled him with “profound personal sorrow”, but stopped short of a formal apology.

UN backs resolution calling slave trade ‘gravest crime against humanity’

For his part, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said it was “not feasible” for the country to pay reparations for slavery, but that “there are things we can work on co-operatively”.

According to reports, Britain could issue a formal apology next year, during its G20 presidency.

Britain played a pivotal role in the slave trade, which saw between 10 and 15 million enslaved Africans taken to the Americas over four centuries.

The country abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833. It paid financial compensation, but to plantation owners rather than to the enslaved people themselves.

UN resolution

In March this year, the United Nations adopted a resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity”, in a motion spearheaded by Ghana.

Ghana backs Jamaica’s petition to push UK for slavery reparations

For many countries, the time has come for formal apologies and concrete plans for slavery reparations.

To find out how these issues are being tackled on the African continent and in the Caribbean, RFI spoke to a panel of four guests:

Edem Adotey: professor at the Institute of African Studies in Accra, Ghana,

Joel Kibazo: Commonwealth spokesperson,

Matiangai Sirleaf: professor at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law in the United States,

Verene A. Shepherd: Jamaican historian and one of three vice-chairs of the Caricom Reparations Commission.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.
