World.title: ¿Cuánto se nota la huelga? La caída del consumo eléctrico en tiempo real
World.content:
La electricidad es un termómetro aproximado de una huelga general. Cuando paran fábricas, oficinas y comercios, se consume menos energía, y podemos verlo en directo con datos de Red Eléctrica. No dice cuánta gente hace huelga, pero sí cuánto se frenan ciertas actividades. Lo muestra el siguiente gráfico. Compara el consumo de hoy con el que Red Eléctrica había previsto para un miércoles sin huelga. La zona sombreada es la caída que atribuimos a la huelga:

¿Por qué comparamos con la previsión? Es la mejor referencia. Red Eléctrica predice cada día cuánta electricidad se va a consumir. Y suele acertar: un miércoles normal de octubre falló el consumo del día por un 0,2%. Su modelo tiene en cuenta el día de la semana, la época del año o el tiempo que se espera, pero no —y esto es clave— la convocatoria de una huelga (lo hemos comprobado: su previsión para hoy es prácticamente igual a la del martes). Además, usamos otras dos referencias: el consumo del martes, un laborable normal, y el del domingo.

Para hacerse una idea de las magnitudes, un domingo se consume entre un 17% y un 20% menos que un día laborable. Si la huelga llega a esos niveles, el país estaría consumiendo como en domingo.

Por supuesto, los datos de Red Eléctrica son solo una señal. El consumo eléctrico no es un proxy perfecto del seguimiento trabajador a trabajador. Quien hace huelga sigue gastando luz en casa, los servicios mínimos mantienen parte de la actividad y una fábrica puede parar aunque no todos sus trabajadores secunden el paro. Hay también un efecto composición, porque no todos los sectores pesan igual: un horno industrial parado se nota más que cien dependientes de comercio. Y hay ruido. Un día más frío de lo previsto también mueve el consumo. Pero siguen siendo un buen indicador relativo: si la caída es grande, la huelga se está notando.

Comparar con el pasado es complicado

¿Es mucho o poco? Podemos mirar las huelgas generales anteriores, aunque es una comparación imperfecta. En las dos de 2012, el 29 de marzo y el 14 de noviembre, el consumo cayó un 14% y un 11% frente a lo previsto, según los cálculos que hice entonces para Politikon. Pero han pasado años y las cifras no son del todo homogéneas: hoy hay más autoconsumo solar y menos industria pesada, por poner dos ejemplos. También cuentan la época del año y la economía de cada momento. Por eso, una caída menor que la de 2012 no significa necesariamente que la huelga se siga menos.

Metodología. Usamos la demanda eléctrica en tiempo real que publica Red Eléctrica cada cinco minutos, y actualizamos la pieza con la misma frecuencia. La comparamos con la previsión que el operador publicó de madrugada (y que dejamos ahí congelada). La cifra principal compara la energía consumida desde las 0.00 con la prevista para esas mismas horas. Damos también la caída en la última hora completa y, en el gráfico, la de cada cinco minutos, que son más ruidosas. Como referencia mostramos el consumo del martes 10 de noviembre, un laborable normal, y el del domingo 8, un día de poca actividad.

World.title: El PP descalifica la huelga como “preventiva” contra Feijóo y Vox como “circo general”
World.content:
El PP se ha precipitado a concluir que el seguimiento de la huelga general no está siendo un éxito y, antes de acabar la mañana, su secretario general, Miguel Tellado, ha aprovechado varias comparecencias para subrayar además que los sindicatos convocantes ya no representan a los trabajadores. Tellado ha insistido en la idea de que el paro se convoca de manera “preventiva” ante el gobierno de Alberto Núñez Feijóo, que podría salir de las urnas fijadas para el 29-N. El portavoz oficial del PP, Borja Sémper, descalificó la huelga como “un despropósito” contra “el sentido común”. En Vox la tildaron de “circo general”.

El Gobierno ha mantenido un perfil bajo durante toda la mañana, a diferencia de los portavoces y representantes de la derecha. El secretario general del PP, Miguel Tellado, ha insistido en las consignas de los últimos días contra las centrales sindicales organizadoras de la huelga. Manifestó primero que respetaba el derecho constitucional de la convocatoria, pero consideró después que se trata de una “huelga general preventiva contra el próximo gobierno de España”, en alusión al PP de Feijóo.

Para Tellado, esta cita es “un pago de los sindicatos” al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez, que entiende que está necesitado de este tipo de ayudas. Luego mencionó, casi uno por uno, los 23 tipos delictivos, 17 sumarios y 131 imputados que el PP ha clasificado de distintos escándalos, investigaciones o sumarios que podrían afectar a dirigentes o cargos del PSOE.

El PP, además y en su cuenta oficial de X (antes Twitter) ha publicado un tuit con una fotografía de supuestos sindicalistas disfrutando entre risas de una opulenta mariscada y el siguiente mensaje: “Se acerca un momento crítico de la huelga… el aperitivo". El PSOE ha replicado ese tuit con otro contenido: “Feijóo dice que la huelga es un “disparate”. Ayuso habla de “basura sindical”. Y ahora esto. Este país y sus trabajadores se os quedan grandes. El 29N frenaremos esto. Vais a estar cuatro años más comiendo oposición".

Sobre CCOO y UGT, el número dos del PP incidió en que los firmantes del paro auspiciado por el Sindicato de Inquilinas “tienen una crisis de representatividad” para la que nada les beneficia apoyar este parón empresarial. Tellado ensalzó que otros sindicatos de clase, como USO o de los funcionarios como Csif, no han suscrito esta huelga. También apuntó que, si una de las razones de la cita es la crisis de la vivienda, deberían apuntar contra el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez, que lleva ocho años en La Moncloa.

Los partidos dentro de la coalición gubernamental y sus socios han apoyado y hasta animado a la participación en esta movilización sindical porque defienden que sus reivindicaciones, vivienda, mejores salarios y servicios públicos, son transversales e interpelan a todos los poderes.

Sí se han pronunciado dirigentes de Frente Amplio, como Antonio Maíllo, coordinador general de Izquierda Unida, que ha concluido que la jornada estaba siendo un “éxito” y que, en cualquier caso, supondrá un antes y un después para poner en primer lugar las reclamaciones para mejorar los precios de la vivienda en España. Este es uno de los factores determinantes para la organización de esta huelga general planteada inicialmente por el Sindicato de Inquilinas tras el desahucio de la anciana Maricarmen Abascal de su vivienda de toda la vida de un barrio céntrico de Madrid. La anciana falleció en el hospital tras el desalojo. La candidata de Podemos, Irene Montero, ha participado en algunos piquetes por la capital y ha destacado la relevancia de las demandas planteadas por los convocantes.

En Vox, su secretario general, Ignacio Garriga, fue el primero que aludió al parón como “circo general” y el secretario general del sindicato de esta formación, Solidaridad, Jordi de la Fuente, acusó a a Comisiones y UGT de ser “unas milicias y altavoces” al servicio del Gobierno: “Ocho años callados como tumbas ante la pérdida de poder adquisitivo y de bienestar de los trabajadores”. De la Fuente aprovechó para denunciar desde la madrileña plaza de Castilla el fracaso de la huelga y el activismo político de los sindicatos.

World.title: Aluvión de críticas al PP por ridiculizar a los sindicatos como unos ‘comegambas’: “Este país y sus trabajadores os quedan grandes”
World.content:
El PP de Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha pasado en tres años de cuidar su relación con los sindicatos —se reunió con los líderes de Comisiones Obreras y UGT antes de su investidura fallida en septiembre de 2023— a arremeter contra ellos y ridiculizarlos en su cuenta de X. En plena jornada de huelga general, los ha retratado como comegambas en otra polémica recreación realizada con Inteligencia Artificial en su cuenta oficial de la red social X. Los populares han recibido un aluvión de críticas por parte de los líderes sindicales, dirigentes políticos de izquierdas y usuarios indignados con la publicación.

La cuenta del PP en la red social X retrata a dos hombres y una mujer con chalecos de UGT y Comisiones Obreras rodeados de bandejas a rebosar de langostinos y cigalas. “Se acerca un momento crítico de la huelga… el aperitivo”, reza el mensaje del montaje realizado con IA, según aparece en una marca de agua de la imagen. El término “comegambas” es un calificativo despectivo utilizado por la ultraderecha contra los sindicatos. Sin citarlo de forma expresa, el PP lo ha sumido en su cuenta oficial en un post publicado poco antes del mediodía. “Feliz día de la juerga general”, se han sumado a la estrategia de Génova las Nuevas Generaciones del PP de Madrid, con un vídeo de 9 segundos en el que las protagonistas son unas gambas que bailan y beben cerveza. La agrupación del PP del distrito Centro de la capital reutiliza un vídeo asiático en el que un crustáceo es masajeado e incluso es tratado con acupuntura... antes de pasar por los fogones. “Sindicalista promedio con lo que le ha pagado Sánchez estos 8 años”, es el mensaje en castellano.

Las reacciones no se han hecho esperar. El secretario general de Comisiones Obreras, Unai Sordo, con algo más de un millón de afiliados, ha considerado que con este mensaje el PP se equipara a Vox: “Los hijos de aquella Alianza Popular de Fraga/Arias Navarro nunca protagonizaron la España constitucional, sino que la tuvieron que tolerar. Hoy la reencarnación postmoderna de Blas Piñar les come la tostada y sella la deriva ultra de un PP de iletrados”, ha reaccionado en X. “Hoy no estoy para inteligencia artificial, hoy lo que hay es inteligencia natural e inteligencia colectiva, la de buena parte que ha decidido apoyar la huelga”, ha ironizado Sordo en La Sexta.

UGT cuenta con otro millón de asociados. Carmen Castilla, secretaria general en Andalucía entre 2014 y 2023 y diputada en el Congreso por el PSOE, ha arremetido contra el PP por “no tener vergüenza”. “Lo único que sabéis hacer es insultar y engañar”, ha añadido, dudando que al PP le interese “el diálogo social”.

El PSOE también ha arremetido contra el PP por su burla a los sindicatos. “Este país y sus trabajadores os quedan grandes”, le ha recriminado. Los socialistas han recordado que Feijóo ha considerado la huelga general un “disparate” y que la presidenta de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha insultado directamente a las centrales como “basura sindical”. “El 29N frenaremos esto. Vais a estar cuatro años más comiendo oposición”, concluyen su mensaje.

“Puedes estar de acuerdo o no con la huelga general, compartir o no su objetivo, criticarla, lo que quieras… ¿pero faltar al respeto a los hombres y mujeres que defienden a los trabajadores?“, ha denunciado Adrián Barbón, el presidente de Asturias, una de las comunidades donde la huelga general ha tenido más seguimiento. ”Hoy, más que nunca, estamos con la gente", ha compartido María Jesús Montero, la vicesecretaria general del PSOE y secretaria general de la federación andaluza, que ha hecho una mención expresa a los sindicatos y trabajadores “frente a los insultos de la derecha”.

La vicepresidenta segunda y ministra de Trabajo Yolanda Díaz, cree “intolerable” que un partido que aspira a gobernar España como lo es el PP “se burle de un derecho fundamental de la Constitución”. “La huelga nos dio la jornada de ocho horas, las vacaciones pagadas y los derechos de las mujeres. También para los votantes del PP”, ha respondido en su cuenta de la red social Bluesky.

Antonio Maíllo se ha remontado a la elección de Feijóo como secretario general en 2022 y la promesa que entonces realizó de practicar un modelo de oposición alejado del realizado por su predecesor, Pablo Casado, y por Vox. “Esta es ‘la política para adultos’ del señor Feijóo. Están desesperados y se nota”, ha sido la reflexión del coordinador federal de Izquierda Unida. Los discursos iniciales del líder del PP combinaban un tono moderado y abierto a acuerdos con el Gobierno que ha ido abandonando mientras asumía parte de los postulados, y el lenguaje, de la ultraderecha.

La exministra y secretaria general del PSOE de Aragón, Pilar Alegría, ha recordado los descalificativos formulados por la derecha contra la huelga general. “Basura, apesebrados... Y como guinda del pastel, esta mañana el PP los ridiculiza de nuevo con una foto hecha con IA. Insultar, humillar y ridiculizar son comportamientos propios del abuso y el acoso, no del respeto que exige una democracia. Es inadmisible tratar así a quienes representan y defienden los derechos de millones de trabajadores y trabajadoras”, ha cargado en Instagram. La conclusión de la líder territorial socialista es que “no todo vale” contra los sindicatos y la clase trabajadora que “con su trabajo y esfuerzo han conseguido que disfrutemos de importantes derechos laborales y sociales” como el salario mínimo, las pensiones revalorizadas conforme al IPC, o la jornada laboral. Unos derechos que, ha recalcado Alegría, “han costado décadas de lucha”.

El PP considera la huelga un ataque contra la oposición a las puertas de una campaña electoral en la que, según las encuestas, a Feijóo le darían los números para presidir un gobierno de coalición con Vox. “Los sindicatos han decidido despertar de la siesta después de 8 años sin salir a la calle y han decidido salir de esa hibernación”, les ha recriminado Miguel Tellado antes de una reunión con cargos públicos y orgánicos del PP en Huesca. El secretario general de los populares ha tildado los paros generales de “huelga preventiva frente al próximo gobierno de España” en lo que ha interpretado como “el último servicio de los sindicatos a Pedro Sánchez y a su Gobierno”.

Los populares ya suplantaron en octubre la identidad de Begoña Gómez, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero y José Luis Ábalos. También han hecho montajes con Sánchez y Ábalos besándose, en lugar del presidente con su esposa, para trolear la campaña basada en La fuerza del Amor del PSOE en la precampaña. Feijóo defendió el mes pasado los vídeos publicados en la cuenta oficial de su partido y sostuvo que no entendía que el Ejecutivo se molestara por la suplantación de identidad “con el conjunto de delitos del PSOE”.

World.title: D66 and CDA agree deal with Pro to save budget, VVD frozen out
World.content:
Coalition parties D66 and CDA have agreed an eleventh-hour deal with the left-wing Pro to break the deadlock in the Dutch budget talks.

The opposition party announced an amendment to raise an extra €1 billion in taxes on assets and savings, shortly after a 2pm deadline for changes to the cabinet’s tax plan expired.

The third party in the minority government, the right-wing liberal VVD, is expected to vote against the amendment, but enough minor parties are likely to support it to ensure a majority in the Lower House.

Prime minister Rob Jetten has cancelled a trip to Dublin for an EU leaders’ summit so he can attend an extra debate on the budget scheduled for Thursday morning.

The VVD has not responded to the announcement on the deal, but will now have to decided whether to accept the amended budget or withdraw its support altogether, which would trigger a cabinet collapse.

The amendment is a watered-down version of the original plan, tabled by Pro and pro-European party Volt, to raise an extra €1.5 billion by creating a new top tax rate for savers and investors with assets of more than €1.3 million. D66 and CDA described that proposal as “too coarse”.

The updated version will also bring an increase in tax on inheritance and cash gifts, and a pledge to crack down on tax avoidance schemes.

Millionaires’ tax

“This is a breakthrough,” said Pro party leader Jesse Klaver. “In the last few days we have held talks to bring about a compromise to make the Netherlands fairer. If this plan is accepted, the Netherlands will have a millionaires’ tax.”

The VVD was not involved in the negotiations, Klaver added. “We have talked to D66 and CDA. If you want to know if the VVD support it, you’ll have to ask them.”

Earlier the VVD said it was “unthinkable” it could vote for the amendment in its original form, with MP Wendy van Eijk saying the plan crossed her party’s “pain threshold” and was “bad for the Netherlands”.

Now the deadline to submit amendments has passed, the VVD will have to decide whether it can still support the budget with the wealth tax included. If not, it will mean the end of the coalition.

On Tuesday parliament voted for a motion calling on the cabinet to explore alternative coalitions before it decides to call early elections, in an attempt to prevent the third general election in just over three years.

If an election is called, it is expected to take place in March. In the meantime a caretaker government would have to try to cobble together a majority in parliament for a new budget plan.

World.title: Tilburg parties fear local arms deal could supply Israeli army
World.content:
Dutch defence firm AIA has announced plans to manufacture Israeli-designed guns in Tilburg, prompting six local parties to ask whether the council can stop the weapons ending up with the Israeli army.

D66, PRO, Denk, the Party for the Animals (PvdD), the Socialist Party (SP), and local party VoorTilburg013 submitted written questions to the council’s executive, regional broadcaster Omroep Brabant reported on Tuesday.

The parties say ties with Israeli arms maker IWI are undesirable because of the war in Gaza and the situation in the West Bank. Five of the six also want to know whether AIA has permission to make weapons in Tilburg, whether it could be withdrawn, and whether IWI will continue to earn money from the guns.

AIA announced on Monday that it had bought the designs and know-how for two IWI weapons, the Arad 5 rifle and the Negev UX light machine gun, which it says are particularly useful for anti-drone warfare. Production will start in Tilburg before moving to a larger site in Overijssel.

The guns are intended for European countries and Nato partners. It is not clear whether they could also be sold to Israel.

AIA director Gerard Zondervan told broadcaster NOS the deal was “just a business transaction” and that the company had had no contact with the Dutch government about it.

In January, MPs adopted a motion calling on the government to phase out the Netherlands’ dependence on the Israeli arms industry.

It said the Netherlands had bought €2 billion worth of military equipment from Israeli firms in recent years, and that it was undesirable to depend on military industries “involved in war crimes”.

Less than two months later, MPs adopted another motion, from the orthodox Protestant SGP, asking the government to actively seek cooperation with Israel in developing a European air and missile defence system.

World.title: Youth, 16, arrested for shooting of 19-year-old man in garden
World.content:
A 16-year-old youth has been arrested after a 19-year-old man was shot dead while gardening in Schiedam.

The victim was attacked by three people as he tended the front garden of a house in Weverpad with two other people on Saturday afternoon. Both his companions were wounded in the incident, but their injuries are not life-threatening.

One was taken to hospital for treatment, while the other suffered minor injuries and fled the scene. He was arrested by police but has since been released and is not regarded as a suspect.

Police arrested the 16-year-old male youth in Capelle aan den IJssel on Tuesday afternoon on suspicion of murder or attempted murder. The search for the other two suspected assailants is ongoing.

The shooting may have been a case of mistaken identity, police said. A large-scale inquiry led by the prosecution service is ongoing.

The town’s mayor, Harold Bergmann, has placed security cameras outside the scene of the shooting and two nearby houses where explosions took place the following day. Police have not established if the incidents are linked.

World.title: NL and Germany sign deal on faster, more frequent trains
World.content:
The Netherlands and Germany have agreed to increase the number of trains running between them and cut travel times, with a focus on shortening the route to Berlin.

Annet Bertram, junior minister for public transport and rail, signed a joint declaration with German transport minister Steffen Bilger in Berlin on Tuesday. The agreement covers cross-border passenger and freight traffic, including military transport.

Bertram, of the centrist Christian Democrat CDA, told broadcaster NOS that she had wanted to travel to Berlin by train, but that current diversions made it impossible. “That is exactly why it is important that we discuss these issues in Berlin now,” she said.

The two countries will improve the main border routes and give new rail operators more access to the network.

The journey from Amsterdam to Berlin, 660km, takes almost seven hours, compared with three and a half hours for the 500km trip to Paris, according to NOS.

National rail operator NS and Deutsche Bahn run just four direct trains to Berlin, and all of them will be cancelled for three months next spring because of engineering work.

“Interest is not the problem, speed is,” Bertram said. She told NOS she would like to see “several options an hour” to Berlin or Frankfurt within 10 to 15 years.

World.title: Court upholds licence for Amsterdam TikTok sensation Fabel Friet
World.content:
Amsterdam city council was entitled to extend the licence for a chip shop whose long queues have been blamed by local residents for damaging the quality of life in the city centre neighbourhood, a court has ruled.

A judge said campaigners had failed to show that the problems were solely or mainly caused by customers of Fabel Friet, which has become a magnet for tourists drawn by the social media platform TikTok.

The decision is a setback for locals who wanted the court to overturn an extension to Fabel Friet’s licence, which was granted by the city council in 2024. The court was not asked to rule on the current licence issued this year.

They said the queues at the outlet in Runstraat, stretching back to the canal bridge, added to problems with overcrowding in the Negen Straatjes district and attracted seagulls to the area.

“The number of places where they can sit and eat their chips without causing a nuisance is quite limited,” resident Niek van der Heijden told the court at an earlier hearing.

But judges said Fabel Friet was not primarily responsible for the queues and litter problems and the licence was granted correctly.

Exotic toppings

“Other catering outlets in the neighbourhood also attract large numbers of visitors and have queues,” the court said in a press release.

“The court concludes that it cannot be assumed that the problems experiences are solely or primarliy caused by customers of Fabel Friet. The neighbouring residents have not demonstrated this.”

Fabel Friet’s founders, Abel Klatzer and Floris Feilzer, have opened four other branches in the city centre since they launched the business in 2020, but the outlet in Runstraat remains their flagship.

Tourists flocked to the shop after their videos of their fries topped with exotic toppings such as Parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise were widely shared on TikTok.

The owners set up a special queueing system and hired extra security to try to keep order in the neighbourhood. At one stage they also employed a falconer to keep away the seagulls that ripped open the rubbish bags outside the shop and spilled the contents all over the street.

World.title: Johan Cruyff’s grandson called up to play for USA under-18 team
World.content:
The most famous name in Dutch football could appear on an international men’s team sheet for the first time in 30 years after Johan Cruyff’s grandson was called up for the United States’ upcoming matches in Europe.

Shae Cruijff-Beane, the son of Johan Cruyff’s daughter Chantal and her American husband Todd Beane, was included in the squad that will play against Norway and Portugal in the next seven days.

Cruijff-Beane plays as a midfielder for Gimnàstic de Tarragona, a club in the Spanish third tier based near Barcelona. His older brother Jordan also came through the club’s ranks and is currently playing US college football at Westmont College in California.

Shae, 17, is eligible to play for the USA through his father and Spain and the Netherlands through his mother, who spent part of her childhood in Catalonia while Johan Cruyff was playing for Barcelona in the 1970s.

The USA under-18 squad also includes an Ajax player, midfielder Xander Newstead, who grew up in San Francisco and joined the Amsterdam club’s youth team set-up at the age of 10, beforec signing professional terms last year.

Johan Cruyff went on to play in the United States for Los Angeles Aztecs and Washington Diplomats before returning to the Netherlands, winding down his career at Ajax and Feyenoord.

His son Jordi played for Barcelona and Manchester United and won nine international caps in 1996. Last year he was appointed technical director at Ajax, the club where his father began his career.

World.title: What’s on at IDFA 2026: five documentaries to watch
World.content:
The International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA) opens on Thursday for its 39th edition, with 253 films from 80 countries screening until November 22.

The festival was founded in 1988 by Ally Derks, at a time when documentaries rarely made it into Dutch cinemas. The first edition showed 72 films to around 2,000 visitors.

There are prizes for the best films in the International Competition and the Envision Competition, which is for more experimental work.

There are also prizes for the best debut, the best Dutch film and the best use of archive footage. The winners will be announced on November 19.

Here are some highlights to look out for:

White Tiger Column

The opening film follows a group of young recruits through 45 days of training at a jungle camp run by Myanmar’s resistance movement. Canadian directors Robert Mentov, Dwight Jantzi and Bryan Dickie filmed the volunteers’ daily routines as they prepare to fight. The film is in the International Competition and is also nominated for the award for best first feature.

You Can See Everything

Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of blood-testing company Theranos, invited comedian Nathan Fielder and director Lance Oppenheim into her home in the weeks before she went to prison. They filmed her daily life with her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, and their two children. The film was made in secret from 2023 and unveiled at a surprise screening at the Telluride film festival in September.

Musk

Oscar winner Alex Gibney’s portrait of Elon Musk runs to almost four hours. Gibney expanded the film after Musk briefly became one of President Trump’s closest aides and set about cutting the federal government. The film premiered at the Venice film festival in September.

30 mei, 1969 (gritu di un pueblo)

On May 30, 1969, aworkers in Curaçao went on strike, which grew into a popular uprising against exploitation and inequality. The Dutch government sent troops to the island, causing political turmoil. Curaçao-born filmmaker John Leerdam made the film 25 years later, interviewing people who were involved and drawing on archive footage. It first screened at IDFA in 1995, and is returning this year in a new restoration by Amsterdam’s Eye Filmmuseum.

No Man’s Air

On July 20, 1974, the last flight landed at Nicosia Airport before Turkey invaded Cyprus. The airport has sat ever since in the no man’s land between the Greek and Turkish parts of the island. In this 42-minute film, Dutch filmmakers Peter Delpeut and Gerco de Ruijter use found footage to reconstruct that flight, with the Cypriot captain narrating off screen.

World.title: No sign of breakthrough as deadline looms on Dutch tax plans
World.content:
The Dutch government is running out of time to find a majority in parliament for its tax programme for next year, with no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations with opposition parties.

Prime minister Rob Jetten has repeatedly said he wants to secure a broad agreement with concessions on the left and right, but the two sides’ demands are proving irreconcilable.

Junior finance minister Eelco Eerenberg, who is responsible for the tax plans, called on MPs to “look with a clear head and a new day at what is on the table”, at the end of a debate that brought the parties no closer to ending the deadlock.

The minority coalition of D66, CDA and VVD need to find 10 votes in the lower house and 17 votes in the Senate from at least two opposition parties to pass their legislation.

The parties have until 2pm on Wednesday to table fresh amendments, after which the tax plans will go to a vote in the lower house, which is scheduled for Thursday. The Senate is due to vote in December.

The left-wing Pro, who have teamed up the pro-European liberal minor party Volt, are pressing the cabinet to raise another €1.5 billion in taxes on people with high levels of assets and savings to fund tax cuts for working people.

But the move is being blocked by the right-wing liberal VVD, who favour doing a deal instead with a right-wing block of JA21, the farmers’ party BBB and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

Split vote

The coalition parties have not ruled out splitting their vote on Pro’s amendement, an unprecedented move that would allow D66, CDA and Pro to pass the measure with support from other opposition groups while the VVD vote against.

The tax service has warned that if the plans are not passed before November 20 it will not be able to include the new rates in next year’s tax demands, meaning millions of taxpayers will be sent incorrect bills that have to be adjusted later.

Employers’ payslips will also be calculated on the basis of the 2026 rates for at least the first quarter.

With the prospect of a cabinet collapse looming, MPs backed a motion on Tuesday requiring parliament to explore alternative combinations before resorting to fresh elections.

The motion, tabled by the Christian parties ChristenUnie, SGP and CDA, would change the parliament’s procedural rules, to say MPs “will consult on a new formation” after a cabinet resigns rather than “can consult”.

Only one of the last seven Dutch governments has lasted the full term and a general election in March 2027, the earliest it could be held, would be the third in less than three and a half years.

World.title: Annual Polish Independence March passes through Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier. Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks. This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”. The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.” On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared. Czas odciąć sznurki obcych wpływów i marionetkowych decyzji! W naszym własnym kraju to my – polscy obywatele – jesteśmy jedynym suwerenem i to my ustalamy reguły! 🇵🇱 POLAK W POLSCE GOSPODARZEM! pic.twitter.com/8Htr8s0klx — Marsz Niepodległości (@StowMarszN) November 11, 2026 The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right. Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march. A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000. That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One. The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government. “It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.” Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”. “Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.” Na Marszu Niepodległości jesteśmy u siebie! Przyjeżdżamy z różnych stron, mamy różne doświadczenia i poglądy, ale pod biało-czerwoną flagą tworzymy jedną wspólnotę. Każdy jest w niej potrzebny. Także ten, kto dziś czuje się samotny, odrzucony i traci poczucie sensu. Ta wspólnota… pic.twitter.com/L5pYU1RVv0 — Krzysztof Bosak 🇵🇱 (@krzysztofbosak) November 11, 2026 However, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a picture of himself at the march in front of a banner showing images of both Tusk and Kaczyński crossed out, alongside the word “Reset”. While Bosak’s nationalist faction of Confederation is seen as more amenable to the idea of working with PiS to form a potential future coalition government, Mentzen’s libertarian faction is less enthusiastic about the idea. In the past, the march has sometimes seen violence, with participants clashing with police. However, in recent years it has generally passed peacefully, and that was again the case today. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaszkowski, who is a deputy leader of KO, said on Wednesday afternoon that, other than the illegal use of pyrotechnics (such as a flare held up by Mentzen), the march was proceeding without incident. Local authorities in Warsaw had put in place additional security measures following Saturday’s terrorist attack in Kraków, in which a 24-year-old Polish man, Michał Oksiński, killed six people and injured over a dozen more by shooting an AR-15 rifle from his car. Oksiński’s rampage was quickly brought to a halt in a shootout with armed police, and he died from his injuries on Monday. On Tuesday, the justice minister revealed that evidence uncovered so far shows “strong traces of right-wing extremism” in Oksiński’s activity. There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister. His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 Tusk, meanwhile, celebrated Independence Day in the city of Szczecin in northwest Poland. “All of us, without exception, are responsible for ensuring that Poland remains strong, secure, free and independent forever,” said the prime minister. “Everyone who holds Poland in their hearts must understand that independence, freedom and a secure republic are a common good.” Tusk noted that, since the recent crisis around the constitutional court broke out, Nawrocki has refused his offer to meet and discuss how to find a solution to a crisis that has pitted judges appointed under the former PiS government against those chosen by the current ruling coalition. The prime minister today renewed that offer, inviting Nawrocki and his family to visit Tusk’s home in the build-up to Christmas. “We must be able to discuss things together, without bitterness, without hatred,” said the prime minister. Note: This article has been updated to include the official estimate of attendance at the march. Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries. “Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”. The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared. Wicepremier W. @KosiniakKamysz z #Waszyngton: to chyba moja najważniejsza i przełomowa wizyta w USA. To moment, w którym mogę powiedzieć, że Polska jest nie tylko modelowym sojusznikiem, ale stała się strategicznym partnerem USA. pic.twitter.com/75xdgzIaG0 — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz was welcomed by Hegseth in Washington to discuss a range of issues relating to security cooperation. A major item on the agenda was Poland’s desire for a new permanent US military base on its territory. After the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters that there was a “green light from the Pentagon” for the base, with the final decision now resting with the White House. He said that was expected to be made in early December. Hegseth, meanwhile, praised Poland for embracing the “NATO 3.0” concept, under which the US wants Europe to take on more responsibility for its own defence. “Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” said the Secretary of War, who noted that Warsaw is “leading by example” with its high levels of defence spending. Hegseth also welcomed the fact that Poland is investing significantly in US equipment, including Abrams tanks, F-35 fighter jets, Apache helicopters and Patriot air-defence systems. “You are building a fully modernised, interoperable force, and our two nations are…giving military cooperation industrial depth as well,” said the secretary of war. Hegseth also reaffirmed Washington’s desire for a peace deal in Ukraine and “encouraged Kosiniak-Kamysz to continue Poland’s steadfast support of Ukraine”, said Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell. American defense technology is driving innovation and creating new opportunities for transatlantic industrial cooperation.@USAmbNATO Matthew Whitaker, Assistant Secretary of Commerce David Fogel @CommerceGov and @USAmbPoland Tom Rose met with Deputy Minister of Defence… pic.twitter.com/5etw1L3X5A — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the statement of intent he had signed with Hegseth was aimed at ensuring more US equipment was manufactured and maintained in Poland itself, including technology transfers. He also said that he wants to secure European funds for jointly produced US equipment. The EU’s SAFE programme of defence loans, for example, largely excludes US manufacturers. “We want American equipment manufactured by Polish-American companies to benefit from European funding. I will present such a position next Tuesday at the meeting of EU defence ministers,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz. “Poland is the US ambassador to the EU.” The meeting between the two defence secretaries also coincided with the Transatlantic Defence Industry Access Forum, which brought together 70 Polish and 80 American firms, with the aim of strengthening ties between the two countries’ defence industries. W ostatnich dniach dobra decyzja o utworzeniu w Polsce centrum serwisowego rakiet Patriot, a dziś podpisaliśmy kolejne porozumienie z USA, które przyspieszy współpracę naszych przemysłów zbrojeniowych. Chcemy, by więcej uzbrojenia powstawało i było naprawiane w Polsce. To nowe… pic.twitter.com/j24E2xON66 — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 10, 2026 Last month, the United States chose Poland as the location for a planned facility for servicing and maintaining Patriot missiles – the first to be located outside the US itself. In July, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks. That same month, President Donald Trump announced that his country would station an additional 5,000 troops in Poland, prompting Warsaw to formally request the establishment of a new US military base, which President Karol Nawrocki has suggested should be called “Fort Trump”. World.title: Two Ukrainians charged with spying and sabotage for Russia in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia. The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych. ▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026 The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics. According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office. Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life. At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months. In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage. World.title: “Strong traces of right-wing extremism” in activity of Kraków terrorist, says justice minister
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, says that investigators have so far found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the activity of Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out Saturday’s mass terrorist shooting in Kraków that left six people dead. The perpetrator’s search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist who killed 77 people during two attacks in 2011. Żurek’s comments come amid intense debate and dispute in Poland over the beliefs and motives of Oksiński, who on Monday died from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police that brought his rampage to an end. W. Żurek ujawnia nowe ustalenia po zamachu w Krakowie. Tłumik w samochodzie sprawcy i ślady zainteresowania Breivikiemhttps://t.co/nd1XPBlmrI — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) November 10, 2026 On Tuesday, Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, spoke to local broadcaster Radio Kraków about the progress of the investigation into Oksiński. He confirmed that the perpetrator had not left behind any letter or other kind of message revealing his motives. “Those motives are being investigated,” said the minister. “There are very strong traces of right-wing extremism. I can already confirm some information because the services have access to the perpetrator’s computer. Indeed, visits to websites related to Anders Breivik are visible.” Żurek also pointed to the fact that, as prosecutors announced on Sunday, a so-called Gadsden flag (showing a snake above the words “Don’t tread on me”) had been found in Oksiński’s home. Prosecutors say a "Don't Tread on Me" flag was found hanging at the home of the perpetrator of the attack in Kraków They emphasise that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation and that they are still trying to determine the shooter's motives and beliefs pic.twitter.com/yoNfh7cHwU — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026 Although the National Prosecutor’s Office emphasised that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation, Żurek noted that it was displayed during the attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of Donald Trump in 2021. “We know well that during the attack on the Capitol, there were quite a few of these flags among far-right groups in the United States,” said the minister. “This flag [in Oksiński’s home] also sends a signal to the security services and the prosecutor’s office.” Żurek added that a search of the perpetrator’s workplace had also identified “symbolism there that could point to this thread [of right-wing extremism]”, but provided no further details. The minister noted, however, that investigators are also taking into account the potential for “mental disorders” playing a role in the actions of Oksiński, whose parents and sister were found shot dead in his home. Żurek’s remarks come following controversy in Poland over a statement by interior minister Marcin Kierwiński on Saturday, in the immediate aftermath of the attack, when he said that early indications suggest that Oksiński had held “very radical views”, including a “fascination with far-right ideologies”. Over the following two days, Kierwiński refused to provide evidence supporting those claims, and in a TV interview on Sunday evening said that he had simply been sharing “first hypotheses”. That led some right-wing opposition politicians and commentators to accuse Kierwiński of spreading false claims, either through incompetence or as a deliberate attempt to associate the attack with the right. However, speaking to Radio Kraków on Tuesday, Żurek said that “it seems that what Minister Kierwiński communicated in those first hours is confirmed by the evidence”. Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, is facing growing pressure to present evidence to back his claim that the Kraków shooter was driven by far-right ideologies, amid criticism from opposition parties that he is seeking to exploit the tragedy for political reasons. — Jakub Krupa (@JakubKrupa) November 9, 2026 On social media, many people have also been sharing alleged images of Oksiński’s past activities, both online and in real life, claiming that they show he held left-wing views. However, some of those images have proven to be false, such as one purporting to show him at a pro-refugee rally (the photograph is genuine, but the person in it was not Oksiński) and another purporting to show him shaking hands with Kierwiński (the image was AI-generated). Further alleged images from Oskiński’s social media accounts remain unverified and also depict posts that were made six or seven years ago. Another fake that is being widely shared. While the photo is genuine, the person highlighted is not the Kraków shooter. Other images from the event clearly show it isn't him, while fact-checkers @konkret24 actually tracked down the guy in the photo: https://t.co/4HeofUdOUm pic.twitter.com/pTfdkCZlAL — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026 On Monday, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told Polsat News that there had been an “enormous wave of disinformation” in the wake of Saturday’s tragedy. He criticised “pseudo-journalists and politicians” who had shared such content. “Digital platforms acted very responsibly, removing this content quickly,” said Gawkowski. However, he added that X, the social media service owned by Elon Musk, had been an exception and was “where the most radicalisation occurred”. Meanwhile, the interior ministry’s spokeswoman, Karolina Gałecka, announced on Monday that they would notify prosecutors about the creation and dissemination of the AI-generated image of Kierwiński shaking hands with Oksiński. She said it had been spread by social media accounts associated with right-wing broadcaster Republika. World.title: What is at stake in Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal dispute?
World.content:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk. But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court. It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

World.title: Coalition of the Willing military exercises begin in Poland to prepare support for postwar Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia. The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November. The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​ 🇫🇷🇬🇧 KOALICJA: The MNF-U is training to ensure a solid and lasting peace in Ukraine The Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U), formed from the Coalition of the Willing and under 🇫🇷🇬🇧command, is launching its first major exercise: KOALICJA 📅 November 9–22, 2026 📍In Poland,… pic.twitter.com/Ikcl1uY8N2 — The 🇫🇷 Joint Staff – Military operations (@FrenchForces) November 7, 2026 The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition. “This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U. The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”. France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”. Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft. In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey. Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”. However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support. Nederland doet met enkele honderden militairen mee aan oefening Koalicja in Polen. De Coalition of the Willing traint er met 11 landen op snelle verplaatsing, commandovoering en bevoorrading ter voorbereiding op mogelijke steun aan Oekraïne na beëindiging van de oorlog. pic.twitter.com/JLE6W91HnZ — Ministerie van Defensie (@Defensie) November 9, 2026 France says that the deployment of forces to Ukraine would include sending instructors to help the country rebuild and strengthen its armed forces, while air missions would enable civlian aircraft to resume flying in Ukrainian airspace. At sea, MNF-U forces could help clear mines from shipping routes in the Black Sea. The maritime component of the current exercises is being led by Turkey through a simulated operational exercise, without deploying troops to Poland itself. France, the UK and Poland have emphasised, however, that the MNF-U forces would only be deployed once fighting in Ukraine has ceased and would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. He also declared Poland's willingness to permanently host more troops from its European allies https://t.co/couian4FrP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 On Saturday, the spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, Maria Zakharova, condemned the exercises, saying that they make “absolutely clear that the West remains unwilling to take Russia’s legitimate security concerns into account and continues to fuel the spiral of escalation”. She described the deployment of any foreign armed forces to Ukraine as “absolutely unacceptable” and said they would “create additional threats to Russia’s security”. “Any military units in Ukraine will be regarded by the Russian armed forces as legitimate targets, with all the risks and consequences that entails,” warned Zakharova. Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova’s answer to a media question in connection with the first military exercises of the so-called Multinational Force – Ukraine under the Coalition of the Willinghttps://t.co/GiouEAmT6J — Jeff Franzius (@jk55044) November 9, 2026 The exercises come as Ukraine and Russia meet the United States and others for peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week. Ukraine has repeatedly insisted that European security guarantees would be necessary for any peace agreement. British defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested the exercises forecast precisely such a scenario: “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops.” Zakharova, however, says that the exercises are “yet another confirmation that the Europeans have no place at the negotiating table”.
