He alleged that the repeated involvement of police forces from other States and central agencies in detecting alleged criminal networks operating in Karnataka reflected serious lapses in law enforcement and intelligence gathering. The Congress government should take moral responsibility for the failure, he demanded.

Mr. Yaduveer also sought to know why the State intelligence wing had failed to detect the racket, what surveillance mechanisms were in place to identify organised drug networks and who would be held accountable for the alleged lapses.

Calling for a comprehensive investigation, he urged the government to uncover the entire network behind the racket, fix accountability for the alleged intelligence lapses, strengthen inter-State police coordination and take stringent action against all those involved.

World.title: Boy killed after two-wheeler collides with private van in Vandalur
World.content:
A six-year-old boy was killed, and his father and sister sustained serious injuries on the Vandalur flyover near Tambaram on Wednesday,

A senior official of the Tambaram police Commissionerate said Saravanan was a resident of Vandalur and worked as a delivery person. He had two children comprising a daughter named Dishana and a son named Miliran. Both were studying at a private school in Perungalathur.

On Wednesday, Saravanan was taking his children to school on his motorcycle. While travelling from Vandalur towards Perungalathur, they were reportedly moving in the wrong direction on the Vandalur flyover of the GST Road. At that moment, a private company van proceeding from Perungalathur towards Vandalur collided head-on with the motorcycle. In the impact, the boy Miliran being seated at the front of the motorcycle was thrown off the vehicle and was killed after getting trapped underneath the van. Similarly, his father, Saravanan and sister, Dishana, suffered serious bodily injuries and were rushed to a private hospital for treatment.

The Guduvanchery Traffic Investigation Wing police on being alerted recovered the boy’s body and sent it to the Chromepet Government Hospital for a post mortem.

World.title: Tiruppur man killed, wife injured in accident on Neelambur bypass
World.content:
A 56-year-old man from Tiruppur died and his wife suffered injuries when the car they were traveling in collided head on with a bus on Neelambur bypass in Coimbatore on Wednesday (November 11).

The police said that V. Ravikumar (56), a resident of Aishwarya Garden at Ammapalayam in Tiruppur, died in the accident and his wife R. Krishnaveni suffered injuries. The accident took place around 4 p.m. when the couple and their daughter R. Athishya (23) were travelling from Thrissur towards Tiruppur. The car collided with a bus when it was approaching Neelambur.

World.title: Swachh Survekshan: Guntur wins ‘Super Swachh League’ award
World.content:
Guntur has won the ‘Super Swachh League’ award after finishing third among cities with a population of three lakh to 10 lakh under the Swachh Survekshan 2025-26 rankings.

Guntur Municipal Corporation Commissioner K. Mayur Ashok received the award from President Droupadi Murmu at a ceremony held at Vigyan Bhavan in New Delhi on Wednesday, along with Municipal Administration and Urban Development Minister P. Narayana, Principal Secretary S. Suresh Kumar and APTIDCO Managing Director B. Sunil Kumar Reddy.

Andhra Pradesh has secured six national awards, emerging as the second-best performing State in the country.

Mr. Ashok attributed the achievement to the collective efforts of municipal officials, sanitation workers and public participation. He said several initiatives had been implemented to improve sanitation and scientific waste management in the city.

A waste-to-energy plant is operational, while a Letter of Award has been issued for establishing a new Bio-CBG plant to generate green energy from waste. The civic body has also introduced electric autos, compactors and modern sweeping machines to strengthen garbage collection, he said.

Scientific removal of legacy waste, the ‘Swarnandhra-Swachh Andhra’ programme and the 30-day ‘Operation Clean Sweep’ drive contributed to improving urban cleanliness, he said.

The Municipal Commissioner pledged to continue efforts to transform Guntur into a cleaner and better-maintained city.

World.title: Man gets life for rape, murder attempt in Pulicat
World.content:
The Principal Sessions Court in Tiruvallur on Wednesday sentenced a man to life-imprisonment for raping a woman and attempting to murder her in Pulicat in 2021.

The accused, R. Panneerselvam, 20, of Vairavan Kuppam in Pulicat, was also slapped with a fine of ₹65,000. Judge Juliet Pushpa pronounced the verdict.

According to the prosecution, the incident took place around 3 p.m. on April 23, 2021, near the Pulicat Forest Office.

Panneerselvam, who allegedly knew that she was there, dragged her to a secluded spot and raped her. He also attempted to murder her.

The Ponneri All Women Police Station registered a case and arrested the accused. Both the survivor and the accused were subjected to medical examination, and the accused was subsequently remanded in judicial custody.

Police examined 24 witnesses and recorded their statements. The investigation was subsequently taken over by then Ponneri Deputy Superintendent of Police Kalpana Dutt. After completing the investigation, the police filed the final report before the court.

During the trial, the prosecution established the charges against the accused. Public Prosecutor Ramesh Babu appeared for the prosecution.

World.title: 10 cops martyred, 18 terrorists killed as police party comes under attack in KP's Kohat
World.content:
PESHAWAR: Eighteen terrorists were killed while 10 cops were martyred on Wednesday when the police team came under attack on its way back after completing an operation against elements involved in illegal gold mining, police said.

In a statement, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police public relations director said the personnel were conducting a joint operation with the local civil administration in the Darabukach locality near Kohat city.

“When the police party was returning after completing the operation, Fitna al Khawarij attacked the police party at the behest of criminal elements,” the statement read.

“Police personnel fought the attackers with great bravery and courage, as a result of which 18 khawarij were sent to hell,” it noted, adding that 10 personnel of KP Police “embraced martyrdom while fighting bravely”.

Fitna al Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan.

According to images shared by KP Police on their X account, the martyred cops included Deputy Superintendent of Police Haidar Zaman.

In its statement, the KP police said the “mutual nexus between criminal elements at the behest of external forces and Fitna al Khawarij and the joint attack on the police party is clear evidence that the criminal mafia and Fitna al Khawarij maintain organised connections”.

“This incident once again proves that Fitna al Khawarij has no connection with Islam and Pakistan. These elements are working together with the criminal mafia for their nefarious purposes,” they declared.

The police vowed that “all possible action will be taken against criminal elements working with foreign backing and Fitna al Khawarij”, asserting that facilitators of terrorists and criminal mafias would not be spared under any circumstances.

“No illegal activity will be allowed.”

The statement noted that policemen martyred in the incident hailed from KP, particularly Kohat, and that their “sacrifices will always be remembered”.

Earlier, Rescue 1122 spokesperson Jawad Afridi said in a video message that the rescue service had taken 12 injured cops to a hospital after “an incident where the police party came under fire”.

The incident came a day after the Kohat deputy commissioner imposed a 60-day ban on parking excavators within the limits of Block-C, Block-D of placer gold and adjacent mining areas.

The order issued from the DC office stated that certain individuals, groups and locals had parked excavators at their residences near mining areas, which could easily be used for the unauthorised mining of placer gold.

It said that despite several operations conducted by the district administration to vacate areas of illegal mining, the presence of excavators within residential areas continued to facilitate and encourage such activities, posing a grave risk to public order and state interest

It said that the district administration, in order to curb the illegal mining activities, was compelled to take stringent measures to prevent the misuse of excavators, which have become a key tool in facilitating unlawful placer gold extraction.

Through another order, the administration had also banned the sale, purchase and supply of petroleum products in open containers/bottles for use in unauthorised mining of gold in the district.

Governor seeks report

KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the martyrdoms and sought a detailed report, as per an official statement issued by his office.

While the police statement said the attack took place after the operation, Kundi’s statement said it occurred during the operation against illegal mining.

“This cowardly act by terrorists is highly condemnable,” Kundi was quoted as saying, vowing that the attackers would be brought to justice.

“The supreme sacrifices made by the police personnel will not go in vain,” the governor asserted, stressing that the martyrs’ sacrifices were a “source of pride” for the nation.

“In this difficult and sorrowful time, I fully share the grief of the families of the martyrs,” he said. He also reiterated the same in a post on X.

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry also expressed grief and sorrow at the “loss of human lives” due to “firing by terrorists” on the police team.

“The sacrifices of the police against terrorism and criminal elements are a source of pride for the entire nation,” he said on X.

“The government and relevant institutions should bring the elements involved in this cowardly act before the law as soon as possible so that they may be brought to justice,” he said.

Last week, two policemen were martyred, and another was injured when unidentified gunmen opened fire on them in KP’s Mohmand district.

Last month, a police officer was martyred after terrorists attacked a police post in KP’s Bajaur. On October 20, an additional station house officer (SHO) of the Miranshah police station was martyred in firing by unidentified individuals near Miranshah Bypass Road in North Waziristan.

On Oct 7, seven policemen were injured when terrorists attacked a police checkpost in Kohat.

According to Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , the country’s security environment continued to show considerable volatility from Oct 30 to Nov 5, with renewed terrorist activity in parts of KP and the former tribal districts, alongside intensified counterterrorism operations and changing patterns of militant violence.

World.title: Fuel prices slashed once again; high-speed diesel cut by Rs7 per litre, petrol by Rs3
World.content:
In another reduction of fuel prices, the government on Wednesday cut the price of petrol by Rs3 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs7.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs335 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs364 on Nov 12 (Thursday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation.

The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc.

The government and Jamaat-i-Islami held another round of negotiations today to formulate a way forward on relief in petroleum prices.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: PTI lawyers meet Imran, Bushra 'for 3 hours' at Adiala jail following IHC orders
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Lawyers representing the PTI met party founder and former prime minister Imran Khan on Wednesday, a day after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) issued orders allowing the meeting.

On Tuesday, the IHC, while hearing appeals filed by Imran and his wife, Bushra Bibi, against their convictions in the £190 million reference , directed authorities to facilitate meetings between Imran and his legal team.

Subsequently, Barrister Salman Safdar and Advocate Latif Khosa met the incarcerated couple at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail, both confirmed in separate statements.

Barrister Safdar said on X that a “nearly three-hour-long meeting with Imran Khan [sahib] and Bushra Bibi was allowed” by jail authorities. Meanwhile, Khosa also told reporters that the meeting lasted “3-4 hours” and included Bushra Bibi.

Safdar said that given the “extraordinary duration” of the meeting from 4pm-7pm, the legal and medical issues of both Imran and Bushra “were discussed in detail and comprehensive legal instructions were given by both”.

He said that “categoric and clear instructions were given” that he (Safdar) would continue to represent the two in the main appeals of the Al Qadir Trust case before the IHC.

In addition, he said that Advocate Khosa would assist the bench alongside him on Bushra Bibi’s pending petition before the IHC relating to her eye complications and granting of relief.

In a video shared by PTI of Khosa speaking to reporters about the meeting, the smiling lawyer replied in the affirmative when asked whether Bushra Bibi was also present for the meeting.

He said that discussions focused on Imran’s health and the cases against him. Khosa said that details regarding Imran’s health and what he himself saw would be released later.

Asked about Imran’s health, the lawyer said that Imran had a “blood pressure problem”. He said that the ex-premier’s blood pressure fluctuated to a “terrifying extent”, but added that he was “completely active and his will was very strong”.

Confirming that discussions had also covered a possible 28th constitutional amendment, Khosa said that he would not go into more detail at this time.

Asked why the meeting took so long, Khosa laughed and said, “Ask those who allowed the meeting.”

He noted that the IHC had ordered that the meeting should not be less than an hour long.

Speaking to Dawn earlier, PTI lawyer Awais Younus Chaudhry said the Safdar and Khosa’s meeting with Imran and Bushra was to “discuss under-trial cases”.

The lawyers remained at Adiala for four hours and left without speaking to the media or PTI lawyers, Chaudhry had said.

The meeting took place hours after the ex-premier was again taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) for his eye ailment.

According to the hospital, Imran was brought to Pims last night for a medical check-up and follow-up eye treatment. It added that his vital parameters were “normal”, he was clinically “stable” and his general physical examination was “normal”.

Imran has been in prison since August 5, 2023 , while his wife was arrested on January 17, 2025, in a separate case in which the couple were sentenced.

The IHC has allowed Imran twice-a-week meetings — on Tuesdays and Thursdays — with his family, lawyers and other associates. Despite multiple court directives , Imran’s meetings with his family and party leaders have been largely restricted .

On Nov 2, Safdar met Imran after a gap of seven months for less than an hour. When he had met Imran in April, months after the ex-premier’s eye condition had surfaced, the Supreme Court had designated Safdar as amicus curiae. However, on Nov 2, he met Imran as his lawyer.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram, speaking to Dawn after the Nov 2 meeting, said that no political issues were discussed as Safdar spoke about the cases and asked about future strategy.

When asked about Imran’s health, Akram replied that although health issues were discussed, the PTI would only speak about the legal cases.

World.title: PM Shehbaz highlights Pakistan's solar 'revolution by ordinary citizens' at COP31
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday highlighted Pakistan’s solar power boom at the COP31 in Turkiye, where world leaders gathered to discuss joint solutions to combat climate change.

This year’s summit focuses on transitioning toward a low-carbon future. Delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya as global greenhouse gas emissions show little sign of falling and wars, inflation and other crises compete for political attention.

Addressing a high-level dialogue on clean energy transition, titled ‘ 35 by 35: Powering the Future ’, PM Shehbaz said: “In my country, an extraordinary transition has already taken place.

“In just two years, Pakistan has added nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity — a quiet revolution by ordinary citizens seeking affordable power and a cleaner, more predictable future.”

He affirmed that Pakistan fully supports the ‘35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge’, wherein countries agree to aim to increase electricity’s share of total final energy consumption to around 35 per cent by 2035 in line with global climate objectives.

The premier recalled the recent inauguration of a “key section” of Pakistan’s seventh nuclear power plant, Chashma-5, referring to its dome placement. He explained that the project will add 1,200 megawatts of clean energy to Pakistan’s energy mix.

“A second transformation is now underway on our roads and highways. Clean sources now provide nearly 55pc of our energy mix,” PM Shehbaz declared.

The prime minister then highlighted that Pakistan’s newly drafted auto policy builds on the country’s aim to have 30pc of its new vehicles be electric by 2030 by offering “incentives for them through lower tariffs”.

“All future government buses and motorcycles will be electric. This year, for the first time, more than one in every 10 motorcycles sold in Pakistan was electric,” he stated.

“The momentum is real and it is accelerating,” PM Shehbaz remarked, while cautioning that “momentum without finance cannot be sustained”.

“Our grids must expand quickly and reliably. Storage must keep supply steady. New technologies must be affordable for all. Yet, this burden falls on countries already under heavy debt,” he emphasised.

The prime minister noted that Pakistan alone needs around $138 billion by 2035 for low-carbon power and $50 billion more to replace coal with solar.

He stated that the ‘35 by 35’ clean energy goal could only be achieved “if finance flows at the speed of ambition through concessional capital and the transfer of affordable technology”.

“Let us resolve to power our economies without impoverishing our people and light up our homes without darkening our planet. That is the promise of 35 by 35, and it is a promise we must deliver together and under all circumstances,” the premier remarked.

He thanked Turkiye President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, whose country has the COP31 presidency, for convening the “important dialogue”.

Earlier in the day, PM Shehbaz was received by Erdogan and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres upon his arrival at the venue, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said.

The premier and other world leaders then gathered for a group photograph at the summit.

In his speech at the Antalya Leaders’ Summit, PM Shehbaz will highlight Pakistan’s climate priorities and emphasise the urgent need for enhanced global climate action and strengthened international cooperation to mitigate the adverse impacts of climate change, according to PMO.

The Foreign Office (FO) said the prime minister will also highlight “Pakistan’s steps towards rapid solarisation and expansion of its renewable energy capacity, as part of its transition towards a cleaner and more resilient economy, along with its efforts to strengthen disaster preparedness and early-warning systems”.

He will call for predictable, adequate and accessible climate finance for developing countries to strengthen their resilience and pursue sustainable development, it added.

According to the PMO, a “Pakistan Pavilion” has been established at the COP31 venue where 54 events will be hosted on various themes.

Turkiye’s Erdogan highlights Gaza ‘ecocide’

Dozens of leaders were to speak during the “high-level segment” taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, including Erdogan, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose country hosted last year’s climate talks.

“Nature — no less than people — is also paying a heavy price for armed conflicts. The starkest example of this is Gaza… what has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide, but it is also an ecocide,” Erdogan said to applause.

Turkiye did not invite Israel to COP31, The Jerusalem Post reported.

“As the host country for the leaders’ summit, we did not send an invitation to Israel,” it quoted Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum as saying.

“Of course, we will discuss the climate and climate justice here. We say that there can be no climate justice where peace does not prevail.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, and the United Kingdom’s PM Andy Burnham were also scheduled to speak on Wednesday.

The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, has skipped the talks for the second year in a ‌row after ⁠President Donald Trump — who has called global warming a hoax — withdrew the US from climate cooperation following his return to office in 2025.

Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.

As the third day began, the UN chief told world leaders at the summit that the slow international response to climate change so far had placed the world on a path to destruction.

Governments must fight harder to preserve the planet for future generations, he said, in comments that set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders.

“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” Guterres said, pointing to rising emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters.

“But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder.”

PM meets world leaders

On the sidelines of the summit, the prime minister held conversations with leaders of various countries and international bodies.

The premier and his delegation also had a separate meeting with Iran’s Pezeshkian and his team.

The meeting was to “discuss bilateral relations and the promotion of mutual cooperation between Pakistan and Iran”, as well as the regional situation and matters related to regional peace, PMO stated.

PM Shehbaz, in a post on X, said he was “delighted to meet my brother”.

While reaffirming the “deep and enduring bonds” between the two neighbours, the prime minister said he “conveyed Pakistan’s deep concern over the prolonged conflict in our region”.

“Dialogue, restraint, de-escalation and sustained diplomacy are the only path to lasting peace,” he stressed.

“Building on the understandings reached under the Islamabad MoU, Pakistan continues to play a sincere and constructive role for peace and stability in the region and beyond.”

PM Shehbaz also met with Kuwait’s PM Ahmad Al-Abdullah Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, with both leaders discussing the longstanding fraternal relations between their countries.

They “reaffirmed their resolve to further strengthen cooperation in a range of areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, energy, development cooperation and people-to-people exchanges”, PMO said.

The two premiers expressed the hope that the recent ratification of the Pak-Kuwait defence agreement would “further promote bilateral cooperation”. They also exchanged views on international developments and challenges to regional peace.

PM Shehbaz’s informal meetings included those with Bangladesh’s PM Tarique Rehman, Palestinian PM Mohammad Mustafa, Saudi Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, Saudi State Minister for Foreign Affairs Adel bin Ahmed al-Jubeir and Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa, according to PMO.

He also met Organisation of Islamic Cooperation chief Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, World Bank President Ajay Banga and Türkiye’s First Lady Emine Erdoğan.

In his conversation with his Palestinian counterpart, PM Shehbaz expressed Pakistan’s full solidarity with Palestinians.

According to PMO, Mustafa thanked the government and people of Pakistan for “effectively raising their voices on the global level against the injustices inflicted on the Palestinian people and for supporting the Palestinian stance”.

“During these cordial meetings, the prime minister and the world leaders discussed strengthening bilateral relations and the situation in the region,” PMO said.

It added that the meetings also stressed the importance of highlighting the challenges faced by countries most affected by climate change at the international level.

Year of extreme weather

A UN report last month found the world on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.

Meanwhile, 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.

Former French prime minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, said on Tuesday the leaders’ speeches should give political impetus to the negotiations.

“It is an opportunity for leaders to make some announcements, and more this time, to explain how they will implement, because the key word in Antalya is implementation,” he told Reuters.

Several other nations, including France, Germany, Japan, Italy and Canada, did not send their top leaders to the talks this year and won’t be represented in the speeches.

“The world’s biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others,” said Mohamed Adow, director of climate and energy think tank Power Shift Africa.

Age of electricity?

COP31 host Turkiye has been pushing for countries to put a goal on electrification at the centre of a final deal, though critics say it may do little to curb warming.

The proposal targets a rise in electricity’s share of total global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, up from a little over a fifth now, theoretically reducing greenhouse gas emissions from cars, factories and buildings.

But the proposal does not include language requiring new power to be generated by clean energy sources, and governments have yet to clarify a broader plan to transition away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

Guterres urged countries to speed their transition to clean energy sources.

He said the world’s dependence on fossil fuels was also damaging economies, not just the climate, an apparent nod to surging petroleum prices since the start of the US and Israeli war against Iran that has disrupted Middle East oil exports.

“Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did not create and cannot control,” he said.

“Recent conflicts make clear that this is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown.”

Ahead of the conference, negotiators had been locked in discussions late on Sunday over demands by developing nations to include items on climate finance in the official agenda.

“This has already been a difficult start for COP31,” said Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace’s COP31 delegation.

Under UN climate agreements, developed countries, which are historically responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions, have provided financial support to help developing nations adapt to climate impacts and transition to cleaner energy. But poorer countries say the sums remain insufficient.

Inventor said developed countries were “taking a hard line” over whether to include a platform, agreed at COP30 in Brazil last year , aimed at discussing how wealthy nations should provide funds to developing nations.

African countries are also pushing for the agenda to include discussions on the tripling of adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops.

Observers say few major breakthroughs are expected at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war on Iran and Russia’s conflict in Ukraine.

World.title: ‘I stand by it’: Chaudhry Salik sticks to Punjab corruption claims despite Maryam's ire
World.content:
Minister for Overseas Pakistanis and PML-Q leader Chaudhry Salik Hussain on Wednesday asserted that he stood by his claims regarding corruption in Punjab.

Last week, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz sent a Rs5 billion defamation notice to Hussain for levelling allegations of corruption against her government and demanded that he retract his remarks.

“Reality is reality. I stand by it and will continue to,” he said on Geo News programme ‘Capital Talk’ while responding to a question about his brother Shafay Hussain being a minister in the same Punjab government he had criticised.

Salik said he did not think about hesitating to make the remarks because of this connection.

The PML-Q leader further said he would present evidence for his accusations before the court when furnishing his response to CM Maryam’s defamation notice.

“Making statements about dragging someone to court does not suit a politician,” he regretted, while referring to the Punjab CM’s remarks.

In response to a question, Salik said he had not been contacted by any government official or PML-N after the incident; except for an earlier meeting with Information Minister Attaullah Tarar during which he explained the context.

However, the latest “below-the-belt” remarks by Maryam and earlier responses by her minister worsened the row, Salik added.

On CM Maryam’s demand for him to resign from the ministry, the minister noted that his party was a coalition partner of the government under an arrangement and recalled Maryam was not even present during meetings at that time.

However, the PML-Q leader said it was up to the PML-N if it considered it no longer needed coalition partners.

In her Nov 3 speech, the Punjab CM had claimed that Salik’s anger stemmed from neither corruption nor progress; rather, the issue was that she had changed the deputy commissioner of Gujrat a few days earlier, whereas Salik allegedly wanted a DC of his choice to be appointed.

Asked about this on the show, Salik said: “We had very good working coordination with the former Gujrat deputy commissioner (DC), who had been working for the past 1.5 years.

“When DCs were being appointed 1.5 years ago, we asked that the official should be experienced in construction and urban development, as the development projects in the region were facing delays.”

However, after the appointment of the new DC, we did not raise any objection, he clarified.

The PML-Q leader further argued that his interview in Lahore was recorded on Sept 25 — rather than earlier this month when the remarks surfaced — while the DC was appointed on Oct 31.

“The Punjab chief minister made these remarks based on incorrect information,” Salik said.

The minister also regretted the withdrawal of his security by the provincial government after the incident.

He said that the Punjab government had deployed Elite Force officials at his Gujrat residence; however, after the incident, they were ordered to report back to the Police Lines.

What did Salik say?

During a talk show on a private television channel, the PML-Q leader praised the performance of his uncle Chaudhry Pervez Elahi as a former Punjab chief minister, further criticising the incumbent provincial administration headed by CM Maryam and alleging that he regularly heard complaints of corruption.

He also questioned lavish government spending , particularly the use of an official aircraft , arguing that public representatives should remain mindful of the country’s economic difficulties.

He said officials using government aircraft should be required to demonstrate the tangible outcomes and public benefits of their trips.

He also called for greater ministerial accountability, proposing that federal and provincial ministers should be empowered to perform their duties while also being held accountable for their performance.

Salik’s remarks carry particular political significance given the fractured relationship between the Chaudhry family and the PTI leadership.

Salik, the younger son of PML-Q president Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain, belongs to a family whose political loyalties have diverged sharply since the ouster of Imran Khan’s government in 2022 through a no-confidence vote.

While Elahi and his son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, aligned themselves with the PTI, the Shujaat family chose to stand with the Sharifs. Salik’s elder brother, Shafay Hussain, is also part of CM Maryam’s cabinet in Punjab.

World.title: UK police question Nato-assigned US soldier accused of spying for Russia
World.content:
UK police were questioning on Wednesday a senior American soldier assigned to Nato and suspected of spying for Russia, after his arrest amid a joint investigation with the US military and law enforcement.

The espionage case, the latest involving suspected Kremlin agents in Britain and elsewhere in Europe, comes with tensions heightened between Moscow and various European capitals after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

It also follows recent security scares at two British air force bases hosting the US military, which officials have accused Iran of being behind. Tehran has denied the allegations.

UK Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) have said the 41-year-old American soldier was detained near Gloucester, southwest England, on suspicion of violating national security laws and taken to a London police station.

Later on Tuesday, a senior Nato military official confirmed the soldier was assigned to its Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), the alliance’s 20-nation, high-readiness force led by the British Army.

Based at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, it can deploy at short notice anywhere in Europe or globally under the direct operational command of Nato’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe.

Imjin is also just a few miles from the UK’s sensitive GCHQ intelligence, security and cyber agency headquarters.

Probe ‘ongoing’

Vicki Evans, CTP’s senior national coordinator, said the “significant” arrest and investigation followed close collaboration between UK and US authorities.

“The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing,” she said in a statement late Tuesday.

US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director Kash Patel thanked British authorities — including the country’s domestic spy agency, MI5 — and their American counterparts “for their outstanding work”.

“This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies,” he said in a statement.

Police arrested the US soldier under two sections of the UK’s national security laws, one relating to obtaining or disclosing protected information and the other to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The law allows them to hold him without charge for up to 14 days.

Police said “the country to which the allegations relate is Russia”, adding officers were carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire.

But asked about the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday: “This arrest has nothing to do with us. We do not know what it is connected with.”

Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said the arrested person was a “senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information”.

He called it a “sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent”.

The UK-US probe is not linked to any other ongoing investigations, the police statement said.

Western countries have for years accused the Kremlin of espionage within their borders, as well as masterminding a string of incidents to undermine support for Ukraine as it battles Russia’s invasion.

In September, a British man appeared in a London court over allegations that he was preparing to sabotage a drone factory and drone manufacturing sites on behalf of Russian military intelligence.

Last year, a 66-year-old British man was jailed for seven years for his attempts to spy for Russia.

Beyond Britain, a number of European countries have made similar arrests, while Russia has also detained individuals it has claimed are spies.

On Wednesday, Russian security services said two “agents” working for Polish intelligence had been arrested in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania.

It followed Poland — a key supporter of neighbouring Ukraine in its war — announcing last week that it had arrested six people suspected of spying for Moscow and supplying its military.

World.title: World urged to tackle fossil fuels but big names skip COP31
World.content:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres railed against the oil and gas lobby on Wednesday, telling world leaders fossil fuels “must go the way of the dinosaurs” at a climate summit missing several prominent figures.

The two-week COP31 talks kicked off in Turkiye this week with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal.

“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us,” Guterres told dozens of world leaders assembled in the Mediterranean city of Antalya for two days of speeches by heads of state and government.

But few major breakthroughs are anticipated at the COP31 negotiations, which run until November 20, as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war with Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Since agreeing in 2023 for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver of climate change — nations have struggled to advance that goal at the annual UN conferences.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan (C), flanked by UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres (C-L), Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev (C-R), and other heads of state pose for a family photo during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) at the Antalya Expo Center in Antalya, Turkiye on November 11, 2026. — AFP

At his final COP before stepping down in December, Guterres said governments cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to support the fight against climate change.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” he said in another salvo against an industry he has long accused of fuelling climate chaos.

“Their strategy is simple: Distort the science. Delay the policy. Delay the action. Delay the accountability. It’s time to kick the habit — and end the fossil fuel addiction,” he said to sustained applause.

Climate silence

But some big names are missing at COP31, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only leader from a G7 country scheduled to address the summit.

“Since the start of this year, climate change has disappeared from speeches and documents from our global leadership,” recently re-elected Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva told fellow leaders.

“We’ve turned to talking more about arms and tariffs than the survival of future generations,” he said.

Climate campaigners breathed a huge sigh of relief when Lula, who has overseen a dramatic drop in deforestation in the Amazon, defeated right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro in last month’s presidential election.

“Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet,” Lula said.

Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva delivers a speech during the High-Level Segment for Heads of States and Government at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) at the Antalya Expo Center in Antalya, Turkiye on November 11, 2026. — AFP

While European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen spoke in Antalya, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni were among the European leaders not present.

The leaders of Canada, Japan and India are also expected to skip the event, while Chinese President Xi Jinping, who rarely attends COPs, was represented by Vice President Han Zheng. Unsurprisingly, President Donald Trump, who pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement, is also not attending.

Fossil fear

Climate activists singled out two of Wednesday’s higher-profile speakers – the EU’s von der Leyen and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – for failing to mention fossil fuels by name during their speeches.

Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine, whose Pacific nation is threatened by rising sea levels, said, “Every new oil well drilled, every new piece of coal extracted is a threat to my country’s future.

“The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate, but something to fear,” she said.

Her message stood in stark contrast to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who earlier this week announced the “good news” that his country had discovered new oil fields.

In his address on Wednesday, Erdogan said the world needed a “fair” energy transition that “takes into account the energy security and different development needs of different countries”.

Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, warned that “the quest for carbon neutrality without guaranteeing energy security can undermine our efforts”.

“The measures that are aimed at protecting the climate should not constitute barriers facing countries and impede their achievements of economic development,” he said.

Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman delivers a speech during the High-Level Segment for Heads of States and Government at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) at the Antalya Expo Center in Antalya, Turkiye on November 11, 2026. — AFP

Finland announced concrete plans to phase out fossil fuels, becoming just the fourth country after France, Germany and the Netherlands to do so.

COP31 host Turkiye is championing a voluntary initiative to accelerate the electrification of transport, buildings and industry, with a target of raising electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035.

The EU has stressed that electrification must be “clean”, which could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.

World.title: Nadra launches chatbot that tells families exact papers needed for succession certificates
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Families dealing with inheritance can now get the exact process and list of documents for their case from an automated chatbot, introduced on the revamped succession website of the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra).

The chatbot, called “ID”, works in Urdu and English on any phone or computer.

It asks the user a few simple questions about the deceased, the legal heirs and the assets, and then generates on its own the steps to follow and a checklist of only those documents that the particular case needs. No Nadra official is involved in the exchange.

Nadra spokesman Syed Shabahat Ali said the chatbot runs entirely online through a series of questions and answers, without asking for CNIC numbers or other personal details. Heirs living abroad are guided to complete their biometric verification online through the Pak ID facility.

The chatbot also tells users which office can take up their case. It warns them early if the matter will have to go to court, such as when an heir is a minor or the heirs are in dispute.

The chatbot interface advises the public to use it as a reference tool only, and to “always confirm final requirements” with the nearest Nadra registration centre.

The authority has been issuing succession certificates and letters of administration in uncontested cases since 2021. The chatbot offers guidance before the applicant reaches a Nadra office with a formal application.

Almost every family in Pakistan has to go through succession at some point, yet the requirements differ from case to case.

The law varies with the faith and sect of the deceased, and the procedure changes from province to province. Sindh, for instance, requires three newspaper s, while other jurisdictions require two.

Many applicants usually learn such details only at a Nadra counter, often after travelling from another city.

A screengrab from Nadra’s succession website. — succession.nadra.gov.pk

The website makes it clear that Nadra can issue a succession certificate or letter of administration only in uncontested cases, where all legal heirs agree and have no dispute among them, no heir is a minor or mentally disabled, and the matter is neither pending before a court nor already decided by one.

The deceased must be in Nadra’s records and the heirs must be registered in the Family Registration Certificate (FRC), while the applicant must hold a valid CNIC, Nadra card or Pakistan Origin Card (POC), as the old manual NIC is no longer accepted.

A legal heir has to visit a Nadra centre in person, except in Sindh and Balochistan, where a lawyer can appear on his behalf. If any condition is not fulfilled, Nadra does not issue the certificate and the family has to approach the court.

For an application to be accepted, the family has to produce the death certificate of the deceased issued by the relevant union council, municipal authority or cantonment board, along with the receipt of cancellation of the deceased’s CNIC, FRC, and copies of the CNICs of all legal heirs.

They also need a Schedule-I letter of authorisation attested by an oath commissioner, and the original property documents, as photocopies are not accepted.

In some cases, additional documents are required. For immovable property in Sindh, a search certificate has to be obtained, while in Sindh and Balochistan, a wakalatnama (power of attorney) is also required if the application is filed through a lawyer. If the deceased was a government or private employee, a letter from the concerned department about pension or service dues is also needed.

The fee for a succession certificate or letter of administration is Rs10,000 where total assets are less than Rs100,000, and Rs20,000 where assets are Rs100,000 or more, except in Sindh where it is Rs22,000. A duplicate certificate costs Rs5,000.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side.
