World.title: Nintendo sells 5.2 million copies of ‘Zelda’ remake in four days
World.content:
Nintendo sold 5.2 million copies of its “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” remake in just four days, invigorating the Switch 2 platform that had been waiting for a blockbuster hit.

Released on Nov. 5 for $59.99, the 2026 edition is a complete recreation of the 1998 classic action-adventure game for the Nintendo 64 console, replete with new graphics, level and character designs. It ranks among the best-reviewed video games of recent times, earning a score of 96 out of 100 from both players and professional reviewers on aggregator Metacritic.

The Switch 2 console has had an uneven first year on the market, challenged by the rising cost of memory pushing hardware prices up. The fast start by the new “Ocarina of Time” takes the Zelda game past the cumulative sales of “Donkey Kong Bananza,” another popular title from 2025. Only “Mario Kart World,” which was part of a launch bundle with the Switch 2 console, has sold more units so far.

The first Switch, released in 2017, got a huge boost from having “The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild” as a launch-day title that helped draw in gamers from outside the Nintendo ecosystem. Though a remake, the new “Ocarina of Time” may have a similar effect as Nintendo heads into the crucial holiday season.

World.title: Nissan pares car sales forecast on tougher China competition
World.content:
Nissan lowered its annual car sales outlook due to weak demand and mounting competition in China, where buyers are shifting to locally made electric vehicles faster than it expected.

The Japanese manufacturer now projects at most 3 million vehicle deliveries this year, from 3.15 million previously, it said Wednesday. Nissan reported second-quarter operating profit that came in significantly below analyst expectations.

“China remains our biggest challenge,” Chief Executive Officer Ivan Espinosa told reporters in Yokohama.

The results show how far the embattled Japanese carmaker still has to go in its efforts to come back from its worst financial crisis. Nissan has started a broad cost-cutting campaign that includes cutting jobs and shutting down factories. But it still faces sizeable debt obligations and is struggling to compete with the industry’s shift toward EVs with complex software, particularly in China.

Nissan’s sales in the world’s biggest car market fell 15% during the first half of the fiscal year. The company is looking to turn things around by adding more EVs and plug-in hybrid cars to its lineup, some of which will be exported to other markets.

Business was better elsewhere. Deliveries increased 6.3% in Japan and 2.1% in North America — regions where the shift to EVs is happening at a slower pace.

Nissan’s operating profit came in at ¥2.12 billion ($13.3 million) for the three months through September. That’s well below the ¥49.3 billion projected by analysts. The company maintained its full-year financial forecast on expectations that profitability will improve in the second half due to new models and higher sales volumes.

Nissan will announce a new business strategy in February that will go beyond its current restructuring plan, Espinosa said.

World.title: Exiled Cambodian opposition leader urges Japan to aid democracy
World.content:
Sam Rainsy, a Cambodian opposition leader currently living in exile in France, called on Japan to provide support for democracy in his country.

In a recent interview in Tokyo, Rainsy criticized former Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, 74, and his family for establishing a “dictatorship” in the Southeast Asian nation.

Rainsy said that he asks “the Japanese government to help consolidate democracy in Cambodia, because Japan is a model of democracy in Asia.”

After serving as prime minister for 38 years, Hun Sen stepped down and handed the position to his son, Hun Manet, in 2023. Since then, however, Hun Sen has filled influential positions and currently serves as president of Cambodia’s Senate.

In recent years, the Cambodian government has taken an authoritarian approach to suppress anti-government forces, resulting in the dissolution of the Cambodia National Rescue Party, the country’s largest opposition party, in 2017. Rainsy once served as head of the party.

Rainsy said that he was visiting Japan to inform the Japanese government and lawmakers of Cambodia’s current situation.

Democracy in Japan is “deep-rooted,” with the country having the “most stable democracy in Asia,” he said.

“Japan is a model ... at least for Asia, to ensure that there is respect for human rights, respect for the fundamental freedoms and respect for the democratic principles,” he said.

In October last year, Rainsy announced the establishment of a so-called independent government in Paris. “We conduct our activities to express the will of the Cambodian people inside Cambodia,” he said.

“The main objective is to ... give hope to the Cambodian people,” he said.

“You don’t trust (and) you don’t believe in the current government in the country, but there is a government in exile outside which represents you,” he said. “We give them an alternative.”

World.title: Japan, eight others get fossil award over leaders skipping climate talks
World.content:
An international nongovernment environmental group on Tuesday gave Japan and eight other countries its Fossil of the Day award for inadequate climate action, citing their leaders’ failure to attend the ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is absent from the two-day leaders’ meeting of the climate talks through Thursday for scheduling reasons, marking the third straight year that a Japanese prime minister has skipped the summit.

From the Group of Seven countries, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is the only leader expected to attend the summit.

The Climate Action Network said that the absence of the leaders from the meeting could delay the progress of negotiations and raise concerns that climate change measures would be put on the back burner.

The fossil award will be presented daily until the conference ends on Nov. 20.

World.title: ‘Three Millimeters to You’: A hokey but heartfelt tale of cross-cultural first love
World.content:
Teenagers in the first flush of love can do the darnedest things. Tatsuhiko (Soya Kurokawa) is an unambitious high schooler living in a sleepy coastal town in Kyushu, southern Japan, who falls hard for visiting South Korean exchange student Yoon-seul (Kim Ji-an).

They embark on a tentative courtship, only for her to suddenly get whisked back to her native Busan after parting on less-than-amicable terms. Determined to make amends in person, Tatsuhiko pulls out a ruler and measures a map in his textbook to determine the distance between their respective homes: just three millimeters! He initially tries to swim it, then elects to take the ferry instead.

Yes, we’re firmly in seishun eiga (youth film) territory, a genre in which no expression of adoration is too ridiculous, as long as it doesn’t involve the characters getting past first base.

World.title: Japan Supreme Court rules 2025 election was held in unconstitutional state
World.content:
The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the July 2025 Upper House election was conducted in an “unconstitutional state” due to vote-value disparities of up to 3.13.

The top court’s Grand Bench, presided over by Chief Justice Yukihiko Imasaki, issued the ruling on a total of 16 lawsuits filed by two groups of lawyers seeking to invalidate the election across the country. It dismissed requests to invalidate the election.

Imasaki said that the maximum disparity in the election was at a level that raises constitutional concerns. The ruling was backed by 10 of the 15 justices, while the other five found the 2025 election to be constitutional.

This is the first time the top court has found an Upper House election with a maximum vote-value gap of less than 4.00 to be held in an unconstitutional state. The court last recognized such a state for an Upper House election in 2013, when the maximum disparity was 4.77.

The 2025 election was held under the same framework as the previous poll in 2022. However, the maximum disparity rose to 3.13 from 3.03.

Prior to the top court’s decision, high court rulings were split on the lawsuits, with 11 finding the election to be in an unconstitutional state and five finding it constitutional.

World.title: Action thrills best treacly drama in ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’
World.content:
The sequel to the 2023 smash hit “ Godzilla Minus One ,” Takashi Yamazaki’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” had a Nov. 3 domestic opening as thunderous as the titular monster trampling a Tokyo street: ¥910 million ($5.75 million) from 590,000 admissions, a first-day box office record for a live-action film in Japan.

The film’s monster action, with Yamazaki himself supervising the VFX work, justifies those spectacular figures. Seen by this reviewer at the recently concluded Tokyo International Film Festival , “Minus Zero” explodes with visual excitement when Godzilla, risen from the watery grave into which he sank in the previous film, confronts another kaijū (giant beast), King Ghidorah.

World.title: As JET Programme turns 40, alumni and ministers stress its importance in age of AI
World.content:
Japan celebrated the 40th year of its flagship international exchange program this month, marking four decades of a project that has brought young people from around the world into Japanese classrooms and communities.

The Japan Exchange and Teaching Programme, more commonly referred to as JET, was launched in 1987 to promote foreign-language education and grassroots cultural exchanges, and has grown from an initiative involving 848 participants from four countries into one of the world’s largest international exchange programs.

However, the program is facing mounting pressure in recent years as translation work dries up due to the proliferation of artificial intelligence and as a weak yen makes Japan a less attractive destination for prospective participants.

World.title: 30 Japanese porn stars denied entry into Hong Kong, forcing adult expo’s cancellation
World.content:
A large-scale adult entertainment expo billed as Hong Kong’s first has abruptly been cancelled after nearly 30 Japanese adult-video (AV) performers were refused entry upon arrival at Hong Kong International Airport.

Organisers of the “Mega Fans Expo 2026” (MFE) released a statement on Wednesday announcing with regret the immediate cancellation of the three-day show, scheduled for Friday to Sunday at the Regal Airport Hotel, as well as a preview event on Thursday.

The statement did not give a reason for the abrupt cancellation, saying only that refund arrangements would be disclosed later through official channels.

World.title: Hong Kong aims for global police role with new academy to train 1,000 a year
World.content:
Hong Kong police aim to train 1,000 officers per year and bolster the city’s ties with overseas law enforcement agencies through a new international academy, which opened on Wednesday.

At the opening ceremony for the Hong Kong International Academy of Policing, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the institution was an investment in collective security that would bolster the city’s international partnerships.

“By bringing new enforcement leaders together, it would strengthen Hong Kong’s international partnerships,” Lee said.

World.title: Garage owner, 72, dies after car falls on him in Hong Kong
World.content:
A 72-year-old garage owner has died after a car he was repairing fell on him in Hong Kong.

Police received a report from a passer-by at 2.50pm on Wednesday that a man had become trapped beneath a private car off Wing Lai Road in Tseung Kwan O Upper Village.

Emergency personnel arrived to find the man unconscious, with his upper body trapped under the vehicle and only part of his legs visible.

World.title: Hong Kong rules out talent scheme caps despite squeeze on jobs for local graduates
World.content:
Hong Kong authorities have no plans to adjust talent-hunting schemes or cap the number of non-local graduates permitted to seek employment in the city, the labour chief has said, pointing to a rapidly ageing population and persistent manpower shortages across pillar industries.

But lawmakers representing workers said that local university graduates were finding it hard to secure jobs, particularly those without a background in innovation and technology (I&T), and faced keen competition from both Hongkongers and non-locals.

Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han told the legislature on Wednesday that the city’s policy of trawling for and retaining talent was driven by the peak in its working population in 2018 and an ageing demographic shrinking the workforce.

World.title: Hong Kong bid-rigging trial hears trio offered HK$2m bribes to win HK$20m tender
World.content:
Three alleged middlemen in a Hong Kong bid-rigging syndicate offered HK$2 million (US$256,410) in bribes to an owners’ corporation chairman and member to secure a HK$20 million renovation tender for an ageing building, a court has heard.

The prosecution’s opening statement in the District Court on Wednesday accused Chong Chun-to, 60, Lam Suet-pin, 53, and To Hon-sum, 47, of conspiring to offer bribes to two members of the owner’s corporation of Hing Tat Mansion in Kwun Tong during the bidding for major renovation works in 2022.

Corporation chairman Cheung Kin-wah, 55, and member Zhan Qingbo, 49, were also accused of conspiring with the men to influence owners to vote for companies affiliated with the syndicate.

The ICAC’s headquarters in North Point. Photo: Jelly Tse

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) has cracked down on corruption crimes in relation to bid-rigging in recent years, prosecuting 35 individuals and two companies.

World.title: 6 girls filmed vaping in Hong Kong school toilet, investigation under way
World.content:
A video showing six schoolgirls puffing on e-cigarettes inside a school toilet cubicle in Hong Kong has gone viral, prompting education authorities to say they are “highly concerned” and contact the school.

The 20-second clip, titled “Six people gathered in one room for hotpot”, was posted on Threads, Meta’s microblogging platform, on Tuesday. The post said the video had been reposted from Snapchat, where it was filmed last week.

It shows six students in school uniforms crammed into a single toilet cubicle, with a Snapchat filter applied.

World.title: Hong Kong considers tougher site operation rules after spike in construction scandals
World.content:
Hong Kong’s Construction Industry Council will form a task force to review site operations and address quality concerns after a series of substandard works were uncovered at building and infrastructure projects across the city.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho announced plans for the task force on Wednesday, saying that it would explore measures to improve the construction industry’s performance. These could include requiring frontline workers to wear body cameras while carrying out critical work procedures.

The announcement came after the government outlined plans to step up construction supervision by requiring contractors to photograph or video steel reinforcement before concrete pouring, with inspections by an independent laboratory afterwards.

01:35 Dozens of defective columns found at Hong Kong MTR station ‘unimaginable’, engineers and lawmakers say

“Having complete recordings will have a significant deterrent effect on the industry because all evidence will be right there,” Linn said, responding to lawmakers’ questions in the Legislative Council.

World.title: How Hong Kong can double asset holdings: target world’s ‘patient’ capital, FSDC advises
World.content:
Assets under management in Hong Kong would double with the addition of just a small portion of the money global insurance and pension funds have to invest, according to a member of the Financial Services Development Council (FSDC).

Hong Kong should do more to attract this so-called patient capital – assets that insurance companies and pension funds invest for the long term, said the government think tank that promotes the city as an international financial centre, in a report on Wednesday.

Globally, pension funds had total assets of US$68 trillion at the end of last year, while global insurers had investment assets of US$42 trillion at the end of 2024, according to data from the FSDC.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.content:
“Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.

“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”

“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.

Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Urinals installed in a women’s restroom at a bar in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019251/Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.title: Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019251/Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.content:
SHANGHAI — The ninth China International Import Expo ran from Nov. 5 to 10, with 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 162 countries, regions and international organizations.

More than 480 exhibits made global, Asian or Chinese debuts. Qualcomm brought a 6G terminal prototype out of the lab. Medtronic’s China-developed Kanghui orthopedic surgical robot had its world premiere. And a rare type of durian tree fruit, the Malaysian white durian, made its global debut.

Robots at the expo could be found working hotel front desks, taking photos for visitors, and running booth demos on their own — visibly more advanced than in past years. In place of the mechanical arm designed to play ping-pong featured last year, at this year’s expo, a company debuted an entire humanoid robot playing the sport. At the forum held alongside the expo, Xiong Jijun, Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology, said humanoid robots must be upgraded from performing simple actions to being “able to think and work.”

Sixth Tone photographers spent the week in the halls, capturing the new products, technologies and services on display.

(Header image: CIIE attendees play table tennis against a robotic opponent, Shanghai, Nov. 9, 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.title: From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.content:
The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

U.S. wireless chipmaker Qualcomm exhibited the world’s first 6G terminal prototype — the first time the device has been shown publicly outside the lab. The prototype has been used in joint tests with China Mobile, China’s largest telecom operator, and Chinese telecom equipment manufacturer ZTE. The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.

The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, Nov. 6, 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.title: Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.content:
China has opened its first school dedicated to declining and obscure fields of study, with a focus on ancient and classical Chinese texts.

The School for Rare and Endangered Disciplines was inaugurated in Beijing on Nov. 6 under the University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (UCASS). At the opening, the university also announced the launch of a national alliance of more than 80 universities, museums, and cultural and research institutions to share resources, conduct collaborative research, and cultivate talent in related fields.

The school comes as the number of scholars studying ancient Chinese scripts dwindles. Nationwide, only about 500 people work in ancient Chinese writing studies, and of the roughly 4,500 known oracle bone characters — the oldest known fully developed form of Chinese writing and widely used for divination purposes during the Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) — nearly two-thirds remain undeciphered, underlining the need for further research.

The initiative also builds on previous attempts by UCASS to preserve such fields, such as establishing an institute for rare and endangered studies in 2024 to train future talent in fields such as bamboo and silk studies, which examines script on the two materials, as well as classical studies, Turkic studies, and Assyriology, or studies of the Ancient Near East.

Each student of the new school’s bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree courses will be mentored by two members of the school’s more than 140 faculty members. UCASS has also built dedicated laboratories for the school’s use.

Students may pursue research in oracle bone studies, bamboo and silk studies, and classical studies. They may also train in over 10 ancient ethnic scripts, including Turkic, Tangut, Khitan, Jurchen, Manchu, Old Tibetan, Old Yi, Phags-pa, Naxi Dongba, and Zhuang.

“Ancient scripts like oracle bone script are on the verge of being lost, and some frontier history research relies on the survival of the country’s cultural roots and its long-term development,” Huang Dekuan, director of the Research and Conservation Center for Unearthed Texts at Tsinghua University, told state broadcaster CCTV.

Such disciplines are also hampered by scattered resources and research institutions working in isolation — key obstacles to research and transmission, according to CCTV.

China has called for increased focus on cultural heritage preservation in recent years. At an October press conference on cultural heritage protection, government officials called for advancing cultural heritage as a discipline, cultivating interdisciplinary talent in the field, and encouraging qualified universities to establish cultural heritage schools.

In a Nov. 7 commentary, domestic media outlet The Beijing News wrote that by emphasizing rare and endangered disciplines, the new school offers a lesson to other universities: schools should develop their own distinctive majors, resist the urge to offer only popular fields, and actively strengthen less mainstream majors.

“Only then can a university truly serve education,” it stated.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.title: Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.content:
Coming from a Shanghai family with a strong academic background, Yang Fan had always felt studying at university was his destiny. The only problem was, he was flunking middle school.

“He’d make the same mistake with a character the entire semester. I just couldn’t get him to do it right,” says his mother, Zhao Xuan, who could only look on in frustration as Yang struggled with his homework night after night. “Given how much it was taking for him to get through middle school, I felt high school would crush him.”

Last summer, with the conventional academic pathway looking a bad fit for their 15-year-old son, Zhao and her husband began to consider China’s integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program. Launched as a 2014 pilot in Shanghai, the initiative sees students spend up to three years at a vocational school before transitioning to a partner university to complete a related four-year bachelor’s degree program.

Over the past 12 years, the number of participating educational institutions has rapidly expanded, now covering at least seven provincial regions, and applications have soared.

Shanghai alone has established 91 majors across 38 vocational schools and 18 universities, enrolling about 20,000 students and producing six cohorts of graduates. Planned enrollment this year was 2,756, up from just 120 in 2014 and a 17.5% increase from 2025.

Programs cover diverse fields including robotics, accounting, digital media arts, big data engineering, logistics, environmental design, hospitality management, cultural heritage restoration, smart manufacturing, performing arts, sound recording, information security, and materials science.

The trend reflects a sea change in attitudes toward vocational education in China. Technical skills training has long been stigmatized as “low status” and a “fallback option,” but as the country’s workforce undergoes a massive restructuring driven by an aging population, advancements in artificial intelligence, and an economic slowdown, more people feel it now makes students more employable compared to those with purely academic backgrounds.

In real terms, most students in the integrated program say their experiences are far less stressful than those of their peers at traditional Chinese high schools, and that they are encouraged to focus more on their personal strengths rather than sticking to a one-size-fits-all curriculum.

However, because most applicants are only in their mid-teens, it’s often parents who make the final decision, with research suggesting that more-passive children have only a vague idea of, or interest in, what might lie ahead.

The path less traveled

It was only when Zhao learned that the prestigious Shanghai Maritime University (SMU) would join the integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program in 2026 that she was sure the pathway was a “realistic match” for Yang.

Soon, Zhao and her husband, who holds a Ph.D., had researched the job prospects of various degree holders and consulted with their son, who was willing to give vocational school a try. For him, it was an opportunity to follow his growing interest in mechanics and spend time on activities he’d been forced to drop in middle school, such as table tennis and learning to play guitar.

In the 2026 zhongkao, the national high school entrance exam, Yang scored highly enough to earn a place this fall in the mechanical design, manufacturing, and automation major run jointly by Shanghai Harbour School and SMU.

With the increase in applications, programs have been setting higher admission thresholds. More than 80% increased their cut-off in 2026, and over half by 20 to 30 points. To secure a place in either of the two majors run in partnership with SMU, students must score at least 690 points out of a maximum 750.

In the final year of middle school, “we really pushed ourselves to the limit,” says Zhao, though she dismisses the idea that her son’s zhongkao score was a reflection of any academic acumen. “We got lucky. The exam was on the easy side.”

Kuang Ying, a professor specializing in vocational education at Shanghai’s East China Normal University, points out that students and parents today have far more information about the integrated program compared to when it started.

“People weren’t familiar with these programs, and many working-class families lacked the information they needed to make a reasoned decision back then,” she says.

Pan Yuxiao, who grew up in Shanghai’s northern Chongming District, was among the first students to enroll in the pilot in 2014. He’d wanted to continue his studies at a high school closer to the city center, but his zhongkao score was too low.

By chance, he came across a brochure about the integrated program. “There was hardly any information back then. The teachers didn’t know about it, and neither did the parents,” recalls Pan, who eventually enrolled in the mechanical engineering major offered by Shanghai Industrial Technology School and Shanghai Polytechnic University (SSPU).

Kuang believes that not only has awareness of such courses substantially improved since the inaugural cohort but parents’ priorities have also changed. “Now people are looking for a more certain future,” she explains. Families are no longer solely fixated on school rankings and prestige; they are taking a more honest look at their child’s academic standing relative to their peers and what they can realistically achieve. This allows them to make more informed, pragmatic choices tailored to a child’s abilities and circumstances, she adds.

The reason many have chosen the integrated program over a standard high school, then and now, is simple: It virtually guarantees a spot on a bachelor’s degree course. However, for some, mental health is another major factor.

Wu Yulu, a sophomore student at SSPU, scored 640 in the 2022 zhongkao, enough to get into a selective local high school in Shanghai. But she doubts she would ever have made it to college through the traditional route. “I just wouldn’t have had the stamina for it,” she says.

The pressure of middle school took its toll on Wu. In her first year, she would work on her homework late into the night and often woke up at her desk. When her grades began to drop, she took a leave of absence due to stress.

A 2022 report by the China Youth and Children Research Center based on interviews of 24,758 students in 10 provinces found that 23% of middle school students were at risk of depression, while 31% showed signs of anxiety.

When Wu returned to middle school the following fall, she had lots of material to catch up on but had learned to “let myself off the hook.” It was around then that she heard about the integrated vocational-to-undergraduate major in taxation that led to a bachelor’s from SSUP.

For Wu and her parents, it seemed a fitting path forward. “I wouldn’t have to wear myself out,” she says. As the program was still relatively unknown in 2022, she was one of only two students in her class who applied.

Same but different

As in Yang’s case, Jia Xinyi’s parents first suggested she join an integrated program, recommending she study early years education. This was 2017, and China had just relaxed its one-child policy. Her family predicted a baby boom and reasoned that Jia could land a stable job at a kindergarten, yet she had little interest in the subject.

When it came time to decide, Jia was torn. “No one could guarantee how things would turn out, but the integrated pathway offered a clearer route,” she says. She eventually settled on a major in materials science and engineering because a relative already worked in the field.

Once enrolled at Shanghai Material Engineering School, Jia found the daily schedule fairly typical: four morning classes, another four after lunch, and 30- to 90-minute study sessions in the evening. Chinese, mathematics, and English formed a core part of the curriculum for all three years, with students using standard textbooks. However, she feels the homework was far more manageable than at regular high schools.

Wu agrees. She says the learning atmosphere at her vocational school was relatively relaxed; she was no longer plagued by the workload-induced sleep deprivation she’d experienced in middle school.

However, on top of core academic subjects, vocational school students also take practical classes in their chosen field.

While preparing for a vocational qualification exam, Jia learned to conduct chemical analyses of construction materials, received skills training in cement production, and was given a factory tour. Pan says his teachers at Shanghai Industrial Technology School introduced him to 3D printing technologies and a five-axis machine center, an advanced cutting tool.

Professional skills competitions also offer a different dimension. Wu took the opportunity to enter contests in intelligent finance and taxation, and won awards for several videos she made after teaching herself how to use editing software. These achievements helped her come to terms with her tough middle school years and showed her that she could shine through her strengths.

In most provinces, students on the integrated pathway take a transition exam after three years.

Wu recalls that the test was undemanding. For the academic section, the pass mark was 180 points out of 300, while the only vocational requirement was that candidates reach 70% of the class average. “The pass rate was very high,” she notes, adding that only one student in her year had failed.

Parental guidance

Twelve years in, the integrated program is still a work in progress. Local education officials commonly visit participating schools to solicit student feedback on the teaching quality and the curriculum. Jia recalls that some of her classmates called for more class hours in physics and chemistry, as well as better-qualified teachers.

However, for her, the major challenge was what came next. While studying for her bachelor’s at the Shanghai Institute of Technology, Jia discovered that she needed to take the kaoyan, China’s national postgraduate entrance exam, to progress to one of the university’s master’s programs. To prepare, she had to start from scratch in several foundational academic subjects because her vocational school had devoted so little time to them. She believes this has since been addressed in training plans for subsequent cohorts.

Meanwhile, education experts are concerned by the fact that it’s typically parents pushing their children to choose the integrated program, rather than driven by personal interest.

According to an education industry magazine article written this June by a finance tutor at Shanghai Economic Management School, surveys show that roughly 80% of students on the integrated program had primarily followed their parents’ wishes in applying, “placing themselves in a passive stance” and leading to a “lack of initiative.”

Pan notes that several of his vocational school classmates had “no interest in their major and felt that their potential was being wasted.” Whenever Jia posted about her studies on social media, she also noticed that the vast majority of comments and questions were from parents.

Kuang believes few adolescents have the ability to think clearly about decisions with such far-reaching consequences. “Middle school students are often bewildered when it comes to making choices. Even high school graduates are,” she says, adding that China’s education system doesn’t provide children with enough formal career guidance or expose them to different professions early.

It’s been five years since Pan’s inaugural 40-strong cohort graduated from university. He estimates that only 25% to 33% of his classmates work in fields related to their majors. He initially found a job working with machinery after graduation but has since switched to the medical industry.

Jia is completing a postgraduate internship in environmental, health, and safety management, far removed from her academic focus of materials science. She believes it’s highly unlikely she’ll end up working in her field of study.

Switching track

As China’s real economy develops and the central government places greater emphasis on skilled professionals, Kuang says the integrated program’s growing popularity is inevitable. “Technical skills will become one of the major pathways to success,” she predicts.

Since 2014, the public has gained a better understanding of how the integrated program differs from conventional vocational education. Schools are committing quality resources and assigning their most capable teachers. “These positives give Chinese parents greater confidence in choosing this once-stigmatized pathway,” Kuang adds.

In Pan’s view, much of what students learn in high school is irrelevant to real life, while those who choose the integrated route are making a conscious decision to use their time and energy wisely.

Jia adds that parents are having to consider alternatives because the days when graduating from a prestigious university guaranteed a secure job are gone. However, she still worries that some see the integrated vocational route as a “back door” to a bachelor’s degree.

Yang started at Shanghai Harbour School this fall and hopes to take part in many extracurricular activities and competitions. On registration day, the incoming cohort was encouraged to pursue independent learning, which Zhao was glad to hear.

“We don’t want our child spending his time in a passive learning environment, simply being dragged along by others,” she says. “Choosing the integrated pathway doesn’t mean taking the easy way out. It means stepping onto a different track, one that still demands hard work but puts my son in the driver’s seat.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Yang Fan, Zhao Xuan, Pan Yuxiao, and Jia Xinyi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Chen Lei, Wang Zhaoxue, and Zhang Zhenyao.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.title: More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.content:
More Chinese regions are implementing autumn and spring breaks in compulsory education, expanding a decadelong national initiative. Some have also waived fees for students on break and rolled out support measures to help parents take leave at the same time as their children.

Spring and autumn holidays across all compulsory education schools have been rolled out provincewide in at least 15 provinces, as well as numerous cities in other provinces, such as the southern megacity of Shenzhen, domestic media reported last week. In China, compulsory education lasts nine years, encompassing primary and middle school. Breaks will occur in November and April for four to five days each.

The reform dates back to 2004, when Hangzhou, capital of the eastern province of Zhejiang, piloted the breaks. In 2013, the initiative expanded nationally when the State Council issued an announcement encouraging local governments to adopt it, and the rollout accelerated again in 2025 when central authorities urged more schools to implement the holidays.

Chu Zhaohui, a researcher at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, told domestic media outlet Red Star News that the holidays actually boost learning.

“Learning isn’t confined to schools or taught only by teachers and parents,” Chu said, adding that the holidays give students space for self-exploration.

At the same time as introducing spring and autumn holiday policies, many cities have also added supporting measures so parents can sync their leave. In October, Longnan city in the northwestern Gansu province encouraged employers to implement paid leave and prioritize compensatory rest for employees with school-age children, aligning staff leave with school holidays.

Foshan, a city in the southern Guangdong province, also issued a proposal on Nov. 3 calling on employers to prioritize arranging leave for employees with children during the autumn holiday. The city’s five-day autumn break begins Nov. 11.

Many tourist spots are also waiving entrance fees for children during the upcoming fall break. In the eastern city of Wuxi, a theme park dropped entry fees for students 16 and under throughout November; 15 top tourism sites in Huangshan in the eastern Anhui province, a city known for its mountain of the same name, are now entry-free for children under 18; and the Dujiangyan scenic area in the southwestern Sichuan province waived fees for primary and middle school students between Nov. 12 and 16.

The breaks have significantly boosted travel demand, according to online travel booking platform Qunar. Data from Qunar revealed that in November, air ticket bookings for children 12 and under increased 1.6 times year on year, while parent bookings rose by 50%.

Wang Qiyan, director of the Leisure Economy Research Center at Renmin University, told Red Star News that spring and autumn breaks “enable off-peak travel, avoiding the packed scenic spots of winter and summer vacations.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Tourists take photos of St. Sophia Square during the autumn break in Harbin, Heilongjiang province, Nov. 4, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.title: A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.content:
On Oct. 6, 2026, a female customer posted complaints on multiple social media platforms about a fried skewer stall in Gao County, Yibin, in southwestern China’s Sichuan province. “Avoid XX Copper Pot Potatoes. The owner can’t take the heat,” she wrote. She had bought a 10-yuan ($1.40) fried food combo from the stall, run by a 33-year-old woman surnamed Hu, but was dissatisfied with the portion of potatoes. “She just refused to add potatoes afterward,” the customer added. Her location-tagged posts quickly spread, and negative comments about Hu and her stall flooded the comment sections.

Hu responded to the criticism, writing, “I stand behind my portions.” Three days later, on Oct. 9, she jumped into a river and died by suicide.

Hu had run the stall for more than four years, sleeping less than six hours a night. In her suicide note, she described the enormous pressures she faced in life. She had hoped to watch her child grow up, she wrote, but the video telling people to avoid her stall had been the straw that broke the camel’s back.

She also wrote: “These past two days I have experienced what I consider cyberbullying. One person complained about no potatoes in her order, and then the comments came flooding in about bad service and poor-tasting food.”

This was not the first tragedy of its kind. In August 2025, a 57-year-old obstetrician-gynecologist surnamed Shao in Zhoukou, central China’s Henan province, jumped to her death. According to her family, she had endured more than seven months of cyberbullying over a medical dispute. In 2023, after a primary school student in Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, was killed in a traffic accident on campus, his mother was subjected to online attacks and later jumped to her death. In cases like these, public opinion often attributes the tragedies to cyberbullying.

But in Hu’s case, labeling the entire incident “cyberbullying” and placing the blame on the customer who posted the negative review would exaggerate the power of a single act of expression.

The customer maintained that she was simply describing a genuine experience, with “no malice, incitement, or falsehood.” She did not insult or personally attack anyone, disclose private information, or call for coordinated attacks online or offline. Her criticism may have been harsh, subjective, or exaggerated, but based on the content of her posts alone, it is difficult to characterize it as cyberbullying.

Many negative comments about the stall owner appeared beneath the posts, but there is currently no evidence that they were all malicious. Public criticism can be harsh, but legal liability must rest on provable facts.

In July 2026, China released a draft Anti-Online Violence Law for public comment. It defines online violence as “concentrated or sustained” acts involving “insult and abuse, rumor-mongering and defamation, incitement of hatred,” and similar behavior. A negative review based on a genuine transaction cannot automatically be classified as cyberbullying because it has harmful consequences. Moreover, the draft has not yet become law.

A common misconception is that anything posted online will inevitably spread and attract attention. That is simply not true. People publish vast amounts of content every day, but only a tiny fraction attracts widespread attention.

Consider Dr. Shao’s case. Following an investigation, the platform disclosed that her account had received more than 10,900 comments, about 60 of which were suspected of containing attacks or other inappropriate content. The rest were classified as normal or neutral interactions. Although the platform’s findings should not be treated as a definitive record of every offensive interaction, they serve as a reminder that not every comment should be regarded as a malicious attack.

None of this excuses genuine cyberbullying. In 2018, a female doctor surnamed An in Deyang, Sichuan, became involved in a dispute with a boy at a swimming pool. The boy’s family posted edited surveillance footage online accompanied by inflammatory text. After enduring sustained online attacks, An died by suicide. In 2021, a court sentenced three defendants to prison for criminal insult.

The law is not powerless against cyberbullying. Precisely because it has the power to punish such behavior, however, we must distinguish criminal incitement and insults from harsh criticism.

Tragedies often result from a combination of factors. We cannot draw a direct causal line from a single negative review and the comments that followed to a person’s suicide. The negative review was one link in a chain of events, but it was neither the sole cause nor something that made the outcome inevitable.

Hu’s final message makes clear the immense pressures she faced in her personal life and as a small business owner. Her psychological state and the support available to her at the time also deserve attention.

The platform’s decision to promote the post to nearby users is just how online reviews work. Positive and negative reviews must be visible to help consumers distinguish good businesses from bad ones. But regulating them presents a dilemma.

Any screening system risks two types of errors: false positives, in which legitimate criticism is flagged as malicious, and false negatives, in which malicious comments go undetected. Tightening controls reduces false negatives but increases false positives, while relaxing them has the opposite effect. Platforms must therefore balance the costs of both.

For platforms such as the consumer review service Dianping and the short-video app Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, determining a post’s motives is difficult, and predicting its consequences even harder. Siding with businesses risks suppressing legitimate criticism, while siding with consumers risks allowing malicious attacks. There is no one-size-fits-all solution.

Anyone who has maintained a blog or public social media account knows how pervasive online negativity can be, with abusive comments and private messages a common occurrence. We cannot expect everyone to tolerate such abuse, but where should we draw the line in regulating it?

Cyberbullying typically involves a series of acts including verbal abuse, defamation, and insults. Such behavior may constitute a civil infringement and, in serious cases, give rise to criminal liability. But the definition of cyberbullying must not become so broad that it exaggerates the harm caused by ordinary expression.

The “clear and present danger” standard in U.S. legal history offers a useful reminder that speech should not be restricted merely because it causes discomfort. However, that standard arose in a specific legal context and cannot be directly applied as a general principle of Chinese law.

If we endlessly magnify the psychological harm that speech can cause and attribute tragic outcomes solely to what people say, the argument that “speech can be harmful” risks becoming a blanket justification for restricting expression.

If we blame every tragedy on the criticism that preceded it, consumers may hesitate to post negative reviews, and others may begin to self-censor. Free expression would suffer, potentially undermining market competition.

Such a focus on cyberbullying also overlooks two critical issues: the pressures facing small business owners and the need for better mental health support. Long hours, unstable incomes, and the stresses of running a business can make a single bad review feel overwhelming. China’s national mental health hotline, 12356, also has an important role in identifying and responding to people in crisis.

We must confront genuine cyberbullying without silencing legitimate criticism, while also addressing gaps in mental health care and support for small businesses. Blaming a single review may offer a convenient explanation for Hu’s death, but it brings us no closer to understanding the tragedy or preventing the next one.

Translator: Gabriel Kwan.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.content:
As it expands its weather-warning systems across the Global South, China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU — an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration — to Sri Lanka, one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

The device, described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox, was presented to Sri Lanka’s meteorological department on Nov. 1. It will form part of a system designed to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year.

Launched in July 2025, MAZU takes its name from a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It combines AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from the country’s weather satellites.

Conventional weather forecasting relies on supercomputers to calculate how the atmosphere will change using equations based on physical laws. AI models, by contrast, learn from years of weather data.

“Chatbots familiar to the public learn patterns in language, while AI weather models learn how the atmosphere evolves,” Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led the development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, told Sixth Tone. “By training on years of meteorological data, these models can predict future weather conditions based on current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity.”

Once trained, AI models can produce forecasts faster and more cheaply than conventional methods. One model can generate a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods. For forecasts covering 15 to 60 days, AI models can reduce computing costs to one-thousandth of those of conventional methods.

But most of the savings come from running routine forecasts, Niu said. Training models, building datasets, and maintaining systems still require investment — resources many countries in the Global South lack.

MAZU’s cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, according to domestic media, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years.

In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data to develop warnings for heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods. In Djibouti, the model developed by Niu’s team helps provide tailored weather warnings for the East African country’s port.

Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, for which there is little historical data. Local weather in complex terrain also remains difficult to forecast, and it is not always clear how AI models arrive at their predictions.

The models also need to be adapted to local conditions, Niu said. “Our approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, conduct independent evaluations, and make local adjustments.”

Even with AI, he added, “human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: The weather warning system Mazu at the China Meteorological Administration booth during 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. VCG）

World.title: COP31 leaders try out new sales pitch for climate action: Do it for the economy
World.content:
FAMILY PHOTO. Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pose for a family photo with other leaders during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 11, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, says he likes the reframing of the issue

ANTALYA, Turkey – Leaders at the COP31 summit in Turkey are trying out a new sales pitch for climate action that is tailored to the times: do it to bolster the economy and bring down the cost of living.

The message, being repeated in the hallways and on the plenary stage of the annual UN conference, reflects efforts by organizers to capture the attention of governments wrestling with crises that have pushed global warming down the list of priorities.

Among those is rampant inflation driven in part by disruptions to Middle East crude oil shipments since the onset of the Iran war. Consumer price pressures from fuel to food were a major driver in the US midterm elections that handed control of Congress to Democrats, and are an important vulnerability for leaders across Europe, Asia and elsewhere.

“Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did not create and cannot control,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders attending the summit on Wednesday, November 11.

“Recent conflicts make clear that this is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown,” he added, saying the clear solution is a shift to renewable energy.

Simon Stiell, head of the UN’s climate office, made the same point. “Today, chaos in global energy markets and climate disasters are supercharging inflation, slamming government budgets, pushing household bills up and living standards down,” he told the conference.

“The political costs of fossil fuel dependency are unforgiving. Climate action can help relieve the pressures.”

John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, said he liked the reframing of the issue.

Climate change has become a massively divisive political issue in recent years, including in the US, where President Donald Trump last year withdrew the world’s top historical greenhouse gas emitter from international climate cooperation after calling warming a hoax.

“I think everybody who is working on climate needs to change the way they talk about it,” Kerry told reporters on the sidelines of the summit.

“I think that grouping of security, health, jobs, stability of communities and food supply are all very real and very much on people’s minds when I talk to them.”

To be sure, speakers at COP31 tended to agree the primary motivation for climate action should center on the overwhelming scientific evidence that warming is human-driven and dangerous.

“It is our responsibility to turn scientific evidence into political action and ensure that our decisions are guided by fact, not short-term political interests,” Slovenian President Natasa Pirc Musar said in a speech to the summit on Wednesday.

But European energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen said emphasizing the other benefits of cutting emissions could help build a consensus for action that could even include climate sceptics.

“Because even if you don’t believe in climate change, which I obviously do, we should be able to agree that moving away from a dependency on fossils is extremely smart for security reasons,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: DSWD: More than 1,300 vendors affected by ASEAN Summit
World.content:
AYUDA. Vendors in Pasay City affected by the ASEAN Summit receive P10,000 from the Department of Social Welfare and Development on November 11, 2026.

The vendors whose livelihoods have been disrupted are receiving cash aid and family food packs from the Department of Social Welfare and Development

MANILA, Philippines – There are more than 1,300 vendors whose livelihoods have been affected by the Philippines’ hosting of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits, according to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said on Wednesday, November 11, that the Parañaque City government forwarded to the DSWD a list of vendors affected in Baclaran, a bustling market area, amid security measures implemented for the event.

The city government said street vendors are “temporarily prohibited” from operating along Roxas Boulevard and its service roads, from Redemptorist Road to Quirino Avenue, as well as the road beneath the Light Rail Transit (LRT) until November 20.

Since Baclaran is near Pasay City as well, the DSWD is also coordinating with the local government to identify more affected vendors in the area.

“Bagamat humihingi kami ng paumanhin sa mga naantala ang hanapbuhay dahil sa napipintong ASEAN Summit, ang direktiba ng ating Pangulo ay masigurado na mabigyan sila ng tulong pinansyal kasi alam natin na wala silang kikitain sa mga araw na ‘yon,” Gatchalian said on the sidelines of cash aid distribution in Pasay City.

(We apologize to those whose livelihoods were put on hold because of the upcoming ASEAN Summit, but the directive of the President is to ensure that they will be given financial support because we know they will not have earnings during those days.)

Play Video

In Pasay City, around 50 ambulant vendors and eatery workers received P10,000 from the DSWD’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program on Wednesday. They were also given family food packs.

It was the second batch following the aid distribution to some 30 individuals on Sunday, November 8.

Most of the beneficiaries were located along Diokno Boulevard.

“Malaking tulong na rin naman po kahit papaano…. Pagkakasyahin hangga’t walang trabaho (This is still a great help somehow. We’ll make do with it while we have no work),” said Anabel de Luna, 34. The eatery where she works temporarily closed on Monday, November 9, and may resume operations on November 20 or 21.

But others like Rizal Villaula, a 40-year-old pares cart owner, had to stop selling on October 22 amid road clearing operations. He has since entered into multiple gigs, like towing services.

Maria Joanna Cristina Samarro, a 46-year-old ambulant vendor, has been selling cigarettes for the past weeks to earn just enough for some meals.

But she took the chance to set up her table in front of the Senate building, also along Diokno Boulevard, to sell various items such as bread, coffee, and soft drinks, as protesters gathered there on Wednesday morning.

When there are no road restrictions, she can earn up to P500 a day.

Gatchalian said affected vendors in Parañaque City will receive their cash aid and food packs by Thursday, November 12.

Malacañang earlier declared November 16 to 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila to make way for the ASEAN Summit. – Rappler.com
