Across both Batangas and Laguna, these initiatives form part of Manila Water Philippine Ventures’ broader strategy to strengthen climate resilience, secure alternative water sources, improve operational efficiency, and ensure reliable water service amid increasingly challenging weather conditions. Through sustained investments in infrastructure and preparedness measures, MWPV continues to support the long-term water security of communities throughout the South Luzon corridor.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: Myanmar Junta Seeks Record Military Budget as Millions Struggle With Poverty
World.content:
The Myanmar regime plans to increase the military budget to a record high for the 2026-27 fiscal year, even as approximately one-third of the country’s population lives in poverty.

Since 2021, the regime has been waging war against several established ethnic armed organizations as well as newly emerged resistance forces, including the People’s Defense Force, across the country, spending a large portion of its budget on military expenses.

Last Thursday, the regime’s rubber-stamp Union Parliament (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw), where the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and its allies hold a majority of seats, debated a supplementary budget allocation bill.

The proposed allocation would bring total defense spending to 10.53 trillion kyats (US$5.01 billion), combining the initial 2026-27 fiscal year estimate of 7.95 trillion kyats with a supplementary grant of 2.58 trillion kyats.

Chit Swe, an Upper House lawmaker representing Ayeyarwady Region’s Constituency No. 11 and first deputy chair of the Joint Public Accounts Committee, urged parliament on November 5 to approve the regime’s proposed budgets, including the record-high military budget.

He said the committee had only eight days to verify the budget, with some items requiring ground observation, and that at least two weeks would be needed for verification.

If the supplementary allocations are approved, the budget deficit is projected to surge from 8.98 trillion kyats to 11.41 trillion kyats, he stated.

The military budget has surged continuously since the coup.

Under the last civilian government, led by ousted democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, defense expenditure for the 2020-21 fiscal year stood at just 3.4 trillion kyats.

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, it increased to over 5.6 trillion kyats. Although defense expenditures for the remaining years were not officially released, the current budget figures show that spending has nearly doubled compared to 2023-24.

Meanwhile, approximately 17.9 million people are “multidimensionally poor”, while two-thirds of the population are either poor or at risk, according to a UN Development Programme (UNDP) report published on October 8.

After five years of military regime rule, Myanmar people continue to suffer from soaring prices of basic goods and living costs amid the civil war, and face personal safety and security concerns.

Although the budget is still in draft form, the proposed military expenditure has drawn widespread criticism from the public.

“The budgets that should be spent on the country’s education, health, social welfare and nation-building are instead being used to kill the people,” said Naung Yoe, a military defector who now works with the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute.

According to the MDSI, the Directorate of Defense Industries, which manufactures ammunition and aerial bombs used in the regime’s indiscriminate attacks, has consumed the largest share of the military’s budget since the coup.

“It is deeply tragic and unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Mideast Crisis Fuels Oil Conflict in Myanmar’s Heartland
World.content:
Myanmar’s small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry that is becoming increasingly lucrative amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

“As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us,” said Htun Aung, a worker on an oil well in Myanmar’s arid heartlands.

“But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder,” said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.

Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

But the central region of Magwe hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.

The area is dubbed “Anyar Dubai,” associating the Anyar or central dry zone landscape with the oil boom emirate, despite the pitiable US$50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.

With prices at Myanmar’s petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground “black gold” is a coveted prize.

“We just want to live in peace,” said Htun Aung. “But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other—they keep attacking each other.”

“We’ve had to flee three, four, five times already,” he added. “We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again.”

Digging in

Pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magwe’s Myaing Township since 2023.

They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy River in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.

Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025’s total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the 2021 putsch.

Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.

Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of meters down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.

Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill, one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.

Some wells yield dribbles while others gush, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel.

“Anyar Dubai” has been “going viral” for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when regime-held areas are rationing petrol.

He touted recent offensives fending off military advances but admitted being battered by counter-attacks.

“We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us,” said the 35-year-old.

Myanmar’s military could not be reached for comment.

In September, the military claimed a month-long military operation captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighboring Pakokku Township.

Black market

Scores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic armed groups are fighting the military.

As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill their war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.

Oil projects are not generally contested.

The major ones are under staunch military guard, and on-the-books output is tiny by international standards at around 6,000 barrels a day last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

But the artisanal fields are coveted by rebels precisely because of their modest size, according to Thomas Kean, a Myanmar consultant for the International Crisis Group.

“Part of the reason why they’re significant is because they’re not globally significant,” he said, explaining that they are small enough to thrive under the radar yet big enough to fund guerrillas.

Spiking oil prices may not directly drive conflict, said Kean, highlighting a broader military campaign to evict rebels from heartland footholds by squeezing revenue sources.

But as the spoils of war become more profitable, the stakes get higher.

“We’re talking about millions of barrels a year coming out of these oil fields,” he added. “With global prices what they are, that’s a significant amount of money.”

World.title: Shan State’s Scam Industry Expands Under Protection of Regime-Aligned Militias
World.content:
More than two years after high-profile anti-regime military offensives shattered many of Myanmar’s most notorious scam enclaves near the Chinese border, cyber-fraud syndicates have metastasized across the interior of Shan State, the country’s largest state.

Rather than wiping out the illicit multi-billion-dollar industry, the fall of Kokang’s capital, Laukkai, in January 2024 triggered an influx of scammers deeper into Myanmar—chiefly into Shan State’s interior and Karen State in the country’s south.

By mid-2026, cyber-scam syndicates had expanded across more than 63 percent of Shan State’s 55 townships, establishing footholds in at least 35 of them. This assessment is based on official enforcement and crackdown data published by the military regime’s Ministry of Information, alongside reports from four ethnic armed organizations (EAOs)—the United Wa State Army (UWSA), the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

The entrenchment of telecom fraud comes as Shan State continues to bear the brunt of decades of civil war. Observers point out that these conditions have fostered an acute crisis in which the unchecked proliferation of scam syndicates not only expands organized crime networks, but also threatens local socioeconomic stability and lures local young people into the illicit economy.

Operation 1027, an anti-regime offensive launched by the Three Brotherhood Alliance on October 27, 2023, toppled the cross-border empires run by Kokang’s notorious “Big Four” families—the Bai, Wei, Ming and Liu clans. The alliance comprised the TNLA, MNDAA and Arakan Army. Parallel crackdowns were launched in areas controlled by the UWSA and NDAA. Yet far from marking the demise of the scam industry, the dismantling of those border scam complexes simply scattered the surviving networks, driving them deep into Shan State’s interior.

From the border to the interior

According to local residents, hundreds of Chinese nationals arrived in southern Shan State’s Laihka Township around November 2023, approximately a month after Operation 1027 began. Locals said the newcomers first erected compounds near Manpang Village before launching scam operations.

Instead of operating out of massive, conspicuous complexes housing huge numbers of people as they previously did, they rented homes dispersed throughout residential neighborhoods to fragment their workforce, and even set up makeshift tent encampments in rural villages and forests.

Starting in February 2026, the regime began conducting raids against online scam compounds in Laihka. According to official releases, as of the end of October, 129 Chinese nationals had been arrested, comprising the majority of those detained.

According to statements given by detainees, they crossed into Myanmar from Xishuangbanna, in the far south of China’s Yunnan Province, entering UWSA-controlled Panghsang and the NDAA-controlled Mong La area. From there, coordinated networks facilitated their phased, step-by-step relocation across northern, southern and eastern Shan State.

Similarly, in northern Shan, residents noted that telecom fraud operators began trickling into Tangyan town in early 2024.

According to UWSA statements, during crackdowns on scam operations in Tangyan in November 2024 and July 2025, Wa forces arrested over 1,000 people, 829 of whom were Chinese nationals.

The military junta likewise launched its own raids and arrests in Tangyan across 2024 and 2025.

Despite raids conducted by both the junta and the UWSA, a military sweep proved that these criminal syndicates were still operating in Tangyan in April 2026. During a raid on an online scam camp near Kaung San Village, the military reported arresting 123 individuals, 103 of whom were Chinese nationals.

“Local youths worked at the scam centers. Usually, whenever there’s a raid, those who can run simply flee. Some get away, some don’t. But we’ve never heard of the actual bosses being caught,” a Tangyan resident said.

Throughout 2025, these fraud networks spread rapidly into numerous townships in Shan State: Mongyai and Hsipaw in northern Shan; Nansang and Mongpan in southern Shan; and Kengtung and Mong Hsat in eastern Shan.

In October 2026, the regime announced the arrest of 75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar citizens involved in online scams in southern Shan State’s Hopong Township, along with the seizure of related equipment. This indicates that scam operations have spread to the doorstep of Taunggyi, the capital of Shan State.

Ko Michael, an analyst who tracks cyber-scam activities, said the crackdowns by both the regime and local armed groups have stalled because they consistently fail to net the masterminds.

“They aren’t shooting the birds; they’re just shaking the trees. So the birds simply fly from one tree to another. Everything gets scattered around. That’s why this problem has become so difficult to contain,” he said.

At the same time, while scam operations have proliferated into the interior, they have by no means vanished from the borderlands. None of the ethnic armed groups conducting anti-scam crackdowns have declared their regions entirely free of fraud hubs. Operations persist in the border town of Muse, and recruitment s seeking workers for scam centers in Tachileik on the Thai border continue to appear daily on social media. The fact that cyber-scam operations continue to operate on Shan State’s borders while simultaneously spreading inland raises a key question. Who is enabling this aggressive proliferation?

Who is providing protection?

The vast majority of individuals arrested in Shan State’s scam hubs are Chinese nationals; in some locations, nearly every person detained was from China. Yet it would be utterly impossible for foreign nationals to arrive in large groups and establish, let alone operate, these telecom fraud enterprises without local assistance.

Crucially, armed organizations and security outfits controlling the territory in these areas are the linchpins ensuring the survival of these organized crime syndicates. When cyber-scams first proliferated across the Kokang, Wa and Mong La borderlands, they took root strictly under the control of local armed actors.

In many parts of Shan State, regime-aligned armed factions have turned these operations into lucrative revenue streams, according to local residents and individuals formerly involved in the trade.

“The total proliferation of scams across Shan State didn’t happen because of just one group. But I want to stress this: it would be completely impossible to run without the military’s involvement,” said Ko Michael, the scam-operation monitor.

In December 2025, after the military raided an online scam compound in Hsipaw Township, state media reported the arrest of three members of the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), one of the major Shan armed groups. Concurrently, residents point out that in Muse, Laihka and several other areas, local militia outfits—including the Namhkam Myoma, Pansay, Kaungkha, Manpang and Wanpang militias—receive payoffs in exchange for facilitating relocations, providing physical security and protection, and transporting workers to scam centers.

“The scam business and armed groups are inseparable. Without an armed group, you simply cannot run a scam operation. It’s the armed groups that provide the protection,” said a resident of Muse.

The nexus between armed actors and telecom fraud extends to Myanmar’s most powerful ethnic armed organization, the UWSA, which has been heavily implicated in the scam industry despite its current anti-scam crackdowns.

“The ones who really laid the solid groundwork and operated these scam rings at scale were the Wa. Top Wa leaders were directly involved,” said Dr. Hla Kyaw Zaw, a veteran analyst of China-Myanmar affairs.

The Chinese state-produced documentary “The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar,” which covered the anti-scam crackdowns and was aired last month, identifies UWSA-controlled territory as the incubator for northern Myanmar’s scam economy. It claimed that Bao Yanban, chief of Mong Pawk, a town in the Wa region, amassed so much wealth from the scams that he would sun-dry banknotes on rooftops to prevent mold.

Protection for scam operators has come not only from local militias, but directly from the regime itself.

In late 2023, as the Three Brotherhood Alliance was attempting to capture Laukkai during Operation 1027, the military regime sheltered top Kokang scam kingpins from the Big Four families in Naypyitaw. Among them was Bai Suocheng, the former leader of the Kokang Self-Administered Zone and head of the regime-aligned Border Guard Force.

It was only under immense pressure from Beijing in January 2024 that the regime finally handed these high-profile suspects over to Chinese security forces in Naypyitaw. They were subsequently tried in Chinese courts, where harsh penalties—including death sentences—were handed down.

What is the impact?

Despite the crackdowns and legal cases, online scam syndicates have continued to fan out from the northern Shan-China border across the entirety of Shan State, causing severe social harm in every community they penetrate.

With legitimate employment opportunities devastated by the country’s ongoing military conflict, cyber-scam compounds have emerged as places where local youth can make quick money.

A northern Shan resident who previously worked in a scam compound explained that the prospect of “easy money” causes those who have worked in the industry to lose interest in conventional jobs.

“When you return from there [working at a scam center], you come back with a lot of money. You just don’t want to do outside manual work anymore. Once that money runs out, you don’t go looking for decent, ordinary jobs. That’s true for about 80 percent of the people who go to work there,” the northern Shan resident explained.

As the industry has expanded, training courses designed to teach people how to run telecom scams have begun popping up in Shan State, according to sources close to the industry.

“There are training courses opened by people who worked inside scam compounds. They teach combined computer and communication skills. They teach basic things like how to defraud people out of money. How many words per minute you need to type—that’s something only people who worked there can teach,” said a resident of Kyaukme in northern Shan State. Citing security concerns, the resident declined to disclose the exact locations or other details of the training centers.

Scam operations also serve as a seemingly safe and profitable haven for young people trying to escape military conscription by the regime. The conscription law, which has been on the books for years but only enforced since 2024, requires men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve up to two years in the military.

A Kyaukme resident who sought to evade conscription by working in a scam compound said he did so for his own safety. “My name came up on the conscription list. A lot of people from our area worked there. They said things were going well there, inviting us to come over,” he said.

“Quite a lot of young people ended up going,” he added.

World.title: Regime Summons German Envoy Over Call for Coup Releases
World.content:
YANGON—The Myanmar regime’s Foreign Ministry said it summoned Germany’s top resident diplomat on Tuesday over a Facebook video calling for authorities to “unconditionally release” ousted politicians, including Aung San Suu Kyi.

Germany’s mission head Mathias Licharz posted the video on Sunday, standing outside the former Yangon residence of Win Myint, the president of Aung San Suu Kyi’s government that was removed in a 2021 coup.

The junta behind the coup organized elections installing a nominally civilian government this spring, although analysts regard it as a fig leaf for ongoing military rule.

Licharz said in his message, scheduled for Win Myint’s 75th birthday, that the United Nations still regards him as the “legitimate president” of Myanmar.

Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said Licharz was summoned for a meeting with deputy minister Ko Ko Kyaw, “warned against the video” and handed an aide-memoire.

“Should the Chargé d’Affaires choose to recognize U Win Myint as President and wish to discontinue his service in Myanmar, the Ministry would have no objection,” a statement said.

Myanmar has been riven by civil war since the 2021 coup, as pro-democracy guerrillas rose up and long-simmering ethnic minority insurgencies challenging central rule boiled over.

The ministry statement accused Licharz of “intentional conduct” that “appeared to fuel opposition to the host country and its Government, thereby inciting internal unrest.”

“The Deputy Minister strongly warned against recurrence of such act and informed him that any similar conduct would be treated with utmost seriousness and would take appropriate actions,” it said.

Germany’s embassy in Myanmar did not respond immediately to a request for comment.

Win Myint was jailed in the February 2021 coup, which ended Myanmar’s decade-long democratic experiment.

Authorities said in April he had been pardoned of his post-coup convictions—charges that supporters and analysts say were confected to oust the government.

However, Licharz said in his video message his efforts to meet Win Myint had been unfruitful.

“There is only one conclusion,” he said. “U Wint Myint is not a free man. He’s not allowed to meet with whom he would like to meet and he’s not allowed to communicate independently.”

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained but was moved to house arrest in the capital Naypyitaw this year, authorities say, where access to the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains tightly controlled.

Licharz called for authorities to “unconditionally release all those who are arbitrarily detained including U Win Myint and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi.”

World.title: Myanmar Embassies Push Tax, Remittance Rules as Migrant Backlash Grows Across Asia
World.content:
Embassies operated by Myanmar’s cash-strapped military regime have intensified efforts to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, even as migrant opposition grows across Asia.

For the past two weeks, Myanmar missions have repeatedly ordered that all passport applications must be accompanied by official evidence of remittance and tax payments.

The regime enforced a mandatory 25 percent remittance requirement alongside 2 percent income tax on migrant workers in 2023 — measures widely seen as a bid to bolster foreign currency reserves amid severe shortages.

In the latest notices, Myanmar missions in Singapore, Hong Kong and Macau declared Monday that migrants applying for a Passport for Job (PJ) or PJ extension must include proof of tax payment and remittance of a quarter of their earnings over the past three months through official regime channels.

“The Myanmar embassy is issuing the order but nobody wants to use official remittance channels,” a 30-year-old Myanmar national working at a florist in Singapore told The Irrawaddy.

“Applicants may comply with the rule for three months, but otherwise, they will continue to use alternative channels that are convenient, pay more, and don’t siphon money to the military.”

He added that waiting times for passport extension appointments have also expanded dramatically under the regime’s new digital identification system (UID), prompting worker fears of being stranded in a legal limbo.

“A friend of mine has been waiting three months for an appointment; previously it took just two weeks to extend a passport.”

The precise number of Myanmar migrants in Singapore is unknown, but Myanmar labor department data from 2024 suggested a sharp increase since 2021, prompting predictions they could reach 200,000 in a few years.

Other major destinations for Myanmar migrant workers are South Korea and Japan, which recruit through formal MOU frameworks and offer comparatively higher wages.

Regime embassies in Seoul and Tokyo were among the first to double down, issuing notices that workers must comply with remittance and tax rules in exchange for passport extensions.

“It’s a new requirement. Even If workers have not used official channels before, they must do so before applying for an extension,” a South Korea-based Myanmar national who assists migrant workers told The Irrawaddy.

“Workers have no option if they need their passports extended. So, they have to comply for at least three months,” she said.

She echoed the complaints of long appointment waiting times, higher application costs, and workers’ reluctance to use official channels that offer lower exchange rates while funneling money to the military regime.

Meanwhile, the regime’s embassy in Thailand — home to the largest Myanmar migrant community of roughly four million — is reportedly demanding remittance and tax evidence before it issues or extends PJs. Agents say the embassy requires proof of payments, adding that appointment waiting times are unpredictable.

“The process is really complicated now. We have been told to submit remittance proof, even though they haven’t publicly announced it,” a Bangkok-based agent told The Irrawaddy.

The regime’s Certificate of Identity (CI) process to identify undocumented workers in Thailand was rejected by over 2 million migrants in a recent poll. Only 15,000 out of nearly 750,000 ID-less migrants have shown up at Thai CI centers amid a widespread boycott triggered by the tax and remittance rules.

Thailand’s Labor Ministry has voiced opposition to the rules, which it views as a violation of worker rights. However, regime Labor Minister Maung Myint pressed the issue on Sunday, insisting that CI applicants must abide by the remittance and tax mandates.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Routs Resistance HQ on Bago–Mon Border
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has seized 11 resistance bases along the border of Bago Region and Mon State, including the shadow National Unity Government (NUG)’s Special Region Military Command.

Regime media said the military launched a major “counter-terrorism operation” from Theinzayat along the mountainous route through Mon State’s Kyaikhto and Bago’s Shwegyin townships on Nov. 3.

From Nov. 4 to 7, it seized four temporary posts of the ethnic Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) in Kyaikhto.

On Nov. 8, the regime seized another five resistance bases, including the Special Region Military Command northeast of Theinzayat, which it said was the nerve center of regional operations of the heartland People’s Defense Forces (PDF) loyal to the shadow government.

Here the resistance manufactured “homemade mortars, firearms, ammunition and explosives for their operations,” the report said.

The regime previously bombed the command on Sept. 24, killing six people including prominent Air Force defector Nay Win Aung.

A PDF fighter in the southern region confirmed the loss of the regional HQ.

“Yes, it’s true, the situation is worse than in the news,” he told The Irrawaddy.

Other resistance sources said intense fighting continues, ranging from ground battles to airstrikes using drones and fighter jets.

Neither the KNLA nor the NUG responded to inquiries from The Irrawaddy.

The regime said it seized 97 small arms, 12,285 ammunitions, 362 drops bombs, 139 mines as well as drones and two vehicles but attached no figures to the resistance’s “heavy casualties.”

Prominent military defector Zin Yaw said the regime raid seems to have taken the resistance by surprise, quoting sources as saying it involved roughly 1,000 troops.

“We have to wait and see how far they can advance into resistance territories since resistance forces are on high alert now and the clashes will become more intense,” he added.

World.title: Blue Tsunami Claims a Congressional Champion of Myanmar’s Cause
World.content:
It is now widely known that Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in last week’s U.S. midterm elections. Some voters simply disliked the Republican candidates running in their districts, while others, who might ordinarily have voted Republican, chose to vote against them simply because they belonged to Trump’s party. Their thinking was essentially this: “I want to teach Trump a lesson. As long as it’s not your guy, I’ll vote for anyone else.”

Take Senator Susan Collins of Maine, for example. Known as a moderate Republican, she defied her own party by voting alongside Democrats during Trump’s second impeachment trial to convict him for his role in the January 6 insurrection, earning his lasting enmity in the process. Yet she, too, lost her seat in this election.

Another casualty of the election was my own congressional representative, Congressman Bill Huizenga, who represents Michigan’s Fourth Congressional District. His defeat represents a painful loss for those of us who support Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement. We have lost someone who has done a great deal to advance our cause.

Huizenga is a seasoned congressman who has served eight terms since 2011. As a senior member of Congress, he held influential positions on several important committees. He served as vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, and vice chair of the Congressional Burma Caucus.

Through his involvement with the Burma Caucus, in particular, he supported Myanmar’s cause both publicly and behind the scenes. Some of these efforts are ones I am sharing publicly for the first time.

One such instance involved Ashin Nat Zaw, a Myanmar-born monk from Buffalo, New York, who was detained by the junta during a visit to Myanmar. The U.S. government, through the State Department and its embassy in Myanmar, sought his release, as he had returned to Myanmar as a U.S. citizen. Huizenga played a role in that effort.

I know this firsthand because a community liaison from Buffalo contacted me and asked for help connecting her with Huizenga’s office. I facilitated that connection. These were the kinds of things he did quietly, behind the scenes, without seeking publicity.

On the public front, he worked to advance the BRAVE Burma Act and helped push for its passage by the House. After Trump issued his order terminating Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Myanmar nationals, not a single Republican member of Congress seemed willing to speak up. Huizenga, however, joined Democratic Congressman Ami Bera of California, Gregory Meeks of New York and others in introducing legislation seeking to restore TPS for Myanmar nationals. However, the protections were ultimately terminated in August despite a temporary court-ordered reprieve.

Just last month, he also spearheaded a letter, signed by five other bipartisan members of the Burma Caucus, urging the United States to continue supporting Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun as Myanmar’s permanent representative to the United Nations.

But none of these efforts happened in a vacuum. We must recognize that members of Congress are elected to represent the people of their own districts—their American constituents—and to address their concerns. They have no obligation to do anything for Myanmar. It is the responsibility of the Myanmar community in each congressional district to educate, persuade and encourage its representatives to take an interest in our cause.

And this does not happen overnight. It takes time, patience and the cultivation of relationships. There are various ways to establish that initial connection. Someone who already knows the congressman might introduce us. We might repeatedly write letters, submit statements and request meetings until we finally get an opportunity to speak with him. We might also reach out through religious channels, among other approaches.

One thing is certain: unlike some wealthier communities, we Burmese have never had the financial resources to buy our way into political influence.

Before the 2021 military coup in Myanmar, Huizenga knew little about the country. Although there was a Burmese community in his district, it was nowhere near as large as those in Indianapolis or Fort Wayne. To put things into perspective, approximately 350,000 votes were cast in this congressional district in the 2026 election, while the entire Burmese community’s voting strength amounted to only about 4,000 votes.

We had to work extremely hard to break through and get him to pay attention to Myanmar’s affairs. The fact that our city already had a Burma Center, established some 15 years ago, gave us an advantage. Through five years of cultivating relationships, explaining our cause, and educating his office, we developed close ties with him and his staff. Even the recent letter supporting Kyaw Moe Tun was the result of our activists suggesting to his office that such a letter would be worthwhile and guiding them toward issuing it.

This is how grassroots advocacy works.

Losing someone with whom we had built such a close and trusting relationship is an enormous loss for us. The newly elected Democratic congressman who replaces him will likely know little or nothing about Myanmar. We will have to start all over again, building relationships and educating him about our cause from scratch. Furthermore, as a freshman congressman, he will have little influence in the House and is unlikely to secure a position on any of its important committees.

We did everything we could to help Huizenga win reelection. But, as mentioned earlier, our community’s approximately 4,000 votes were a mere drop in the ocean compared with the 350,000 votes cast in the district. He, too, was swept away by the blue tsunami.

I hate to say it, but even within our own Burmese community, there were people who did not want to vote for him because they viewed him as something of a MAGA Republican—a Trump supporter.

In my view, however, even if he had been reelected, his presence alone would not have significantly altered the balance of power between Democrats and Republicans in Congress. But among the 435 members of the House of Representatives, only four or five genuinely understand and support Myanmar’s cause. Losing even one of them is a significant setback, and finding a replacement is no easy task.

That is why, when it came time to vote, I encouraged members of our community to consider splitting their tickets. They could vote for Democrats in other races if they wished, but I urged them to vote for Huizenga, the Republican, in our congressional race. Unfortunately, our efforts still fell short.

In addition to Huizenga, Representative Young Kim (R-California), another member of the Burma Caucus, lost her reelection bid. Longtime supporter of Myanmar Senator Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) will retire from his Senate position and political career in January 2027. Myanmar desperately needs newer members of Congress to champion its cause.

I would like to take this opportunity to express my deepest gratitude and respect to Congressman Huizenga for his unwavering support of Myanmar’s cause. In appreciation of his efforts, I am sharing some of his behind-the-scenes contributions that many people may not have known about. I would also like to extend my special thanks to his entire staff, who worked closely with our community and with whom we developed a close and trusting relationship.

Thank you, Congressman Huizenga, for standing with the people of Myanmar.

Than N. Oo is a co-founder of advocacy group Free Myanmar and writes frequently about Myanmar’s political developments.

World.title: Tokayev Highlights AI-Driven Security Risks at CSTO Summit in Moscow
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for stronger cooperation among member states of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) to combat international terrorism, counter illicit drug trafficking and strengthen information security amid the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on Nov. 11, Akorda reported.

Tokayev thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for hosting the meeting and praised Russia’s chairmanship of the CSTO this year, describing it as productive.

The meeting was attended by Belarus’ President Alexander Lukashenko, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon and CSTO Secretary General Taalatbek Masadykov. The leaders reviewed key aspects of cooperation within the organization, assessed its activities in 2026 and outlined priorities for the coming period. They also exchanged views on pressing international and regional security issues.

The meeting concluded with the adoption of a Joint Statement by the CSTO Collective Security Council. The leaders also signed a series of documents aimed at further strengthening the organization’s collective security framework based on the shared interests of its member states.

Kazakhstan also called for stronger international dialogue and mutual trust at the International Forum on Collective Security in Moscow, held on Nov. 10. Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi emphasized that a stable international order should be grounded in international law and the willingness of countries to maintain dialogue despite serious disagreements, stressing that Eurasia’s future should not be shaped by confrontation or dividing lines.

World.title: Kazakhstan Invites US Businesses to Partner in Critical Minerals Sector at B20 Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has invited U.S. businesses to develop long-term industrial and technology partnerships in critical minerals, highlighting its resource base, infrastructure, regulatory framework and skilled workforce.

Kanat Sharlapayev, chairman of the Presidium of the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, outlined these advantages at a B20 Summit panel on Central Asia-U.S. public-private partnerships in Washington on Nov. 9-11.

Sharlapayev described Kazakhstan’s competitive advantages as Superfecta, combining four factors: diverse mineral resources, developed infrastructure, predictable regulation and qualified personnel, the chamber’s press service reported on Nov. 11.

“From 2022 to 2025, capital investment in metal ore mining in Kazakhstan increased by approximately 62%, while total investment in geological exploration grew 2.5 times to reach $1 billion,” he said.

He highlighted opportunities in deeper mineral processing, technology transfer and industrial development, citing the Sarytogan graphite project, with resources exceeding 65 million tons, Taza Metal Technologies’ high-purity manganese sulfate production and the Akbulak joint exploration project between Kazgeology and Cove Kaz Capital Group, where rare earth elements, including neodymium and praseodymium, have been identified.

International companies operating in Kazakhstan include Rio Tinto, Fortescue, Ivanhoe Mines, Arras Minerals, B2Gold and East Star Resources.

On the sidelines of the summit, Sharlapayev met with Dan Levine, founder and managing partner of Tenfore Holdings, to discuss cooperation in advanced manufacturing, robotics, smart logistics and artificial intelligence.

He also met Heidi Crebo-Rediker, senior fellow in the Center for Geoeconomic Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), to discuss private investment in infrastructure and critical minerals, public-private partnerships and long-term financing for small and medium-sized businesses.

The B20 Summit is taking place in Washington on Nov. 9-11 as part of the U.S. presidency of the G20. Kazakhstan’s business delegation includes representatives from industry, energy, agribusiness and transport and logistics.

World.title: Kazakhstan Wins Coursera Award for Digital Transformation of Higher Education
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Science and Higher Education has received the Coursera Learning Excellence Award 2026 for integrating international online education into the national higher education system and expanding digital and artificial intelligence (AI) skills development.

The award was presented at the London FWD event, which brought together education technology platforms Coursera and Udemy and key partners from Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). Other organizations recognized included consulting firm EY, British bank Nationwide and Italian technology company bIP. The event was led by Coursera Chief Executive Officer Greg Hart, the ministry reported on Nov. 6.

The award recognizes Kazakhstan’s progress in integrating international online courses into university curricula and developing digital competencies relevant to the modern economy.

More than 292,000 students earn Coursera certificates

Kazakhstan began its partnership with Coursera in 2022, making the initiative an important part of its higher education transformation.

Through the program, students have gained access to thousands of international online courses and professional certification programs offered by leading universities and industry partners.

More than 292,000 students have earned certificates, bringing the total to more than 682,000. Cumulative learning time has surpassed 5.35 million hours, and Kazakh universities have recognized 163,098 academic credits.

This year, the ministry allocated 38,184 Coursera licenses across 100 higher education institutions. More than 100 universities are integrating platform courses into their academic programs and recognizing online learning outcomes as part of formal education.

The latest award follows the 2025 recognition of Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek, who received the Coursera Learning Hero Award.

The ministry continues to prioritize digital education, international partnerships and the development of skills needed in the modern labor market, including AI competencies and entrepreneurship.

World.title: Foreigners to Obtain IIN in Kazakhstan Within One Working Day Under New Online Pilot
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs is launching a pilot project allowing foreign citizens to apply for individual identification numbers (IINs) online through the QazETA mobile application. The service will be available via the MAQ digital migration services platform, with applications processed within one working day, according to a ministry order.

The pilot project was introduced under Order No. 825 of Nov. 2, which entered into force on Nov. 9.

Under the new procedure, foreign applicants must register or log in to the QazETA application and consent to the processing of their personal data. They must then photograph their identity document, complete biometric authentication and a liveness check, and confirm their geolocation, reported inbusiness.kz on Nov. 10.

The system will automatically generate an application, allowing users to review the information and provide any additional details if necessary.

Authorities will then verify the applicant’s entry into Kazakhstan through the Berkut Unified Centralized System. If the verification is successful, the application will be forwarded to the Ministry of Internal Affairs for review.

The ministry will check the application’s completeness and accuracy, verify that the submitted information matches the attached identity documents, and ensure that no duplicate IIN has been issued.

Once all requirements are met, the ministry will generate an IIN and forward it to the relevant information system. Applicants will be able to check the result through the MAQ platform in the QazETA application, using the sections titled “View IIN Application List” or “View IIN.”

Users will also be able to view and download their IIN registration certificate.

World.title: PTPA Criticizes Tennis Calendar Following Elena Rybakina’s WTA Finals Withdrawal
World.content:
ASTANA – The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) has criticised the demanding tennis calendar following Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina’s withdrawal from the WTA Finals due to a viral illness.

In a statement released on Nov. 10, the PTPA said the world No. 1 had already withdrawn from the Tokyo tournament the previous week due to a neck injury.

Despite winning two Grand Slam titles and four titles overall in 2026, Rybakina was unable to compete in the season-ending event.

“Players shouldn’t reach the biggest event of the year running on empty,” the association said, reiterating its call for a season calendar that allows players to remain healthy through the final tournaments.

Meanwhile, tennis commentator Andrei Pak said Rybakina’s limited public communication had contributed to speculation surrounding her withdrawal and professional relationship, reported Tengri Sport on Nov. 11.

“She is the world No. 1, and she needs to change something in this regard. If Rybakina does not start speaking publicly and clarifying situations herself, speculation and unconfirmed rumours surrounding her name will continue,” Pak said.

He also suggested that her relationship with coach Stefano Vukov could be at the root of the situation, while acknowledging that such claims remained his personal assessment.

“In my subjective opinion, the root of the problems lies there,” he said, referring to what he described as a complicated personal relationship between Rybakina and Vukov.

World.title: Kazakhstan Launches Climate Investment Platform at COP31 With Up to $1 Billion in Potential EBRD Financing
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has officially launched its Just Energy Transition Investment Platform (QaJET) at COP31 in Antalya, with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) offering up to $100 million in concessional financing and grants, alongside up to $1 billion in potential direct financing on a non-committal basis.

“From ambition to partnership. From partnership to investment,” wrote Cristian Carraretto, Head of Energy Transition – Sustainable Business and Infrastructure at the EBRD, in a Nov. 10 LinkedIn post announcing the launch.

Developed with the Government of Kazakhstan, the platform aims to accelerate renewable energy development, modernize electricity grids, introduce energy storage systems and expand electrification. It aims to commission at least 10 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2035.

Broader climate investment framework

QaJET is part of the Kazakhstan Country Climate Investment Platform (QCIP), presented at the National Pavilion. It brings together government agencies, international financial institutions, climate funds and private investors to develop priority projects and attract domestic and international financing.

The platform operates under the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, with the International Center for Green Technologies and Investment Projects (IGTIC) serving as its secretariat, the ministry’s press service reported.

Two memorandums were signed, one between IGTIC and the Development Bank of Kazakhstan, and another between the Ministries of Energy and Ecology and QaJET partners led by the EBRD.

National pavilion showcases green initiatives

Operating under the theme Continuity of Times: Past, Present and Future, Kazakhstan’s 250-square-meter pavilion presents environmental projects, green technologies and investment opportunities.

Its exhibits include AI-powered digital guides representing Turan tigers Umit and Amur, biodiversity conservation projects, the restoration of the Northern Aral Sea, saiga population recovery and saxaul forest planting on the dried seabed.

Other initiatives include the Central Asian Green Shield program, the KazMethane MRV digital platform for monitoring emissions and detecting methane leaks, industrial waste recycling and the introduction of best available technologies.

Traditional Kazakh craftsmanship is represented through a quraq korpe (quilt mattress) installation highlighting resource efficiency and the Zero Waste concept.

38 events focus on climate finance

The pavilion will host 38 thematic events covering climate finance, industrial decarbonization, energy transition, carbon markets, water security, biodiversity and technological innovation.

Regional priorities include protecting the Caspian Sea ecosystem, restoring the Northern Aral Sea, combating desertification and developing renewable energy.

Kazakhstan views COP31 as an opportunity to move from climate commitments to practical projects, measurable results and stronger international partnerships.

World.title: EDB: Gulf Investment in Central Asia Triples to $31 Billion as Trade Nears $4 Billion
World.content:
ASTANA – Investment stock from Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries in Central Asia increased 3.4-fold to $31.1 billion by mid-2026. In comparison, trade between the two regions nearly quadrupled over five years to reach $3.9 billion in 2025, reflecting growing economic ties and the Gulf’s expanding role in the region, according to a report by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) released on Nov. 10.

The report, titled Trade and Investment Cooperation Between Central Asia and the GCC Countries, identifies the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as the leading trade and investment partner, accounting for approximately 94% of trade between the two regions and 66% of their total investment stock.

Trade expands nearly fourfold

Trade between Central Asia and the GCC countries increased from $1 billion in 2020 to $3.9 billion in 2025. The Gulf countries’ share of Central Asia’s foreign trade also grew from 0.7% to 1.7%.

Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan accounted for approximately 85% of the total trade in 2025. Uzbekistan became the largest trading partner, with trade reaching $1.75 billion, or around 45% of the regional total. Turkmenistan followed with $1.6 billion.

Kazakhstan’s trade with the GCC countries exceeded $300 million in 2025. Its exports have become more diversified, extending beyond metallurgical products to include agricultural goods, meat and other food products, chemicals and certain types of equipment. Imports are dominated by pharmaceutical and chemical products, as well as machinery and equipment for the oil and gas industry.

The EDB estimates additional trade potential between Central Asia and the GCC countries at $4.9 billion by 2030. High transportation and logistics costs, limited access to trade finance and shortcomings in the mutual recognition of standards remain among the main barriers to expanding trade.

The Economic Partnership Agreement between the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the UAE, which entered into force on Oct. 6, is expected to create additional opportunities by eliminating or reducing tariffs on more than 85% of the product range.

Gulf investment shifts toward energy

According to the EDB’s Monitoring of Mutual Investment, investment stock from GCC countries in Central Asia increased from $9.1 billion in 2020 to $31.1 billion by mid-2026.

Turkmenistan remains the largest recipient, with investment stock reaching $14.4 billion. Uzbekistan recorded the fastest growth, with investments increasing more than 25-fold to $11.3 billion. Kazakhstan’s investment stock reached $5.3 billion.

The UAE leads among Gulf investors with a portfolio of $20.6 billion, accounting for 66% of the total. Saudi Arabia and Qatar are also expanding their presence, with investment stock reaching $6.5 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively.

The sectoral structure of investment is also changing. The electric power sector’s share rose from 2% in 2020 to 34%, with investment stock reaching $10.5 billion. Meanwhile, the commodities sector, although still accounting for the largest share at 49%, declined from 82% in 2020.

The expansion of renewable energy projects, notably solar and wind power plants in Uzbekistan, is a major driver of this shift.

Emirati company Masdar is a key investor in the region’s renewable energy sector. Its projects include a 500-megawatt wind power plant in Zarafshan and a solar power plant in the Surkhandarya Region. In Kazakhstan, construction began in June on a 1-gigawatt wind power plant in the Zhambyl Region, with Masdar participating in the $1.4 billion project.

Saudi Arabia’s investment presence is largely driven by ACWA Power, which accounts for more than 95% of the country’s investment portfolio in Uzbekistan. Its projects include wind and solar power plants across several regions.

Qatar’s investment portfolio is more diversified, covering telecommunications, finance, manufacturing, electric power, transportation and logistics. In Kazakhstan, major projects include Power International Holding’s acquisition of Mobile Telecom-Service, operating under the Tele2 and Altel brands, for approximately $1.1 billion, and Lesha Bank’s purchase of Bereke Bank.

The EDB expects trade and investment ties between Central Asia and the GCC countries to continue expanding, supported by economic growth in Central Asia, the international expansion of Gulf businesses and stronger economic cooperation within the Islamic world.

World.title: Astana Airport Handles Special Delivery of Nearly 1,000 Kilograms of Chicks
World.content:
ASTANA – Nearly one ton of day-old chicks arrived at Astana International Airport from Luxembourg on Nov. 7 aboard a cargo flight operated by Cargolux Airlines International.

The shipment weighed 951 kilograms and occupied 252 cargo positions. Upon arrival, the airport reported that the chicks were handed over to a domestic poultry farming enterprise for raising and breeding.

Astana International Airport handles various categories of cargo, including industrial equipment, medical supplies, artworks, fresh flowers, seafood, and breeding cattle and small livestock. Delivering day-old chicks adds to its experience in handling live cargo that requires special transportation conditions.

The airport said coordinated work between its cargo terminal, ground services, and the airline helps ensure each shipment is handled according to its specific requirements.

From January to October, Astana International Airport handled 593 cargo flights and processed 13,617 tons of cargo.

The airport currently works with major international cargo carriers, including Cargolux Airlines International, Europe’s largest specialized cargo airline and one of the world’s top 10 carriers by scheduled international freight volume.

The airport is also working to attract new airlines, expand its route network and improve cargo infrastructure to increase freight volumes and strengthen Astana’s position as an international transport and logistics hub.

World.title: ‘Who could be closer friend to us than Armenia?’ – Key takeaways from Iran’s vice-president’s visit to Yerevan
World.content:
Вице-президент Ирана – об объемах поставок газа в Армению

Iranian Vice-President Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi arrived in Yerevan to attend the 19th session of the Armenian-Iranian Intergovernmental Commission. Armenian journalists asked him about economic ties and Iran’s position on the Armenian-American TRIPP project project, known as the “Trump Route”, which would run through Armenian territory. Armenian media also wanted to understand why Iran’s religious and secular authorities hold different positions on the issue.

Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi stressed that Tehran’s official position was reflected in statements by Iran’s Foreign Ministry.

“Armenia and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan are our reliable partners, and we remain in constant contact. Tehran considers it important that the countries of the region themselves ensure and maintain security and peace. Iran welcomes any steps aimed at preserving and strengthening peace and security among the countries of the region,” the Iranian vice-president said.

Just days earlier, Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, had sharply criticised Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan over the TRIPP project. Velayati accused Pashinyan of making Armenia increasingly dependent on the West, saying this “opens a new chapter of hostility and tension in the South Caucasus”. Velayati’s remarks prompted a response from Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. He stressed that the Armenian authorities had assured Tehran that the implementation of the TRIPP project, near Iran’s borders, would involve neither the deployment of US military forces in the region nor any changes to existing borders. Baghaei added that, although Iran enjoys excellent relations with Armenia, it would continue to monitor developments and make its position public if necessary.

On increasing Iranian gas supplies to Armenia

Against the backdrop of discussions about a possible increase in the price of Russian gas supplied to Armenia, journalists asked whether Iran could increase its gas exports to the country.

“Iran is one of the countries with the largest gas reserves in the world. And if we have the capacity to export gas, who could be a closer friend to us than Armenia, to whom we would export it?” the Iranian vice-president replied.

Pourmohammadi said that one of the commissions established under Armenian-Iranian cooperation deals specifically with energy issues. According to him, the two sides discussed all possible areas of cooperation in this sector, including supplies of gas and diesel fuel, as well as issues related to Armenia’s long-term energy security.

However, the specific details of the agreements reached with Iran have not been disclosed.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan, who co-chairs the intergovernmental commission on the Armenian side, offered only the following details:

“There is not a single area in which we have not reached agreements. These include trade, energy (particularly gas and electricity), opportunities to expand existing project agreements, as well as infrastructure development and its mutual integration.”

The Iran–Armenia gas pipeline has a designed capacity of more than 2 billion cubic metres of gas a year. However, only a small fraction of this capacity is currently being used. Since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline has been under the control of Russian company Gazprom. Some experts believe that Iran cannot increase its gas exports without Russia’s consent. However, in July this year, Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan said there were no restrictions on receiving gas under the Armenian-Iranian “gas-for-electricity” programme. The programme began in 2009 and has already been extended until 2030. The minister assured that Armenia could at least double its gas imports from Iran.

Outcomes of the intergovernmental meeting

The Armenian government said that the intergovernmental meeting covered the implementation of joint projects in the following areas:

energy;

transport;

trade;

infrastructure;

business ties.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan particularly emphasised Armenia’s readiness to develop regional connectivity. He expressed confidence that unblocking regional transport links “would create new opportunities for the countries of the region”. In this context, he stressed the importance of Iran’s support for the Crossroads of Peace initiative. The Armenian government’s project aims to fully unblock transport links to and from Armenia in all directions.

The two sides also signed a memorandum of understanding following the intergovernmental commission meeting.

Connectivity also on the agenda of bilateral meetings

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Nikol Pashinyan discussed joint Armenian-Iranian programmes during his meeting with the Iranian vice-president. He said their successful implementation would “help develop and expand bilateral relations”.

“The interlocutors discussed issues related to the development of Armenia-Iran border infrastructure, joint road construction projects, as well as cooperation in energy, agriculture and other sectors,” the statement said.

Pashinyan and Pourmohammadi also discussed the unblocking of regional transport links and the opportunities this process could create for both countries.

Armenian Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan also discussed regional connectivity and the unblocking of transport links with the Iranian vice-president. Following their meeting, officials said that both countries saw “great potential” for further developing trade and economic ties and elevating bilateral relations to a strategic level.

World.title: Georgian authorities respond to Metropolitan Iov’s scathing sermon
World.content:
Georgian metropolitan criticises government



Metropolitan Iov (Akiashvili) of Ruisi and Urbnisi has sharply criticised the Georgian government, saying the ruling team has run out of steam and that the country needs better governance. In his sermon, the clergyman also addressed relations between the Church and the state, accusing the authorities of seeking to bring the Church under their control, turning a blind eye to corruption and neglecting national interests.

A sermon delivered on 10 November at Urbnisi Cathedral was published on the diocese’s social media page. Particular attention was drawn to Metropolitan Iov’s remarks, in which he criticised not only the government but also the Church’s senior leadership.

The metropolitan said the Georgian authorities lacked faith and were distant from the Church, warning that growing ties between the Church and the state threatened the independence of the clergy. He noted that, as the state provides funding to the Church, it is becoming increasingly difficult for clergy to speak openly about the government’s failings.

He also addressed the situation within the Church, saying that a significant proportion of the clergy had come to resemble government officials. He pointed out that while priests urge their congregations to endure poverty, help those in need and practise humility, their own behaviour is quite different.

The metropolitan also raised the issue of transparency in state funding for the Church. In his view, parishioners should know how every tetri (the smallest unit of Georgian currency) allocated to the Church is spent.

“Each of you, as parishioners, should know what the money is spent on and where every tetri goes,” he said.

Metropolitan Iov also recalled the reigns of David the Builder and Queen Tamar, noting that during periods of Georgia’s historical greatness, secular rulers worked in harmony with the Church. In his assessment, however, the current government has departed from this historical example.

A significant part of the sermon was also devoted to the so-called State Security Service “dossiers”. According to the metropolitan, the circulation of materials documenting private conversations and the personal lives of members of the clergy was intended to discredit the Church. He also recalled a statement by Bidzina Ivanishvili, in which he suggested that it was legitimate to criticise the Patriarch because he, too, was human and could make mistakes.

The so-called “dossier scandal”, involving the State Security Service (SSS), concerns alleged secret recordings and documents that emerged in the media in September 2021. The materials reportedly contained recordings of private conversations and phone calls, as well as information about the personal lives of senior representatives of the Georgian Orthodox Church, including metropolitans, bishops, priests and monks.

The documents pointed to widespread surveillance and wiretapping of the clergy. They covered internal Church disputes, relationships between members of the clergy, their private lives and political views. The authenticity of the recordings and the precise circumstances in which they were obtained have never been fully established.

The scandal became particularly serious because the State Security Service was named as the alleged source of the leak. The authorities were forced to respond to the allegations and seek to identify those who had made the documents public. However, it remains unclear to much of the public who was behind the collection and dissemination of the material.

Iov questioned why the identities of those who circulated the recordings had still not been established, despite promises from the authorities.

The metropolitan criticised the government over the spread of drug addiction and gambling addiction, the promotion of casinos, corruption and demographic problems. He noted that young people were leaving the country and villages were becoming deserted, while the scale of new construction, against the backdrop of a declining population, raised questions.

Iov also addressed the issue of David Gareji (the subject of a long-standing territorial dispute between Georgia and Azerbaijan over an undemarcated section of their border running through the sixth-century monastery complex – JAMnews), saying that the authorities’ response to the territorial challenges facing Georgia was inadequate.

“We must sound the alarm, because things cannot continue like this. It has become clear that the current government has completely exhausted its potential. Just as changes of government are commonplace around the world, we too should choose a better government in the future,” the metropolitan said.

He added that discussing the need for a change of government did not mean being hostile towards it, and that pointing out the government’s mistakes was a duty of the clergy.

Government and opposition reactions

The metropolitan’s sermon prompted mixed reactions from representatives of the government and the opposition.

Levan Machavariani, a Georgian Dream MP, said Metropolitan Iov’s political assessments were detached from reality and incorrect. He said he regretted that a senior clergyman was using the Church and the pulpit to make political statements.

Machavariani said the authorities were ready to provide comprehensive answers to any questions raised by the clergy. However, he stressed that such issues should be discussed through consultations before being made public.

“The people of Georgia know perfectly well how our government treats the Mother Church. If any problems or questions arise, we are accustomed to discussing them in a constructive manner,” the MP said.

Metropolitan Iov’s remarks were also criticised by Giorgi Gabunia, chairman of the parliamentary Committee on Culture. He described the metropolitan’s accusations as unfounded and said any confrontation between the Church and the state ran counter to the country’s interests. According to Gabunia, attempts are being made both inside and outside the country to provoke a conflict between the Church and the state.

The opposition took a different position from the ruling party. Pikria Chikhradze, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, described Metropolitan Iov’s sermon as significant and forceful. In her view, the Church’s criticism of the authorities may even have come too late.

Chikhradze drew attention to the so-called State Security Service “dossiers”, noting that the materials contained information about the private lives and correspondence of members of the clergy. In her view, it was virtually impossible to imagine that information on such a scale could have been collected without state involvement.

She also recalled the so-called “cyanide case” (a high-profile criminal scandal in 2017 involving allegations of a plot to murder a senior figure within the Georgian Orthodox Church – JAMnews), which, she said, still left many questions unanswered. Chikhradze argued that both cases were linked to attempts to undermine the Church’s authority.

The opposition politician said that Bidzina Ivanishvili could not tolerate the existence of independent institutions or influential figures capable of shaping public opinion. As an example, Chikhradze cited a plan to establish cannabis plantations, noting that the Church’s firm opposition had played an important role in halting the project. She also pointed out that, despite the Church’s objections to tax breaks for casinos, the authorities had gone ahead and adopted the relevant legislative amendments.

Pikria Chikhradze

Levan Bezhashvili, one of the leaders of the Unity – National Movement party, welcomed the metropolitan’s remarks. He said that Iov himself often criticises the party and is not a supporter of the National Movement, but that this did not diminish the significance of his latest statement.

“He made a very good statement – well done,” Bezhashvili said.

He added that Metropolitan Iov’s assessment reflected a reality recognised by both society and the Church.

Representatives of People’s Power, a pro-Russian movement that supports the ruling party, also responded to Metropolitan Iov’s criticism.

Tamta Megrelishvili said the metropolitan had used the church pulpit to deliver a political appeal, presenting his partisan position as a religious duty. She argued that accusing the authorities of “lacking faith” and calling for a change of government undermined the Church’s authority.

“In essence, this is an open political call from the church pulpit for a change of government,” Megrelishvili wrote.

Another People’s Power representative, Davit Kartvelishvili, took a much harsher view of Metropolitan Iov’s remarks. He accused the cleric of aligning himself with Saakashvili’s political camp and suggested that his calls for a change of government were driven by personal interests. Kartvelishvili also recalled previous allegations against Iov concerning the situation within his own diocese.

Pro-government commentator Davit Chikhelidze said Metropolitan Iov was accusing the authorities of “turning away from faith”, even though, in Chikhelidze’s view, the metropolitan’s own actions did not reflect the values he claimed to defend. He argued that the sermon harmed the country’s interests and was “playing into the enemy’s hands”.

The Church and Georgian Dream: Why Metropolitan Iov’s Statement Matters

The Georgian Orthodox Church occupies a unique position in the country’s political life. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has established itself not merely as a religious organisation but as one of the most influential institutions in Georgian society. For decades, its authority has far outweighed that of individual political parties or government officials. As a result, maintaining good relations with the Church has been a major source of political legitimacy for virtually every Georgian government.

Georgian Dream, which came to power in 2012, forged particularly close ties with the Church. Bidzina Ivanishvili and members of the ruling team publicly emphasised the unique role of the Orthodox Church, while some influential members of the clergy openly expressed support for the new government. Over time, these ties became a key element of the ruling party’s political and ideological identity.

However, relations between the Church and the authorities have not always been smooth. Clergy members have previously criticised decisions made by the ruling team on a number of issues, including an initiative to legalise cannabis cultivation, as well as gambling and other matters of public concern. Nevertheless, such direct criticism of the government’s overall political course by senior Church figures remains rare.

What makes Metropolitan Iov’s statement particularly noteworthy is that he goes beyond criticising individual government decisions. He questions the established relationship between the state and the Church, raises concerns about the clergy’s financial dependence on the government and internal problems within the Church, and directly tells the authorities that they have exhausted their capacity to govern the country.

The statement carries additional weight given that, following the political changes of 2012, a significant part of the Church was favourably disposed towards Georgian Dream. Metropolitan Iov himself acknowledges that Church representatives supported the government, although he no longer regards that support as unconditional loyalty.

Trust between the Church and the government became a particularly contentious issue in 2021, when media outlets published materials suggesting possible covert surveillance by the State Security Service (SSS). Thousands of documents pointed to possible surveillance of clergy members, politicians, journalists and diplomats. The scandal raised serious questions both within the Church and in Georgian society more broadly, but those responsible have yet to be identified.

It is also worth noting that, according to the Centre for Social Justice, the Orthodox Church received more than 283 million lari (approximately $109,158,525) from central and municipal budgets between 2020 and 2024.
