World.title: One Nation's 'missing' aircraft located at hangar in outback city
World.content:
The mystery of One Nation's missing first aircraft has been solved: the plane was sold to a private pilot and is now locked in a hangar in far-western New South Wales, an ABC investigation has confirmed.

One Nation’s national director James Ashby has indicated he received the proceeds from the sale of the plane.

The discovery of the Jabiru 230D, tail number 24-8637, at Broken Hill, about 1,000km west of Sydney, is likely to trigger more questions for the party about the handling of proceeds from the sale of the aircraft.

In September, One Nation declined to answer questions from the Sydney Morning Herald about the location of the plane and if it had been sold.

Yesterday, when the ABC contacted Mr Ashby via text to ask how the plane ended up in Broken Hill, he confirmed he had sold it to a NSW pilot.

He also said he had phoned Victorian businessman Bill McNee, who gave him the money to buy the plane, to seek his permission for the sale.

One Nation's first aircraft is now located at a hangar in Broken Hill. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Asked if he, Mr Ashby, had received the funds from the sale, he texted back a thumbs up. He did not respond to a text asking how much it sold for.

Aircraft sales websites recently listed several J230s for sale at prices ranging from about $80,000 to just over $100,000.

The plane's Broken Hill-based operator, a state public servant, does not appear to have any connection to One Nation.

He did not want to be identified and declined to say how he came to obtain the plane or whether he had any contact with Mr Ashby or One Nation about the plane.

Locals told the ABC they believe the white-painted aircraft has been kept at the Broken Hill airport for more than five years.

Questions over funding for plane

The light sports aircraft was first associated with One Nation when the party announced it would be used by Mr Ashby, who has a pilot's licence, and leader Pauline Hanson to fly around the country while campaigning in 2015.

Footage of James Ashby flying the Jabiru in 2017. (Supplied)

Decorated with Ms Hanson's face and the One Nation logo, and featuring her campaign slogan of "Fed Up", the plane made its maiden flight from Caloundra Airport after Hanson told reporters she was "thankful" for its use to visit remote communities.

But at the time it was unclear who paid for the plane, and in 2017 controversy erupted after ABC's Four Corners program aired allegations that funding for the plane had come from Mr McNee.

The program raised questions that the plane and the funding were not declared to the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) as a donation.

Mr McNee at the time denied to Four Corners that he had any involvement in the organisation of the plane and had not had communications with One Nation staffers about the plane.

In 2015, One Nation announced that Pauline Hanson and James Ashby would use the aircraft while campaigning. (ABC News: Jacob Kagi)

Following the program, the AEC launched an investigation into whether the party had breached rules around donation declarations regarding the plane and its funding.

While the AEC investigation was underway, amendments relating to One Nation's political donations were made.

Do you know more about this story? Email Callinan.Rory@abc.net.au

In March 2018, Mr Ashby lodged an individual donor return declaring a donation to the party of $30,375 for use of a Jabiru aircraft for 243 hours.

In May 2018, a Melbourne development company linked to Mr McNee lodged two amended organisation donor returns with the AEC, according to the AEC.

One was for the 2014 to 2015 period declaring a donation to the party of $10,908 and the other was for an amended declaration relating to the 2015-2016 period and for $98,175, says the AEC.

In December 2018, the AEC concluded its report and found that these returns and amended returns lodged with the AEC during the course of the investigation in respect of the party, Mr Ashby and the development company, had provided the relevant disclosure.

Gina Rinehart donated a new plane to Pauline Hanson earlier this year. (X: Pauline Hanson)

While the AEC appeared satisfied, questions remained over who actually owned the plane and whether it had been sold.

There was nothing in the declarations to say the party was the owner of the plane.

In 2017, Mr Ashby gave an interview to News Corp where he said he purchased the plane.

In 2018, the plane was photographed at Caboolture Airfield painted plain white, with just a One Nation website address on the tail.

Then, earlier this year, the plane, painted all white this time without any One Nation advertising, turned up at Gunnedah Airport in western NSW.

The Jabiru tied down at Gunnedah Airport in January this year. (Supplied: Russell Legg)

The ABC was able to trace the plane from Gunnedah to Broken Hill, where it is being kept at the airport by the public servant.

The plane is stored in a locked hangar that was used by a now-closed flight school at the airport.

The ABC does not suggest the owner has acted inappropriately.

Efforts to contact Mr McNee have been unsuccessful.

Earlier this year, it was revealed that Gina Rinehart had gifted the use of a new Cirrus SR22 aircraft worth about $1.5 million to One Nation.

World.title: Setting timber ceilings on fire in the name safety and research
World.content:
Queensland researchers investigating how to improve the safety of timber houses have set ceiling compartments on fire at temperatures of about 1,000 degrees Celsius.

Firefighters supervised the tests, which were monitored with live streaming cameras and heat-and pressure-sensing instruments.

"It was a pretty unreal experience," University of Queensland's PhD candidate Josh Madden said.

The research is central to a PhD project he led and part of a wider body of work at the ARC Research Hub to Advance Timber for Australia's Future Built Environment.

"For me, being a researcher, I know all the theory behind it … It was pretty eye-opening," he said.

Josh Madden has led research into timber buildings and fire safety. (Supplied: University of Queensland)

Mr Madden, who has worked as a fire safety engineer, said mass timber was becoming increasingly common in the building sector.

"Current fire safety guidance was generally built around the assumption that structural materials don't burn," he said.

"But the issue with timber is that timber actually burns."

Mass timber is engineered layers of wood compressed, glued, or nailed together to form uniform panels and slabs.

The product is a faster alternative to steel and concrete and can be constructed off-site.

"In traditional concrete building, you need to wait a month for the concrete to cure," Mr Madden said.

The fire testing was carried out at the Queensland Fire Department's training ground at the Port of Brisbane. (Supplied: University of Queensland)

"Whereas a timber building can just essentially be like Lego bricks. You can just go in, click it all together."

The experiment, conducted at the Queensland Fire Department's (QFD) training ground at the Port of Brisbane, each time slightly changed the design parameters of the cross-laminated timber ceiling compartments, such as the ventilation and ceiling's height.

"We built these large 12-metre-long compartments which are about 2.5 metres wide," Mr Madden said.

"We essentially ignite the fire down one end and watch how fire spreads underneath the ceiling."

Timber loses strength at about 60C and loses all its strength at roughly 300C onwards.

Researchers investigate how the fire spreads through the structures. (Supplied: University of Queensland)

"We got some of our temperature readings going up to about 1,000 degrees Celsius."

UQ and the QFD have been sharing information to help improve public safety since 2014.

QFD fire engineer Mick Conway said understanding new materials and innovative design was crucial to building safer timber structures.

"By burning materials under experimental conditions, our firefighters are learning things that they otherwise might have had to experience for the first time in a live scenario," he said.

The test results are being analysed and will be presented in Mr Madden's final thesis.

"What we're trying to develop is this sort of design methodology or framework for fire safety engineers to go out and have the confidence to be able to build these buildings," Mr Madden said.

"If we have the knowledge and expertise to be able to design these safely, hopefully the idea will be that we'll see lots more of these beautiful massive buildings."

World.title: Farm worker health fears as Q fever vaccine shortage hits rural Australia
World.content:
The vaccine that protects Australians from a serious bacterial infection is expected to run out this week.

Q fever is spread by animals, including sheep and cattle, and causes severe flu-like symptoms that can become chronic and, in some cases, lead to serious cardiovascular complications.

Last year Australia recorded 991 Q fever cases; the highest number since national monitoring began in 1991

Australian manufacturer CSL Seqirus is contracted by Australia's Department of Health (ADH) to supply the vaccine.

"Unfortunately, we actually expect a short temporary stock out starting now through to the end of the year," senior vice-president of operations Chris Larkins said.

"We've expedited the next two batches that are being manufactured. They'll be available, we believe, late December.

"We are very sorry. We know it affects public health, especially in the country and also affects businesses financially out there."

Mr Larkins said stabilising supply was the company's highest priority "given how critical it is to public health and getting our agricultural businesses back up and functioning".

Farmers left in the dark

Rawsonville dairy owner Erika Chesworth said she had been unable to vaccinate her staff since March.

"We've just had very short responses from the only local clinic saying they are unable to source the vaccine," she said.

Erika Chesworth from Little Big Dairy. (Supplied)

"It's just been dead ends everywhere; there's been no communication from anyone in any capacity."

Ms Chesworth said the situation left staff and the business "vulnerable to a disease that animals can't be vaccinated for".

"It puts us at a high risk. It's hard enough to secure staff with skills," she said.

"We had an experience two summers ago when two staff members contracted Q fever and they were really sick.

"We had a seven-year-old grandson contract Q fever … people can't be done until they're 15, there are so many problems."

A perfect storm

Mr Larkins said the Q fever vaccine was "an exceptionally complex product to manufacture", with each batch taking nine months to produce using an inactivated form of the bacteria.

"Over the last 12 months we've seen an unfortunate situation where we've had a combination of raw material supply issues … and then we've had unexpected manufacturing equipment issues on our filling lines with our electronic system," he said.

A Q-fever vaccination is already mandatory for those working in meat processors across Australia. (ABC Rural: Tom Major)

"It's been a perfect storm where we've been unable to release about three or four batches to the market that were coming through this nine-month cycle period.

"We think from later this year or early next year the constrained supply situation will ease up and we'll be able to get that product out to customers."

Mr Larkins said the company expected production issues to ease after moving operations to two new, state-of-the-art sites in Melbourne.

A 'public health' issue

Nurse and shearer Carol Mudford said she waited five years to get a Q fever vaccine after she started working in the sheds in 2020.

"It's either not been available or very difficult to get for the last five, six years," she said.

" People want it and need it and it will save lives. "

Ms Mudford said Q fever was a public health problem, not just an agricultural issue.

"A lot of people still don't know about Q fever; we need more awareness because anyone in rural Australia is at risk," she said.

Carol Mudford (left) after receiving a Q fever vaccine in Dubbo. (Supplied)

"It is highly contagious as a bacteria that travels in the dust.

"It spreads very well; it can linger on clothing that comes back to a family home, through dust that flies off a livestock truck or spread through mowing lawns."

A spokesperson for the Health Department said in a statement that CSL Seqirus was responsible for managing the manufacture and commercial supply of Q-VAX, "including distribution arrangements and the allocation of available stock".

"This arrangement with CSL Seqirus, over 10 years and worth $1 billion, supports the continued availability of domestic manufacturing capability," they said.

World.title: The women's RLWC final is a fight against fate
World.content:
The women's Rugby League World Cup has ended up exactly where it was fated to be, with Australia to face New Zealand in the final for the third tournament in a row.

Barring the kind of upset that sends bookies broke, this was the only way it could be given the Jillaroos and Kiwi Ferns have romped their way through with a near contemptuous ease.

Only Fiji, a delightful surprise packet in their maiden tournament who lost to New Zealand by six in the group stage and Australia by 16 in the semi-final, managed to run either of them close. The former is the only game of the World Cup to be decided by one score or fewer.

Australia names teams for World Cup finals Australia has named its men's and women's sides for this Sunday's Rugby League World Cup finals against New Zealand.

Even counting the valiant efforts of the Bulikula, Australia and New Zealand have outscored their opponents by a combined 272-20 and 182-24 respectively.

Fiji's emergence and Papua New Guinea and Samoa's continued development are positives but if the journey truly matters more than the destination this one has been a trudge.

It has felt inevitable from the start and perhaps it was. There could have been improvements to the draw — Australia had no business playing a team like Wales — but none that would have changed this outcome.

A tournament like this and a final like this, where Australia are deserved 20-point favourites given they've only lost to New Zealand once in the past ten years, is the wrong end of the double-edged sword women's rugby league is trying to wield.

The Jillaroos are the game's lone superpower, without peer or rival, because they are the end-product of almost a decade of transformation via the NRLW.

Australia have done it easy through much of this World Cup. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

They play the same sport as developing nations, but they're in a different game to nations like Wales, France and Papua New Guinea.

There's a value in having a team that stands so tall because they're a gold standard to aspire to for some and a target to aim at for others.

They are proof of what is possible for women's rugby league with investment from the bottom up and the top down, as well as giving it the patience for that investment to rise to the top.

It makes the Jillaroos an incredible creation and victory on Sunday would confirm what most already know — that this is the greatest collection of talent in the history of women's rugby league.

Lopsided women's rugby league The rise of Pasifika rugby league teams in the international men's game contrasts with a widening gulf in the women's game.

Just as the 2017 final, the last before the start of the NRLW, signalled the beginning of a new kind of history so would a Jillaroos win here be the capstone on Australia remaking the game in their own image.

It would mark their fourth World Cup final win in a row, pulling them past New Zealand who currently have three with the last coming back in 2008.

Their dominance is a by-product of the game's progress but it's also so complete and smothering it's become a problem. The things that have made them great have worked too well.

Australia have moved so far and so fast not only is there nothing left for them to overtake, they can barely see New Zealand over their shoulders. They must keep looking though, because there is nobody else to see.

New Zealand are the only team to come close to Australia in recent years. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

They are Everest and New Zealand are the only other team who have even been able to try to climb a mountain before. Everybody else is stuck at base camp.

As talented as their opponents are — and with Raecene McGregor at halfback, Mele Hufanga and Stacey Waaka in the centres and inspirational captain Georgia Hale leading a forward pack who could skin a crocodile their talent is considerable — just playing well is not enough for New Zealand to win.

They'll need an off night by the Australians, a few bounces of the ball, perhaps a referee call or two falling their way, just to bring them into the contest.

A win is possible, but it would be the greatest upset of this era and when the second-best team in the world needs a fair bit of luck to take it to the best, things have gotten way too top heavy.

Australia's World Cup record breaker helps nobody Australia ran up the biggest win in women's international rugby league history with its World Cup victory over Wales but it was the kind of result that served little purpose other than stuffing the stats sheet.

Australia have taken giant strides while everyone else is trying to catch up with smaller steps.

The great-grandparent rule might help in the short-term if it allows more elite talent to filter through to other nations.

Any potential NRL investment in Super League would surely include a women's component and that would give the game in the northern hemisphere a boost it sorely needs.

Both moves would build on the progress of this World Cup, which has mainly come through in excellent television ratings even if the contests haven't been close.

But further development is required before there's any thought of a standalone World Cup, which will likely be tabled until 2034 at the earliest because it cannot happen until this game is for more than one player.

There are glories that lie outside ultimate victory and those can be easier to find once teams like Fiji, Samoa and Papua New Guinea have more time to develop but when it comes to Australia that's a hard thing to remember.

They are the best by such a margin the rest are barely in sight, a grim fate they can confirm with glory on Sunday.

World.title: Labor pledges to boost regional rail and attacks Liberal costings
World.content:
Regional and outer suburban commuters would get an extra 550 weekly V/Line train trips if Labor is re-elected, as the party costs Jess Wilson's commitment to reduce the public service to claim she cannot reach her promised cash surplus.

Premier Ben Carroll will today commit $420 million to increase the regional train network by 24 per cent, targeting voters in regional and outer-fringe seats where Labor is under pressure from both the Coalition and One Nation.

Transport in the outer-west and south-west has been especially painful for the government. Melton and Wyndham Vale still rely on V/Line, two elections after Daniel Andrews promised to electrify the tracks.

Under Labor's announcement today, Melton would get an extra 162 weekly trips from 2027 so that services run every 20 minutes. Longer nine-car trains previously announced will also run from next year.

The plan to increase regional rail services has been costed by Labor at $420 million. (ABC News: Ethan Seiderman)

Wyndham Vale would get a dedicated new service with 249 weekly trips, to minimise crowding.

Geelong would get more express services as a result, cutting 10 minutes from the journey with double the number of total services. An extra two services would also run on Sundays to Geelong and Waurn Ponds.

Government attacks Liberal surplus claim

Labor has separately turned to the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) in an attempt to undercut the opposition leader's commitment to reach a cash surplus by 2032, a key plank of Ms Wilson's election platform.

Ms Wilson has largely relied on her announcement that she would reduce the Victorian Public Service through attrition to save $22 billion over a decade to reach the cash surplus.

But analysis by the PBO, requested by Labor, found the majority of the savings would not be realised until after 2032. The budget office estimated the Coalition policy would save $8.5 billion by 2032, billions short of what would be necessary.

Treasurer Colin Brooks used the findings to claim Ms Wilson would need to cut essential services, in particular health, to meet their commitment.

Labor is challenging Liberal leader Jess Wilson's pledge to reach a budget surplus. (ABC News Melbourne)

In a statement, Ms Wilson said she would not take lectures on costings from Labor.

"Only our Liberal and Nationals team has a costed and credible plan to repair the budget, underpinned by more than $26 billion in responsible and disciplined savings," she said.

Ms Wilson has not released the full copy of her version of the PBO's analysis, and has been under pressure to explain how she can scrap taxes, make a suite of spending commitments while also bringing down debt — on track to reach almost $200 billion by 2029-2030.

PBO analysis can vary depending on the assumptions put to them.

More express trains from regional centres

Under Labor's transport announcement, the Seymour line to the outer-north through Wallan and Donnybrook would get an extra 29 services from 2028.

Another 101 weekly services would also run through the Bendigo line from 2028; 21 to Bendigo and 80 to Kyneton, allowing most off-peak trains to run express from Bendigo.

The Warrnambool line would also get an extra eight weekend services from next year, while the Traralgon line would wait until 2028 for an additional Sunday service.

V/Line services have been plagued by overcrowding as demand increases. (Supplied: Kate Young)

Most weekday off-peak trains from Ballarat would also run express to Melbourne from next year, shaving up to 10 minutes off the journey, Labor said.

The Coalition has previously promised $1.7 billion to run hybrid trains to Melton and Wyndham Vale, though the government disputed this was feasible with the rest of the network.

After delaying electrification, the government now says the new Sunshine station hub must be built first to separate the V/Line and Metro tracks.

World.title: Alien-like wasps destroy pests in historic Sydney garden from the inside out
World.content:
Once considered a form of "black magic", an army of predatory insects is being used to tackle pests in a popular century-old Sydney garden.

Centennial Park in the city's east was formerly a swamp that was turned into a drinking water source, before it was transformed into parklands and opened to the public on Australia Day in 1888.

About 20 years later, then-park director Joseph Maiden planted a rosarium, which in Latin means "rose garden".

Today, it is home to 33 different varieties of roses, with an estimated 800 plants overlooking Busbys Pond.

Geese are often seen walking among the floral bursts of colour, giving it a somewhat fairytale appearance.

Unfortunately, it is not just humans and birdlife that enjoy the sweet scents. Pests do too.

Centennial Park's popular rose garden was established in 1909. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Aphid infestation

A team of ladybirds and parasitic wasps, led by Western Sydney Parklands senior horticulturalist Tristan Harman, have been tasked with managing "a fairly heavy aphid infestation".

Mr Harman said it was normal for new shoots to attract thousands of the bugs each year after the roses were pruned back in winter, but they had to be managed.

"If these aphids were just left to do their business, the roses wouldn't be roses anymore," he said.

"They're pretty amazing survivors, like they pump out clones if they need to."

Mr Harman is leading the charge against pests at Centennial Park's rose garden. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Aphids can cause roses to become distorted and puckered. The pest can also pass on viruses between plants.

They are also quite unsightly, often encouraging black mould to develop.

Alien-like bug warfare

Thousands of parasitic wasps and their eggs have been released into the garden. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Although aphids can significantly damage roses and other plants, they are no match for the thousands of "gruesome" predatory parasitic wasps.

"The adult lays its eggs inside the body of the aphid and the egg hatches within the body, then [the wasp] eats the aphid from the inside out," he said.

"Then the wasp, once it's done that, goes on to complete its life cycle, goes into its adult phase."

Ladybirds being tipped onto a rose. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

About 1,000 ladybirds, otherwise known as ladybugs, are far tamer in comparison and easier to spot, eating the aphids as they appear.

The insects are released annually, and this is the second time Mr Harman has been in charge.

Five batches are distributed among the garden beds from September to early November: two in the first fortnight, then every fortnight after.

After just the second release this year in late September, Mr Harman said the insects were victorious in their conquest.

Protecting the bees

The insects have been released throughout the 800 roses. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

The ladybirds and three types of parasitic wasps, including their eggs, were supplied and sent to Sydney by a company based in South Australia.

"They're in a little polystyrene sort of esky type thing with a tiny little cooler bag thing in there that keeps the insects cool," Mr Harman said.

"The wasps are in vials and the lady beetles are in a little ice cream container ... and they send them out with shredded newspaper.

"As long as you get them out within a day or two of their arrival, they're fine."

The parasitic wasps were delivered in a vial. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

The delivery included wasp eggs and live adult insects.

"It was decided that it's obviously better to use an integrated pest management plan rather than just spraying with toxic chemicals for every possible pest disease," he said.

Ladybirds are a gardener's best friend when it comes to aphid control. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Mr Harman said this year's batch cost about $1,300, but came with added benefits.

"I think it would probably work out comparable in the overall growing season to be releasing these insects, especially when you think of some of the chemicals you can use that are toxic to bees," he said.

" If you're spraying chemicals to kill aphids, you'll kill things you're not trying to kill. "

From taboo to a common practice

Mr Harman says it feels great to be using natural means to deal with pests. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Mr Harman said when he was studying almost 30 years ago, using predatory insects to deal with pests seemed like "some sort of black magic".

"In previous jobs I've had, there was never any talk of using these sorts of methods, even though it was something that, after, 15, 20 years, it was something that was common," he said.

"You got these beautiful little insects walking on you and you put them on the flower and they go and they do their thing and they're part of what's beautiful in the garden.

" It feels great. "

Mr Harman said about 17 million people visited Centennial Park each year, including those attending weddings.

"So we try to keep it at its highest standard as we possibly can without spraying unless we absolutely have to," he said.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Albanese defends Australia as climate leader after UN boss pushes him to step up commitments; Russia and Ukraine talks end with no major breakthrough
World.content:
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie says it is “a great privilege and responsibility to wear the baggy green,” and that Australian coach Pat Cummins should call a press conference to address Khawaja’s claims that the whole team knew about a 2018 ball tampering plot during a test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

“Khawaja is either telling the truth or he’s not. I think it’s a real disappointment that he’s not fronting up and backing his version of the truth in with you today. At the end of the day, and this is a question for Cummins, you know, leadership is about courage,” she told the Today show.

McKenzie said there would be grave consequences if Khawaja had lied, and that Australia’s defamation laws would protect the players who were telling “the truth”.

“We have defamation laws for a reason. I mean, we can’t have our cricket team under this sort of cloud … people running, dropping the bomb, and then running for cover.”

Yesterday, Khawaja cancelled all of his planned TV and radio appearances following a grilling on ABC’s 7.30 on Tuesday night.

World.title: ‘He’s a warrior’: Ikitau pledges defensive fix as he reunites with Suaalii
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘He’s a warrior’: Ikitau pledges defensive fix as he reunites with Suaalii Iain Payten November 12, 2026 — 6:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Wallabies centre Len Ikitau conceded the merry-go-round of midfield combinations has made life tricky this year but backed “warrior” Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to shut out his critics and thrive in another spicy showdown with a Scottish rival at Murrayfield. Suaalii is set to return to outside centre for the Wallabies against Scotland on Monday (AEDT), reuniting with Ikitau in the midfield after Isaac Henry’s tour-ending hamstring injury. The change is expected to be one of only a small handful, with also Carter Gordon expected to come into the side at No.10 and bullocking backrower Rob Valetini also returning to the run-on team. Loading Ikitau and Suaalii was a settled combination throughout the Joe Schmidt years but this year the Wallabies stable of centres – also including Henry and Hunter Paisami – have chopped and changed repeatedly. In 11 Tests in 2026, the Wallabies midfield has changed seven times, and used six unique combinations. Some of the change has been forced due to injury and suspension, but it has also been a tactical choice at times, with coach Les Kiss deploying Suaalii at wing in recent Tests. Paisami withdrew late from the spring tour due to personal reasons.



All that rotation has come at a cost, however, with frayed defensive connections, and stilted attacking flow as well. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii training with the Walalbies. Alfred Naupoto/Rugby Australia “It is pretty tough being able to stick with the same centre pairing, and being able to play consistently with the same people has been tough for us lately,” Ikitau said. “But I feel like we’ve got a lot of good centres. You know, it’s unfortunate for ‘Zack’ who’s not playing for the rest of the tour, but we’ve got Filipo [Daugunu] who was outstanding when he came on, brought a lot of energy. “And then Joseph can come back to the centres. We’ve got a good relationship there in the centres, so if he needs to come back in, then we’ll just go with that.” Kiss will name his side on Saturday morning (AEDT). Returning to the reliable defensive duo of Ikitau and Suaalii – as opposed to more attacking players like Kurtley Beale or Daugunu – makes sense in a week when the Wallabies will not only come up against a lethal Scottish 10-12 duo in Finn Russell and Tuipulotu, but after the side was defensively exposed by England.



Australia’s defence was routinely beaten by the up-tempo English attack, and coming after two massive Bledisloe losses before, the Wallabies conceded an average of 46 points per Test in their last three. In the four games where Ikitau and Suaalii started together in the midfield this year, the Wallabies conceded an average of 28 points; second only to Paisami-Henry (Japan in Townsville and Argentina in Jujuy) who conceded an average of 19. Ikitau said the Wallabies had been working hard on fixing problems in defensive connection this week in Edinburgh, and which he frankly described as “all over the shop at the moment”. “England gave it to us from the start and put us under a lot of pressure … and we kind of sat back and watched them in a way. We can’t be doing that against Scotland. We really want to be going at them, especially in defence, putting them under pressure,” Ikitau said.



Related Article Australian rugby ‘Unfair’: Wallabies teammate jumps to Suaalii’s defence after Ashton bake “It’s just our connection. We need to be able to connect well with our forwards and with our backfield, too. We’re all over the shop at the moment, and some major fixes for us as a backline [are needed], and we’re working at it at training.” Suaalii’s aggression may also be an asset, particularly up against Tuipulotu, and after getting panned by former England winger Chris Ashton as not being a Test-standard rugby player. “Who?” Ikitau said pointedly, when asked about the Ashton comments, and their impact on Suaalii. “He [Suaalii] is a rugby player. He focuses on his role as a rugby player, as we all do. We don’t really listen to that outside noise.” Ikitau said Suaalii will be excited for another clash with Scotland at Murrayfield, two years after a running battle with Aussie-raised Tuipulotu at the same venue. Suaalii nailed the Scotland captain with a monster tackle, but had to come off with a shoulder injury, leading to a spray from Tuipulotu.



Sione Tuipulotu is hammered by Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii at Murrayfield in 2024. PA Images via Getty Images Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Sione Tuipulotu trade words at Murrayfield in Edinburgh. Getty Images “That was a good hit,” Ikitau said. “Joseph, he’s a warrior. He does all the prep in the world. He’s the first one into the gym, he’s the last one to leave. In terms of his preparation, he’s always ready to play. On the field, you know that he’s going to go out and give it his all. He just needs to be able to contain himself “He’s excited for this match-up this week and he’s ready to go.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: How Pete Hegseth suddenly went from ‘out the door’ to safe as houses
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS politics How Pete Hegseth suddenly went from ‘out the door’ to safe as houses Michael Koziol November 12, 2026 — 6:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The conventional wisdom around the corridors of Washington a few weeks ago was that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was headed for the exit. Indeed, speculation raged for months that President Donald Trump wasn’t happy with Hegseth. In particular, a Washington Post story from August reported that Trump and Hegseth clashed at Camp David about munitions shortages caused by the war in Iran, and why the president had apparently been misled about the problem. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, and his wife Jennifer Rauchet at a Veterans Day ceremony in Arlington on Wednesday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein It was the latest in a series of controversies that seemed to pit the Pentagon against the White House. Earlier, reports indicated Hegseth’s department had unilaterally paused weapons shipments to Ukraine and scaled back the US troop presence in Romania. Moreover, Hegseth clashed with top military personnel, and replaced several of them. There was an air of chaos and churn around the defence secretary, and Trump acknowledged receiving complaints.



There were strong parallels with 2006, when Republican president George W. Bush fired his defence secretary, Donald Rumsfeld, the day after a devastating midterm election when the GOP lost control of both chambers. That dismissal also took place amid the increasingly unpopular war in Iraq, which had become the exact kind of quagmire that Rumsfeld famously said “I don’t do”. Rumours of Hegseth’s removal from the cabinet were in overdrive, but now the president is digging in behind him. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Even though Hegseth was executing Trump’s orders in Iran, he loomed as a potential fall guy for a war that was never popular and grew less so after initial peace plans collapsed. But the midterm election results – delivering control of both chambers to the Democrats, with big majorities – changed the equation.



The Trump White House is now under siege, and preparing to fight. Trump has said so himself, and appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller as his chief of staff, replacing the more establishment Republican Susie Wiles. This is a White House that is going to war, and its instinct is to defend its people. So when Hegseth faced an impeachment push from a Republican congressman, Thomas Massie, he was no longer liability but a potential victim – and Trump does not want to lose. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller at a White House Halloween event. AP “In any normal political environment, getting impeached would be a bad thing for a cabinet member,” said Josh Rogin, security analyst at the Washington Post’s WP Intelligence unit, on CNN this week. “But in Trump’s mind and in Hegseth’s mind, this is a badge of honour. And what Thomas Massie has done is inadvertently throw Pete Hegseth a lifeline.



“A week ago, we all thought he was on his way out the door. Now he’s got the full backing of the president, and he’s making content off of it.” The administration managed to keep every House Republican in line to defend Hegseth from impeachment on Tuesday (US time), except for Massie. President Donald Trump addressing a Veterans Day ceremony on Wednesday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein The attempt failed after 11 Democrats failed to show up to vote, including former speaker Nancy Pelosi, who returned to San Francisco for a Veterans Day event. Others said they were stuck in traffic after attending an off-site “new member reception”. While next year’s changing of the guard will mean Democrats can easily impeach Hegseth in the House, they would not have anywhere near the two-thirds majority needed to convict him in the Senate.



As Rogin observed, it allows Hegseth to play the martyr, while Trump can decry the Democrats’ impeachment attempts as lawfare and weaponisation. In a performance that won praise from the president, Hegseth used a rare Pentagon news conference to link his plight with Trump’s. “They” had impeached Trump twice before, he said. “Now, they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his cabinet. Loading “They will fail again. And if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.” Trump gave Hegseth a shout-out during his Veterans Day remarks on Wednesday, prompting a resounding cheer from the crowd. “I had a feeling that was going to happen,” the president remarked.



Hegseth’s survival is now a marker of Trump’s success, while his removal would be a signal of the president’s failure. Related Article Updated

US politics Republicans shield Hegseth from impeachment after Trump, Vance circle wagons The defence secretary could still be forced out if it becomes politically expedient. He is reportedly interested in a Senate vacancy caused by the Republican senator for Tennessee, Marsha Blackburn, being elected governor of that state. But Hegseth is now the face of two wars: the one against Iran, and the one against the Democrats. And it’s the latter that will keep him in the job. Read more on US politics:

World.title: Chinese car giant BYD apologises after putting wheels on the wrong way
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

BYD apologised for an assembly mistake that meant some of its Great Tang electric sport utility vehicles had their front and rear wheel rims installed in reverse.

An investigation traced the problem to a Hubei-based supplier, BYD said in a statement on its official Weibo account. The carmaker has fixed the system responsible for the problem, while the supplier has introduced additional visual inspections on the production line, it said.

BYD is the world’s biggest electric carmaker by sales. AP

BYD said its own testing found that the affected vehicles’ handling wasn’t compromised and there was no safety risk. Owners of affected cars are eligible for replacement and the warranty period will be restarted , it said. The automaker didn’t disclose how many vehicles were involved.

The assembly error came to light after several owners complained online that the wider rear-wheel rims had been installed on their front tires and the narrower front-wheel rims were put on the back. Some said they were concerned about the possibility of excessive wear on their tires, as well as potential safety risks while driving.

World.title: Albanese defends Australia as climate leader after being pushed on world stage to do more
World.content:
PoliticsFederalClimate policy Albanese defends Australia as climate leader after being pushed on world stage to do more Natassia Chrysanthos and Nick O'Malley Updated November 12, 2026 — 6:18am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Antalya, Turkey: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has insisted the country is playing its part as a climate action leader, as the head of the United Nations pressures Australia and COP hosts Turkey to push a more ambitious agenda on fossil fuels at this year’s climate conference. Outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders on Wednesday (Antalya time) that “fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs”. Anthony Albanese speaks at the COP31 UN Climate Summit in Turkey on Wednesday. AP Guterres’ comments came as COP31 president Turkish Climate Minister Murat Kurum and Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who is presiding over negotiations, called on more than 190 nations to rapidly ramp up electrification rather than focus on fossil fuels, in the hopes of sidestepping a bitter fight at this year’s conference. Albanese addressed the opening ceremony of the leaders’ summit minutes afterwards, declaring it “a historic moment for my country”.



“Australia is proud to be playing a leading role with Turkey on climate change negotiations for the world at this United Nations Conference of the Parties … and proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” Albanese said. “COP31 must be where our cooperation delivers practical results. Unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, and unlocking climate finance for those who need it most.” But Guterres, who is making his last addresses to a major UN event before the end of his term next month, appeared to signal to Australia and Turkey that it was not enough. UN Secretary-General António Guterres (second from left) during the COP31 group photo. Getty Images “It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable. Now, here at COP31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it and delivering it. I thank [Brazil] for its leadership. We must leave Antalya with clear next steps to advance this road map,” he said at an earlier forum on Tuesday.



“I encourage the current and future COP presidencies to carry this work forward. We must give the world reason to believe in the commitment made in Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels.” Guterres reinforced his message in a second speech on Wednesday, saying the case for fossil fuels was collapsing as global conflicts created price shocks and insecurity for three-quarters of the world’s population living in countries that import coal, oil and gas. Related Article Paris Agreement Greenhouse pollution down but global warming surges as climate talks begin “That [eliminating fossil fuels] won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” he said. “That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach. Slashing methane emissions … and those who profit most from fossil fuels must help foot the bill for the damage they have caused.



“It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits – and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.” Leaders pose for a family photo at the COP31 climate conference. Getty Images Australian Conservation Foundation chief executive Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader who is at the conference, said the comments could be read as criticism of Australia, which has focused on electrification in lieu of pursuing the more diplomatically difficult task of securing agreement to specifically target fossil fuels. “In a very significant intervention, the UN secretary-general and last year’s COP president Brazil have put coal, oil and gas squarely on the agenda here in Turkey. They’re saying it’s not enough to talk about renewables and electrification if you’re also opening new coal and gas mines,” Bandt said. “Australia is getting called out. The bar is now set for this summit and Australia and Turkey must deliver a concrete road map for getting out of coal and gas.”



Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of this year’s conference in Antalya. Australia has also faced criticism from climate activists and some Pacific leaders for its continued exports of fossil fuels and the expansion of coal and gas extraction. As Bowen prepared to leave for Turkey last week, a group of 500 climate scientists and experts distributed an open letter to Albanese, saying Australia “cannot credibly lead on climate abroad nor ensure national nor regional security while it expands coal and gas at home”. At the same time, the Coalition and One Nation have relentlessly attacked the government over its net zero policies and spending of taxpayer money on Bowen’s role as president of negotiations. Albanese quoted 13-year-old Tuvalu school student Melelusi Sokotia as he advocated on behalf of Pacific nations, while promoting Australia’s record. “Australia is playing our part. Our target is ambitious. Our progress is strong. And our successes are significant,” he said.



“In just six years, Australia has doubled renewables generation, which now accounts for half our electricity mix. We proudly have one of the largest rooftop solar and battery markets in the world, [with] more than 600,000 home batteries installed in the past year alone.” Related Article Climate policy 35-by-35: A catchy slogan, a mammoth negotiation and a plan to save the world In response to Albanese’s address, Nicki Hutley from the Climate Council said electrification was the right plan, and Australians were backing it by taking up rooftop solar and electric cars. “But building renewables while approving new coal and gas is like filling the bath with the plug pulled out,” she said. “The prime minister is right that our Pacific neighbours are asking for help, and they’ve been clear that means cutting climate pollution from coal, oil and gas.”



Bowen made a strong call to action on electrification in his own address on Wednesday. “Let’s be frank. We meet at a time in which the world is being buffeted, when our populations and communities are seeing daily reports of crises and uncertainties, when these crises are putting the cost-of-living pressure up in every single country we represent,” he said. “We are accelerating, not stepping back. And we will act in solidarity to address the climate crisis.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: It’s the golden age of pancakes, and this is Sydney’s top five
World.content:
Eating outBest of It’s the golden age of pancakes, and this is Sydney’s top five From pancakes lacquered in thick golden crusts, to those made from literal cake batter, these chefs are pushing pancakes to their culinary limits. Bianca Hrovat November 12, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Before the Good Food team visited Surry Hills cafe A.P Bread and Wine for brunch in October, I thought I’d experienced everything pancakes had to offer. There have been classic diner pancakes with sides of streaky bacon; souffle pancakes, like wobbly breaths of sugared air; and sourdough skillet pancakes so hefty they came with a warning (“You won’t be able to finish one by yourself,” said the waiter at Pina in Potts Point, failing to appreciate my commitment to the bit). But there has never been a pancake in Sydney quite like this. A.Pancake at A.P Bread and Wine, Darlinghurst. It is round, thick and as large as the plate it sits on, lacquered in toffee-brown kithul syrup (reduced floral sap from the Sri Lankan kithul palm). A generous scoop of whipped honey butter sits on top, slowly melting down one side. Then, the crust: a burnished coat so crisp it crackles like brulee beneath your fork, making way to reveal a fluffy, sunshine-yellow interior. Obviously, it’s delicious. It’s a pancake. But it’s that unexpected play on texture, that contrast of biscuity crunch, smoky-sweet syrup and baked batter that pushed the A.Pancake (as it’s called) to top spot on my personal list of Sydney’s best (no small feat, as editor of Good Food’s 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries guide). Too bad a side of berries costs another $6.50. The signature pancake at Pina in Potts Point.



The dish (exclusively available at A.P Bread and Wine) was developed about six months ago by chef Mat Lindsay, co-founder of the A.P Bakery empire and the man behind revered Sydney venues including Poly (Surry Hills), Ester (Chippendale) and its new neighbour, dine-in bar Pig Mary. He says he was inspired by the Golden Diner pancakes, which attracted queues of up to two hours when they debuted at chef Sam Yoo’s New York cafe in 2019. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Both use a pre-fermented yeast batter, and both are briefly cooked on the stove before going into the oven (“It’s more of a hotcake as opposed to a pancake,” says Lindsay). But it’s on the stove where Lindsay pushes his version further by using clarified butter to shallow-fry the batter and set the crust. It’s exactly what Lindsay was aiming for, he says: crisp yet fluffy, substantial without being a day-ender. Creme brulee pancake at Jinius, Dawes Point. In Sydney, pancakes have been a source of culinary innovation since, at least, the introduction of Bill Granger’s amorphous ricotta hotcakes at his eponymous Darlinghurst cafe more than 30 years ago. The tradition continued with the popularity of the supersized sourdough pancake at Pina, which debuted in Potts Point in 2020. This week, another contender for city’s best entered the fray at Jinius, a cafe-bakery in Dawes Point led in partnership by Yeongjin Park (former head baker at Tenacious Bakehouse) and Jerry Jeong (former chef at Quay and Saint Peter). Here, Park repurposes chiffon cake batter to create a creme brulee pancake that’s as light as can be, without sacrificing substance. Souffle pancakes err too far from the original, says Park, and he didn’t want to serve something that could disappear within a few bites.



The final product is a thing of beauty: two slabs of pancake layered atop a spoonful of house-made strawberry jam and bruleed vanilla custard, all of it glazed in maple brown-butter syrup. One perfect, fridge-cold square of butter is placed on top, then gently torched until it starts to melt. World.title: Piper-Lily didn’t think she would graduate. Now she’s off to university
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHigh school Piper-Lily didn’t think she would graduate. Now she’s off to university Catherine Strohfeldt November 12, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Piper-Lily Daniel received her university offer on her mum’s birthday in early October. “She really wanted me to finish year 11 and 12,” Daniel said. About 18 months ago, Daniel didn’t believe she would. BUSY School Brisbane City year 12 student Piper-Lily Daniel has accepted an early offer from Griffith University. Catherine Strohfeldt Now she’s weeks away from graduating from The BUSY School Brisbane City campus, a special assistance school designed to help disengaged young people.



The Fortitude Valley school runs a different curriculum to a standard high school, steering students towards employment rather than grades, and focusing on rebuilding trust. Related Article Exclusive

Schools These schools might have saved the state $456 million: report Its roughly 250 students attend classroom lessons for the equivalent of three days each week, studying applied subjects in English, maths, and social work. The students’ remaining two school days are spent in industry settings pursuing vocational education and training (VET) subjects, which can sometimes include courses on the campus. About 86 per cent of students complete this subject mix, making them eligible for a Queensland Certificate of Education.



Daniel was among this number, having completed certificate courses in hospitality and social work. Related Article High school Year 12 exam exemptions spark debate on future of Queensland testing The year 12 student said her new school environment had not been a cure-all for the barriers she had faced in her previous traditional high school. “I still struggle to do schoolwork in the school environment, but at my last school, I would just give up ... now, I get all my assessments done,” she said. The BUSY School’s focus on rebuilding trust in education systems was echoed across the sector.



“I think when they see that we actually do support them, and then we follow through with those supports, they actually do feel a sense of safety that they potentially haven’t felt before,” said Ashleigh Maas, a teacher at Y Schools Queensland, another alternative education provider. Most schools offered wraparound student support, with teacher-student ratios typically falling below state standards, as many teachers were accompanied by a youth worker. Y Schools Queensland secondary teacher Ashleigh Maas. Catherine Strohfeldt Students are also supported by on-site counsellors and pathways officers, and many campuses offer free food to students, including breakfasts. At The BUSY School campuses, uniforms, classroom supplies and school-owned laptops are provided for free, and the school charges no fees to families.



A McCrindle report commissioned by industry body Independent Schools Queensland surveyed 410 families and 271 alumni from several dozen special assistance schools across the state. About 60 per cent said their school had an extremely or very positive index on either their wellbeing or that of their young person, which included impacts to their safety, relationships, and health. Among parents, 82 per cent said they also felt they were respected and understood by school staff. South Brisbane mother Sharni Welsh said teachers at Y Schools South Brisbane had spoken highly of her son, Levi, since he joined in term 2 this year.



“It’s nice to have other people see in Levi what I do,” she said. Y Schools Queensland year 8 student Levi Welsh. Catherine Strohfeldt The year 8 student said he had rekindled an interest in school, enjoying maths, English, science, and geography. World.title: ‘He’s a warrior’: Ikitau pledges defensive fix as he reunites with Suaalii
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘He’s a warrior’: Ikitau pledges defensive fix as he reunites with Suaalii Iain Payten November 12, 2026 — 6:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Wallabies centre Len Ikitau conceded the merry-go-round of midfield combinations has made life tricky this year but backed “warrior” Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to shut out his critics and thrive in another spicy showdown with a Scottish rival at Murrayfield. Suaalii is set to return to outside centre for the Wallabies against Scotland on Monday (AEDT), reuniting with Ikitau in the midfield after Isaac Henry’s tour-ending hamstring injury. The change is expected to be one of only a small handful, with also Carter Gordon expected to come into the side at No.10 and bullocking backrower Rob Valetini also returning to the run-on team. Loading Ikitau and Suaalii was a settled combination throughout the Joe Schmidt years but this year the Wallabies stable of centres – also including Henry and Hunter Paisami – have chopped and changed repeatedly. In 11 Tests in 2026, the Wallabies midfield has changed seven times, and used six unique combinations. Some of the change has been forced due to injury and suspension, but it has also been a tactical choice at times, with coach Les Kiss deploying Suaalii at wing in recent Tests. Paisami withdrew late from the spring tour due to personal reasons.



All that rotation has come at a cost, however, with frayed defensive connections, and stilted attacking flow as well. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii training with the Walalbies. Alfred Naupoto/Rugby Australia “It is pretty tough being able to stick with the same centre pairing, and being able to play consistently with the same people has been tough for us lately,” Ikitau said. “But I feel like we’ve got a lot of good centres. You know, it’s unfortunate for ‘Zack’ who’s not playing for the rest of the tour, but we’ve got Filipo [Daugunu] who was outstanding when he came on, brought a lot of energy. “And then Joseph can come back to the centres. We’ve got a good relationship there in the centres, so if he needs to come back in, then we’ll just go with that.” Kiss will name his side on Saturday morning (AEDT). Returning to the reliable defensive duo of Ikitau and Suaalii – as opposed to more attacking players like Kurtley Beale or Daugunu – makes sense in a week when the Wallabies will not only come up against a lethal Scottish 10-12 duo in Finn Russell and Tuipulotu, but after the side was defensively exposed by England.



Australia’s defence was routinely beaten by the up-tempo English attack, and coming after two massive Bledisloe losses before, the Wallabies conceded an average of 46 points per Test in their last three. In the four games where Ikitau and Suaalii started together in the midfield this year, the Wallabies conceded an average of 28 points; second only to Paisami-Henry (Japan in Townsville and Argentina in Jujuy) who conceded an average of 19. Ikitau said the Wallabies had been working hard on fixing problems in defensive connection this week in Edinburgh, and which he frankly described as “all over the shop at the moment”. “England gave it to us from the start and put us under a lot of pressure … and we kind of sat back and watched them in a way. We can’t be doing that against Scotland. We really want to be going at them, especially in defence, putting them under pressure,” Ikitau said.



Related Article Australian rugby ‘Unfair’: Wallabies teammate jumps to Suaalii’s defence after Ashton bake “It’s just our connection. We need to be able to connect well with our forwards and with our backfield, too. We’re all over the shop at the moment, and some major fixes for us as a backline [are needed], and we’re working at it at training.” Suaalii’s aggression may also be an asset, particularly up against Tuipulotu, and after getting panned by former England winger Chris Ashton as not being a Test-standard rugby player. “Who?” Ikitau said pointedly, when asked about the Ashton comments, and their impact on Suaalii. “He [Suaalii] is a rugby player. He focuses on his role as a rugby player, as we all do. We don’t really listen to that outside noise.” Ikitau said Suaalii will be excited for another clash with Scotland at Murrayfield, two years after a running battle with Aussie-raised Tuipulotu at the same venue. Suaalii nailed the Scotland captain with a monster tackle, but had to come off with a shoulder injury, leading to a spray from Tuipulotu.



Sione Tuipulotu is hammered by Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii at Murrayfield in 2024. PA Images via Getty Images Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Sione Tuipulotu trade words at Murrayfield in Edinburgh. Getty Images “That was a good hit,” Ikitau said. “Joseph, he’s a warrior. He does all the prep in the world. He’s the first one into the gym, he’s the last one to leave. In terms of his preparation, he’s always ready to play. On the field, you know that he’s going to go out and give it his all. He just needs to be able to contain himself “He’s excited for this match-up this week and he’s ready to go.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: How Pete Hegseth suddenly went from ‘out the door’ to safe as houses
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS politics How Pete Hegseth suddenly went from ‘out the door’ to safe as houses Michael Koziol November 12, 2026 — 6:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The conventional wisdom around the corridors of Washington a few weeks ago was that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was headed for the exit. Indeed, speculation raged for months that President Donald Trump wasn’t happy with Hegseth. In particular, a Washington Post story from August reported that Trump and Hegseth clashed at Camp David about munitions shortages caused by the war in Iran, and why the president had apparently been misled about the problem. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, and his wife Jennifer Rauchet at a Veterans Day ceremony in Arlington on Wednesday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein It was the latest in a series of controversies that seemed to pit the Pentagon against the White House. Earlier, reports indicated Hegseth’s department had unilaterally paused weapons shipments to Ukraine and scaled back the US troop presence in Romania. Moreover, Hegseth clashed with top military personnel, and replaced several of them. There was an air of chaos and churn around the defence secretary, and Trump acknowledged receiving complaints.



There were strong parallels with 2006, when Republican president George W. Bush fired his defence secretary, Donald Rumsfeld, the day after a devastating midterm election when the GOP lost control of both chambers. That dismissal also took place amid the increasingly unpopular war in Iraq, which had become the exact kind of quagmire that Rumsfeld famously said “I don’t do”. Rumours of Hegseth’s removal from the cabinet were in overdrive, but now the president is digging in behind him. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Even though Hegseth was executing Trump’s orders in Iran, he loomed as a potential fall guy for a war that was never popular and grew less so after initial peace plans collapsed. But the midterm election results – delivering control of both chambers to the Democrats, with big majorities – changed the equation.



The Trump White House is now under siege, and preparing to fight. Trump has said so himself, and appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller as his chief of staff, replacing the more establishment Republican Susie Wiles. This is a White House that is going to war, and its instinct is to defend its people. So when Hegseth faced an impeachment push from a Republican congressman, Thomas Massie, he was no longer liability but a potential victim – and Trump does not want to lose. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller at a White House Halloween event. AP “In any normal political environment, getting impeached would be a bad thing for a cabinet member,” said Josh Rogin, security analyst at the Washington Post’s WP Intelligence unit, on CNN this week. “But in Trump’s mind and in Hegseth’s mind, this is a badge of honour. And what Thomas Massie has done is inadvertently throw Pete Hegseth a lifeline.



“A week ago, we all thought he was on his way out the door. Now he’s got the full backing of the president, and he’s making content off of it.” The administration managed to keep every House Republican in line to defend Hegseth from impeachment on Tuesday (US time), except for Massie. President Donald Trump addressing a Veterans Day ceremony on Wednesday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein The attempt failed after 11 Democrats failed to show up to vote, including former speaker Nancy Pelosi, who returned to San Francisco for a Veterans Day event. Others said they were stuck in traffic after attending an off-site “new member reception”. While next year’s changing of the guard will mean Democrats can easily impeach Hegseth in the House, they would not have anywhere near the two-thirds majority needed to convict him in the Senate.



As Rogin observed, it allows Hegseth to play the martyr, while Trump can decry the Democrats’ impeachment attempts as lawfare and weaponisation. In a performance that won praise from the president, Hegseth used a rare Pentagon news conference to link his plight with Trump’s. “They” had impeached Trump twice before, he said. “Now, they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his cabinet. Loading “They will fail again. And if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.” Trump gave Hegseth a shout-out during his Veterans Day remarks on Wednesday, prompting a resounding cheer from the crowd. “I had a feeling that was going to happen,” the president remarked.



Hegseth’s survival is now a marker of Trump’s success, while his removal would be a signal of the president’s failure. Related Article Updated

US politics Republicans shield Hegseth from impeachment after Trump, Vance circle wagons The defence secretary could still be forced out if it becomes politically expedient. He is reportedly interested in a Senate vacancy caused by the Republican senator for Tennessee, Marsha Blackburn, being elected governor of that state. But Hegseth is now the face of two wars: the one against Iran, and the one against the Democrats. And it’s the latter that will keep him in the job. Read more on US politics:

World.content:

BYD apologised for an assembly mistake that meant some of its Great Tang electric sport utility vehicles had their front and rear wheel rims installed in reverse.

An investigation traced the problem to a Hubei-based supplier, BYD said in a statement on its official Weibo account. The carmaker has fixed the system responsible for the problem, while the supplier has introduced additional visual inspections on the production line, it said.

BYD is the world’s biggest electric carmaker by sales. AP

BYD said its own testing found that the affected vehicles’ handling wasn’t compromised and there was no safety risk. Owners of affected cars are eligible for replacement and the warranty period will be restarted , it said. The automaker didn’t disclose how many vehicles were involved.

The assembly error came to light after several owners complained online that the wider rear-wheel rims had been installed on their front tires and the narrower front-wheel rims were put on the back. Some said they were concerned about the possibility of excessive wear on their tires, as well as potential safety risks while driving.

World.title: Albanese defends Australia as climate leader after being pushed on world stage to do more
World.content:
PoliticsFederalClimate policy Albanese defends Australia as climate leader after being pushed on world stage to do more Natassia Chrysanthos and Nick O'Malley Updated November 12, 2026 — 6:18am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Antalya, Turkey: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has insisted the country is playing its part as a climate action leader, as the head of the United Nations pressures Australia and COP hosts Turkey to push a more ambitious agenda on fossil fuels at this year’s climate conference. Outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders on Wednesday (Antalya time) that “fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs”. Anthony Albanese speaks at the COP31 UN Climate Summit in Turkey on Wednesday. AP Guterres’ comments came as COP31 president Turkish Climate Minister Murat Kurum and Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who is presiding over negotiations, called on more than 190 nations to rapidly ramp up electrification rather than focus on fossil fuels, in the hopes of sidestepping a bitter fight at this year’s conference. Albanese addressed the opening ceremony of the leaders’ summit minutes afterwards, declaring it “a historic moment for my country”.



“Australia is proud to be playing a leading role with Turkey on climate change negotiations for the world at this United Nations Conference of the Parties … and proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” Albanese said. “COP31 must be where our cooperation delivers practical results. Unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, and unlocking climate finance for those who need it most.” But Guterres, who is making his last addresses to a major UN event before the end of his term next month, appeared to signal to Australia and Turkey that it was not enough. UN Secretary-General António Guterres (second from left) during the COP31 group photo. Getty Images “It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable. Now, here at COP31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it and delivering it. I thank [Brazil] for its leadership. We must leave Antalya with clear next steps to advance this road map,” he said at an earlier forum on Tuesday.



“I encourage the current and future COP presidencies to carry this work forward. We must give the world reason to believe in the commitment made in Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels.” Guterres reinforced his message in a second speech on Wednesday, saying the case for fossil fuels was collapsing as global conflicts created price shocks and insecurity for three-quarters of the world’s population living in countries that import coal, oil and gas. Related Article Paris Agreement Greenhouse pollution down but global warming surges as climate talks begin “That [eliminating fossil fuels] won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” he said. “That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach. Slashing methane emissions … and those who profit most from fossil fuels must help foot the bill for the damage they have caused.



“It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits – and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.” Leaders pose for a family photo at the COP31 climate conference. Getty Images Australian Conservation Foundation chief executive Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader who is at the conference, said the comments could be read as criticism of Australia, which has focused on electrification in lieu of pursuing the more diplomatically difficult task of securing agreement to specifically target fossil fuels. “In a very significant intervention, the UN secretary-general and last year’s COP president Brazil have put coal, oil and gas squarely on the agenda here in Turkey. They’re saying it’s not enough to talk about renewables and electrification if you’re also opening new coal and gas mines,” Bandt said. “Australia is getting called out. The bar is now set for this summit and Australia and Turkey must deliver a concrete road map for getting out of coal and gas.”



Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of this year’s conference in Antalya. Australia has also faced criticism from climate activists and some Pacific leaders for its continued exports of fossil fuels and the expansion of coal and gas extraction. As Bowen prepared to leave for Turkey last week, a group of 500 climate scientists and experts distributed an open letter to Albanese, saying Australia “cannot credibly lead on climate abroad nor ensure national nor regional security while it expands coal and gas at home”. At the same time, the Coalition and One Nation have relentlessly attacked the government over its net zero policies and spending of taxpayer money on Bowen’s role as president of negotiations. Albanese quoted 13-year-old Tuvalu school student Melelusi Sokotia as he advocated on behalf of Pacific nations, while promoting Australia’s record. “Australia is playing our part. Our target is ambitious. Our progress is strong. And our successes are significant,” he said.



“In just six years, Australia has doubled renewables generation, which now accounts for half our electricity mix. We proudly have one of the largest rooftop solar and battery markets in the world, [with] more than 600,000 home batteries installed in the past year alone.” Related Article Climate policy 35-by-35: A catchy slogan, a mammoth negotiation and a plan to save the world In response to Albanese’s address, Nicki Hutley from the Climate Council said electrification was the right plan, and Australians were backing it by taking up rooftop solar and electric cars. “But building renewables while approving new coal and gas is like filling the bath with the plug pulled out,” she said. “The prime minister is right that our Pacific neighbours are asking for help, and they’ve been clear that means cutting climate pollution from coal, oil and gas.”



Bowen made a strong call to action on electrification in his own address on Wednesday. “Let’s be frank. We meet at a time in which the world is being buffeted, when our populations and communities are seeing daily reports of crises and uncertainties, when these crises are putting the cost-of-living pressure up in every single country we represent,” he said. “We are accelerating, not stepping back. And we will act in solidarity to address the climate crisis.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
