World.title: It’s the golden age of pancakes, and this is Sydney’s top five
World.content:
Eating outBest of It’s the golden age of pancakes, and this is Sydney’s top five From pancakes lacquered in thick golden crusts, to those made from literal cake batter, these chefs are pushing pancakes to their culinary limits. Bianca Hrovat November 12, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Before the Good Food team visited Surry Hills cafe A.P Bread and Wine for brunch in October, I thought I’d experienced everything pancakes had to offer. There have been classic diner pancakes with sides of streaky bacon; souffle pancakes, like wobbly breaths of sugared air; and sourdough skillet pancakes so hefty they came with a warning (“You won’t be able to finish one by yourself,” said the waiter at Pina in Potts Point, failing to appreciate my commitment to the bit). But there has never been a pancake in Sydney quite like this. A.Pancake at A.P Bread and Wine, Darlinghurst. It is round, thick and as large as the plate it sits on, lacquered in toffee-brown kithul syrup (reduced floral sap from the Sri Lankan kithul palm). A generous scoop of whipped honey butter sits on top, slowly melting down one side. Then, the crust: a burnished coat so crisp it crackles like brulee beneath your fork, making way to reveal a fluffy, sunshine-yellow interior. Obviously, it’s delicious. It’s a pancake. But it’s that unexpected play on texture, that contrast of biscuity crunch, smoky-sweet syrup and baked batter that pushed the A.Pancake (as it’s called) to top spot on my personal list of Sydney’s best (no small feat, as editor of Good Food’s 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries guide). Too bad a side of berries costs another $6.50. The signature pancake at Pina in Potts Point.



The dish (exclusively available at A.P Bread and Wine) was developed about six months ago by chef Mat Lindsay, co-founder of the A.P Bakery empire and the man behind revered Sydney venues including Poly (Surry Hills), Ester (Chippendale) and its new neighbour, dine-in bar Pig Mary. He says he was inspired by the Golden Diner pancakes, which attracted queues of up to two hours when they debuted at chef Sam Yoo’s New York cafe in 2019. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Both use a pre-fermented yeast batter, and both are briefly cooked on the stove before going into the oven (“It’s more of a hotcake as opposed to a pancake,” says Lindsay). But it’s on the stove where Lindsay pushes his version further by using clarified butter to shallow-fry the batter and set the crust. It’s exactly what Lindsay was aiming for, he says: crisp yet fluffy, substantial without being a day-ender. Creme brulee pancake at Jinius, Dawes Point. In Sydney, pancakes have been a source of culinary innovation since, at least, the introduction of Bill Granger’s amorphous ricotta hotcakes at his eponymous Darlinghurst cafe more than 30 years ago. The tradition continued with the popularity of the supersized sourdough pancake at Pina, which debuted in Potts Point in 2020. This week, another contender for city’s best entered the fray at Jinius, a cafe-bakery in Dawes Point led in partnership by Yeongjin Park (former head baker at Tenacious Bakehouse) and Jerry Jeong (former chef at Quay and Saint Peter). Here, Park repurposes chiffon cake batter to create a creme brulee pancake that’s as light as can be, without sacrificing substance. Souffle pancakes err too far from the original, says Park, and he didn’t want to serve something that could disappear within a few bites.



The final product is a thing of beauty: two slabs of pancake layered atop a spoonful of house-made strawberry jam and bruleed vanilla custard, all of it glazed in maple brown-butter syrup. One perfect, fridge-cold square of butter is placed on top, then gently torched until it starts to melt. The final product practically gleams – the pancake emoji sprung to life, if it tasted like burnished caramel with a hint of vanilla. Diner-style pancakes at SIT, Marrickville. Dion Georgopoulos My top five pancakes (and hotcakes) in Sydney 1. A.Pancake at A.P Bread and Wine, Darlinghurst $22



An exceptional skillet-baked hotcake with a fluffy interior and crust unlike any other. A side of berries will set you back an additional $6.50. 32 Burton Street, Darlinghurst, apbakery.com.au 2. Creme brulee pancake at Jinius, Dawes Point $26 An entirely new take on pancakes using chiffon cake batter to create something that’s more fine-dining dessert than standard brunch fare. World.title: Piper-Lily didn’t think she would graduate. Now she’s off to university
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHigh school Piper-Lily didn’t think she would graduate. Now she’s off to university Catherine Strohfeldt November 12, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Piper-Lily Daniel received her university offer on her mum’s birthday in early October. “She really wanted me to finish year 11 and 12,” Daniel said. About 18 months ago, Daniel didn’t believe she would. BUSY School Brisbane City year 12 student Piper-Lily Daniel has accepted an early offer from Griffith University. Catherine Strohfeldt Now she’s weeks away from graduating from The BUSY School Brisbane City campus, a special assistance school designed to help disengaged young people.



The Fortitude Valley school runs a different curriculum to a standard high school, steering students towards employment rather than grades, and focusing on rebuilding trust. Related Article Exclusive

Schools These schools might have saved the state $456 million: report Its roughly 250 students attend classroom lessons for the equivalent of three days each week, studying applied subjects in English, maths, and social work. The students’ remaining two school days are spent in industry settings pursuing vocational education and training (VET) subjects, which can sometimes include courses on the campus. About 86 per cent of students complete this subject mix, making them eligible for a Queensland Certificate of Education.



Daniel was among this number, having completed certificate courses in hospitality and social work. Related Article High school Year 12 exam exemptions spark debate on future of Queensland testing The year 12 student said her new school environment had not been a cure-all for the barriers she had faced in her previous traditional high school. “I still struggle to do schoolwork in the school environment, but at my last school, I would just give up ... now, I get all my assessments done,” she said. The BUSY School’s focus on rebuilding trust in education systems was echoed across the sector.



“I think when they see that we actually do support them, and then we follow through with those supports, they actually do feel a sense of safety that they potentially haven’t felt before,” said Ashleigh Maas, a teacher at Y Schools Queensland, another alternative education provider. Most schools offered wraparound student support, with teacher-student ratios typically falling below state standards, as many teachers were accompanied by a youth worker. Y Schools Queensland secondary teacher Ashleigh Maas. Catherine Strohfeldt Students are also supported by on-site counsellors and pathways officers, and many campuses offer free food to students, including breakfasts. At The BUSY School campuses, uniforms, classroom supplies and school-owned laptops are provided for free, and the school charges no fees to families.



A McCrindle report commissioned by industry body Independent Schools Queensland surveyed 410 families and 271 alumni from several dozen special assistance schools across the state. About 60 per cent said their school had an extremely or very positive index on either their wellbeing or that of their young person, which included impacts to their safety, relationships, and health. Among parents, 82 per cent said they also felt they were respected and understood by school staff. South Brisbane mother Sharni Welsh said teachers at Y Schools South Brisbane had spoken highly of her son, Levi, since he joined in term 2 this year.



“It’s nice to have other people see in Levi what I do,” she said. Y Schools Queensland year 8 student Levi Welsh. Catherine Strohfeldt The year 8 student said he had rekindled an interest in school, enjoying maths, English, science, and geography. World.title: Wānaka soon to be home to $180m alpine resort
World.content:
Work on a $180 million hotel and resort development in Wānaka is expected to begin next year.

The Mount Iron Wānaka development would include a 136-room Sudima hotel, 72 townhouses and apartments, shared swimming pools, landscaped gardens, dining and conference spaces.

It would be built on 1.8 hectares of land at the foot of Mount Iron and was expected to take four years to build.

Sudima Hotels and Hind Management founder and chief executive Sudesh Jhunjhnuwala said the hotel would bring much-needed amenities to the town.

"Wānaka has grown significantly but its hotel offering hasn't kept pace and we see a real gap in the market for a high-quality, full-service hotel," he said.

The development includes 39 three to four bedroom townhouses and 33 apartments priced from $1.4 million. Supplied / Mt Iron Developments Ltd

Despite its rapid growth, Wānaka has not had a new hotel of any significance since the 106-room Edgewater opened in 1986.

That growth has not been without teething issues with concerns about a shortage of housing and the cost of living as well as pressure on existing services including healthcare and wastewater.

The development was originally proposed in 2022 but was put on ice due to the economic downturn and changes in planning requirements.

The existing resource consent allowed construction to start but an amendment to the consent was also needed as the masterplan had been revised with more focus on creating an alpine resort.

KR Capital, which was part of engineering and design consultancy Kirk Roberts, came up with the project.

An aerial view of the planned $180 million Mount Iron Wānaka development, which includes a 136-room Sudima hotel and 72 residential properties. Supplied / Mt Iron Developments Ltd

Kirk Roberts chief executive Jade Kirk said a development of this scale created jobs, supported local businesses and added opportunities for hospitality, tourism and retail.

"We wanted to rethink the traditional resort model and create something genuinely different - bringing together residential living, tourism, hospitality, recreation, and health and well-being within one integrated destination," she said.

"As the region continues to grow, we see an opportunity to introduce something that complements its natural environment while contributing positively to its long-term economic future."

Audio player for " Quentin Smith discusses Wanaka's new $180m resort " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2548528%2Fwanaka-soon-to-be-home-to-180m-alpine-resort

Quentin Smith discusses Wanaka's new $180m resort Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Queenstown Lakes deputy mayor Quentin Smith said the new development was "the right thing in the right place".

"It'll probably represent the tallest building we have in Wānaka at this point in time, so it is a major thing, but it's also an area called Three Parks and it's not close to existing residents," he told Morning Report.

He said Wānaka was in need of a new hotel.

"We're in the tourist circuit and we get a lot of visitors here, and there hasn't been a lot of large scale accommodation," he said.

"One of the downsides of that is it means a lot of houses are rented out for accommodation. We want houses for residents and for locals."

Hind Management, which operated Sudima Hotels, would manage the hotel and residences.

Local Sotheby's International Realty agent Sheryl Alty said the development would bring a completely fresh offering to Wānaka.

"We see it appealing to buyers at different stages of life, from those seeking a holiday base to those making Wānaka their permanent home or planning their next chapter in retirement," she said.

"For buyers who divide their time between Wānaka and elsewhere, the option of managed rental arrangements adds another layer of appeal. It allows them to explore how personal use and rental accommodation could fit their ownership plans."

The planned hotel and plaza at Mount Iron Wānaka. Supplied / Mt Iron Developments Ltd

Earthworks were expected to start early next year with work on residential properties occurring later in the year, but timing would depend on the amended consent being granted.

The $300m privately-owned Wānaka Health Precinct was also under development about 700 metres away from the Mount Iron Wānaka resort.

World.title: 'No longer a remote threat': Law enforcers unite to tackle trans-Pacific drug smuggling
World.content:
Law enforcement decision-makers met in Nouméa last week in an attempt to better coordinate the fight against trans-Pacific drug smuggling, under the theme "Pacific United Against Drug Trafficking at Sea".

"Narco traffic is no longer just a remote threat for the Pacific. It is a reality that directly affects our maritime spaces, our territories and our population," French High Commissioner in New Caledonia Jacques Billant told the gathering on 5 and 6 November.

The audience included about 150 high officials from fifteen neighbouring countries, including Australia and New Zealand.

He said the two-day meeting did not aim to sign any regional treaty, but to initiate a more efficient cooperation between countries and territories in the region in terms of fighting against the transhipment of narcotics.

Law enforcement officers taking part in the Nouméa 'Pacific United Against Drug Trafficking at Sea' seminar. Consulat NZ en Nouvelle Calédonie, Polynésie française et Wallis & Futuna

Trans-Pacific highway'

The traffic volume has significantly risen over the past few years, on what is now dubbed a "Trans-Pacific highway", mainly from Central and South America (where the substances are produced) to the Western Pacific, mostly destination markets such as Australia and New Zealand.

Seventeen tonnes of drugs, mostly cocaine, were seized in the Pacific region during the first half of 2026.

"It's four times as much as 2025," Billant told the Pacific law enforcers, mainly police, army, customs, maritime forces and legal officers.

Some of these recent catches involved New Caledonia, as well as French Polynesia.

The New Zealand delegation included representatives from police, customs and the PACPOL Secretariat hosted in Wellington.

The New Zealand delegation at the Nouméa seminar. Consulat NZ en Nouvelle Calédonie, Polynésie française et Wallis & Futuna

Intelligence sharing

"We have exchanged and compared our methods, our challenges," Billant said.

The participants also exchanged intelligence on how drug traffickers were operating and constantly adapting to an ever-evolving regional criminal environment.

Once relying on transport via sailboats and commercial cargo ships, the delivery method for drugs is now shifting to the "drop-off" technique in coastal areas, where floating shipments, sometimes unmanned and equipped with GPS transmitters, are later recovered by smaller vessels.

In one of the latest finds, in late October 2026, one of these GPS-fitted floating packages was found by a fisherman in Wallis and Futuna.

In French Polynesia, a total of eight tonnes of cocaine was seized in January and February 2026.

Off New Caledonia's coastlines, in June 2025, 2.5 tonnes of cocaine were seized onboard a Peru-flagged vessel.

"What we have facing us is organised, mobile and patient. It would be a mistake to believe that just one country can address the issue on its own. If we don't do anything we are at risk of being affected more quickly than we think," Billant told local media.

"Drug industry is an economy. So a market is a market, this is business. These organisations have a phenomenal financial power," Nouméa-based public prosecutor Camille Miansoni said.

French Ambassador for the Pacific Véronique Roger-Lacan said: "Our objective is not to create yet another platform."

"We want to insert ourselves in the existing regional architecture, as reiterated at the latest Pacific Islands Forum Leaders' meeting in August in Palau," Roger-Lacan said.

She added a recently created "Pacific Academy" could contribute to the regional effort by training more Pacific security forces.

World.title: The Warehouse staff defecating in distribution centre aisles, union alleges
World.content:
More than 300 staff from The Warehouse's distribution centres in Auckland and Christchurch are striking on Thursday over fears that technology will take over their jobs.

Workers First Union claimed its members' bathroom breaks were being tracked by artificial intelligence, leading to instances of staff urinating and defecating in distribution aisles.

The Warehouse strongly denied these claims, and said it was shocked and appalled that they were being made.

Union organiser Hayley Courtney told RNZ she had been fighting the issue for eight months.

"Having supervisors and managers follow people to the toilet and telling them off for a fundamental right is absolutely ludicrous."

Drones used for stocktaking had been introduced to the distribution centres, which Courtney said had cut down the size of the physical inventory team.

She said workers were striking for employment security, seeking assurances in contracts that they could not be easily replaced when technology arrived.

Ratifying an employment agreement without achieving any protection over future employment "would be like signing their own death warrant", she said.

Hayley Courtney is a First Union organiser. RNZ / Blessen Tom

The Warehouse Group people officer Richard Parker said he was "shocked and appalled by the union's claim that our team members are urinating and defecating on the floor at work".

"This has never happened."

Parker said bathroom use was not tracked, and this was made very clear to teams.

"We use technology, which is not AI as claimed, that has been commonly used in distribution centres around the world for decades to monitor efficiency through scanning devices. It has nothing to do with bathroom use."

He said there had been no job losses as a result of introducing stocktaking drones at distribution centres.

"In fact, we currently have three additional temp roles in this area. The drones improve stock accuracy and the customer experience, while making our distribution centres safer by removing the need for people to work at height in machinery every night."

He said no employer could guarantee what roles would look like in the future, but that they would consult, retrain, and redeploy people where they could.

"The new automation is designed to increase capacity and efficiency, and our team are doing an excellent job learning new skills and working with new technology."

World.title: 'No future here for them': Cafe owner despairs for Kaitāia's young people
World.content:
Audio player for " Maryjane Manukau on life in a struggling Kaitaia " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2550395%2Fno-future-here-for-them-cafe-owner-despairs-for-kaitaia-s-young-people

Maryjane Manukau on life in a struggling Kaitaia Morning Report Download MP3 8m

Many people in Kaitāia can barely afford food and the probable closure of the Triboard Mill is set to worsen the town's plight, business owner Maryjane Manukau says.

Efforts to save almost 160 jobs at the town's only remaining timber mill appear to have failed.

The Far North town's Triboard Mill, which is owned by Japanese forestry company Juken New Zealand, has been on the market since March.

However, the company said this week it had been unable to find a buyer willing to take on the current workers.

The news comes just a week after new labour force data showed Northland's unemployment rate was the highest in the country at 8.3 percent.

The unemployment rate among 15 to 24-year-olds is 25 percent.

Maryjane Manukau and her husband own MJ'z Seafood & Whānau Kai in Kaitāia.

Their business is on the main street and the owners are well known for their kindness along with their hangi, seafood chowder, paua pies, and mussel burgers.

She told Morning Report when she returned to Kaitāia recently from Auckland she was dismayed to see how much poverty had spread in the community.

The town had been struggling for a while with a lot of unemployment and people finding it hard to pay for basics like food.

She was seeing people looking through rubbish bins or begging and that "was massive for me".

"I see more and more young people walking the streets these days. A lot aren't going to school.

"The future here in Kaitāia for our young people is not very good ...There is no future here for them."

Manukau said 15-year-olds were asking her for jobs and she tells them they should be at school.

She said while she couldn't provide them with jobs, she would bring them in and teach them basic skills such as using a coffee machine and getting "used to being around people".

She was seeing more people unable to afford to come in for a cup of coffee or other customers might spend several hours in her cafe and spend as little as $5.

"I end up having my building quite full because I allow them to sit here forever and a day.

"I do what I do. A lot of elderly come in and it's a catchup time for them and I'll do something on the sidelines, take them out a plate of scones no charge, just feed them up."

Some people also weren't on mains water which meant buying it at a cost of $700 for half a tank.

"That's a big cost and we're not even in summer yet."

The Triboard Mill RNZ / Peter de Graaf

As for the mill, Juken NZ executive director Yasufumi Tsuchiya said negotiations to sell the land, buildings and machinery were continuing with a potential buyer, who could restart the mill in future with a new workforce.

If the sale fell through the mill would be closed down and efforts to sell the land and assets would continue.

Either way, the company would stop operating the mill by March next year at the latest.

Northland MP Grant McCallum told Midday Report he was still hopeful a buyer would be found for the land and buildings, who would then restart the mill.

Permanent closure would be "a disaster" for the town, he said.

World.title: RNZ's unlawful overdraft was signed off by the board
World.content:
RNZ has confirmed its request for a $5m overdraft, which breached the Crown Entities Act, was signed off by the board.

The public broadcaster on Monday revealed a shock $12 million budget blowout, after a litany of financial blunders.

CEO Paul Thompson took responsibility for the result and said internal reports gave an inaccurate picture of the finances, meaning the scale of the loss only became clear in October.

RNZ CEO Paul Thompson VNP / Phil Smith

While carrying out the broadcaster's annual audit, EY identified a breach of the Crown Entities Act - emphasising it in RNZ's annual report.

"We draw your attention to Note 12 on page 32 about the Group not complying with sections 160 and 162 of the Crown Entities Act 2004, in that the Group entered into a financing arrangement without the authority of the Minister for Media and Communications and the Minister of Finance."

The breach concerned a $5m overdraft that was set up without ministerial approval.

RNZ said the $5m overdraft was initiated to provide RNZ with a safety net in the event one of its land sales was delayed, so the company could manage significant one off costs, but was never used.

By law, RNZ needs sign-off from two ministers to borrow money, which it last received in 2006 for up to $3.5m.

On Checkpoint, RNZ board chair Brent Impey accepted the organisation had broken the law.

"Now, how did that happen? That's very difficult to explain. That there was a loan with Westpac and again, the Crown Entities Act was breached."

A RNZ spokesperson said the board approved a temporary $5m overdraft facility on 9 June, 2026.

Former RNZ chief financial office Hilary Parker LinkedIn

The former chief financial officer, Hilary Parker - who resigned unexpectedly in early October - initiated setting up the overdraft, which RNZ's executive took to the board, the spokesperson said.

Public law expert and barrister Mai Chen said the fact that ministerial approval wasn't obtained raises questions.

"You've got people in highly paid positions who don't seem to understand that they're a Crown entity, they're subject to the Crown Entities Act," she said.

"Why did they do it without going through the right process?"

Chen said it was concerning that the board appeared to be unaware of the breach and more broadly in the dark about RNZ's financial position.

A RNZ spokesperson said the $5m overdraft was set up to provide RNZ with a safety net in the event one of its land sales was delayed, "while the company also managed a significant number of one-off costs".

They noted the overdraft was undrawn as at 30 June 2026.

Asked if RNZ management was aware of its obligations under the Crown Entities Act, RNZ pointed to section 160 of the Act - that outlines the need for ministerial sign-off - in its borrowing policy.

They said no internal or external legal advice was sought prior to entering into the overdraft.

"The independent review will establish what happened and why," the spokesperson said.

A Westpac spokesperson said the bank didn't comment on specific customers' banking details.

World.title: Papua Nw Guinea's  Violet Apisah to compete for a spot at Australian Open
World.content:
Papua New Guinean tennis player Violet Apisah has been given a wildcard entry into a qualifying tournament for the Australian Open.

PNG Tennis said she will play in the main draw of the Asia-Pacific Australian Open Wildcard Playoff from 23-28 November.

The winner of that tournament, held in Chengdu, China, gets direct entry into the main draw of the 2027 Australian Open, the first Grand Slam of the year held in Melbourne in January.

"Violet will have the opportunity to compete against some of the best players in the Asian region, including girls ranked inside the world's top 200, all battling for that coveted Australian Open spot in January 2027," the association said.

The tennis organisation said Violet Apisah has reached number 992 on the WTA rankings, and she achieved this after only a couple of tournaments.

In 2018, her aunty Abigail Tere-Apisah narrowly missed the chance to become the first Papua New Guinean to reach a Grand Slam main draw.

PNG tennis coach Coach Abigail Tere-Apisah at the Regional Coaches Conference in Hong Kong. Papua New Guinea Tennis Association Facebook

Tere-Apisah competed on the International Tennis Federation lower-tier women's circuit, and reached a career-high WTA (Women's Tennis Association) world ranking inside the world's top 300.

She also won multiple gold medals representing Papua New Guinea at the Pacific Games.

World.title: Winegrowers pulling out vineyards due to global oversupply of wine
World.content:
Hundreds of hectares of vineyards are being pulled out across the country as the industry reacts to a global over supply of wine.

The New Zealand Winegrowers Association estimates about 2000 hectares of grapes have been uprooted, so by 2027 the total planted area of vineyards would be down three percent to 42,357 hectares.

A combination of several years of large vintages and falling alcohol consumption had contributed to a reduced demand for wine that'd seen a flurry of larger wine companies exiting the industry.

The worst hit region in New Zealand was Gisborne, where Indevin Group had halted supply contracts with its growers.

Ed Massey from the New Zealand Winegrowers Association told RNZ that'd resulted in 46 percent of the region's vineyards being ripped out.

"From 1138 hectares down to 614. That's a substantial change and we recognise the concern for growers and the wider community in that region.

"It's tied to that general reduction in demand for Sauvignon Blanc from regions that have traditionally supplied Marlborough," he said.

He said Hawke's Bay had also lost 9 percent of its vineyards, while Nelson was down 7 percent.

Hawke's Bay winemaker Leith Ashworth owned a boutique organic vineyard in Bridge Pa called Ash Ridge, and was seeing vines being removed all around him.

"It costs money to run a vineyard and if you're not able to sell the grapes, then the next best thing is basically to pull the vineyard out.

"I'm not sure what the numbers in Hawke's Bay are, but I guess it's well over 500 hectares. I've had 35 hectares just on my boundary removed in the last year. And at this stage I can't see it being replanted as a vineyard," he said.

He's hoping smaller wine producers would be more resilient to what the bigger companies had gone through.

"I'm being optimistic that we'll see a swing the other way quite fast. But whether it's two years away or five years away, it's pretty hard to predict.

"The way the industry's been changing so, so fast ... and trying to predict what people want, it's pretty hard at the moment. People seem to swing wine trends pretty regularly," said Ashworth.

Viticulturist Ryan Fraser has pulled out five hectares of merlot at Paritua Vineyard in Hawke's Bay. Supplied

That's something that viticulturist Ryan Fraser was trying to work out too. He's the vineyard manager for Paritua near Hastings and was pulling out a five hectare block of merlot vines.

"Constellation, they were a big buyer of Merlot for rosé and they've gone, they've sold to Poulter Group because they can get a cheaper rosé out of Europe, which is closer to the market at a better price point.

"It's left a lot of contract growers who supplied that rosé for a very long time and are sort of forced to change now or find a new home for all that Merlot. That's probably one of the bigger changes that's happened in Hawke's Bay," said Fraser.

He said many winegrowers were hitting pause while they figured out their next move.

"It's the apprehension of where people are going to land. You know, people aren't necessarily putting a whole bunch of plants in the ground at the moment because they don't know where the markets are that are going to stabilise," said Fraser.

But depsite all the uncertainty out there, the Winegrowers Association was feeling optimistic.

"The world wants sustainably produced premium wine that New Zealand produces, those lighter, fresher varieties, championed by Sauvignon Blanc, but others as well.

"I think we are in a good position to continue to grow the industry," said Massey.

World.title: Swimming embraces short and sharp with new Swim GP competition
World.content:
No sport is immune from a fight for relevance in a jam-packed sporting marketplace.

And Swim GP is Swimming Australia's latest attempt to blend sporting entertainment, just 12 months on from its last foray into the genre, Australia vs The World in Brisbane.

This year, the nation is keeping things in-house with a slightly tweaked format involving teams of domestic swimmers.

"I think it's a really exciting opportunity," three-time Commonwealth Games champion Jenna Forrester told ABC Sport.

"I wasn't actually at Aus vs The World last year, so this is going to be my first time doing an event like this.

"But I got to watch some of it on TV and I thought that it was a really cool concept."

Swimming's revolution begins with pumping night at The Valley Swimming stepped out of its tried and trusted format in a novelty, multi-event competition in Brisbane on Friday night.

A cool concept but not an unfamiliar one.

Swimming has toyed with events like this for more than 30 years, since the Qantas Skins events in the mid-1990s.

Before COVID, the International Swimming League (ISL) came in to shake up the perceived monotony of conventional competition and act as a vehicle to keep interest in the sport high between Olympics.

The league has not been seen since 2021, partially as a result of COVID, partially due to the Russia-Ukraine war. The ISL's principal backer is Ukrainian businessman Konstantin Grigorishin.

However, later this year, the ISL will return with a one-off All-Star Match at the London Aquatics Centre on December 19.

The International Swimming League (ISL) took place before COVID. (Getty Images: Catherine Ivill)

That is despite there being legal issues between World Aquatics and the ISL: World Aquatics settled with a group of 263 swimmers in September 2025, who said they were denied a chance to compete, and therefore earn money, in ISL competitions.

World Aquatics paid those swimmers a combined $US4.6 million, and allowed them to participate in independent competitions such as the ISL without losing their ability to compete in the Olympics.

There is also a separate, ongoing lawsuit between the ISL and World Aquatics.

The ISL also played a role in forming the College Swimming League (CSL) in the USA, which had its first competitions in September.

The league brings together 12 programs from three of the biggest NCAA conferences: the SEC, ACC and Big Ten.

The ISL aimed to give international swimmers more visibility, and hopes to do the same for college swimmers with the CSL. (Getty Images: Catherine Ivill)

The league featured multiples, four-team competitions, with 30 events at each competition. That includes Skins events and a "jackpot" scoring rule.

Chief executive Rob Kent told Reuters the league was designed for a TV audience and for each meet to last a TV-friendly two and a half hours.

TV-friendly is exactly what Swim GP is going for too.

"I think it's just going to be a year-by-year thing that will just keep getting better and better as the event progresses," Forrester said.

"It is really exciting and it definitely is a bit different to what we're used to."

Skins matches, multi-round elimination races, play a big role in Swim GP, as do mystery relays and power plays, much in the same way they did in Brisbane last year.

It will also provide high-intensity race prep for swimmers outside of the major championships.

"It's a really exciting opportunity, and short course as well, so it'll be short and fast," Forrester said.

Jenna Forrester's versatility was instrumental in her early selection. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"It'll be good race practice and good race practice in coming together as a team, because that's something that's really important in swimming.

"It is an individual sport, but when we go away on the Australian team we really focus on the culture and bringing that Australian spirit.

"I think this will be kind of a good practice into turning swimming into more of a team sport."

At Swim GP, Australia's best and brightest able-bodied and para swimmers have been split into four teams: Team Kraken, Wahoo, KingTide and Tsunami.

Each team has platinum athletes as their headliners: KingTide has Flynn Southam and Lani Pallister; Kraken selected Kyle Chalmers and Mollie O’Callaghan; Wahoo had Meg Harris and Sam Short; Tsunami went with Kaylee McKeown and William Petric.

The first overall pick went to Wahoo, who selected sprint specialist Ben Armbruster.

Ben Armbruster is a versatile sprinter. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Armbruster is as versatile a sprinter as they come.

The 24-year-old won Commonwealth and Pan Pac gold in the 50-metres butterfly, having reached the semifinals of the 50m freestyle at the Paris Olympics and the final of the 50m backstroke at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham.

Mel Marshall used her first pick, second overall, to select Forrester for KingTide.

"To be second pick, that was kind of crazy to be honest," Forrester said.

"I'm curious to see what events they have because I feel like a lot of it will be kind of sprint events. I'm interested to see how I go trying to do some of those.

"It really just shows that I've had a pretty good year, I guess.

"Maybe that hasn't really settled in for me yet, maybe some other people are seeing it before I am."

World.title: Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows
World.content:
AFLW sides are more likely to finish down the bottom of the ladder when their players rate their workplace culture low, the players' association says.

Data collected from the union around the middle of the season suggests a strong correlation between workplace culture and on-field performance.

"If we look at AFLW, what we're seeing is there is a bit of a widening gap between the best of our workplace culture data and that which is more at the bottom," AFL Players Association chief executive James Gallagher told ABC Sport.

"We're seeing some of the highest scores ever reported at the top end, so that's fantastic. That's what we want to see, but we are seeing a gap between the best and the bottom end."

Collingwood's woeful AFLW season Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has criticised the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

This year, four teams were assessed as having the best workplace culture on record and four teams the worst.

This was evaluated according to club care, mental breaks, off-field expectations, relationships, schedule flexibility and study/work support.

Five of this year's finals teams were in the top seven for "overall workplace culture". Non-finalist teams overwhelmingly rated on the lower end for workplace culture scores.

It comes after widespread media scrutiny on struggling clubs, particularly Collingwood.

James Gallagher says there is a correlation between successful AFLW sides and workplace culture ratings. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

The Magpies, along with St Kilda, finished with one win each this season, while GWS and Essendon had just two victories out of their 12 games.

Of those four bottom-ladder clubs, all but the Giants parted ways with their head coaches.

The Magpies and Saints are now set to undertake external reviews of their women's programs,. Essendon has opted to conduct an expanded internal review.

North Melbourne, Geelong, Melbourne, Carlton, Gold Coast, Sydney, Western Bulldogs and Hawthorn finished in the top eight this year.

Sydney and the Western Bulldogs featured in the finals series this year. (Getty: Darrian Traynor)

The Kangaroos have lost one game in three years and the Demons have regularly finished in the finals.

The data also showed some players as having rated respect for the men's AFL club head of performance and head coach as low to extremely low.

Furthermore, men's players being embroiled in off-field news, such as the Sydney Swans saga involving allegations of sexual assault or GWS' "controversial couples" night leading to player sanctions, can impact the women's programs.

"There's no doubt they are extraordinarily challenging for all to navigate. I mean, do they have an impact on AFLW playing groups? In some cases, they do for sure," Mr Gallagher said.

"Making sure there's an opportunity for those players' views to be heard and considered is a really important part of how footy clubs in 2026 now operate."

Pies launch AFLW review As a tough season nears its end, Collingwood announces a strategic review into the struggling AFLW program, with the club's president admitting the Pies had not "got it right".

Crucially, with the seasons overlapping more every year, men's and women's programs require access to the same facilities, including the gym and communal areas.

Just half of all players said they felt their men's and women's programs were aligned.

"Those clubs that report the strongest workplace environments are much more likely to be successful, and that's reflected in the final series in front of us," Mr Gallagher said.

"The game is a high-performance game and to enable that to be successful you do need people who are fronting up, comfortable, confident, feeling like they're really well supported, and we're seeing that reflected in the wins and losses column now, for sure."

Women's teams with strong workplace culture are more likely to make the finals, according to the AFLPA. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

Workplace culture includes club support for players outside football commitments, including work and study.

While players have seen huge strides in increased contact hours since season one, more than half of all players still work outside football.

Sixty-four per cent engage in casual work, 32 per cent work part-time and 4 per cent full-time. None of the 45 Irish players can work due to their visas.

The players' association expects next year's AFLW season to accommodate more double-headers. The start date is yet to be announced.

World.title: The rebuild is on as Labuschagne makes shaky return to Shield cricket
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne's return to first-class cricket following his axing from the Test team lasted 36 balls for Queensland in the Sheffield Shield on Wednesday.

Labuschagne made 12 runs before nicking off to Tasmania's Jake Doran off the bowling of Riley Meredith.

The 32-year-old's dismissal looked similar to so many of his recent failings at Test level, prodding on fourth stump without a hint of foot movement.

Ordinarily Sheffield Shield games retain some semblance of importance for Test players searching for form ahead of The Summer of Cricket.

Uniquely for Queensland's captain, this match means nothing — at least in the short-term.

He's already been flung on the Test scrap heap, a dire run of form eventually hastening his demise from an Australian Test team that crushed England in last year's Ashes, but has won just two of its last five Tests against Bangladesh and South Africa, without claiming a series victory.

Spectators didn't mind that though, and more than a handful had turned out to show support to their beleaguered skipper.

Those who arrived on time had to wait an hour and 20 minutes before Labuschagne came to the crease after Angus Lovell (18 off 60 balls) edged Beau Webster into the slips. The opener furiously smacked his bat after doing so much of the hard work on a pitch that offered plenty of zip.

Labuschagne's arrival was greeted with warm applause, the clapping briefly drowning out the incessant jackhammering of the building sites around the Gabba.

"Come on Marnus," one punter among the hundred or so faithful called out as he took his mark.

Marnus Labuschagne lasted 36 balls in his first return to the crease since South Africa. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Labuschagne wasted no time in getting into the thick of the action, crushing a square drive for four off the very first ball he faced from former Test teammate Webster.

A streaky edge past third slip off the bowling of Jackson Bird though, reiterated that Labuschagne's rebuild could be a process as drawn out as the redevelopment around the ground.

As good as his opening salvo was, the idiosyncrasies that all too often verged towards idiocies during his faltering stays in the middle during Test matches, were still there.

There was a wave of his hands here, a period of shadow-batting there that were as prevalent at the Gabba as they were in Gqeberha, where he scored 14 and 39 in Australia's innings defeat.

As Bell got closer to the off-stump, Labuschagne's leaves became ever more flamboyant, a batting matador daring the bull to crash into his stumps.

He lasted until lunch, walking off with eight runs to his name.

His demise came soon after the break when edged a delivery he didn't need to play at into the gloves of the keeper.

Labuschagne waited a moment at the crease, miffed at his dismissal, before trudging off.

Fortunately for him, it was far from a bumper day of scores around the country.

Sam Konstas scored 24 and Kurtis Patterson a duck for New South Wales as they were bundled out for 204 against South Australia, while Marcus Harris managed just 15 on an MCG pitch that looked good for batting, given Peter Handscomb's century for Victoria.

It is far too soon after his return from South Africa to rectify any wrongs in his technique or banish the demons residing within his head.

As much as the hammering taking place outside the Gabba, the work to build Labuschagne back into a principle Test batter will take time.

World.title: How a small scrap of sandpaper shed light on cricket's so-called dark arts
World.content:
Eight years after then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull felt the need to weigh in on Australia's ball tampering in the Cape Town Test, sandpaper and cricket are back in the headlines together.

Usman Khawaja's book, featuring revelations, allusions and confirmations of what most everyone already believed, has reignited conversations about the Australian team's conduct during that 2018 tour of South Africa.

But whatever the team did, who did it and who knew about it, one thing is for sure: they weren't the first to fiddle with the ball.

So why did they do it and why was the reaction so extreme?

'A beautiful art'

Reverse swing can make even the best batters look silly. (Getty Images: Tom Shaw)

In the wake of Khawaja's exclusive interview with Nine Newspapers on the weekend, outspoken former Australia fast bowler Geoff Lawson added to the conversation with a brilliantly headlined article.

" I don't know a bowler who hasn't licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball. "

Thanks for those mental images, Geoff.

Evocative wording or not, the 46-Test veteran is right. But why?

Explaining the mysteries of swing bowling It is one of the most devastating weapons a fast bowler can own — but the art of swing is steeped in mystery and myths that only science can explain.

The science of conventionally swinging a cricket ball through the air is relatively simple and adheres to some basic rules of drag, air pressure and laminar flow (a lot of the same stuff that keeps an aeroplane in the air).

When a cricket ball is new, its stitched seam is standing at its tallest, allowing a bowler to angle that seam towards or away from the batter and the air will get caught on the seam, dragging the ball in that direction.

But the proud seam on a dark red ball is clearly visible to a batter, and the best ones can see what's happening and account for it.

Reverse swing is a little more complicated and prized due to it being more difficult to deliver, predict and face.

Conventional swing (left) vs reverse swing (right). (ABC News: Gabrielle Flood and Nina Maile Gordon)

"As a batter it's the hardest thing to face. It's a beautiful art," former Proteas captain Faf du Plessis told The Grade Cricketer podcast on the eve of Australia's return to Cape Town last month.

The ball swings towards the side of the ball that looks smoother due to small abrasions on that "shiny" side of the ball, more of which is facing the batter and therefore offering more surface area and turbulent airflow, this time dragging the ball in the opposite direction to the way the seam is facing.

It also happens later in the ball's flight, often too late for the batter to react.

It only comes after the ball has been bowled for a few dozen overs and whacked around the field a bit; once the seam has flattened out, and the leather has been, crucially, roughed up and dried out.

Weather conditions have to be perfect, the bowlers have to be incredibly skilled and the care for the ball has to be spot-on, to the point that former England captain Alastair Cook was prized as a ball shiner because he barely sweats.

Of course, there are other ways to help this along.

Spit, sunscreen and swing

There are plenty of legal ways to shine the ball. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Once a cricket pitch has flattened out from the start of a game, the new ball has lost its shine and proud seam, and before it becomes a spinner's paradise on days four and five (although this is becoming more and more rare), reverse swing is one of the few tools in fast bowler's arsenal.

For decades, cricket teams have worked on the ball feverishly to try to work on conventional and reverse swing.

Often players will shine the ball on their groin or hip, or some sweat from their forehead (or spit in pre-COVID times).

In those processes, there are some grey areas.

Any sensible cricketer will be wearing sunscreen, some will be wearing hair products, many will be chewing gum or chomping on a lolly.

Sweat can be used to shine the ball but keeping it dry is key to reverse swing. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

All of that gives a little extra viscosity to the sweat or saliva used on the ball, but match referees couldn't very well force players to spit their gum into a hanky on the boundary line or force them to have a shower before entering the field of play, so there is not much they can do.

Then there's the flip side, where players try to create a rougher surface to generate that turbulent airflow, which can include simple things like picking at the seam of a ball or fielders intentionally throwing the ball in short to ensure it bounces on the coarse pitch block.

Ironically enough, du Plessis, South Africa's captain on that fateful 2018 tour, twice stumbled from lightish grey into gun-metal territory earlier in his career.

In 2013, after a failed attempt with his fingernails, du Plessis was caught on camera blatantly scratching the ball on the zip of his pants pocket, mere centimetres from legal territory.

Teams work hard on the ball to create the conditions for conventional and reverse swing bowling. (Getty Images: Santanu Banik/MB Media)

A few years later, as he skippered the team during a 2016 tour of Australia, he was again seen on the field opening his mouth, touching his fingers to a massive white mint on the middle of his tongue, then applying that sugary saliva directly to the ball.

Had he simply sucked the mint, popped it into his cheek and then touched his tongue, he could have avoided his own chase through the airport and a hefty fine.

Du Plessis described the fallout from his 2013 zipper incident as "a week of hell", so it's no wonder he expressed so much sympathy for Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith (curiously no mention of David Warner) as the world closed in on them.

After massive bans and public disgrace, you would think the world would have moved on, but between the long-awaited Test return to South Africa and now Khawaja's book, the controversy seems never-ending.

Why the sandpaper saga?

One part absolutely boils to down to Australian cricket's sense of exceptionalism and perception of itself as arbiter of what is and isn't acceptable on a cricket field.

But the brazen nature of the ball tampering is perhaps the biggest reason that this was and remains such a big story.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

England skipper Michael Atherton was caught rubbing dirt into the ball and his reputation remains pristine but, like the various fructose or lotion-enhanced bodily fluids, that's the sort of thing one could use on the ball opportunistically or even inadvertently.

Perhaps that's why Bancroft's first feeble attempt at deflection was claiming he "saw an opportunity to potentially use some tape [and] get some granules from the rough patches on the wicket", rather than bringing some 300 grit onto the field where its only purpose could be ball tampering.

There are legendary tales of bottle caps being used to help out reverse swing kings like Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis in Test matches way back when, and Khawaja wrote about some of the methods he had seen or heard of in Sheffield Shield cricket.

But in a high-profile Test series, to be so obvious when the team knew they already had heat on them betrayed a sense that they thought they were untouchable or that winning was worth the risk.

Alas, the SuperSport cameras caught him in high definition and super slow-mo and put the so-called dark arts very much under a spotlight.

After du Plessis's minty moment, Dirk Nannes said in commentary at the time for ABC Sport: "It's an art and some of the art is doing it and not getting caught."

If that is the case, consider Cameron Bancroft less Gauguin and more Gallagher.

World.title: ACL battles haven't halted these AFL draft hopefuls
World.content:
In just the second game of this year's footy season, Gus White did not realise he had suffered an ACL injury when he hurt his knee.

"I landed a bit funny and hyperextended my knee … it didn't hurt that bad," he said.

" I went and got scans a couple of days later, the result came back with the ACL, which was really devastating. "

The 18-year-old is one of many teenage footballers vying for a chance in the AFL draft later this month — and is hopeful he will be in contention, despite only playing one full game of football this year.

"I'm obviously really nervous, not having much control over my playing this year," he said.

For months, White has been firmly focused on recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said he initially sat in the emotions of the injury but quickly shifted his focus.

"I just gave myself 24 to 48 hours to sit in my thoughts and really feel it and from then move on and accept that it's happened," he said.

" 'Control the controllables' was the main goal — and [to] just stay as positive as I could. "

The South Adelaide product just hit the six-month milestone of recovery, a significant halfway mark of an injury that sidelines most players for about a year.

'Every journey's different'

When the injury first happened, White spoke to someone who had trodden the same path a year earlier.

North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL last year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

It was round 2 of the 2025 SANFL season when North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL.

"The 12 months was long, but I made strategies and figured out ways to get through it," he said.

Webb decided to step away from football for the year as he recovered.

"I learnt a lot about myself, because before that my life had pretty much just been football," he said.

" Obviously it wasn't great not playing footy for a year, but it was almost a blessing as well. "

Webb stepped away from football for a year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The 18-year-old said the recovery process had given him a lot of time to reflect, and had reignited his love for football when finally returned to playing in round 4 this year.

"I was like a little kid again, playing footy for the first time," Webb said.

The midfielder said he was at the match, but not yet back playing, when White did his ACL against North Adelaide in round 2.

"We had a good chat about things to expect for him — I just said, 'Every journey's different, don't try and compare to other people'," he said.

Webb returned to the field earlier this year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said Webb was one of the first people he went to about his injury.

"I asked him how he dealt with things and what worked for him, what didn't," White said.

White, who is also a midfielder, said seeing someone else experience the same injury and return to the field after such a hard time was motivating.

"It sort of opens that light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

White says discussion with Webb helped boost confidence in recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

'Dream to play AFL footy'

White was invited to the AFL Draft Combine, where top junior prospects undergo physical testing and interviews, but was unable to be involved.

He was hopeful his junior years of footy had been enough to show prospective AFL clubs what he could achieve.

"Ever since I was four years old, it's been the dream to play AFL footy, so if my name were to be called out on draft night, I'll be over the moon," he said.

Webb is prepared for all eventualities. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Webb was also invited to the national combine but instead featured at the state event due to sickness.

While feeling nervous ahead of the draft, he was grateful for the experience so far.

"Not many people my age get to experience this journey that I've been on," he said.

" I'm just looking forward to it, whatever happens will happen. "

The AFL draft will be held over two nights on November 19 and 20.

World.title: Minjee Lee set to end horror 2026 season with Tour Championship absence
World.content:
Minjee Lee will miss the LPGA's rich and prestigious Tour Championship for the first time in more than a decade after calling an end to her deflating 2026 season.

Australia's triple major champion has opted out of The ANNIKA, the all-important penultimate event of the year starting on Thursday, rendering Lee no chance of scraping into next week's $US11 million ($16 million) showpiece in Florida.

Lee hasn't missed the season-ending championship since 2014.

But after slumping from third in the world rankings last October to 24th, her equal-lowest standing in 11 years, the WA superstar has opted for a reset following her last-place finish at the Japan Classic on Sunday.

Battling swing issues, the 30-year-old has slumped to 79th in the season-long point standings, with only the top 60 to qualify for the Tour Championship in Naples from November 19-22.

The 11-times LPGA Tour winner tied for 13th last year, with her best result in the event being a share of seventh on debut as a teenager in 2015.

While Lee will be absent this week, four Australians will be striving to punch their tickets to the Tour Championship at Pelican Golf Club in Belleair.

Perched safely in 11th place in the points race, Hannah Green is also sitting out The ANNIKA tournament.

But Cassie Porter (47th), Grace Kim (51st), Karis Davidson (54th) and Robyn Choi (61st) are all teeing it up.

Currently one spot outside the qualification zone, Choi likely needs a top-30 finish to clinch a maiden berth at the Tour Championship after enjoying a fruitful Asian swing.

Having become the first woman ever to clinch player-of-the-year honours before the Tour Championship, world No.1 Nelly Korda is chasing more history this week.

The American can become the first LPGA professional to win the same event for the fourth time since The ANNIKA tournament namesake Annika Sorenstam in 2005.

Korda also has a chance to become the fifth player in LPGA Tour history to win the same tournament at least four times and the first since Se Ri Pak at the Jamie Farr Kroger Classic in 2003.

AAP

World.title: Warner jabs former Australian coach Lehmann over Sandpapergate sanctions
World.content:
David Warner has fired an indirect jab at Darren Lehmann, suggesting the ex-Australian coach knew of the use of sandpaper in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Warner agreed with former International Cricket Council match referee Chris Broad, who said that Lehmann must have known of Australia's use of sandpaper on the ball, and if he did not, then he should not have been coach.

"Darren Lehmann surely knew all about it," Broad told Track Radio.

"And if he didn't, he shouldn't have been the coach at the time.

"He has got away lightly because he, OK, he left his job a few months later, but he didn't get any sanctions."

Warner replied to Track Radio's social media post of Broad's comments, writing on X: "I couldn't agree more and that's hard for me to say!"

Lehmann, who stepped down as Australia's coach in the aftermath of the 2018 scandal in South Africa, has denied personal knowledge of the Test team using sandpaper on the ball.

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann, who will co-host the ABC's cricket podcast this season, told Summer Grandstand on the weekend.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case-by-case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

Loading...

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Lehmann's comments are at odds with Usman Khawaja's claims the whole team knew of the sandpaper plans, and the illegal tactic was also used in the match prior to being uncovered by television cameras at the infamous 2018 Test in Cape Town.

Cricket Australia (CA) has ruled out reopening its investigation into the scandal.

Warner on Monday night backed Khawaja's claims, labelling CA's investigation as "rushed and botched" after it found only he, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith knew of the plan.

CA banned Smith and Warner from playing any cricket for one year and also suspended Bancroft for nine months. Smith and Warner were also stripped of their respective captain and vice-captain roles.

Paceman Mitchell Starc repeated his denial of the sandpaper plot when he became the first player from the match to front media, citing a statement he and his fellow bowlers made in 2021.

Usman Khawaja's (left) claims that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper has been backed by David Warner (second from left), denied by Darren Lehmann (right), while Steve Smith (second from right) is yet to comment. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"We [bowlers] weren't aware anything was taken on to the field to be tampered with," Starc said on Tuesday.

"We saw [the sandpaper] on the big screen in Cape Town."

Asked why he and Khawaja had differing views, Starc responded: "That's a question for him."

"I'll stick to what I said … at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people."

Australian Cricketers Association chief executive Paul Marsh said on Tuesday it was understandable players' versions of events could differ.

Loading...

"Players and staff at the heart of the issue are entitled to share their experiences, just as others are entitled to put such a challenging period in their life behind them," Marsh said in a statement.

"There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened.

"But we must recognise that there are humans in the centre of this and we are calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

Marsh's statement attracted the ire of former Test batsman Damien Martyn, who posted on X: "This statement from our players union does not reflect all ex players' opinions."

Meanwhile, the author of a review into Australia's cricket culture said he may have been lied to by players.

Simon Longstaff led an Ethics Centre team tasked with examining the sport's culture, but not the sandpaper scandal itself.

"Those matters had been investigated by Cricket Australia, and the findings were concluded," Longstaff wrote in the Australian Financial Review on Wednesday.

"Even so, we picked up whispers — few and very faint — that, perhaps, the public record did not tell the full story.

"All I can say is that if what Khawaja alleges turns out to be true, then I was also lied to.

"It is easy enough to understand how a group of players might perpetuate — either by act or omission — what could turn out to be a lie."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Usman Khawaja makes changes to book tour after tense 7.30 interview
World.content:
Usman Khawaja's publisher Penguin has confirmed that "adjustments" have been made to his book tour following a tense TV interview.

Khawaja's book, Sabr, released on Tuesday, contains an entire chapter titled "Sandpaper" dedicated to Australia's infamous 2018 tour of South Africa, which resulted in Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft being suspended for ball-tampering.

The 37-year-old appeared uncomfortable during an appearance on the ABC's 7.30 on Tuesday night, when he dodged questions from host Sarah Ferguson about the aforementioned chapter.

Khawaja denies starting 'witch-hunt' over Sandpapergate claims Usman Khawaja rejects claims he has reopened some of Australian crickets biggest wounds just to sell copies of his new book as he admits concerns it may have damaged friendships.

In a written statement to ABC Sport, Penguin pushed back on reports suggesting Khawaja's book tour had been cancelled altogether.

The publisher would not confirm what specific interviews had been cancelled, but that "adjustments" had been made.

"The book tour is 100 [per cent] still going ahead, we've just had to make some adjustments this week but no major cancellation of the tour at all," the statement read.

Penguin also confirmed Khawaja will be doing further interviews regarding his new book.

In the 7.30 interview, Khawaja was adamant that he did not want a "witch-hunt" to take place as a result of his claim that the entire Australian team was aware of the plan to tamper with the ball against South Africa.

Khawaja's account has been backed by Warner, who described it as being "100 per cent accurate" in his own statement on Monday night.

Bancroft refused to speak in depth on Khawaja's claims in a short interview with reporters as he arrived at Melbourne Airport prior to a Sheffield Shield clash between Western Australia and Victoria at the MCG this week, while Smith is yet to speak publicly regarding the new book.

Australian paceman Mitchell Starc denied suggestions the bowlers were in on the sandpaper ploy in a media appearance on Tuesday afternoon.

Tech.title: Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
Tech.content:
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.

“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”

Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:

A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.

A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”

Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.

Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.

Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.

Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.

Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.

Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.

The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”

Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.

“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”

Tech.title: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, “Scion by Toyota” is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator — and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana.

Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan’s light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported into the US since 2020, with roughly 7,500 units entering the country each year. Even President Trump is a fan, telling reporters last year that he authorized the Department of Transportation to approve their production.

Toyota looks to be the first to test the American market’s appetite for the tiny trucks. The choice to use the Scion brand, which was discontinued in 2016, would seem to indicate that the automaker is hoping to appeal to younger car buyers. But more than that, Toyota says it sees Scion as a testing ground for utility, outdoor adventure, and customization that wouldn’t typically fit in any of its other models.

When it lands in the second half of 2027, Scion’s KEI-01 sports a 660cc three-cylinder gas engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. It won’t win any drag races, but it should delivery enough power for stop-and-go driving while using a minimum amount of fuel.

Previous Next

















1 / 10

It’s true super power comes from its diminutive dimensions. At roughly 11 feet long and under 5 feet wide, the KEI-01 is about half the footprint of a full-size pickup. It can easily thread through cramped alleys, narrow barn aisles, garden gates, or busy campus pathways where standard trucks can’t fit.

The truck features an on-demand 4WD system with a push-button locking mode. If you’re cutting across muddy farm turf, gravel work paths, or wet slush, power splits to all four wheels to keep the truck from spinning out or getting stuck.

Inside, the vehicle looks pretty cheap, with lots of black plastic and a noticeable absence of any premium materials. That will hopefully help keep the price nice and low — though Toyota hasn’t disclosed any trim options yet. Japanese imports typically range from $6,000 to $12,000.

Because it is certified under federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) rules — also used for golf carts and golf cart-adjacent vehicles — its top speed is strictly capped at 25 mph. The truck bed features three sides that fold completely flat, removing the need to lean over high-metal sides to drop in cargo. The KEI-01 can hold up to 600 pounds of soil, tools, or gear, and can easily tow small utility trailers or mowers.

Unlike an open utility cart or ATV, this tiny truck has a fully sealed cabin equipped with both heating and air conditioning. The extended roofline gives drivers extra headroom, reclining seats, and interior storage behind the seats to keep tools dry and secure. True to classic Japanese utility imports, the steering wheel is on the right side of the cab. Beyond the cool factor, curbside delivery and stepping directly onto sidewalks or worksite shoulders is quicker and safer.

To make the KEI-01 to conform to the rules and regs of auto manufacturing in the US, Toyota is investing $34 million into its Princeton, Indiana manufacturing plant to stand up local assembly and add roughly 50 jobs. Production kicks off in the second half of 2027, but everyday drivers won’t be able to buy one off the lot immediately.

Scion by Toyota is launching the mini-truck strictly as a fleet-focused pilot program targeting corporate campuses, farms, municipalities, and local delivery operators, distributed through a specialized group of existing Toyota dealerships. While Toyota notes it may consider opening up sales to consumer retail down the road if demand justifies it, the initial rollout is very much treated as an experiment to evaluate real-world US utility.

The KEI-01 was joined by two adventure-themed concepts that show Scion’s new focus extends far beyond budget hatchbacks. The SxS Concept packs a 300-plus-horsepower hybrid turbo setup for high-speed off-roading, while the modular BKE Concept explores compact personal mobility. Together, they signal that Scion’s second act is aimed squarely at niche utility and experimental recreation.

Tech.title: Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
Tech.content:
Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. The Tabletop platform shares some visual similarities with workplace management apps like Asana and Monday, but with a built-in AI feature that allows you to vibecode personalized interactive tools by describing them, such as savings trackers, chore charts, event plans, and more.

“Just add in your links, files and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets,” Google Labs design and engineering lead Roman Nurik said in the blog post. “Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time like a Google Doc.”

Access to the Tabletop beta is rolling out via a waitlist, and currently limited to people over the age of 18 in the US. Some of the example use cases that Nurik provides in his video above would clearly require giving kids or teens access to Tabletop, however, and using this for personal family planning looks like a compelling alternative to stuffy workplace software, so that age requirement might only be in place while Tabletop is in public testing.
